The same befell the distinguished D. Stephen Blancus, whose Theological Disputation on the soul's origin and how original sin is propagated appeared in 1648. In Thesis XLII he argues: all sinned by the sin that entered the world through one man; yet not in their own person, for they did not yet exist; therefore they sinned in Adam, for in him they died (1 Cor. 15:22). The conclusion could stand if rightly taken; but the minor looks like nothing but a denial of what article XI asserts in our Churches. He denies that the vice is the sin which entered the world—that is, all men—through one man; yet that article says the vice is truly sin and makes every human being liable to eternal death before God, which it could not do unless it had entered every human being.

source_text: Quod etiam subiungit, quippe in quo mortui sunt, confirmat nostram sententiam: non enim cum in Adamo mori omnes dicuntur, mors ipsius Adami intelligitur, una numero, omnibus imputata; sed mors secundum hominum numerum multiplicata, ac sua cuique propria. Addit, & mortui unius illius hominis offensa Rom. 5. 15. unde, inquit, promptum est colligere, illam offensam fuisse omnium offensam, puta imputatione: repugnat enim justitiae divinae ut quis alienae poenae sit particeps, & non sit ullo modo particeps culpae. Si quis similiter diceret, nos fuisse productos unius illius hominis operatione vel virtute, num inde sequeretur, illam operationem vel virtutem fuisse omnium communem imputatione? Si repugnat justitiae divinae, ut quis alienae poenae sit particeps, & non sit ullo modo particeps culpae, certe eidem etiam justitiae repugnat, ut fiat particeps culpae judicis imputatione, is, qui alioqui non esset culpae particeps. Si judex facit injuste ei poenam irrogans, qui nullo modo est particeps culpae, quanto major erit injustitia, si non modo poenam irroget, sed eum faciat etiam sua actione & judiciaria imputatione participem culpae, atque adeo peccatorem & reum, alioqui non peccatorem nec reum? Miror hoc a viris piis & doctis non considerari. Quis enim innocens puniri juste non poterit, si facit imputatio commune esse peccatum quod alioqui non fuisset commune, & esse vere peccatorem & reum, qui alioqui peccator non fuisset?
english: His added words—'inasmuch as in him they died'—confirm our view. When all are said to die in Adam, we do not mean Adam's single death imputed to everyone, but death multiplied by the number of men, each his own. He adds that they died by that one man's offense (Rom. 5:15), and from this thinks it easy to gather that the offense was everyone's by imputation, since divine justice will not let someone share another's punishment without sharing the guilt somehow. If someone likewise said we were produced by that one man's power, would that power therefore be common to all by imputation? If justice forbids sharing another's punishment without sharing guilt, it also forbids making someone a sharer of guilt by the judge's imputation who otherwise would not share it. If a judge already acts unjustly in punishing one who shares no guilt, how much worse if by his own act and judicial imputation he also makes that man a guilty sinner who otherwise was neither? I marvel that pious and learned men miss this. Who that is innocent could not be 'justly' punished, if imputation makes common a sin that was not common, and makes a true sinner of one who otherwise was not?

source_text: Tandem, ait vir doctus, vox illa ἁμαρτίαν in loco Paulino non significat habitum peccati, seu habitualem corruptionem, quae ipsis etiam infantibus inest, sed actum peccandi, eumque praeteritum, quo non potest intelligi aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Hoc vero est Calvino & aliis viris maximis, quos sequimur, contradicere, illud peccaverunt de vitio originali exponentibus. Affert tamen rationes. Quia I. inquit, loquitur Paulus de peccato quod introiit in mundum. i. in omnes homines, per Adamum, quem vocat unum hominem. Supponit vitium originale, aut non esse peccatum, aut non introiisse in omnes homines per unum illum hominem naturaliter procreatos. II. quia, hoc peccato involvuntur etiam infantes: sunt enim in censu hominum, & ex eorum numero, in quos mors transiit, nec moriuntur propter aliud peccatum actuale quam imputatum, quia aliud actuale in eos non cadit: actuale autem imputatum non est aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Non moriuntur quidem infantes propter aliud peccatum actuale quam primum illud Adami: sed cur non moriuntur proxime propter vitium illud habituale, quod omnes & singulos homines reos mortis aeternae coram Deo peragit? Hoc est quod jam non semel observavi, non posse imputationem immediatam primi Adae peccati actualis astrui, nisi negato habitualis vitii reatu. III. inquit, cum Paulus dicit vers. 17. mortem regnasse per unam offensam & vers. 19. multos esse constitutos peccatores unius hominis inobedientia; verba ista una offensa, & unius hominis inobedientia, non possunt aliud respicere quam ipsum factum Adami. i. divini mandati violationem. Esto, quid tum postea? Num inde sequitur, verbum ἁμαρτίαν non significare habitum peccati? aut primum Adami peccatum actuale nobis imputari immediate, seu prius quam nascamur corrupti? Mors regnat per unam offensam ita secundum habitum propagatam in omnes, ut in omnibus regnet mors, quia regnat peccatum. Unius hominis inobedientia secundum habitum propagata & multiplicata multi sunt constituti peccatores. Cur proximam mortis nostrae causam in alio quaerimus, cum se prodat ipsa in nobis, in corpore nostro, ac membris nostris, inhaerens, nempe illud peccatum, quod nisi crucifigatur gratia Christi, tam impotenter in nobis regnat?
english: At last the learned man says the Pauline word ἁμαρτίαν does not mean the habit of sin—the habitual corruption even in infants—but a past act of sinning, which can mean nothing but Adam's first sin. That contradicts Calvin and the other great men we follow, who take 'they sinned' of original vice. Still he offers reasons. I. Paul speaks of the sin that entered the world, that is all men, through Adam, called one man. So he assumes original vice is either not sin, or did not enter all naturally begotten through that one man. II. Infants too are wrapped in this sin: they count among those into whom death passed, and they die by no other actual sin than an imputed one, since no other actual sin befalls them; and that imputed actual sin is nothing but Adam's first. Yes, infants die by no other actual sin than Adam's first—but why not die proximately by that habitual vice which makes every human being liable to eternal death before God? As I have often said: you cannot build immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin without denying the guilt of habitual vice. III. When Paul says in verse 17 that death reigned through one offense, and in verse 19 that many were made sinners by one man's disobedience, those phrases can look only to Adam's own deed—the breach of God's command. Grant it—what then? Does it follow that ἁμαρτίαν does not mean the habit of sin, or that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us immediately, before we are born corrupt? Death reigns through one offense so far as it is propagated by habit into all, so that death reigns in all because sin reigns. By one man's disobedience propagated and multiplied by habit, many are constituted sinners. Why hunt elsewhere for the proximate cause of our death, when that inhering sin shows itself in our body and members—and unless Christ's grace crucifies it, reigns so mightily in us?

source_text: Subjungit th. XLIII. Mortem illam, quae per unum hominem in omnes homines pertransiit &c. includere suae significationis ambitu mortem spiritualem, seu animae, quae nihil aliud est, quam privatio justitiae originalis cum positione contrariae corruptionis habitualis &c: Hoc qua facilitate affirmatur, eadem negari potest; itaque probandum erat: quod vir doctus ne conatur quidem. De sola corporis & aeterna morte Confessio Helvetica, omnesque melioris notae interpretes mortem illam accipiunt, esseque accipiendam probabitur alio loco. Quod subiicit, sine imputatione inobedientiae Adami derivationem habitualis naturae humanae corruptionis non posse esse justam, id quomodo verum esse possit considerare oportet. Derivatio enim illa, cum sit aliud nihil quam contagium peccati & propagatio injustitiae, ipsa per se justa non est, nec esse potest. Non enim justum est propagare & multiplicare injustitiam. Sed illius derivationis permissio seu non impeditio divina justa est, nihilque habet justitiae repugnans. Quam adjungit rationem, Qua enim justitia & aequitate sustineremus omnes illius peccati poenam, nempe mortem spiritualem, si peccatum illud nobis non imputatur? Ea primum supponit, id quod inter nos controvertitur, vitium originale nobis a Deo infligi, & esse poenam proprie dictam. Deinde imputatio peccati alieni, qua nostrum fiat, non tollit injustitiam, sed auget potius: quasi Deus aequissimus & sanctissimus omnibus hominibus primum imputaret alienum peccatum, quo eos faceret imputative peccatores & reos, deinde ut illud imputatum puniret eos faceret inhaerenter peccatores. Ita unum tantum hominem Diabolus tentatione sua fecisset peccatorem, Deus sua actione, id est, imputatione, fecisset omnes homines peccatores & perditos. Quomodo fieri potest, ut pia conscientia tale dogma non detestetur? Nihil amplius argumenti apud hunc autorem reperio, quod non sit jam satis refutatum, ut nihil opus sit inani repetitione fastidio esse Lectori. Tantum, quod pene praeterieram, illud sine aliqua censura dimittendum non videtur, quod ait Th. XLI. Palam est, quicquid delinquat aliquis ut caput alicujus societatis, aut multitudinis, illud juste toti communitati imputari. Nam si id verum est, male omnino agebatur cum Romanis, cum eorum caput esset Nero aut Caligula: quippe quibus omnibus & singulis juste imputari poterat quicquid scelerati illi imperatores delinquebant: ita nullus erat in toto imperio Romano, qui non esset parricida, siquidem parricidium a capite commissum omnibus Romanis juste imputabatur.
english: In Thesis XLIII he adds that the death which passed to all through one man includes spiritual death—of the soul—nothing but the loss of original righteousness with the contrary habitual corruption set in its place. What is affirmed so easily can be denied as easily; it needed proof, which he does not even attempt. The Helvetic Confession and every better interpreter take that death of bodily and eternal death alone; that reading will be proved elsewhere. He adds that without imputing Adam's disobedience the derivation of habitual human corruption cannot be just. How can that be true? That derivation is nothing but sin's contagion and the spread of injustice; it is not itself just, nor can it be— for it is not just to multiply injustice. But God's permitting or not hindering that derivation is just and has nothing against justice. His further reason—by what justice would we all bear that sin's penalty, namely spiritual death, if it is not imputed?—first assumes what we dispute: that God inflicts original vice on us as a penalty properly so called. Next, making another's sin ours by imputation does not remove injustice but increases it: as if the most equitable and holy God first imputed another's sin to all, to make them sinners and guilty by imputation, then to punish that imputed sin made them sinners by inherence. So the Devil's temptation would have made only one man a sinner; God's act—imputation—would have made all men sinners and lost. How could a pious conscience not detest such a dogma? I find nothing more in this author not already refuted enough; empty repetition would only weary the Reader. One point I nearly passed: in Thesis XLI he says whatever someone commits as head of a society or multitude is justly imputed to the whole community. If that were true, the Romans were wholly wronged when Nero or Caligula was their head: whatever those wicked emperors did could justly be imputed to each Roman, so that no one in the empire was not a parricide if the head's parricide was justly charged to all.

source_text: CAPUT XIV. Nullam extare in manuscriptis libellis rationem quae peccati Adamici imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem probare possit. De Argumentis typis excusis, quae mihi legere contigit, dictum est, ut ego arbitror, satis. Manuscriptorum vidi complura: Sed in quibus nihil fere animadverti, quod non legatur in scriptis Typographorum opera publicatis; si primum illud excipias, cui Placeus manuscripto illo respondit, quod D. Garissolius posterius appellavit, et in quo refellendo magnam partem libri sui consumpsit.
english: Chapter XIV. That no argument in the manuscript pamphlets can prove the immediate or antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. Of the printed arguments I have managed to read, enough has been said, I judge. I have seen many manuscripts, and in them I have noticed almost nothing that is not already in books issued by the printers—save that first piece to which Placeus answered in the manuscript Garissoles later called the later one, and on whose refutation Garissoles spent a great part of his book.

source_text: Quare nihil mihi videtur consultius, quam ut manuscriptum illud Placei tibi, Lector, exhibeam (Cur enim in illis argumentis vel proponendis, vel refutandis operam meam ponerem, cum id jam fuerit ab ipso Placeo praestitum?) ac, quando id refutare voluit D. Garissolius, ejusque passim frustula et lacinias transcripsit in suum librum, et quantum potuit, confutavit, subjiciam singulis illis particulis viri illius reprehensiones, hisque ipsis Placei defensiones. Ita poteris, Lector aequissime, admodum facile, et citra errandi aleam, de tota hac causa cognoscere, et judicium ferre: id quod alioqui difficile, ne dicam impossibile, foret. Vix enim qua mente, quo sensu quidque dictum fuerit, bene perspici potest, cum lacerae tantum, et suis locis revulsae, ac veluti luxatae et dissipatae partes sermonis legenti offeruntur. Neque est quod quisquam propterea offendatur. Si quid enim in eo scripto reprehensione dignum est, id in iis potissimum partibus habere locum putandum est, quae jam sunt a D. Garissolio vulgatae. Non eo quidem consilio a Placeo compositum fuerat ut ederetur, et ex nimia festinatione irrepsere fortasse nonnulla, si per otium licuisset autori, emendanda atque expolienda: tamen ne voculam quidem tollere, addere, aut mutare voluimus, ne quis de nostra fide vel synceritate conqueri posset. Qualecunque est, Tu aequissime Lector, illud aequi bonique consules, quodque ejus integri legendi, totiusque istius controversiae dijudicandae copiam tibi facimus, aut habebis nobis gratiam, aut saltem non iniquo animo feres.
english: Nothing therefore seems wiser than to set that Placeus manuscript before you, Reader (why should I spend myself proposing or answering those arguments when Placeus has already done it?), and, since Garissoles chose to refute it and copied its scraps and patches into his own book and answered them as he could, to set under each scrap that man's censures and Placeus's own defenses. So you, most fair Reader, may know the whole cause easily and without risk of error, and judge—which would otherwise be hard, not to say impossible. One can scarcely see with what mind or sense each thing was said when only torn, uprooted, and scattered pieces of the discourse are offered. Let no one take offense at that. If anything in the writing deserves blame, it is chiefly in the parts Garissoles has already published. Placeus did not compose it to be printed, and haste may have left spots he would have polished at leisure; yet we would not drop, add, or change even a word, lest anyone doubt our honesty. Take it, most fair Reader, in good part: we give you the whole to read and the whole controversy to judge—thank us, or at least bear it without ill will.

source_text: MANUSCRIPTUM POSTERIUS, HOC EST, EXAMEN Tractatus singularis, De peccato originis, in quo demonstratur primum primi hominis peccatum omnibus hominibus imputari, oppositi Thesibus de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam, disputatis Salmurii die 16. Martii An. 1640. sub Praesidio Josue Placei S. Theologiae Professoris in Academia Salmuriensi. CAPUT I. Capita doctrinae de Peccato originali de quibus inter nos convenit. LICEAT mihi, quaeso, Vir reverende, te, perinde ac si coram sermone res ageretur, compellare et alloqui: Sic enim, uti spero, tua, velut oculis meis obversantis praesentia me torpentem excitabit, et ad tui majorem reverentiam componet. Tu quidem pro tua singulari prudentia voluisti tibi viam ad statum controversiae constituendum munire, praestratis iis de quibus inter nos convenit. Quod tuum consilium valde probo; sed (quod cum tua bona venia dictum velim) visus es mihi neutrum praestitisse satis accurate et enucleate. Patere igitur ut utrumque tuo exemplo faciam breviter quidem, sed ita tamen, ut ab hac nostra amica collatione omnis, si fieri possit, tollatur confusio, omnis ambiguitas.
english: THE LATER MANUSCRIPT, that is, an Examination of a singular tractate On original sin, which argues that the first man's first sin is imputed to all, set against Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, disputed at Saumur on 16 March 1640 under Josue de la Place, professor of theology there. Chapter I. Heads of doctrine on original sin on which we agree. Let me address you, reverend Sir, as if we spoke face to face: so your presence before my eyes may wake my dullness and tune me to deeper reverence. By your singular prudence you wished to clear the state of the question by first laying down what we hold in common. I much approve that plan; yet (with your leave) you seem to me to have done neither part with enough care and clearness. Allow me therefore to do both after your example—briefly, yet so that from this friendly conference every confusion and ambiguity may, if possible, be cleared away.

source_text: Ego arcte teneo, accurateque defendo quicquid de peccato originali Ecclesia vere Christiana adversus veteres novosque Pelagianos, et Semipelagianos cum definivit olim, tum his postremis seculis suis publicis confessionibus se credere professa est. Id autem universum Daniel Chamierus, vir suo merito magni apud Ecclesias nostras nominis, statum controversiae inter nos et Pighium ac Salmeronem constituens ad tria capita revocavit. Catholici, inquit, (Protestantes intelligit) certis argumentis docent, ipsi humanae naturae inesse corruptionem, seu pravitatem cuilibet homini propriam, aliam ab actibus peccati. Secundo, etiam nascenti homini cuilibet eandem inesse. Tertio eandem ab Adamo ortum ducere, et per propagationem derivari in posteros. Quamvis autem subjungat, haec tria capita continere universam peccati originalis naturam. Itaque iis demonstratis nihil fore reliqui factum; tamen uberioris explicationis causa duo addam: unum, hanc corruptionem omnes animae nostrae facultates ita depravasse, ut nisi ex aqua et Spiritu renati fuerimus, neque ullum fructum vere bonum proferre, neque ad Deum converti valeamus. Alterum, hanc corruptionem vere peccatum esse, omnes Adami posteros, solo Christo, in quo nunquam fuit, excepto, mortis aeternae reos peragens.
english: I hold fast, and carefully defend, whatever the truly Christian Church has defined against old and new Pelagians and Semipelagians on original sin, and what she has professed in these later ages by her public confessions. Daniel Chamier—a man of deserved name among our churches—reduced the whole dispute between us and Pighius and Salmeron to three heads. Catholics (he means Protestants), he says, prove by sure arguments that human nature itself has a corruption or pravity proper to each person, distinct from sinful acts; second, that the same is in each even at birth; third, that it rises from Adam and passes to posterity by propagation. Though he adds that these three contain the whole nature of original sin—so that once proved nothing remains—I still add two points for clearer teaching: first, that this corruption so spoils every faculty of the soul that, unless we are born again of water and the Spirit, we can neither bear any truly good fruit nor turn to God; second, that this corruption is truly sin, and makes all Adam's posterity—Christ alone excepted, in whom it never was—guilty of eternal death.

source_text: GARISSOLIUS. Chamierus duo in Peccato originali manifeste distinguit, quod poena est peccati primi, et quod vitium est internum in nobis haerens. Sed prius non veniebat in controversiam cum Pighio, et aliis quos eo libro refutat; itaque eam considerationem non urget hoc loco. Sed quaerebatur tantum, an peccatum originale veram haberet rationem vitii et corruptionis. Affirmat Chamierus, et probat; Et peccatum originale considerans jam, qua vitium est, haud immerito ejus naturam in illis tribus constituit. PLACEUS. Quorsum spectet ista distinctio, nescio? Quis enim unquam peccatum originale dixit esse duplex: unum, poenam peccati primi actualis, alterum, vitium inhaerens; aut duas esse peccati originalis partes: unam poenam peccati primi, alteram peccatum internum in nobis haerens? Sed qui imputationem primi Adae peccati actualis immediatam docent, illi, vel duplex esse dicunt peccatum originale: unum imputatum, alterum inhaerens; vel duas peccati originalis partes; primariam et praecipuam peccatum actuale Adami imputatum, minus praecipuam corruptionem haereditariam. In qua opinione si fuit Chamierus, quomodo in illis tribus, quae commemoravit, universam peccati originalis naturam contineri asseruit? Quomodo addidit; Itaque iis demonstratis nihil erit reliqui factum? Omississet enim praecipuam peccati originalis partem. Adde quod si haeresis Pelagiana in imputationis illius negatione pars sita fuit, ut voluit D. Garissolius, decuit Catholicos eam imputationem inprimis demonstrare, praesertim cum a Stapletono, aliisque nonnullis Pontificiis, aperte negata fuisset. Sed de Chamiero, si opus erit, alibi disputabitur.
english: GARISSOLES. Chamier clearly divides two things in original sin: that it is the penalty of the first sin, and that it is an inward vice inhering in us. The first was not in dispute with Pighius and the others he answers in that book, so he does not press it here. The only question was whether original sin has the true character of vice and corruption. Chamier affirms and proves it; and taking original sin as vice, he rightly sets its nature in those three heads. PLACEUS. I do not see what that distinction is for. Who ever called original sin twofold—one the penalty of the first actual sin, the other inherent vice—or made two parts of it, penalty and inward sin? Those who teach immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin do say either that original sin is twofold (imputed and inherent) or that it has two parts—the chief being Adam's imputed actual sin, the lesser hereditary corruption. If Chamier held that, how could he say those three heads contain the whole nature of original sin, or add that once they are proved nothing remains? He would have left out the chief part. And if Pelagian heresy partly lay in denying that imputation, as Garissoles claims, Catholics ought to have proved the imputation first of all, especially since Stapleton and some other Papists openly denied it. Of Chamier, if need be, elsewhere.

source_text: Tu quidem, observande Symmysta, superiora credis. Sed de hoc ultimo quid sentis? Conceptum est verbis confessionis Ecclesiarum nostrarum Art. XI. quae tu ipse laudas Cap. VII. Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes et singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum, esse vere peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet. Hoc ego ex animo credo ut sacris literis consentaneum, immo rationi, neque everti potest, quin eo ipso thesium mearum quas oppugnas compactio et contextus luxetur. Tu vero num id credis? videris tale quid affirmare Cap. I. et II. tui tractatus, et aliis aliquot locis: sed vereor ne ita loquaris occultandae opinionis tuae gratia: Id enim aliis quibusdam locis exerte negas, eaque negatione tanquam fundamento pars non contemnenda hujus tuae disputationis nititur. Recognosce tua verba: non enim gravabor huc transferre. Cap. V. sic colligis, Ubi mors regnat, nec est reatus ex peccato proprio actuali, ibi necessario est imputatio reatus primi peccati. Item, Cap. V. mors regnavit in infantes. Ergo infantibus reatus primi peccati necessario fuit imputatus. Cum autem videres tibi responderi posse, reatum in illis esse a vitio inhaerente et depravatione haereditaria, tu hanc responsionem cavillum appellasti, et contra sic conclusisti, si pueri in utero matrum, aut recens nati, sunt peccatores, ideo sunt, vel quod actu peccaverint, vel quod primum peccatum primi parentis ipsis imputetur. Tertium siquidem dari non potest, quod illos constituat peccatores. Nam peccator quis dicitur ob peccatum; Nec ullum aliud peccatum potest imputari, nisi illud primum. Relege, si placet, quae sequuntur. Cap. IX. mentem tuam plenius aperis. Non video, inquis, quid sit peccatum originis si negetur ejusmodi imputatio. Potuisset-ne Pighius suam sententiam exprimere clarius?
english: You, observant colleague, hold the points above. But what of this last? It is cast in the words of our Churches' Confession, Article XI, which you yourself praise in chapter VII: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes every person—even little ones still hidden in the womb—guilty of eternal death before God. We also affirm that after baptism this vice is still truly sin as to guilt. I believe this from the heart as agreeing with Scripture and with reason; overturn it and the very fabric of the theses you attack comes apart. Do you believe it? In chapters I-II of your tract and elsewhere you seem to say so; yet I fear you speak so to hide your view, for in other places you openly deny it, and a large part of your case rests on that denial. Hear your own words. Chapter V: Where death reigns and there is no guilt from one's own actual sin, there must be imputation of the first sin's guilt. Likewise: death reigned over infants; therefore the first sin's guilt was necessarily imputed to them. When you saw the reply that their guilt comes from inherent vice and hereditary depravity, you called it a cavil and concluded: if children in the womb or newly born are sinners, it is either because they have sinned in act or because the first parent's first sin is imputed to them—for no third way can make them sinners. One is called a sinner because of sin; no other sin can be imputed but that first. Read on. In chapter IX you speak more plainly: I do not see what original sin is if such imputation is denied. Could Pighius have put his mind more clearly?

source_text: Subjicis rationem: nam quinam mors regnavit tunc in eos quoque qui non peccaverunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam, si hoc peccatum Adami non fuit illis imputatum? Finge puerum recens natum vel in utero ipso matris morientem, quid in illo est quod peccatum dici possit? voluntas in ipso ab omni actione vacat, nec potest propria voluntate peccare. Habet in se, inquies, semina peccati, valeat, sed nondum peccatum proprie, nisi peccatum illud originis, quo in Adamo peccavit. Ergo peccatum illius non in ipso, vel ex seipso, sed in prima origine, id est, in primo parente quaerendum est: Nec est aliud peccatum illud quam inobedientia illa voluntaria Adami etc. Tu igitur nullum peccatum originale agnoscis praeter primum illud peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatum, nullum reatum in infantibus praeter eum qui immediate ex illa imputatione existit. Quo ergo vel animo, vel sensu, corruptionem inhaerentem modo simpliciter peccatum, modo cum epitheto peccatum originale appellas? sic enim in hanc tuam disputationem ambiguitatem et confusionem intulisti, noxiam mihi futuram nisi eam deprehendissem, ac, quod facio, sustulissem. Hic subit animum meum mirari, vir reverende, qui, cum tam aperte a confessione Ecclesiae nostrae abeas, potueris inducere in animum tuum, ut mihi, qui illi religiose adhaereo, quasi ab ea defcivissem, grandem dicam scriberes. Dolet etiam mihi quod te aliis doctrina et sanctitate praelucentem, et quem ex animo diligo, tueri non possim vel ab inconstantia, vel a dissimulatione: ab inconstantia quidem si corruptionem inhaerentem vere peccatum esse, reatum mortis aeternae ex sese fundens modo sensisti, modo non sensisti; a dissimulatione vero, si cum sentires constanter non esse peccatum, tu tamen peccatum esse aliquot locis dixisti et inculcasti, perinde ac si revera et proprie peccatum esse crederes, nec eo contentus, affirmasti inter nos ea de re nullam esse dissensionem, cum te fugere non posset, non solum me, quem refutandum sumpseras, sed Ecclesias etiam nostras vitium illud formaliter et proprie, et, ut loquitur confessio fidei, vere peccatum esse statuere; et eos ipsos, qui tecum imputationem primi peccati urgent, solitos esse peccatum originale in duo peccata dispescere, imputatum et inhaerens, ac suum utrique proprium Mortis aeternae reatum attribuere. Laudarem testimonia nisi libri omnibus noti essent, omnium triti manibus. Hic igitur aut consentis corruptionem haereditariam, seposito peccato Adami imputato, esse vere peccatum damnando generi humano sufficiens, aut dissentis. Si consentis, revoca eas rationes et solutiones, quas in progressu hujus tui tractatus contrariae hypothesi superstuxisti. Si dissentis, haec erit inter me teque unum singularis controversia, quam libentissime suscipiam pro tuenda confessione Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quae mihi videtur verissima.
english: You add the reason: how then did death reign even over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's trespass, if Adam's sin was not imputed to them? Picture a newborn, or a child dying in the womb: what in him can be called sin? His will is idle of every act and cannot sin by its own choice. He has, you will say, seeds of sin—granted—but not yet sin properly, except that origin-sin by which he sinned in Adam. So his sin is sought not in him or from himself but in the first origin, the first parent; and that sin is nothing but Adam's voluntary disobedience, and so on. You therefore own no original sin but Adam's first actual sin imputed to us, and no guilt in infants but what springs immediately from that imputation. With what mind, then, do you call inherent corruption now simply sin, now original sin? So you have poured ambiguity and confusion into your case—harmful to me had I not spotted it and, as I do, cleared it away. I wonder, reverend Sir, that you, so openly leaving our Church's confession, could charge me—who cling to it—as if I had deserted it. It also grieves me that I cannot shield you, whom I love and who outshine others in doctrine and holiness, from inconstancy or from dissimulation: inconstancy, if you have sometimes held and sometimes not held that inherent corruption is truly sin and itself yields eternal death's guilt; dissimulation, if while you steadily held it is not sin you still said and pressed in places that it is, as if you truly believed it, and even claimed we do not disagree—when you could not miss that not only I, whom you set out to refute, but our Churches too hold that vice formally and properly, and, as the confession says, truly sin; and that those who with you urge first-sin imputation usually split original sin into two—imputed and inherent—and give each its own guilt of eternal death. I would cite witnesses if the books were not known to all and worn by every hand. So either you grant that hereditary corruption, apart from Adam's imputed sin, is truly sin enough to damn the human race, or you deny it. If you grant it, take back the reasons and answers you built in this tract on the contrary premise. If you deny it, this will be our one special quarrel, which I will gladly take up to defend our Churches' confession, which seems to me most true.

source_text: CAP. II. Status Questionis. Venio nunc ad statum questionis. Eum non incommode constituisses si poenae nomini, quod in eam introduxisti, ambiguitatem vel non inclusisses, vel sustulisses. Enimvero poenae nomine corruptionem haereditariam complecti vel voluisti, vel noluisti. Si noluisti: debuisti id significare, alioqui erraturo lectori, quippe cum hoc primo capite innuas, et secundo clames, et aliis inculces, corruptionem illam poenam esse primi peccati. Si voluisti, vel putasti corruptionem illam esse poenam proprie dictam primi peccati, non solum quatenus in ipso Adamo fuit, sed etiam quatenus inest in nobis; vel non. Si prius, quaestionem non admitto: Praesupponit enim ut certum, ut inter nos confessum, id quod ego thesibus meis refutavi, quodque versatur in quaestione, nimirum corruptionem haereditariam esse, proprie et stricte loquendo, poenam primi peccati, non solum quatenus fuit in Adamo sed etiam quatenus nobis propagata inest. Si poenam quidem esse voluisti, sed non proprie dictam, nec stricta hujus vocabuli significatione, saltem quatenus est in nobis, decuit te mentem tuam explicare, quoniam apparet ex multis hujus tui tractatus locis te corruptionem illam putare poenam esse sensu strictissimo, maximeque proprio.
english: Chapter II. The state of the question. I come now to the state of the question. You would not have framed it awkwardly if, in the word penalty that you brought into it, you had either left out the ambiguity or taken it away. For by penalty you either meant to include hereditary corruption, or you did not. If you did not, you should have said so—otherwise the reader will go wrong—since in this first chapter you hint, in the second you cry out, and elsewhere you drum into others, that that corruption is the penalty of the first sin. If you meant, or thought, that that corruption is the first sin's penalty in the proper sense, not only as it was in Adam himself but also as it is in us—or not—then, if the former, I refuse the question. It assumes as settled among us what I refuted in my theses and what is still under dispute: that hereditary corruption is, properly and strictly, the penalty of the first sin not only as it was in Adam but also as it is present in us by propagation. If you meant a penalty, but not properly so called, nor in the strict sense of the word—at least as it is in us—you ought to have explained your mind; for from many places in this treatise of yours it is plain that you take that corruption to be a penalty in the strictest and most proper sense.

source_text: Misso igitur poenae nomine, potuisses sic quaestionem instituisse sine ulla ambiguitate: Cur nascamur obnoxii miseriis hujus vitae, morti corporis, et morti aeternae? an quia nobis imputetur proxime et immediate primum peccatum actuale Adami? aut quia sine ejusmodi imputatione, vitiositas ejus ab eo in nos derivata est, et per propagationem naturalem transfusa? Tu prius affirmas, ego posterius. Vel sic, Cur trahimus ab Adamo corruptionem moralem haereditariam, quae peccatum originale dici solet? An quia nobis a Deo Judice primum peccatum actuale Adami imputetur, ac in ejus imputati poenam, ut vindicetur, et justitiae satisfiat, infligatur illa corruptio moralis, quae et ipsa peccatum est, et fons aliorum peccatorum? Aut vero quia, sine ejusmodi imputatione, haec est naturae lex ante peccatum constituta, ut sui quaeque res similem gignat, homo hominem, corruptus corruptum, vitiosus vitiosum, leprosus leprosum? Tu rursus prius asseris, ego posterius. Quamvis autem status questionis, ita propositus accommodate ad mentem tuam, non prorsus incommodus sit, nondum tamen mihi omni ex parte satisfacit: exprimit enim potius partes questionis, quam ipsam quaestionem universam.
english: So drop the word penalty, and you could have put the question without ambiguity: Why are we born liable to the miseries of this life, to bodily death, and to eternal death? Because Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us proximately and immediately? Or because, without any such imputation, his viciousness has come down from him into us and been poured through by natural propagation? You affirm the first; I the second. Or put it this way: Why do we draw from Adam that hereditary moral corruption usually called original sin? Because God the Judge imputes Adam's first actual sin to us, and, as the penalty of that imputed sin—so that it may be avenged and justice satisfied—inflicts that moral corruption which is itself sin and the spring of other sins? Or rather because, without such imputation, this was nature's law before the fall: like begets like—man a man, the corrupt the corrupt, the vicious the vicious, the leprous the leprous? Again you assert the first; I the second. Though the state of the question, framed to fit your mind, is not wholly unserviceable, it still does not satisfy me on every side: it states the parts of the question more than the question as a whole.

source_text: Ut igitur, quando de mea sententia agitur, quid sentiam distincte aperiam, atque statum questionis, quoad ejus fieri a me poterit, dilucide et enucleate constituam, eam dividam in duas, quarum altera est de imputatione primi peccati Adami, altera de poena, qua imputatum vindicari dicitur. Quaeritur enim primum, Utrum primum peccatum Adami omnibus ejus posteris, Christo excepto, imputetur? Deinde, Utrum corruptio haereditaria nobis infligatur a Deo Judice, ut fiat justitia? Priori quaestioni, quia laborat homonymia, non possum per simplicem affirmationem, aut negationem respondere. Distinguendum enim ejus est tum subjectum, tum attributum. Subjectum est primum peccatum Adami: in quo duo distinguenda, Actio tam interna quam externa, qua divinum interdictum violavit, et Corruptio moralis, quam illa actio in Adami naturam intulit. Quae corruptio ipsa quoque spectari potest duobus modis, uno ut fuit in Adamo; altero, ut est in nobis profecta ab Adamo. Hinc fit ut primum peccatum Adami usurpetur quatuor modis.
english: So when my own view is at stake, that I may say plainly what I hold, and set the state of the question as clearly as I can, I divide it in two: one part on the imputation of Adam's first sin, the other on the penalty by which the imputed sin is said to be avenged. First: Is Adam's first sin imputed to all his posterity, Christ excepted? Second: Is hereditary corruption inflicted on us by God the Judge so that justice may be done? To the first I cannot answer with a bare yes or no, for the wording is ambiguous. Subject and attribute must both be distinguished. The subject is Adam's first sin, in which two things are to be marked: the act, inward and outward, by which he broke the divine ban, and the moral corruption that act brought into Adam's nature. That corruption itself may be viewed two ways: as it was in Adam, and as it is in us as it came from Adam. Hence Adam's first sin is used in four senses.

source_text: 1. pro actione qua dei legem est transgressus, quae primum fuit peccatum actuale. 2. pro eadem illa actione non praecise accepta, sed simul cum habituali corruptione quam peperit: habent enim se haec duo velut calefactio et calor, actus et habitus, mutatio actualis et mutatio habitualis. Itaque utrumque conjunctim idem nomen peccati Adami, vel primi peccati nonnunquam complectitur. 3. pro corruptione, quam actualis inobedientia genuit in Adamo, quaeque fuit ejus primum peccatum habituale. 4. denique pro eadem illa corruptione in nos transmissa et propagata, quae nostrum quidem peccatum est, quia nobis inhaeret, nos afficit, et denominat; dicitur tamen peccatum Adami ut authoris, ut primi veluti possessoris, ut fontis unde ad nos defluxit. Si hoc ultimo modo sumatur primum Adami peccatum, aio illud omnibus Adami posteris (uno, in quo locum nullum habuit, Christo excepto) imputari, donec ab eo per Christum justificentur, eorumque sententiam jure damnatam a Synodo Carentonensi arbitror, qui hoc quidem peccatum agnoscere se profitentur, nulli tamen imputari, quantumvis infideli: esse enim hoc saeculo qui id doceant editis libris testatur et deplorat paulo ante obitum suum in quadam Epistola doctissimus Walaeus. Similiter si tertio modo sumatur, fateor nobis imputari, non tamen qua haesit in Adamo, sed qua in nos transit, ac, ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est: est enim nostra corruptio haereditaria eadem specie cum illa, quae olim fuit in Adamo; ac quam suam naturam, tam suam corruptionem moralem nobiscum Adamus communicavit.
english: 1. For the act by which he broke God's law—the first actual sin. 2. For that same act not taken by itself, but together with the habitual corruption it produced: the two stand as heating to heat, act to habit, actual change to habitual change. So both together sometimes share the one name 'Adam's sin' or 'the first sin.' 3. For the corruption that actual disobedience bred in Adam—his first habitual sin. 4. For that same corruption as transmitted and propagated into us, which is our sin because it inheres in us, affects us, and names us; yet it is called Adam's as of the author, the first as it were possessor, the fountain from which it flowed to us. If Adam's first sin is taken in this last sense, I say it is imputed to all Adam's posterity (Christ alone excepted, in whom it had no place) until they are justified from it through Christ; and I judge rightly condemned by the Synod of Charenton the opinion of those who profess to acknowledge this sin yet deny that it is imputed to anyone, however unbelieving—for that some in this age teach so in print, the learned Walaeus testified and mourned shortly before his death in a letter. Likewise if it is taken in the third sense, I grant that it is imputed to us—not as it clung in Adam, but as it passes into us, and, in Calvin's words, because it is within us: for our hereditary corruption is the same in kind as that which once was in Adam; and Adam shared with us his nature and his moral corruption alike.

source_text: Idem de secundo modo dicendum: quam enim vere dicitur peccatum Adami in nos transiisse, derivatum, transmissum, propagatum esse, tam vere etiam dicitur nobis imputari. Propagatum est autem, non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit vitiositas permanens, non qua fuit peccatum personae, sed qua fuit peccatum naturae, non qua olim esse desiit in rerum natura, sed qua naturae humanae adhaeret, cumque ea multiplicatur et propagatur. Porro ut natura mea propagata et derivata ab Adamo differt numero a natura Adami, sic peccatum ab Adamo derivatum et propagatum differt numero a peccato Adami. Hactenus, nisi me fallit animus, inter nos summus est consensus, modo nolis negare corruptionem haereditariam esse vere peccatum irregenitis imputabile, vel potius imputandum ad condemnationem. Quod si id neges, haec tertia exorietur inter me et te controversia, qua quamvis propriis argumentis confici poterit, tamen iis nihil opus erit: nam refutatis (quod feci in Thesibus) exceptionibus Socini, Pelagii, et Pighii, necesse est fateri, universam illam condemnationem, quam Apostolus ad Rom. v.12. inculcat, ex sola illa corruptione, quae a lapsu Adami fluxit, proxime enasci. PLAC. Has tres ultimas peccati Adamici acceptiones D. Gar. mirum in modum exagitat: qua mente? nescio. Nihil enim id juvat statum questionis, aut causam quam agit, et Lectorem inutiliter moratur. Quid enim in ea nominis distinctione reprehendit? Num eam falsitatis arguit? minime. Num negat in ea re consensum esse? nequaquam. Quid ergo agit? ipsum audi.
english: The same holds for the second sense: as truly as Adam's sin is said to have passed into us—derived, transmitted, propagated—so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it was propagated not as a passing act, but as lasting viciousness; not as the sin of a person, but as the sin of nature; not as something that once ceased to exist, but as what clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated with it. And as my nature, derived from Adam, differs numerically from Adam's nature, so the sin derived and propagated from Adam differs numerically from Adam's sin. Thus far, unless I am mistaken, we are in full agreement—provided you will not deny that hereditary corruption is truly a sin to be imputed to the unregenerate, or rather to be imputed unto condemnation. If you deny that, a third controversy rises between us; and though it could be settled by its own arguments, they will not be needed: once Socinus's, Pelagius's, and Pighius's exceptions are answered (as I did in the Theses), we must admit that the whole condemnation Paul presses in Romans 5:12 arises proximately from that corruption alone which flowed from Adam's fall. Placeus. Master Garissoles works up these three last senses of Adam's sin strangely—to what end I do not know. It helps neither the state of the question nor the cause he urges, and only wastes the reader's time. What fault does he find in the distinction of the name? That it is false? Not at all. That there is no consensus on the point? By no means. What then is he doing? Hear him.

source_text: GAR. Primum quidem est, quod suam praestanti Theologo confessionem gratuemur, qui, etsi negat imputari posteris primam illam Adae actionem, qua Dei mandatum violavit, si eam praecise ac seorsim spectemus; agnoscit tamen illam imputari, acceptam simul cum corruptione quam peperit. Hoc enim inde certo consequitur, ergo ipsam criminosam Adami actionem posteris imputari: quoniam quod simul et conjunctim cum alio spectatum imputatur, non eo tantum minus imputari censendum est. Jam vero si Adami actio, non praecise sumpta, sed simul cum corruptione consequenti, imputatur; nemo non videt, eas omnes rationes una veluti litura expungendas, quibus adversus actionis Adamicae imputationem hactenus Viri Docti disputarunt. Illae enim omnes id efficiunt, si quid efficiunt, nos nullo modo esse posse reos propter inobedientiam et actionem injustam alterius nobis imputatam, sive praecise, sive una cum alio vel actu, vel habitu illam considerare libeat. Illud autem si fixum maneat, actionem Adami simul cum corruptione, quam peperit, acceptam unicuique posterorum imputari, pax facile componetur. PLAC. In elogio praestantis theologi, quo me ornat indignum, judicium charitatis agnosco. In reliquis ejus verbis quatuor mihi apparent ὀράματα. Primum enim sententiam mihi tribuit, quae mea non est. Nunquam enim negavi ipsam criminosam actionem Adami posteris ejus imputari. Nunquam affirmavi nos nullo modo esse posse reos propter inobedientiam Adami. Tantummodo negavi illam actionem posteris imputari immediate, et nos esse reos propter illam immediate. Nam illam imputari mediate, propter illam nos esse reos mediate, id est, mediante corruptione ab illa in nos descendente, ego toties dixi, repetiui, inculcavi, ut mirum sit virum doctum ad has meas voces toties iteratas obsurduisse.
english: Garissoles. First we may congratulate the excellent theologian on his confession: though he denies that Adam's first act, by which he broke God's command, is imputed to posterity if we view it precisely and apart, he still grants that it is imputed when taken together with the corruption it produced. From this it surely follows that Adam's criminal act itself is imputed to posterity: for what is imputed when viewed jointly with something else is not for that reason less imputed. And if Adam's act is imputed not taken precisely but together with the following corruption, anyone can see that all the reasons learned men have used against imputing Adam's act are to be wiped out at a stroke. For if those reasons prove anything, they prove that we cannot be guilty for another's disobedience and unjust act imputed to us—whether taken alone or together with some other act or habit. But if it stands fixed that Adam's act, taken with the corruption it produced, is imputed to each of his posterity, peace will easily be made. Placeus. In the praise with which this excellent theologian honors me—unworthy as I am—I recognize charity's judgment. In the rest of his words four ὀράματα (phantasms) appear to me. First, he pins on me an opinion that is not mine. I never denied that Adam's criminal act itself is imputed to his posterity. I never said we cannot in any way be guilty for Adam's disobedience. I only denied that that act is imputed to posterity immediately, and that we are guilty for it immediately. That it is imputed mediately, and that we are guilty for it mediately—that is, through the corruption descending from it into us—I have said, repeated, and pressed so often that it is strange a learned man should have gone deaf to words so often spoken.

source_text: Deinde, non modo perdit operam in eo contra me probando quod passim affirmo, sed, quod deterius est, id inde elicere conatur, ubi non latet. Etsi enim verba mea prima fronte favere videantur ejus collectioni, tamen ei praescindit omnem ansam, quae continuo sequitur explicatio, quam ipse libri sui pag. 33. sic contraxerat, quia, quam vere peccatum Adami in nos transit, tam vere nobis imputari dicitur. Atqui transit et propagatum est, non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit vitiositas permanens, nec qua fuit peccatum personae, sed qua fuit peccatum naturae, quod scilicet naturae humanae adhaeret, et cum ea multiplicatur atque propagatur. Tertio, falsum est nostras omnes rationes, si quid efficiunt, efficere nos nullo modo esse reos propter inobedientiam Adami: Eas enim imputationem illius inobedientiae mediatam nullo modo impugnare tam clare ostendi datis ad eum literis, ut ab eo responsionem nulla etiam agitatione impetrare potuerim. Quarto denique falsum est id quod ait, si fixum maneat actionem Adami simul cum corruptione quam peperit acceptam unicuique posterorum imputari, pacem facile compositum iri. Restabit enim integra quaestio, utrum illa actio praecise sumpta immediate imputetur, hoc est, ita, ut illius imputatae corruptio sit poena proprie dicta. Id quod unum duntaxat et constanter negavi, et negatum volui. Praecisam enim a corruptione, quae in Adamo et nobis haesit, imputari oportet, si quidem illam imputationem corruptio sequitur ut poena.
english: Next, he not only wastes labor proving against me what I everywhere affirm, but—worse—tries to draw it from a place where it is not hidden. My words may at first glance seem to favor his inference; yet the explanation that follows at once cuts off every handle, the explanation he himself had shortened at page 33 of his book: because, as truly as Adam's sin passes into us, so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it passes and has been propagated not as a passing act but as lasting viciousness; not as a person's sin but as nature's sin—what clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated with it. Third, it is false that all our reasons, if they prove anything, prove that we are in no way guilty for Adam's disobedience: for that they do not touch the mediate imputation of that disobedience I showed so clearly in letters to him that I could get no answer from him by any urging. Fourth, and last, it is false that if Adam's act, taken with the corruption it produced, remains imputed to each of the posterity, peace will be easily made. The whole question will still stand: whether that act, taken precisely, is imputed immediately—that is, so that the corruption of the imputed act is a penalty in the proper sense. That alone I have constantly denied, and wished denied. For the act must be imputed cut off from the corruption that clung in Adam and in us, if corruption is to follow that imputation as its penalty.

source_text: GAR. Observo deinde, nulla necessitate, vel magna utilitate, compulsum Virum Doctum, ut ita anxie et scrupulose subjectum in quatuor significata distingueret; cum quicunque hactenus de primi peccati imputatione locuti sunt, nihil aliud eo nomine intellexerint, ut ex ipsorum scriptis satis patere potest, quam ipsius primi hominis actualem illam transgressionem, qua Dei mandatum de non gustando fructu arboris interdictae violavit. Ut quid igitur opus erat per operosas ambages lectoris animum circumducere, et de peccato in nobis inhaerente, sive corruptione nostra originali, deque imputatione ac poena reatum ipsam consequente verba facere, de quibus in hac disputatione nequaquam agi satis notum est? Non enim quaeritur, utrum nobis omnibus insita sit corruptio, propter quam Deus poenas a nobis exigere merito possit, aut eam nobis imputare, quod nemo Evangelicorum unquam revocavit in dubium: Illud unum in Quaestionem hodie vocari quibusdam volupe est, utrum ex primo illo actuali Adae peccato aliquis reatus, et aliqua poenae dignitas posteris incumbat.
english: Garissoles. Next I notice that no necessity, and no great usefulness, drove the learned man to divide the subject so anxiously and scrupulously into four senses. Everyone who has spoken until now of the imputation of the first sin has meant by that name, as their writings sufficiently show, only that actual transgression of the first man by which he broke God's command not to taste the fruit of the forbidden tree. Why then lead the reader through laborious windings, and speak of sin inhering in us—or our original corruption—and of imputation and the penalty that follows guilt, matters everyone knows are not at issue in this dispute? The question is not whether corruption is planted in us all, for which God may justly exact penalties from us or impute it to us—no Evangelical ever called that back into doubt. What some today delight to bring into question is only this: whether from Adam's first actual sin some guilt and some liability to penalty rests on the posterity.

source_text: PLAC. Primum esto; nulla necessitate, vel magna utilitate compulsus peccatum Adae sic distinxerim, modo distinctio non sit falsa, nec noxia, nec prorsus inutilis, mihi satis est. Utinam in eius libro nihil minus verum, minus utile occurreret! Deinde verum non est, quod ait, quicunque de peccati Adae imputatione locuti sunt, eos nihil aliud eo nomine intellexisse, quam ipsius actualem transgressionem: cujus rei eum admonere debuerunt verba illa mea, ac ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est, quae, quia causae suae oberant, consulto omisit. Habentur autem illa Calvini verba Comm. in Rom. 5. vs. 17. integrum locum habes supra p. 92. Perit enim differentia quam illic observat inter Christum et Adamum, nisi peccatum Adae, quod nobis imputatur, intra nos sit, seque habeat ut qualitas nobis inhaerens. Tertio, Quod addit de peccato inhaerente ejusque imputatione in hac disputatione non agi, id ipsum dico hoc loco, ac ut dicerem distinctionem illam adhibui. Separandum enim fuit id quod non est inter nos controversum ab eo quod controversum est, removendaque ab hac quaestione omnis ambiguitas et confusio. Quo neglecto qui mihi in hac causa adversantur non me oppugnant, sed umbram suam. Denique quod dicit in quaestionem vocari, utrum ex primo illo actuali Adae peccato aliquis reatus et aliqua poenae dignitas posteris incumbat, vel falsum est, vel ad me non spectat: Doceo enim constanter ex illo peccato aliquem reatum et aliquam poenae dignitatem, si tamen dignitas appellanda est, posteris incumbere: tantum volo non immediate sed mediante corruptione quam peperit, incumbere.
english: Placeus. First grant it: suppose no necessity or great usefulness compelled me to distinguish Adam's sin this way; so long as the distinction is not false, not harmful, and not wholly useless, that is enough for me. Would that nothing less true or less useful appeared in his book! Next, it is not true that everyone who has spoken of imputing Adam's sin meant by that name only his actual transgression. My own words ought to have warned him of that—and Calvin's phrase, "because it is within us," which he deliberately left out because it hindered his case. Those words of Calvin stand in the Commentary on [[Romans 5.17 >> Bible:Romans 5:17]]; you have the whole place above at p. 92. The difference he marks there between Christ and Adam collapses unless Adam's sin, which is imputed to us, is within us and stands as a quality inhering in us. Third, when he adds that inhering sin and its imputation are not treated in this dispute, I say the same here—and I used the distinction so that I could say it. What is not in controversy among us had to be separated from what is, and every ambiguity and confusion cleared from this question. Neglect that, and those who oppose me in this cause do not fight me but their own shadow. Finally, when he says the question raised is whether from Adam's first actual sin some guilt and some liability to penalty rests on the posterity, that is either false or does not touch me: I constantly teach that from that sin some guilt and some liability to penalty—if liability is even the right word—does rest on the posterity. I only insist that it rests not immediately, but through the corruption that sin produced.

source_text: GAR. Dicant vero, qui eam prae se ferunt in explicanda Quaestione diligentiam, annon ludificationi deputaturi sint, et praestigiarum loco habituri, si quis ex Novis illis Pontificiorum Doctoribus, qui pacificationis studio provincias et urbes obire credi volunt, blandulus accedat, et in causa momentosa, justificationis puta negocio, consensum cum Evangelicis profiteatur: se nimirum haud invito animo doctrinam amplecti de justificatione per imputatam Christi Domini nostri justitiam, dummodo distinctione adhibita rem explicare liceat; Quia scilicet justitia Christi variis modis accipi potest. 1. Pro actionibus illis ad legis divinae regulam exactissimis, quibus Christus et vivens et moriens plenissimum Patris sui mandatis obsequium praestitit. 2. Pro habituali illa et inhaerente justitia, qua Christi anima splendidissime enituit. 3. Pro justitia interna et habituali, qua unicuique fidelium subjective inest, sed quae justitia Christi merito dici possit, quoniam a Christo, Christique Spiritu, tanquam autore, in nos defluit. Hoc ergo ultimo sensu, agnoscere se, in controversia justificationis, imputationem justitiae Christi: at vero si prima et secunda significatione Christi justitiam accipiamus, se justitiae Christi imputationem nullam agnoscere, sed tanquam absurdam rejicere. Consensum certe in hoc negocio ita explicatum, nemo est, qui non conqueratur Ludibrium esse, potius quam consensum. &c.
english: Garissoles. But let those who parade such care in explaining the Question say whether they will not count it a mockery and a piece of prestidigitation if one of those new Pontifical doctors—who wish to be thought to tour provinces and cities in the zeal of pacification—comes on blandly and, in a weighty cause (say the business of justification), professes agreement with the Evangelicals: that he willingly embraces justification by the imputed righteousness of Christ our Lord, provided he may explain the matter by a distinction. For Christ's righteousness, he would say, can be taken in several ways. (1) For those acts most exact to the rule of God's law, by which Christ living and dying rendered fullest obedience to his Father's commands. (2) For that habitual, inhering righteousness by which Christ's soul shone most splendidly. (3) For the inward, habitual righteousness that is subjectively in each of the faithful, yet may rightly be called Christ's, because it flows into us from Christ and Christ's Spirit as its author. In this last sense, then, he would acknowledge, in the justification controversy, the imputation of Christ's righteousness; but if we take Christ's righteousness in the first and second senses, he would acknowledge no such imputation and reject it as absurd. A consensus in this business so explained—no one fails to complain—is a mockery rather than a consensus. And so on.

source_text: PLAC. Hoc simile non est appositum, sed oppositum. Huic enim blandulo praestigiatori tam sum dissimilis quam album nigro. Primo ille se enumerasse prae se ferret omnes acceptiones justitiae Christi, cum tamen unam omitteret in justificationis negotio maxime momentosam, qua justitia Christi accipitur pro singulari illa obedientia quam praestitit patiendo mortem, mortem, inquam, crucis; quae vulgo justitia passiva appellatur, et imputari fidelibus ab omnibus Protestantibus sine dubitatione creditur, cum de imputatione justitiae activae, quam solam D. Gar. commemoravit, sit aliqua sententiarum discrepantia, quae pacem Ecclesiae non turbat. Ego vero primi Adae peccati acceptiones omnes recensui, nullam praetermisi. Secundo ille Christi justitiam eo sensu acceptam imputari diceret, quo sensu accepta imputari negatur constanter ab omnibus Protestantibus. Ego vero peccatum Adami eo sensu posteris imputari affirmavi, quo sensu iis imputari omnes Protestantes constanter tenent. Itaque ille consensum fingeret cum Evangelicis plane falsum: Quis enim unquam Evangelicorum docuit justitiam inhaerentem, quam habemus a Christo, nobis ad justificationem imputari? Quem autem ego profiteor consensum, is verus est, neque negatur, aut negari potest a quoquam non Pelagiano.
english: Placeus. This likeness is not a parallel but an opposite. To that bland prestidigitator I am as unlike as white to black. First, he would pretend to have listed every sense of Christ's righteousness, yet omit the one most decisive in justification: that singular obedience he rendered by suffering death—death, I say, of the cross—which is commonly called passive righteousness and which all Protestants without hesitation believe is imputed to believers, while about imputing active righteousness (the only sense D. Garissoles mentioned) there is some difference of opinion that does not disturb the Church's peace. I, by contrast, reviewed every sense of Adam's first sin and omitted none. Second, he would say that Christ's righteousness, taken in a sense in which all Protestants constantly deny it is imputed, is imputed; whereas I affirmed that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity in the sense in which all Protestants constantly hold it is. So he would invent a plainly false consensus with the Evangelicals: for who among them ever taught that the inhering righteousness we have from Christ is imputed to us for justification? The consensus I profess is true, and no one who is not a Pelagian denies it or can deny it.

source_text: Tertio denique; Ille prae se ferret tertiam illam justitiae Christi acceptionem pro justitia nobis inhaerente, esse eam, quae intelligitur, cum quaeritur, utrum justitia Christi nobis imputetur, necne? Id quod falsum est. Opponitur enim justitia Christi in ea quaestione nostrae justitiae nobis insitae. Ego vero contra istas acceptiones peccati Adamici, quibus illud imputari dixi consensum esse, removi a statu quaestionis inter nos agitandae, et quidem disertissimis verbis. Quare ab omni ludificatione alienissimus fui.
english: Third and last: he would pretend that that third sense of Christ's righteousness—as righteousness inhering in us—is what is meant when we ask whether Christ's righteousness is imputed to us or not. That is false. In that question Christ's righteousness is set over against our righteousness implanted in us. I, on the contrary, removed from the state of the question we are debating among ourselves those senses of Adamic sin concerning which I said there is consensus that it is imputed—and I did so in the clearest words. So I stand wholly alien to every mockery.

source_text: GAR. Quod si aliqua esset in voce peccati Adae, homonymia & ambiguitas, illa tamen omnino sublata est, cum imputatio primi peccati Adae nuncupatur. Ita enim unusquisque per se facile intelligere potest, cum plura fuerint Adami peccata, de uno illo quaeri, quod inter omnia primum fuit, & quo non aliud est in genere humano prius. Ubi enim de numero vel ordine agitur, primum illud dici omnes intelligunt, unde ducitur numeri ordinisque principium, & quo prius nihil est in illo ordine. Itaque non erat hic istis distinctionum argutiis distinguendus, id est obturbandus magis, quam instruendus Lector.
english: Garissoles: But if there were any homonymy or ambiguity in the word "Adam's sin," it is wholly removed once we name the imputation of Adam's first sin. Anyone can see for himself that, though Adam had many sins, the question concerns the one that was first among them—nothing earlier in the human race. Where number or order is in view, everyone understands by "first" that from which the series begins, and before which nothing stands in that order. So the reader did not need to be tangled in these subtleties of distinction—that is, more disturbed than taught.

source_text: PLAC. Parum abest quin credam, hanc primi peccati Adae distinctionem Viro Docto commovisse bilem: adeo eam omni ex parte adoritur & sollicitat. Quid autem probare instituit? illam non necessariam fuisse. Fac ita esse; modo non sit falsa, non sit absurda, non sit causae meae noxia, causam non video, cur tantopere debeat exagitari. At distinguit & obturbat Lectorem. Distinguit forte, sed non diu. Obturbat autem neminem, nisi si quis me damnatum velit & confutatum. Lux distinguit & recreat: tenebrae confundunt & turbant. Praeterea nego non fuisse necessariam illam distinctionem. Ita enim distinctis subjecto & attributo quaestionis irritus fit eorum labor, qui meam sententiam tanto molimine oppugnant: quae causa videtur esse, cur hae distinctiones eis tantopere ingratae fuerint. Sed, inquit, unusquisque per se facile intelligere potest, cum plura fuerint Adami peccata, de uno illo quaeri, quod inter omnia primum fuit. Ergo id expressi, quod quisque per se facile intelligere potest: Grande scilicet crimen, & quod magnam reprehensionem meretur!
english: Placeus: I am nearly sure this distinction of Adam's first sin stirred the learned man's bile: he attacks and worries it from every side. What does he mean to prove? That it was unnecessary. Grant that; so long as it is not false, not absurd, and not harmful to my cause, I see no reason why it should be so fiercely chased. "But it distinguishes and confuses the reader." It distinguishes, perhaps—but not for long. It confuses no one unless someone wants me condemned and refuted. Light distinguishes and refreshes; darkness confounds and unsettles. Besides, I deny that the distinction was unnecessary. Once subject and attribute of the question are distinguished, the labor of those who batter my view with such effort is wasted—which seems why these distinctions so greatly displeased them. "But," he says, "anyone can easily see for himself that, though Adam had many sins, the question concerns the one that was first among them." So I stated what anyone can easily see for himself: a grave crime indeed, and one that deserves sharp rebuke!

source_text: At, inquam, hoc non sufficit. Progredi longius oportet. Peccatum enim Adami inter omnia primum duo complectitur, peccatum actuale, & peccatum habituale: illud omnium peccatorum actualium, hoc omnium habitualium primum: illud transiit, hoc mansit, & in posteros propagatum est, & quin nobis proxime seu immediate, cum intra nos sit, imputetur, nemo non Pelagianus ambigit. De altero illo an imputetur immediate, omnis est inter nos excitata controversia. Haec distinctio, quia audienti nominari primum Adae peccatum non statim veniebat in mentem, multumque habebat ad decidendam quaestionem momenti, constituenda fuit ob oculos Lectoris.
english: But that, I say, is not enough. We must go further. Adam's first sin among all embraces two things: actual sin and habitual sin—the first of all actual sins, and the first of all habitual ones. The former passed; the latter remained and was propagated to posterity; and that it is imputed to us proximately or immediately, since it is within us, no non-Pelagian doubts. About the other—whether it is imputed immediately—the whole controversy among us has been raised. Because that distinction did not leap to mind as soon as a hearer heard "Adam's first sin" named, and because it mattered much for deciding the question, it had to be set before the reader's eyes.

source_text: GAR. Sed & in hac subjecti distinctione nonnulla continentur, quae bene perpendenti vix est ut probari valeant. Nam 1. Quo fructu secunda peccati Adae significatio distinguitur a tertia, cum quicquid de peccato Adae in secunda significatione hic dicitur, ei reapse convenire asseratur, non quatenus est actio transiens, sed quatenus est corruptio habitualis & permanens? Ita enim peccatum Adae secundo & tertio modo dictum in idem revera coincidunt.
english: Garissoles: But in this distinction of the subject as well there are points that, well weighed, can scarcely be approved. For (1) what is gained by distinguishing the second sense of Adam's sin from the third, when whatever is said here of Adam's sin in the second sense is claimed to fit it in reality not as a passing act but as habitual, lasting corruption? So Adam's sin in the second and third modes really coincides in the same thing.

source_text: PLAC. Magnas habeo Viro docto gratias non patienti quicquam a me dici absque fructu. Quanquam fructu, uti spero, non carebit haec distinctio suo tempore & loco. Coincidunt quidem secunda & tertia acceptio in eandem imputationem, sed differunt modo loquendi, & sunt eiusdem nominis acceptiones diversae. Distinguere autem nomen, non rem ipsam, volui. Si quis dicat, id quod verum est, peccatum Adae dividi posse in primum peccatum actuale, & primum peccatum habituale; dividendum erit peccatum Adae acceptum secundo modo: divisi primum membrum erit peccatum Adae sumptum primo modo, & secundum membrum erit peccatum Adae tertio modo. Quibus si addas propagatam in nos corruptionem, quae vetus Adam solet nuncupari, etiam peccatum Adae vocari posse, habebis omnes illas acceptiones quas enumeravi, nihil ut sit, quare tanto conatu rejiciantur.
english: Placeus: I thank the learned man for allowing nothing I say to go without fruit. Still, I hope this distinction will not lack its fruit in due time and place. The second and third senses do coincide in the same imputation, but they differ in manner of speaking and are diverse senses of the same name. I meant to distinguish the name, not the thing itself. If one says—what is true—that Adam's sin can be divided into the first actual sin and the first habitual sin, then Adam's sin taken in the second sense must be divided: the first member of the division will be Adam's sin taken in the first sense, and the second member Adam's sin in the third. Add the corruption propagated into us, commonly called old Adam and able to be called Adam's sin as well, and you have all the senses I listed—so there is no reason to reject them with such zeal.

source_text:
GAR. 2. Quomodo ista componi possunt inter se? Peccatum Adae imputatur nobis, non qua haesit in ipso, & peccatum Adae imputatur nobis qua fuit vitiositas permanens in ipso: nam haerere in Adamo, & esse permanens in Adamo, quid hic differant, ego quidem non video.

PLAC. Propositio, Peccatum Adae imputatur nobis, non qua haesit in ipso, mea quidem est; sed illi opposita, Peccatum Adae imputatur nobis qua fuit vitiositas permanens in ipso, mea non est. Voces enim in ipso, quae contradictionem efficiunt, non invenit in meis scriptis, sed de suo Vir doctus addidit hoc loco: neque vero illae comparent in sententiae meae expositione quam ipse praemiserat § x. Contradictionem igitur istam ipse fecit ac finxit, mihique falso tribuit.
english: Garissoles: (2) How can these be reconciled? "Adam's sin is imputed to us not as it stuck in him," and "Adam's sin is imputed to us as it was lasting viciousness in him"—for what difference is there here between "sticking in Adam" and "being lasting in Adam"? I do not see. Placeus: The proposition "Adam's sin is imputed to us not as it stuck in him" is mine; the opposite, "Adam's sin is imputed to us as it was lasting viciousness in him," is not. The words "in him," which create the contradiction, he did not find in my writings; the learned man added them here from his own stock. Nor do they appear in the exposition of my view that he himself had set out earlier in §x. So he made and invented that contradiction and falsely pinned it on me.

source_text:
GAR. 3. Quando dicitur primi nostri parentis corruptio nobis posteris illius imputari, non quatenus haesit in ipso Adamo, sed quatenus transiit in nos: quanam est illa, quae statim profertur, hujus rei ratio; quod scilicet corruptio nostra haereditaria, sit ejusdem speciei cum corruptione, quae fuit in Adamo? An igitur specifica illa duarum corruptionum identitas id efficit, ut prior nobis imputetur? Quod si est, nihil causae dici potest, cur non omnium nostrorum majorum corruptio nobis imputari dicenda sit &c.

PLAC. Hic quoque monstrum sibi fingit, quod debellet. Meam enim istam rationem & truncat, & perperam interpretatur. Truncat: omittit enim & verba immediate praecedentia, ac ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est, & sequentia, ac quam suam naturam, tam suam corruptionem moralem nobiscum Adamus communicavit. Male interpretatur: Non enim verbis illis, Est enim corruptio nostra haereditaria eadem specie cum illa quae olim fuit in Adamo, rationem reddere volui, cur peccatum Adami tertio modo acceptum nobis imputetur; sed cur dicatur intra nos esse. Quare imputetur ostendi, cum dixi, ac ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est: id quod causalis quia monere eum potuisset, si voluisset attendere. Dixi ergo cum Calvino ad Rom. 5. 17. ideo imputari, quia intra nos est: Posse autem intra nos dici, quia corruptio nostra haereditaria est eadem specie cum illa quae fuit in Adamo. Idque illustravi similitudine ducta ab ipsa natura nostra, quae, quia specie eadem est cum natura Adami, & ab ea propagata, inde fit ut dici possit Adamus naturam suam nobiscum communicasse: non minus autem nobiscum communicavit corruptionem suam, seu peccatum. Potest igitur dici peccatum Adami in nos propagatum, in nos introiisse, intra nos esse. Haec est ratiocinii mei vis; a qua vides, Lector, quam aberret D. Garissolius.
english: Garissoles: (3) When our first parent's corruption is said to be imputed to us his posterity not as it stuck in Adam himself but as it passed into us, what is that reason instantly offered—namely that our hereditary corruption is of the same species as the corruption that was in Adam? Does that specific identity of the two corruptions make the former imputed to us? If so, nothing can explain why the corruption of all our ancestors should not likewise be said to be imputed to us, and so on. Placeus: Here too he invents a monster to slay. He both truncates my reason and misreads it. He truncates: he omits the words immediately before—and, to use Calvin's phrasing, "because it is within us"—and what follows: that Adam shared with us both his nature and his moral corruption. He misreads: by those words "For our hereditary corruption is the same in species as that which once was in Adam" I did not mean to explain why Adam's sin in the third sense is imputed to us, but why it is said to be within us. Why it is imputed I showed when I said, again with Calvin, "because it is within us"—a causal "because" that could have warned him had he cared to listen. So with Calvin on Romans 5:17 I said it is imputed because it is within us; and that it can be called within us because our hereditary corruption is the same in species as that which was in Adam. I illustrated that by a likeness from our very nature: since it is the same in species as Adam's and propagated from him, Adam can be said to have shared his nature with us—and no less his corruption, or sin. So Adam's sin can be said to have been propagated into us, to have entered us, to be within us. That is the force of my reasoning; from it, reader, you see how far Dr. Garissoles strays.

source_text: Est igitur quaestio inter nos instituta duntaxat de primo peccato Adami sumpto primo modo, hoc est, de actuali ejus inobedientia, de actione illa interna & externa, qua Dei legem transgressus est actu, praecisa ab habituali corruptione, qua actionem illam secuta est: num ea nobis nascentibus imputetur? Cui quaestioni nondum negatione simplici, sed distinctione rursus satisfaciendum videtur. Est enim ejus distinguendum attributum. Potest enim animo concipi duplex imputatio. Immediata & Mediata, vel (ut idem aliis verbis dicam) Antecedens & Consequens. Immediatam voco eam, quam solam thesibus, quas tu refutandas tibi sumpsisti, negare volui; qua putatur actio illa Adami, hoc est, vetiti fructus Manducatio ejus posteris omnibus (Christo excepto) proxime, immediate, hoc ipso quod filii sunt Adami, imputari ad duas istas poenas proprie dictas, privationem justitiae originalis quam mortem spiritualem appellas, & mortem aeternam. Hanc solam imputationem actionis illius ego negavi, quia non docetur in sacris literis adaequata fidei nostrae norma, quia pugnat cum sacris literis, quia Deum facit authorem peccati, quia Dei justitiam dehonestat, quia sequitur ex ea Christum esse natura sua peccatorem, quia alia nonnulla trahit secum absurda, mirabilem religionis Christianae puritatem & splendorem obscurantia, quae utinam fratres & conservi nostri a me per theses moniti, aut non prorsus contempsissent, aut non contemptim expendissent!
english: So the question between us concerns only Adam's first sin in the first sense—his actual disobedience, that inward and outward act by which he broke God's law, cut off from the habitual corruption that followed it: is that act imputed to us at birth? A bare no will not settle it; the attribute of the question must again be distinguished. One may conceive a twofold imputation: Immediate and Mediate, or—same point in other words—Antecedent and Consequent. By Immediate I mean the only imputation I meant to deny in the theses you undertook to refute: the view that Adam's act itself—his eating the forbidden fruit—is charged to all his posterity (Christ excepted) immediately, simply because they are Adam's children, unto the two punishments properly so called: loss of original righteousness (which you call spiritual death) and eternal death. That alone I have denied—because Scripture, the adequate rule of our faith, does not teach it; because it clashes with Scripture; because it makes God the author of sin; because it dishonors God's justice; because it would make Christ a sinner by nature; and because it drags other absurdities that cloud the purity and glory of the Christian religion. Would that our brothers and fellow servants, warned by those theses, had neither wholly scorned them nor weighed them with contempt!

source_text: Mediatam seu consequentem appello eam, quae haereditariae corruptionis in nos ab Adamo derivatae intuitum consequitur, eaque mediante fit. Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, ut ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus; ac propterea digni sumus, qui Adamo peccatori annumeremur. Id me Chamierus docuit Panstr. tom. 3. lib. 6. cap. 4. de poenis peccati § XVI. & XVII. Locum, si placet, quaere & lege. Huc transcripsissem (nam est insignis) nisi consulerem brevitatis. Sed tenere me non possum quin Aegidii Hunnii Augustanae confessionis Theologi celebris verba subiiciam, quibus hanc imputationem mediatam docet & explicat. Ostendit ergo (Apostolus Paulus) Lapsum Adami non immediate & per se, sed mediate & propter aliud nobis ejus posteris imputari, quia videlicet per lapsum illum polluta est natura primorum parentum, ut nonnisi peccato corruptos & vitiatos liberos procreare possint sicut scriptum est, genuit Adam filium ad imaginem suam Gen. 5. Alias si fieri potuisset, ut in posteros non vitium proprium derivaretur a primis parentibus, tum lapsus ille tanquam peccatum alienum eis plane non imputaretur.
