Palam igitur ostendit Paulus unum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere tantum Mediate, quatenus per delictum illud actuale introducta est in naturam horribilis corruptio, quam per carnalem generationem propagavit in ipsos posteros. Ita ut a lapsu corruptio Naturae, a corruptione naturae in nos derivata mors & damnatio perveniat, quatenus omnes peccavimus, inquit, id est quatenus ipsi in possessionem illius hereditariam devenimus.
english: By Mediate or consequential I mean the imputation that follows upon hereditary corruption derived into us from Adam and is wrought through that corruption as means. By sharing that corruption we share Adam's sin and, so to speak, consent to it habitually—and so deserve to be numbered with Adam the sinner. Chamier taught me this in Panstratia, tome 3, book 6, chapter 4, on the punishments of sin, sections XVI–XVII. Look up the place and read it; I would have copied it here—it is striking—had I not been watching length. I cannot, though, refrain from adding the words of Aegidius Hunnius, the noted Augsburg Confession theologian, by which he teaches and explains this mediate imputation. "Paul therefore shows that Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of something else—namely because by that fall the first parents' nature was so polluted that they can beget only children corrupted and spoiled by sin, as it is written, Adam begat a son in his own likeness (Genesis 5). Had it been possible that their own vice was not passed to posterity, that fall as another's sin would plainly not have been imputed to them. So Paul clearly shows that that one offense yields to our condemnation only mediately, insofar as through that actual offense a horrible corruption entered nature, which he spread by carnal generation into his posterity. Thus from the fall comes corruption of nature; from that corruption derived into us come death and damnation—inasmuch as all have sinned, he says, that is, inasmuch as we ourselves have come into hereditary possession of it."

source_text: Ut igitur rem verbo absolvam, quaeritur, utrum primum peccatum actuale Adami precise sumptum nobis ejus posteris imputetur a Deo Justo Judice proxime, immediate ac ordine naturae prius quam inhaerenter corrupti simus? Tu venerande frater affirmas: Ego Nego. Uter rectius, sequens disputatio, uti spero in Domino, planum faciet.
english: To put it in a word: the question is whether Adam's first actual sin, taken precisely, is imputed to us his posterity by God the Just Judge immediately and in the order of nature before we are inherently corrupt. You, venerable brother, say yes. I say no. Which of us is right, the disputation that follows will, I hope in the Lord, make plain.

source_text:
GAR. Distinguitur imputatio peccati in Priorem, sive Antecedentem, aut Immediatam; & Posteriorem, sive Consequentem, aut Mediatam. Haud incommode sane; nec dubito, si modo recta explicatio adhiberetur, consensum hic facile stabiliri posse: si nempe utraque imputatio eodem referretur, id est, si intelligeretur de peccato Adami eadem significatione accepto, sive de actione, qua primum Adamus reum se fecit laesae Divinae Majestatis.

PL. Cur ergo consensus non stabilitur? Cur oppugnor? utramque enim illam imputationem eodem retuli, ac nonnisi de illa actione qua primum Adamus peccavit, intellexi. Id sole meridiano clarius est, & miror vocari potuisse in dubium. Illa enim ipsa distinctio, ut alia omittam, hoc clarum facit: non potest enim de peccati habitualis seu corruptionis imputatione accipi. Quis enim dicat corruptionem ante corruptionem, aut post corruptionem; mediante corruptione, aut ea non mediante imputari?
english: Garissoles (§XVI): Sin's imputation is divided into prior—or antecedent, or immediate—and posterior—or consequent, or mediate. Not a bad division; and I do not doubt that if only it were explained rightly, agreement here could easily be reached—namely if both imputations were referred to the same thing, that is, to Adam's sin in the same sense, or to the act by which Adam first made himself guilty of offending the Divine Majesty. Placeus: Why then is agreement not reached? Why am I attacked? I did refer both imputations to the same thing, and understood them only of the act by which Adam first sinned. That is clearer than noon, and I wonder it could be doubted. The distinction itself, to say nothing else, makes this plain: it cannot be taken of imputing habitual sin or corruption. Who would say corruption is imputed before corruption, or after it—through corruption as means, or without it?

source_text: GAR. Ita enim paria ferme faceret cum ea, quam praemisimus, imputationis distinctione in communem & singularem: ut priorem & immediatam intelligeremus, communem illam quam diximus; posteriorem & mediatam quam propriam sive singularem nominavimus. Nam certe communis illa sive immediata, quemadmodum posterior fuit prima actuali Adae transgressione, ita prior fuit personali cujusque hominis ex Adamo prognati existentia, atque adeo etiam corruptione illa, quae in singulos naturali generatione descendit; quatenus ab initio res fuerunt omnes communiter in Adamo, quo sensu dictum est a Bernardo, Adamum & Evam fuisse prius nostros peremptores quam parentes. At imputatio singularis, propria, personalis & mediata, recte dici possit corruptione nobis inhaerente posterior, quatenus nemini personaliter imputari potest peccatum istud, nisi filius sit Adami, adeoque nisi personaliter existat: neque potest aliquis personaliter existere, & pro filio Adami haberi, nisi postquam anima & corpus in unam personam coaluerunt: quae partium hominis essentialium coalitio atque conjunctio, sine dubio conceptione posterior est &c. Ergo in conceptione prima nondum adest anima, nondum homo est, nondum filius Adami: & tamen ab ipso conceptionis momento inest vitiositas in semine, quippe quod habet fomitem illum peccati, quem definiunt, inordinatam carnis qualitatem ex peccato primorum parentium traductam in posteros, &c.
english: Garissoles (§XVII): For that would nearly match the distinction we already set out into common and singular imputation: taking the prior and immediate as that common imputation we named, and the posterior and mediate as what we called proper or singular. That common or immediate imputation, though later than Adam's first actual transgression, was earlier than each person sprung from Adam's personal existence—and earlier also than the corruption that descends on each by natural generation—insofar as from the beginning all were commonly in Adam. In that sense Bernard said Adam and Eve were our destroyers before they were our parents. But singular, proper, personal, mediate imputation may rightly be called later than the corruption inherent in us, since that sin can be charged to no one personally unless he is Adam's son and so exists as a person; and no one exists as a person and counts as Adam's son until soul and body have coalesced into one person—which union of the essential parts of man is without doubt later than conception, and so on. Therefore at first conception the soul is not yet present; there is not yet a man, not yet a son of Adam; and yet from the very moment of conception viciousness is in the seed, which has that tinder of sin they define as a disordered quality of the flesh drawn from the first parents' sin into their posterity, and so on.

source_text: PLAC. Si paria facit, cur non contentus illa distinctione jam recepta & commoda excogitavit novam & incommodam? Melior enim est imputationis distinctio in immediatam & mediatam, quam in communem & singularem. Primo quia illa jam fuerat usurpata ab Aegidio Hunnio & Walaeo, haec vero a quo fuerat usurpata? Deinde, quia illa est in membra non re modo, sed nomine etiam opposita; quae bonae distinctionis nota in hac desideratur. Nam imputatio illa singularis dici potest communis, & vice versa communis singularis. Quid enim? nonne humana natura, corruptio haereditaria, existentia, &c. sunt omnium hominum communes? Atqui imputatio singularis, propria, personalis non minus communis est quam natura humana, quam corruptio, quam existentia (Christum semper excipio) quomodo ergo imputationi communi opponitur? Nam membrorum oppositorum alterum alterius negationem importat. Rursus imputatio communis potest etiam ipsa dici singularis, propria, personalis, siquidem communis dicitur distributive: de singulis enim personis posterorum Adae singulatim praedicatur. Quod si dicitur communis collective, utraque dici debuit communis, altera collective, altera distributive. Deinde quod commune est collective posteris Adami, id quidem de tota collectione posterorum ejus praedicari potest, sed de iis singulis, nullo modo; sicut Apostolis commune fuit collective esse duodecim; ac propterea eorum nullus fuit duodecim. Praeterea, cum per imputationem vir doctus intelligat, vel actum Judicis declarantis aliquem reum, poenaque dignum, vel ipsam poenae inflictionem, palam est inflictionem poenae esse singularem: seu enim illa sit corruptio, seu mors corporis vel aeterna, infligitur singulis. Si igitur imputatio communis est poenae inflictio, utique singularis est. Inflictioni autem poenae respondet condemnatio, seu declaratio Judicis aliquem esse reum & poena dignum. Quaero etiam, quo sensu imputatio dicatur communis & opponatur singulari? An quo sensu solet commune seu universale opponi singulari? Non differt ergo imputatio communis a singulari, nisi ut species ab individuo suo. Non est autem species nisi in aliquo individuo suo. Extra aut ante individua sua frustra quaeritur. Attamen vult Vir doctus imputationem communem diu antequam esset singularis, adeoque extra singularem fuisse. Mitto alia discrimina. Quod si alio sensu, quam fert usus, communem singulari Vir doctus opposuit, singularitatem ipse & obscuritatem affectavit, sibique potius quam Lectori scripsit. Adde quod communis videtur magis communis esse debere quam singularis: alioqui cur id nomen huic opponitur? Attamen non est magis communis, nisi velis etiam iis communem esse hominibus, qui nunquam fuerunt, nec futuri sunt. Plura non addam; nisi hoc unum, quod praetermitti non debet. Ex ratione Viri docti, qua probat imputationem singularem, propriam, personalem corruptione nobis inhaerente posteriorem esse, sequi, imputari posteris peccatum Adae imputatione illa communi, antequam sint filii Adae, & pro filiis Adae habeantur. Quod quomodo verum & justum esse possit, tibi prudens Lector, considerandum relinquo.
english: Placeus: If the two distinctions match, why invent a new and awkward one instead of resting in the received, convenient one? The split into immediate and mediate is better than into common and singular. First, Hunnius and Walaeus had already used the former; who had used the latter? Second, the former divides into members opposed not only in the thing but in the name—the mark of a good distinction, missing here. For that singular imputation can be called common, and the common singular. Are not human nature, hereditary corruption, existence, and the rest common to all men? Yet singular, proper, personal imputation is no less common than human nature, corruption, or existence (Christ always excepted)—so how is it the opposite of common imputation? Opposed members each negate the other. Again, common imputation can itself be called singular, proper, and personal if common is taken distributively: it is said of each of Adam's posterity one by one. If common is taken collectively, both should have been called common—one collectively, one distributively. What is common to Adam's posterity collectively can be said of the whole collection, but of each member not at all—just as it was common to the Apostles collectively to be twelve, and therefore none of them was twelve. Further, since by imputation the learned man means either a Judge's act declaring someone guilty and worthy of punishment, or the infliction of punishment itself, the infliction is plainly singular: whether corruption, bodily death, or eternal death, it falls on individuals. If common imputation is infliction of punishment, it is singular. To that infliction answers condemnation—the Judge's declaration that someone is guilty and worthy of punishment. In what sense, then, is imputation called common and opposed to singular? In the sense in which common or universal is opposed to singular? Then common imputation differs from singular only as species from its individual. But a species exists only in some individual; outside or before its individuals it is sought in vain. Yet the learned man wants common imputation to have existed long before—and outside—the singular. I pass other differences. If he opposed common to singular in some sense usage does not bear, he affected singularity and obscurity, and wrote for himself rather than the reader. Add that the common ought to be more common than the singular—why else oppose that name to this?—yet it is not more common unless you make it common even to men who never were and never will be. One more point must not be skipped. From his proof that singular, proper, personal imputation is later than the corruption inherent in us, it follows that Adam's sin is imputed to the posterity by that common imputation before they are sons of Adam or counted as such. How that can be true and just I leave you, prudent reader, to weigh.

source_text:
GAR. Eam existimo fuisse mentem illis Theologis, qui peccatum Adae docent nobis imputari mediate, sive mediante corruptione & vitiositate nostra. Aegid. Hunnius artic. de pecc. Quaest. 7. Walaeus Defens. Molin. cap. 8. Enimvero longe alius Doctis Viris sensus, qui hac prioris & posterioris imputationis distinctione utuntur. Quandoquidem 1. eam, quam diximus communem, priorem & immediatam, absolute negant &c. 2. Quia posteriorem & mediatam sive singularem longe aliter exponunt, ita scilicet ut eam pretendant nulla ratione ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere, sed ad nostrum ipsorum duntaxat originale vitium nativamque & hereditariam corruptionem referri debere.

PLAC. Utrumque hoc discrimen aperte falsum est. Et primum quidem: Negarunt enim imputationem immediatam Aegidius Hunnius & Walaeus tam diserte, ut disertius non potuerint. Ille ait lapsum Adami non immediate & per se, sed mediate & propter aliud nobis ejus posteris imputari. Item, unum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere tantum mediate. Quid sibi vult illa negatio, non immediate & per se? Quid exclusiva, Tantum mediate? Quid est negare imputationem immediatam, si hoc non est? Hic vero imputationis illius possibilitatem negat, suamque negationem firmat ducto a Dei justitia argumento. Locum habes supra pag. 22. uti superiorem pag. 20. Secundum etiam tam aperte falsum est, ut satis mirari non possim, quomodo a se Vir Doctus impetrare potuerit, ut id proferret. Contra enim contendo imputationem mediatam ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere; nec de alio peccato a me unquam usurpatam fuisse, aut, quod amplius est, usurpari potuisse.
english: Garissoles: I take that to have been the mind of those theologians who teach that Adam's sin is imputed to us mediately—through our corruption and viciousness as means (Aegidius Hunnius, article on sin, Question 7; Walaeus, Defense of Molinaeus, chapter 8). But the learned men who use this prior/posterior imputation distinction mean something quite different. (1) They absolutely deny what we called the common, prior, immediate imputation, and so on. (2) They explain the posterior, mediate, or singular far otherwise—claiming it in no way looks to Adam's actual personal sin, but must be referred only to our own original vice and native hereditary corruption. Placeus: Both differences are plainly false. First: Hunnius and Walaeus denied immediate imputation as expressly as speech allows. Hunnius says Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of something else—and that that one offense yields to condemnation only mediately. What does not immediately and of itself mean? What does the exclusive only mediately mean? If that is not denying immediate imputation, what is? As for this writer, he denies even the possibility of that imputation and props the denial with an argument from God's justice; see above, page 22 (and earlier, page 20). The second difference is so openly false I cannot wonder enough how the learned man brought himself to say it. On the contrary I maintain that mediate imputation looks to Adam's actual personal sin itself; I have never used it of another sin, nor—what is more—could it be so used.

source_text: GAR. Tum in nomine imputationis peccati varie luditur. § XIX. Nam disputationis initio consenseramus, per imputationis vocem in hoc negotio intelligendum, vel actum judicis declarantis aliquem reum poenaque dignum, vel ipsam poenae inflictionem. Nunc in alia omnia itur. Quaeritur enim, an ipsius Adae actuale peccatum posteris imputetur. Agnoscunt Viri Docti verbotenus; sed explicationem audi: ita scilicet, inquiunt, ut imputari dicatur illa transgressio eodem significatu, quo dixit Apostolus, praeputium imputari in circuncisionem, id est, eodem loco haberi ac si circumcisum esset: Nos enim, ob peccatum nobis ab origine inhaerens, dignos esse, qui eo loco habeamur, ac si actualem ipsam inobedientiam commisissemus. Quod aliquis sane haud immerito tergiversationi deputari debere pretenderit. Convenerat enim, imputare peccatum hoc loco non aliud esse, quam alicui peccatum ita adscribere, ut propter illud, & ejus consideratione reatum subeat, & vel poenas det, vel certe poenis dignus existimetur. At quam remotum sit illud ab eo imputationis significatu, quem hic proponunt, nemo non videt.
english: Garissoles: Next, people play various games with the very name of imputing sin (§ XIX). At the start of the dispute we had agreed that in this business 'imputation' means either a judge's act declaring someone guilty and worthy of punishment, or the infliction of the punishment itself. Now everything is shifted. The question is whether Adam's own actual sin is imputed to his posterity. The learned men grant it in words—but hear their gloss: that transgression is 'imputed,' they say, in the same sense in which the Apostle said foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26)—that is, counted as if circumcised. So we, because of the sin that inheres in us from birth, are worthy to be treated as if we ourselves had committed that actual disobedience. Someone might fairly call that tergiversation. We had agreed that to impute sin here is nothing but so to ascribe a sin to someone that, for its sake and in view of it, he comes under guilt and either suffers punishment or is at least judged worthy of it. How far their proposed sense is from that meaning, anyone can see.

source_text: PLAC. Quod ait me, in nomine imputationis varie lusisse, ab eo longissime abfui, & quam maxime potui serio egi, ut veritatis & pacis decebat studiosum. Abhorrui etiam ab omni tergiversatione, & nihil mihi prius fuit quam ut statum quaestionis purgarem ab omni impedimento, & clarum facerem & liquidum, ne ullus vel tergiversationi, vel dissimulationi, vel declinationi locus esse posset. Quod autem me accusat, quasi conventis non steterim, satis mirari nequeo. Quomodo enim consenseramus Disputationis initio, aut convenerat inter nos de vocis imputationis significatu, qui nunquam ea de re inter nos disputaveramus? Virum enim Doctum mihi nunquam datum est, videre, aut coram alloqui. Ut autem de hac quaestione mecum conferre vellet, impetrare nulla ratione potui. Cum autem dicit, Nunc in alia omnia itur, putas fortasse, Lector, eum hoc meum manufcriptum posterius aut saltem tempus quo scriptum est, designare. At non ita est. Quae enim subjungit verba mea non petuntur ex hoc meo Manufcripto, sed partim ex Thesibus meis de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam, quinquennio, antequam inciperet ista controversia, publicatis, partim ex duarum epistolarum quas solas ad eum scripsi, posteriore, duobus aut tribus a Synodo postrema Nationali mensibus: In priore autem nihil disputabam, tantum ex ipso quaerebam modeste, qua de imputatione Decretum Synodi esset intelligendum, de Mediata, an de Immediata? In posteriore vero breviter ostendebam, nec rationes a me in thesibus allatas mediatam oppugnare imputationem, nec defuisse magnos Theologos qui immediatam negarent confessa mediata. Illud enim utrumque rescripserat ostendendum esse, quod ubi a me factum est, aliquamdiu respondere mihi renuit; tandem vero datis ad me secundis literis protestatus est se mihi ea de re non responsurum, neque mecum aut cum alio ullo eo de negotio disputaturum, nisi in proxima Synodo Nationali. Atque ita finem scribendarum invicem literarum fecimus.
english: Placeus: He says I played variously with the name of imputation. I was nowhere near that. I treated the matter as seriously as I could, as one who cares for truth and peace. I also shrank from every evasion. My first aim was to clear the state of the question of every obstacle and make it plain and liquid, so that there would be no room left for tergiversation, dissimulation, or side-stepping. That he charges me with breaking agreements I can scarcely believe. How had we 'agreed' at the opening of the Dispute, or settled between us the sense of the word imputation, when we had never disputed that point with each other? I was never allowed even to see the learned man or speak with him face to face, and I could by no means get him to confer with me on this question. When he says 'Now everything is shifted,' you may think, Reader, that he means this later manuscript of mine, or at least the time when it was written. Not so. The words of mine he quotes are not taken from this Manuscript, but partly from my Theses on the state of fallen man before grace—published five years before this controversy began—and partly from the later of the only two letters I wrote him, two or three months after the last National Synod. In the first letter I disputed nothing; I only asked him modestly how the Synod's Decree on imputation was to be understood—of the Mediate, or of the Immediate? In the second I briefly showed that the reasons I had given in the theses do not attack mediate imputation, and that great theologians have not been lacking who deny the immediate while confessing the mediate. He had written back that both points must be shown; when I had done so, he for some time refused to answer; at last, in a second letter, he protested that he would not answer me on the matter, nor dispute it with me or with anyone else, except in the next National Synod. And so we ended writing letters to each other.

source_text: Ubi igitur aut quando inter nos ea facta fuerit conventio, diviniare non possum. Fac tamen fuisse factam, quid dixi, quod ei vocis imputationis significatui repugnet? Scripsi in Thesibus supra dictis § VII. Actualem inobedientiam Adami dici posse nobis imputari, hoc sensu, quod ob peccatum nobis ab origine inhaerens digni sumus, qui eodem loco habeamur, ac si inobedientiam illam admisissemus. Est-ne id verum, an falsum? Si falsum, debuit ostendere falsitatem. Si verum, utique non repugnat imputationi mediatae, quam esse veram ipse vir doctus non diffitetur: verum enim vero non repugnat. Imo nihil aliud est quam descriptio imputationis mediatae, quam opposui opinioni Pighii, culpam originis unicam statuentis transgressionem Adami. Cumni, inquit Martyr, nos omnes vult nasci obnoxios, non propter aliquod vitium, aut culpam, aut deprauationem, quam in nobis habeamus. Dixi in Epistola, cum vitium hereditarium nos aeque morte dignos ac Adamum faciat, nihil obstare, quominus peccatum Adami nobis eo sensu dicatur imputari quo dixit Apostolus, si quis legem servaverit, illius praeputium in circuncisionem imputari. Est-ne id verum, nec-ne? Neque ait, neque negat D. Garissolius. Quid igitur facit? eum audi. GAR. Dixerit ergo Paulus, imputari praeputium in circuncisionem, quia eodem loco habeatur ac si circumcisum esset. At hic non de imputatione cujusvis rei agitur, sed de imputatione peccati alieni. Quis autem hactenus vel docuit, vel sibi persuasit, per imputationem illam peccati, intelligendam collationem diversorum peccatorum a diversis personis patratorum, vel paritatem inter diversa peccata ratione poenae aut reatus? Hoc neque Scriptura, neque communis ipse loquendi usus admittit.
english: Where or when, then, that agreement between us was made, I cannot guess. Grant it was made: what did I say that contradicts that sense of the word imputation? I wrote in the Theses just named, § VII, that Adam's actual disobedience can be said to be imputed to us in this sense: because of the sin that inheres in us from birth we are worthy to be held in the same place as if we had committed that disobedience. Is that true or false? If false, he ought to have shown the falsehood. If true, it cannot clash with mediate imputation, which the learned man himself does not deny is true—for truth does not clash with truth. It is nothing but a description of mediate imputation, which I set against Pighius's view that the sole guilt of origin is Adam's transgression. 'Cumni,' says Martyr, 'wants us all born liable—not because of any vice, fault, or depravity we have in ourselves.' I said in the Epistle that when hereditary vice makes us as worthy of death as Adam, nothing prevents Adam's sin from being said to be imputed to us in the sense in which the Apostle said that if someone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26). Is that true or not? D. Garissoles neither affirms nor denies. What does he do, then? Hear him. Garissoles: So Paul will have said foreskin is imputed for circumcision because it is counted as if circumcised. But here we are not dealing with the imputation of any thing whatever, but with the imputation of another's sin. Who has ever taught, or persuaded himself, that by that imputation of sin one must understand a comparison of different sins done by different persons, or a parity among different sins as to punishment or guilt? Neither Scripture nor ordinary speech allows that.

source_text: PLAC. Sumpfine verbum imputandi eo sensu quo illud Paulus sumpsit, cum dixit praeputium imputari in circuncisionem, nec-ne? Non negat Vir doctus. Ergo in eo verbo non lusi, nisi velit in eodem verbo similiter lusisse Apostolum. In ea enim significatione illud usurpavi, cujus gravissimum habeo autorem, ipsum Paulum. At hic, inquit, non de imputatione cujusvis rei agitur, sed de imputatione peccati alieni. Quid tum postea? Est-ne aliquid quod prohibeat illud verbum, quo sensu de alia aliqua re usurpatur, eodem etiam usurpari de peccato? At per imputationem peccati non est intelligenda collatio diversorum peccatorum a diversis personis patratorum vel paritas inter diversa peccata. Quid hoc ad me? An per imputationem inobedientiae Adami talem intellexi vel collationem, vel paritatem? Non certe. Diversa peccata a diversis personis patrata sunt ambo peccata actualia; vitium nobis ab origine inhaerens non est peccatum actuale, sed habituale tantum. Illorum peccatorum diversorum unum non est causa alterius: cum tamen inobedientia actualis nobis inhaerentis habitualis causa fuerit. Itaque conferuntur illa diversa peccata, tanquam ut, ita loquar, coordinata, hae vero inobedientiae tanquam subordinatae. Cum ergo inobedientia Adami sit causa vitii nobis inhaerentis, & hoc sit causa reatus nostri, necesse est inobedientiam Adami causam esse nostri reatus, saltem mediatam. Itaque nos esse reos ob vitium nobis inhaerens immediate, eoque mediante ob inobedientiam illam actualem Adami, cujus vitium illud inhaerens habitualis quaedam est consensus & approbatio, & communio: ut ob eam causam magis proprie nobis in peccatum dici possit imputari, quam praeputium in circuncisionem, ob servata Legis δικαιώματα.
english: Placeus: Did I take 'impute' as Paul took it when he said foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26)—yes or no? The learned man will not deny it. Then I was not gaming the word, unless he wants Paul gaming it too. I used Paul's sense; he is my heaviest warrant. But here, says he, we speak not of imputing just any thing, but of imputing another's sin. So what? May a word used of some other matter not also be used, in that same sense, of sin? He adds that imputing sin must not mean lining up different sins by different persons, or a parity of sins for punishment or guilt. How does that touch me? Did I mean by Adam's-disobedience imputation such a lineup or parity? No. Different persons' different sins are both actual; the vice born into us is not actual but only habitual. Neither of those different sins causes the other—yet Adam's actual disobedience caused the habitual vice in us. So those sins sit side by side (coordinated, if I may say so); these disobediences sit under one another. Adam's disobedience causes our inhering vice; that vice causes our guilt; therefore Adam's disobedience causes our guilt—at least as a mediate cause. We are guilty at once for the vice in us, and through that medium for Adam's actual disobedience—of which the inhering vice is a kind of habitual consent, approval, and share. That is why it may more properly be said imputed to us unto sin than foreskin unto circumcision for the Law's kept δικαιώματα.

source_text: Caeterum quod ait in Scriptura nullibi ostendi posse imputationem peccati eo sensu usurpatam, conturbare nos non debet: nam phrasis imputare vel imputari peccatum admodum rara est in Scriptura, nec forte nisi cum negatione adjuncta uspiam occurrit. Considera autem, humanissime Lector, quo sensu phrasis aequipollens ab ipso Domino nostro Jesu Christo usurpata fuerit Matth. 23.34. Propterea ecce ego mitto ad vos Prophetas & sapientes, & scribas, & ex ipsis quosdam trucidabitis & crucifigetis, & ex ipsis aliquos flagellabitis in Synagogis vestris, & persequemini ex urbe in urbem, ut veniat super vos omnis sanguis justus effusus super terram, a sanguine Abel justi usque ad sanguinem Zachariae filii Barachiae, quem occidistis inter templum & altare: hoc est, exponente Luca cap. XI. 50. ut a gente ista requiratur sanguis omnium Prophetarum effusus a jacto mundi fundamento. Quin enim illis verbis significata fuerit imputatio peccati negari nequit. Itaque sic in verba illa commentatus est Calvinus, Tametsi Abel non a Judaeis occisus est, ejus tamen necem ipsis imputat Christus, quia inter ipsos & Cain quaedam erat impietatis cognatio. Facit autem vitiositas inhaerens, ut nobis cum Adamo peccante non qualiscunque cognatio peccati, sed consanguinitas intersit. Imo vitium nostrum inhaerens nihil aliud est quam peccatum Adami secundum habitum in nos propagatum, vel instar pestis aut veneni naturali contagio diffusum. Quid est igitur, cur ob illud vitium nobis imputari dici non possit? Vide ergo, Lector, an me potius hoc loco quam ipsum Dominum, Vir Doctus impugnet.
english: As for the complaint that Scripture nowhere uses 'imputation of sin' in this sense: that need not unsettle us. The wording 'impute / be imputed' of sin is scarce in Scripture, and may never appear except with a negation. Kind Reader, look instead at the equivalent phrasing our Lord Jesus Christ himself used (Matthew 23:34): he sends prophets, wise men, and scribes; some will be killed and crucified, some scourged in the synagogues and hunted from city to city, so that all the righteous blood shed on earth comes upon that generation—from righteous Abel to Zechariah son of Barachiah, murdered between temple and altar. Luke puts the same point (Luke 11:50): that generation must answer for every prophet's blood shed since the world's foundation. Those words plainly signify sin's imputation. Calvin comments: Abel was not slain by the Jews, yet Christ charges them with his death because a kinship of impiety bound them to Cain. The vice that sticks in us does more still—it sets between us and sinning Adam not a loose kinship of sin but blood-relation. Our inhering vice is Adam's sin under the form of habit poured into us, like plague or poison by natural contagion. Why then may it not be said to be imputed to us for that vice's sake? Ask whether the learned man is striking at me here—or at the Lord himself.

source_text: GAR. Denique Socinistae imputationem peccati Adae exerte negant, & agnoscunt tamen nos propter nostrum peccatum eodem loco haberi, ac si Adami actualem inobedientiam commisissemus, quia nimirum imputationem peccati sic explicatam agnoverunt, nullam esse veri nominis imputationem. PLAC. Hic quoque nos traducendi cupido tenebras offudit animo Viri Docti. Ait enim Socinistas agnoscere nos propter nostrum peccatum eodem loco haberi, ac si Adami actualem ipsam inobedientiam commisissemus. Id quod falsum est. Volunt enim nos quidem eodem cum Adamo loco haberi, at non propter peccatum nostrum (peccatum enim ab origine nobis inhaerens nullum agnoscunt) sed quia sumus ab eo procreati, & de liberis idem quod de patre judicium sit. Itaque ab eorum sententia abest nostra toto caelo. Caeterum imputationem peccati Adami Socinus verbis negat, re ponit. Nam si idem sit de filio quod de Patre judicium, & hic judicatur peccator & dignus poena, judicatur etiam poena dignus esse filius: Ille quidem quia ipse peccavit, hic vero quia ejus pater peccavit. Id quod, ipso Viro Docto teste, est peccatum patris filio imputare, & quidem imputatione immediata; quippe cum haereditariam corruptionem neget Socinus, sine qua mediata imputatio esse non potest. Adde quod eadem mors infligitur posteris Adami & Adamo. Ipsa autem poenae inflictio est Viro Docto peccati imputatio. Revera igitur Socinus negat imputationem mediatam quam agnosco; immediatam quam impugno verbotenus tantum negat, re autem ipsa affirmat.
english: Garissoles: Last, the Socinians flatly deny that Adam's sin is imputed, yet still say that because of our own sin we stand where we would stand if we had done Adam's actual disobedience—because they treat that sort of 'imputation' as no real imputation at all. Placeus: Again the urge to blacken us has fogged the learned man's mind. He claims the Socinians admit we are held, because of our sin, as if we had done Adam's actual disobedience. False. They do put us in Adam's place—but not for our sin (they grant no birth-inhering sin). They do it because we were begotten by him, and children get the father's judgment. Heaven and earth lie between that and our view. For the rest: Socinus denies Adam's sin-imputation in speech and installs it in substance. If son and Father share one judgment, and the father is judged a sinner worthy of punishment, the son is judged worthy too—the one for his own sin, the other for his father's. On the learned man's own showing, that imputes the father's sin to the son, and immediately—because Socinus denies hereditary corruption, without which mediate imputation cannot stand. The same death falls on Adam and on his posterity; and for the learned man, inflicting punishment is itself imputing sin. So in fact Socinus denies the mediate imputation I grant, and only verbally denies the immediate imputation I oppose—while affirming it in the deed.

source_text: GAR. Alio deinde colore hanc posteriorem suam imputationem pingunt, cum addunt, nihil obstare, quominus Adami peccatum nobis imputari dicatur, quatenus vitium nostrum haereditarium habitus est, quem primum actuale peccatum reliquit in Adami anima; deinde inclinatio ad similia peccata; tertio consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum. Haec verba ex secunda, quam ad eum scripseram, epistola Vir Doctus deprompsit: sed de suo addidit voces quatenus, deinde, tertio, dividens ea quae conjunxi, ac ex una ratione tres conficiens praeter mentem meam. Locum ex illa epistola Gallice scripta integrum exscribam. Peccatum Adami dici potest nobis ejus posteris imputari tribus modis. Primo, quia (ut innuit Calvinus, vitium quod ab Adamo in nos defluxit peccatum Adami vocans) intra nos est. Secundo, quia cum vitium haereditarium nos aeque morte aeterna dignos ac Adamum faciat, nihil obstat, quominus peccatum Adami nobis eo sensu dicatur imputari, quo dixit Apostolus, si quis legem servaverit, illius praeputium in circuncisionem imputari, hoc est, eodem loco eum haberi ac si fuisset circumcissus. Tertio, quia corruptio haereditaria est habitus, quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & perversa inclinatio ad simile peccatum; ac proinde consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, nihil video quod impediat, quominus nobis imputari dicatur. Hunc ultimum modum, hanc ultimam rationem, Vir Doctus in tres discerpsit, ac mutat quia in quatenus. Sed eum audiamus. GAR. Ubi primum illud mirari subit, quod imputari agnoscunt peccatum Adae, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Haec enim verba praeferre videntur imputationem ipsius habitualis peccati Adae. Quid autem horridius aut absurdius est, in eo quod dicimus, imputari nobis peccatum Adami actuale, quam quod his verbis fatentur, imputari peccatum habituate? praesertim cum imputatio potius ad actus videatur referenda quam ad habitus?
english: Garissoles: They next dress this later imputation in fresh paint: nothing, they say, blocks calling Adam's sin imputed to us inasmuch as our hereditary vice is a habit the first actual sin left in Adam's soul; next, an inclination toward like sins; third, habitual consent to that sin. He lifted those words from my second letter to him—then slipped in of his own 'inasmuch as,' 'next,' and 'third,' carving one joined reason into three against my sense. Here is the whole French-letter place. Adam's sin may be said imputed to us his posterity three ways. First: as Calvin hints (naming Adam's sin the vice that flowed from him into us), it is inside us. Second: hereditary vice makes us as worthy of eternal death as Adam, so nothing stops saying Adam's sin is imputed in the Apostle's sense—if someone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26), i.e. he is counted as circumcised. Third: hereditary corruption is the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul, plus a bent toward a like sin, and so habitual consent to that sin—I see no bar to saying it is imputed to us. That last mode, that last reason, the learned man has shredded into three and warped with 'inasmuch as.' Hear him. Garissoles: First wonder: they grant Adam's sin imputed inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. The wording seems to favor imputing Adam's habitual sin itself. What could be worse—when we speak of imputing Adam's actual sin—than confessing by these words that a habitual sin is imputed? Especially when imputation looks to acts, not habits.

source_text: PLAC. Primum non dixi, imputari peccatum Adae, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Tantum dixi, quia corruptio haereditaria est habitus quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & perversa propensio ad ejusmodi peccatum, atque adeo consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, causam me non videre, cur non possit dici nobis imputari, nimirum primum illud peccatum, quod corruptionem, quae haereditaria vocatur, in Adami anima reliquit. Id autem aliud esse non potest quam primum illud Adae peccatum actuale. Aliud enim nullum illam deprauationem in Adami anima reliquit. Vides Lector, me imputationem illam, quam mediatam appello, referre ad peccatum Adae actuale, ac rationem reddere, cur ob haereditariam illam corruptionem dici possit nobis imputari. Sed quandoquidem Vir Doctus probat corruptionem, quatenus in Adami anima fuit, nobis imputari, vide quaeso quid consequatur. Primum illa nostra erit, ut peccatum actuale, per imputationem; hoc enim est illius sententiae consentaneum. Vultne igitur posteros Adami corruptos esse, ut loquitur, interpretative, seu imputative? Deinde, peto an corruptio, quatenus nobis inhaeret, nobis imputetur, necne? Si negas; igitur non est vere peccatum, non peragit nos reos. Si ais; igitur bis corruptio nobis imputatur, semel quatenus fuit in Adamo, iterum quatenus est in nobis. Ita magis rei sumus quam Adamus. Quis hoc credat? Denique peto an corruptio, quatenus haesit in Adamo, imputetur nobis immediate, an mediante corruptione? Si hoc, cur idem non dicitur de peccato actuali? Si illud, Ergo illius corruptionis Adae, nostra corruptio poena est: Cur enim non aeque imputati habitualis poena sit, ac imputati actualis? Si ergo illius imputati poena est, magis punitur in nobis peccatum habituale Adami, quam in ipso Adamo punitum est. In nobis enim, si viro Docto fides habetur, punitur inflictione corruptionis, cum ea poena non fuerit corruptio Adami in Adamo punita. Postremo, Si nobis imputatur corruptio ut fuit in Adamo, vel nobis imputatur simul cum eius peccato actuali, vel ante, aut post illud peccatum. Cur ante aut post illud imputetur, causa dici non potest. Si nobis simul imputatur, etiam simul cum actuali imputata fuit Adamo, cur non enim aeque simul illi ac nobis duo illa eius peccata imputata fuissent? Si ergo simul imputata fuerunt ipsi Adamo, eius corruptio non fuit poena peccati actualis: fuisset enim semetipsa prior: antecedit enim imputatio poenam; & prius imputata fuisset Adamo, quam in eo fuisset. Id quod non obscure contradictionem implicat. Sed pergat.
english: Placeus: First, I never said Adam's sin is imputed inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in his soul. My point was only this: hereditary corruption is that habit the first sin left there, plus a bent toward such sin, and so habitual consent to it—and I see no reason we may not say the first sin is imputed to us, namely the sin that left what we call hereditary corruption in Adam's soul. That can only be Adam's first actual sin; nothing else planted that depravity in him. So, Reader: the imputation I name mediate I refer to Adam's actual sin, and I explain why hereditary corruption lets us say it is imputed to us. But if the learned man proves the corruption as it stood in Adam's soul is imputed to us, watch what follows. First, that corruption becomes ours as an actual sin by imputation—his own view requires it. Does he then want Adam's posterity corrupt 'interpretatively' or 'imputatively'? Next: is the corruption as it inheres in us also imputed to us? Deny it, and it is not truly sin and does not make us guilty. Affirm it, and corruption is charged twice—once as it was in Adam, again as it is in us—so we are guiltier than Adam. Who believes that? Last: is Adam-stuck corruption imputed to us immediately, or through corruption as a means? If through a means, why not say the same of the actual sin? If immediately, then our corruption is the punishment of Adam's—for why should an imputed habitual not draw punishment as an imputed actual does? If so, Adam's habitual sin is punished harder in us than it was in him: in us, on his showing, by inflicted corruption, whereas that was not how Adam's own corruption was punished in Adam. Finally, if Adam's-as-was corruption is imputed to us, it comes with his actual sin, or before it, or after. Before or after has no cause. If together with us, it was together with Adam too—else why would those two sins not equally have hit him and us at once? If they hit Adam together, his corruption was not the punishment of the actual: it would be earlier than itself, since imputation precedes punishment, and it would be charged to him before it existed in him. That is open contradiction. But let him go on.

source_text: GAR. Deinde, qua ratione habitus ille in Adami anima relictus, dici potest peccatum nostrum haereditarium? habitus ille in Adami anima, nonne diu est cum esse desiit? Quomodo igitur esse amplius potest, aut nobis subjective inhaerere? imo qui fieri potest, ut unicus habitus, id est unum idemque numero accidens, in tam diversa, adeoque infinita pene subjecta transeat?
english: Garissoles: Next—by what account can that habit left in Adam's soul be called our hereditary sin? Has that habit in Adam's soul not long since ceased to exist? How then can it still be, or inhere in us as in a subject? How can one single habit—one and the same accident in number—pass into so many different subjects, nearly infinite?

source_text: PLAC. Dixi in genere corruptionem haereditariam esse habitum, quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit; nempe ut in suo fonte, unde ad nos omnes propagatione naturali manavit. Nonne hoc verum est? Atqui diu est cum esse desiit, nempe in Adamo. Sed nondum esse desiit in Adami posteris. At quomodo habitus in Adami anima relictus dici potest peccatum nostrum? Eo modo, inquam, quo peccatum Adami dicitur a Calvino intra nos esse, & peccatum haereditarium dicitur vetus Adam, & natura Adami dicitur natura nostra, & quod seminatur esse id quod metitur. Nimirum habitus ille in Adamo relictus ab eo in nos propagatus est. Differt igitur numero peccatum nostrum ab Adami peccato, sed est idem specie, nec id tantum, sed ab eo ducit originem quodam quasi naturali contagio. Si dixero naturam humanam esse illam quae creata est in Adamo, num inde sequetur, naturam humanam Adami, & nostram non differre numero?
english: Placeus: In general I said hereditary corruption is the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul—namely as in its fountain, from which it flowed to us all by natural propagation. Is that not true? Yes, it has long ceased to be—in Adam. But it has not yet ceased in Adam's posterity. How then can a habit left in Adam's soul be called our sin? In the same way Calvin says Adam's sin is within us; hereditary sin is called old Adam; Adam's nature is called our nature; and what is sown is what is reaped. That habit left in Adam was propagated from him into us. So our sin differs from Adam's in number, but is the same in kind—and more: it draws its origin from his by a kind of natural contagion. If I say human nature is the nature created in Adam, does it follow that Adam's human nature and ours do not differ in number?

source_text: GAR. Est inclinatio ad peccata similia peccato illi primo Adae. Sane vero; Sed & ad alia Adami peccata. An ideo dicemus, reliqua itidem Adami peccata nobis imputari? Imo nequaquam sufficiens est alieni peccati imputationis causa, ut nostrum peccatum eodem animum nostrum inclinet & flectat. Multi enim inclinationem, & naturalem quendam impetum habent ad similia aliorum peccata, sine omni omnino illorum imputatione. &c.
english: Garissoles: It is an inclination to sins like Adam's first. True enough—but also to Adam's other sins. Shall we therefore say those other sins of Adam are likewise imputed to us? No: it is nowhere near enough, as a cause for imputing another's sin, that our sin bends our mind the same way. Many people have an inclination and a kind of natural push toward sins like other people's, with no imputation of those sins at all. And so on.

source_text: PLAC. Primo tribuit mihi argumentationem non meam. Hoc enim, ut dixi, conjunxi cum superiori, ut ex duobus illis tertium colligerem, in quo ratio imputationis potissimum consistit. Id quod ex tertia illa ratione, quam ex literis meis se collegisse profitetur hoc eodem cap. 2. § x. pag. 35. 36. liquere potest. In ea enim copulantur ista tria quae hoc loco divisit sic ut duplex mutatio notari possit. Primo enim pro corruptione haereditaria reposuit vitium in nobis inexsistens. Deinde omisit conjunctionem causalem propterea, adeo, aut similem, respondentem eo loco vocibus gallicis par consequent, quibus in illa epistola usus fueram, & ex quibus apparet, rationem imputationis me petere a consensu habituali ad illud peccatum in corruptione haereditaria incluso: hunc autem consensum ex eo colligere, quod illa corruptio nihil aliud est quam primi illius peccati actualis pravitas habitualis, quam in Adami anima reliquit, & quae in nos propagata nos ad simile peccatum inclinat. Caeterum nescio annon etiam hoc loco adversus ipsius Domini verba disputare videatur, quae habentur Matth. 23. 34. & Luc. xi. 50. 51. Quid est enim, cur, exempli causa, non possint aliquomodo crudelia facinora Neronis ei, qui sit animo aeque crudeli & immani, imputari, quandoquidem quominus eadem perpetret per ejus voluntatem non stat, aeque videlicet crudelem?
english: Placeus: First he pins on me an argument that is not mine. As I said, I joined this with the prior point so that from those two I could draw a third, where the reason for imputation chiefly sits. That is plain from the third reason he says he gathered from my letters in this same chapter 2 section x, pp. 35-36. There those three points are linked; here he split them so you can mark a double change. First, for hereditary corruption he put a vice that does not exist in us. Next he dropped the causal link—'therefore,' 'so,' or the like—matching the French par consequent I had used in that letter, from which it is clear I take the reason of imputation from habitual consent to that sin as included in hereditary corruption, and that I gather this consent because that corruption is nothing but the habitual depravity of that first actual sin, which it left in Adam's soul and which, propagated into us, inclines us to like sin. I am not sure he is not also arguing here against the Lord's own words in Matthew 23:34 and Luke 11:50-51. Why, for example, could Nero's cruel deeds not somehow be charged to someone equally cruel and savage in mind, when it is not by his will that he fails to do the same—being equally cruel?

source_text: GAR. De habituali consensu quod ultimo loco dicitur, ad rem praesentem magis pertinet, sed tale tamen est, ut Virorum Doctorum causam evertat potius quam stabiliat. Contendunt enim acriter ipsam Adami actualem inobedientiam nemini posterorum imputari, neminem ejus poenas ferre, neminem propter eam reum haberi posse, & tamen fatentur esse in omnibus Adami posteris consensum habitualem ad illud peccatum. Quis non inde consequi videt, eam igitur inobedientiam primi parentis merito posse posteris imputari? Nam consensus in peccatum alterius, justa causa esse potest imputationis illius peccati, juxta dictum Apostolicum, esse dignos morte, non modo qui mala ipsi patrant, sed & qui mala patrantibus consentiunt. Rom. 1. 32. Unde colligitur haec argumentatio. Omnis consensus in alienum peccatum, justa causa esse potest imputationis illius peccati. At consensus habitualis omnium posterorum Adae, est aliquis consensus in peccatum actuale primum Adami. Ergo consensus habitualis, justa ratio & causa esse potest, quare primum Adami peccatum omnibus ipsius posteris imputetur.
english: Garissoles: What is said last about habitual consent bears more on the present point—yet it overturns the Doctors' cause more than it secures it. They press hard that Adam's own actual disobedience is imputed to none of his posterity, that no one bears its penalties, that no one can be held guilty for it—and yet they admit that in all Adam's posterity there is habitual consent to that sin. Who does not see the sequel: that first parent's disobedience can therefore justly be imputed to the posterity? For consent to another's sin can be a just cause for imputing that sin, by the Apostle's word that they are worthy of death not only who do evils themselves, but also who consent to those who do them (Romans 1:32). Hence this argument: Every consent to another's sin can be a just cause for imputing that sin. But the habitual consent of all Adam's posterity is some consent to Adam's first actual sin. Therefore habitual consent can be a just reason and cause why Adam's first sin is imputed to all his posterity.

source_text: PLAC. Itane argumentatio, quae tota mea est, causam meam evertit? Itane contendo acriter ipsam Adami actualem inobedientiam nemini posterorum imputari, neminem ejus poenas ferre, neminem propter eam reum haberi posse? Quid clarius, quam me potius contendere eam Adami posteris imputari, eos ejus poenas ferre, propter eam reos haberi? Alioqui, quorsum seposui corruptionem haereditariam a statu quaestionis? Cur imputationis immediatae & mediatae distinctionem attuli? Cur sic distinguendum censui attributum quaestionis, Utrum actualis inobedientia Adami nobis nascentibus imputetur? Cur constituens statum controversiae ei limitationem ab illa distinctione petitam adhibui? Quorsum etiam pertinent istae ipsae rationes, quas conjunctim proposueram & Vir Doctus disjunxit? Volui certe rationem reddere, cur peccatum aliquod nobis imputetur, nonne? Nimis diserta sunt verba mea quam ut id possit negari. Quod ergo peccatum intellexi? Nullum potui, praeter actuale primum Adami. Dixi corruptionem haereditariam esse habitum, quem primum peccatum reliquit in Adami anima: nonne vides me aliud primum peccatum intelligere non posse, quam actuale illud primum? Dixi illam corruptionem esse propensionem ad similia peccata, nempe similia illi primo actuali, alia intelligi non possunt. Dixi eam esse consensum habitualem ad illud peccatum. Quis non videt per illud peccatum me corruptionem non intelligere, sed actuale illud primum quo se ipse Adamus corrupit?
english: Placeus: Is my own argument suddenly against me? Am I the one insisting that Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to none of his posterity, that nobody bears its penalties, that nobody can be held guilty for it? The opposite is clearer: I insist that it is imputed to Adam's posterity, that they bear its penalties, that they are held guilty for it. If not, why peel hereditary corruption out of the state of the question? Why introduce immediate versus mediate imputation? Why frame the question's attribute as Whether Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to us as we are born? Why, when I fixed the controversy's state, attach a limit drawn from that distinction? And why do the reasons I had set out together—and the Learned Man tore apart—matter at all? I was giving a reason why some sin is imputed to us. The wording is too open to allow denial. Which sin? Only Adam's first actual. When I called hereditary corruption the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul, I could not mean any other first sin than that first actual. When I called it a bent toward like sins, I meant like that first actual—nothing else fits. When I called it habitual consent to that sin, I meant by that sin not the corruption itself, but the first actual act by which Adam corrupted himself.

source_text: Eandem rationem, imputationis mediatae in hoc ipso Manuscrito proposui his verbis. Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, ut ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus. Quis non videt me peccatum Adami cui communicamus, cui habitualiter consentimus, distinguere a corruptione qua ei communicamus & consentimus? Id autem aliud esse non potest quam primum illud actuale Adami. Hoc igitur volui nobis imputari, & quidem ob istum ipsum habitualem consensum. Non igitur me mecum committit Vir doctus, sed cum animi sui figmento.
english: In this very Manuscript I gave the same account of mediate imputation: by sharing this corruption we communicate with Adam's sin, and we consent to it habitually, so to speak. I am plainly distinguishing Adam's sin—the one we share and habitually consent to—from the corruption through which that sharing and consent happen. That sin can only be Adam's first actual. That is what I wanted charged to us, and for that habitual consent. So the Learned Man pits me not against myself but against a fiction of his own making.

source_text: Posterior quaestio de hujus peccati imputati poena etiam ipsa aliquam explicationem desiderat. Primum autem poena distinguenda est; deinde separandus a nobis Adamus. Poena dicitur vel proprie, vel improprie. Proprie rursus multipliciter: sed nihil opus est omnia poenarum genera quae te nosse arbitror, enumerare, id enim cum longum esset, tum ad rem quam agimus inutile. Satis est tenere quo sensu corruptio haereditaria poena dicatur a te aliisque fratribus nostris, quorum sententiam adversus me tueri vis.
english: Before we go further, the later question on the penalty tied to this imputed sin needs clearing. Two moves first: sort out what penalty means, and keep Adam distinct from us. Penalty can be named properly or improperly, and even the proper sense branches many ways. I will not catalogue every species you already know—that would be long and beside our point. Hold only the sense in which you and the other brothers whose case you defend against me call hereditary corruption a penalty.

source_text: Nempe statuis esse poenam strictissime ac propriissime sic dictam, cujus hae sunt conditiones. 1. Lex eam comminatur. 2. Iustitia ut infligatur a Iudice exigit. 3. Iudex eam infligit ut fiat iustitia, sive ut iustitiae satisfiat. Itaque Ursinus in explicat. Catechet. Cum sibi objecisset non debuisse Deum culpam Adami tali poena punire, respondit fiat iustitia & pereat Mundus.
english: On your account this is penalty in the tightest proper sense, and you put three marks on it. The Law must threaten it. Justice must demand that the Judge lay it on. The Judge must lay it on so justice is done—or so justice is satisfied. Ursinus, in the Catechetical Explanation, faced the objection that God should not have punished Adam with such a penalty, and answered: Let justice be done, though the world perish.

source_text: Ego vero talem esse poenam & negavi in Thesibus & non possum impetrare a conscientia mea ut nunc quoque non negem. Scio hanc corruptionem seu concupiscentiam poenam a Patribus appellari, necnon alicubi a Calvino, sed nego sensu ita proprio, ita stricto. Sed ob similitudinem quandam poenae nomen ei accommodatur. Ut enim poena sequitur culpam & cum ea cohaeret, sic corruptio haereditaria secuta est culpam Adami atque ex ea nata est.
english: In the Theses I refused to count it that sort of penalty, and conscience still will not let me reverse that denial. The Fathers do call this corruption—or concupiscence—a penalty, and Calvin does in places; I do not deny the word, only the so-proper, so-strict sense. The name rides on likeness. Penalty tracks fault and clings to it; hereditary corruption likewise tracked Adam's fault and sprang from it.

source_text: Ut non est in ejus qui punitur potestate poenam admittere, vel non admittere aut etiam excutere, sic ab alio corruptione ista afficimur, nec in nobis situm est eam non admittere, aut excutere. Ut poena ejus cui infligitur conditionem mutat in deteriorem, sic hac corruptione inquinatus Adamus deterior, ignobilior, foedior, miserior, quam alioqui fuisset, evasit.
english: A punished person cannot choose to take the penalty, refuse it, or cast it off. We are hit by this corruption from another in the same way: refusing or casting it off is not in our power. A penalty also worsens the state of the one it strikes. Stained by this corruption, Adam became worse—more ignoble, fouler, more wretched—than he would have been without it.

source_text: Denique ut qui inflictam poenam sentit, ingemiscit, & ab ea liberari percupit; sic qui hanc in se corruptionem deprehendunt & agnoscunt serio, vehementer indolescunt & aegre ferunt se hujus mali vinculis illigari. Has ob similitudines merito tetrum istud & horrendum malum poena dici potuit & dicitur a multis.
english: Last likeness: whoever feels a penalty laid on groans and longs for release. Those who seriously find and own this corruption in themselves likewise grieve hard and hate being chained by that evil. For such likenesses many writers have rightly named—and still name—that foul, dreadful evil a penalty.

source_text: Sed quaeritur inter nos duntaxat, num sit poena sensu illo, quem explicavi, maxime proprio & stricto. Has duas quaestiones, quia tu non separasti, ut feret occasio, tua sequens vestigia, Deo favente, tractabo.
english: Among us the sole live question is whether it is penalty in that most proper, strict sense I just marked out. You did not keep the two questions apart. God willing, I will take them up in turn as the chance comes, following your own steps.

source_text: CAP. III. Observata quaedam in primo & secundo Capite Tractatus, & alia laudata, alia refutata. PRIMO Capite tui tractatus statum quaestionis constituisti. Eo constituto Capite secundo digrederis ad probandum, omnes homines esse infectos peccato originali, & ideo omnibus hujus vitae miseriis mortique obnoxios. quo consilio, equidem nescio. Nam tu ipse fateris extremis verbis cap. 2. nullam ea de re inter nos esse controversiam: Et vero id ipsum Thesibus quas oppugnas probaveram, paucis quidem verbis, sed argumentis multis & validis, robore & numero praestantibus, quorum quaedam expolivisti, quaedam praetermisisti. Notavi autem inter legendum nonnulla digna observatu, vel quia vera sunt, sed causae quam agis repugnantia, vel quia tam veritati quam meae sententiae adversari mihi videntur.
english: Chapter III. Certain observations on the first and second chapters of the Treatise—some praised, some refuted.

In your first chapter you set the state of the question. With that settled, chapter two digresses to prove that every human being is infected with original sin and so stands exposed to this life's miseries and to death. To what end, I do not see. You yourself admit, in the closing words of chapter 2, that we have no quarrel on that point. I had already proved the same in the Theses you attack—briefly, yes, but with many sound arguments, strong and numerous; you polished some of them and skipped others. Reading through, I marked several things worth notice: some true, yet hostile to the case you are pressing; others that seem to me to clash both with the truth and with my own view.

source_text: Laudo in primis quae scripsisti non procul a fine Cap. 2. peccatum illud Adami omnium malorum scaturigo, actuale & PERSONALE fuit in ipso, sed infecit naturam: & omnes homines eo inficiuntur, quia sunt ab eo secundum ordinem naturae &c. Dic mihi, amabo te, si peccatum illud personale fuit in Adamo, quo jure illud idem numero quod in Adamo fuit nobis omnibus imputetur? Tu Cap. 1. dicis Deum in verbis illis Ezechielis, filius non feret iniquitatem Patris, loqui tantum de peccatis externis & actualibus, & cum ejusmodi peccata sint personalia, personam tantum spectare. Jam autem tu affirmas hoc loco peccatum illud Adami fuisse actuale & personale. Quis non inde concludat ergo peccatum illud tantum Adami personam spectabat, nec illud ferre filii ejus debent? Quid sibi etiam volunt illa verba in ipso? opponuntur ne his in ejus posteris, vel in nobis? certe in nobis peccatum Adami non est personale, sed totius generis humani, (uno excepto Christo) commune: sed in nobis nihil aliud est quam haereditarium illud vitium, quo omnes infecti nascimur, quodque omnibus, nisi condonatum fuerit per Christum, imputatur.
english: I praise first what you wrote near the end of chapter 2: Adam's sin, the spring of every evil, was actual and PERSONAL in him, yet it infected nature; and all are infected by it because they come from him in nature's order, and so on. Tell me, please: if that sin was personal in Adam, by what right is the very same numerical act that was in him imputed to us all?

In chapter 1 you say God, in Ezekiel's words "the son shall not bear the father's iniquity," speaks only of outward, actual sins, and that such personal sins regard the person alone. Here you affirm Adam's sin was actual and personal. Who would not conclude that it therefore regarded Adam's person only, and that his children ought not to bear it?

What do those words "in him" mean either? Are they set against "in his posterity," or "in us"? In us Adam's sin is not personal; it is common to the whole human race (Christ alone excepted). In us it is nothing but that hereditary vice with which we are all born infected, and which is imputed to everyone unless Christ has forgiven it.

source_text: Minus commode idem dixeras Cap. 1. haec culpa unius hominis fuit, sed poena omnibus hominibus est communis &c. Hoc discrimen observas inter culpam Adami & poenam, quod culpa unius hominis fuit, poena vero communis omnibus. Nonne vides quid sequatur, nimirum poenam non respondere culpae; quippe, culpam enim non communem vindicari poena communi: poenam iis irrogari, quorum non sit culpa. Certe si poena est omnium, culpa tantum unius, omnes, uno excepto, culpa vacant, quomodo igitur puniuntur juste? Si culpa unius hominis est, nec est communis omnibus, cur omnibus imputatur? Si eam dicas, cum unius sit, imputatione fieri communem omnibus, non evades, primum enim quae mea culpa non est, ea mihi imputari non debet. Non enim ideo mihi imputatur ut sit mea, sed contra quia mea est, idcirco mihi imputatur: alioqui mihi imputatur falso & injuste. Deinde si culpa Adami mea non est nisi imputatione, fecit me Deus Judex (cogitans horresco) sua imputatione peccatorem, non invenit: est enim imputatio judicis actus, non meus. Tolle imputationem, culpa illa vaco; mea enim non est, sed fuit unius hominis Adami: me igitur (vide quo ducat ista imputatio & mecum cohorresce) judex, hoc est, Deus fecit peccatorem ac reum, & causa est primi mei peccati, primi mei reatus. Denique de jure non magis ad me poena Adami pertinet quam culpa. Si igitur culpa ejus mea non est reipsa, sed tantum imputatione, idem etiam de poena dicendum est.
english: You had put the same point less happily in chapter 1: this guilt belonged to one man, but the penalty is common to all. You mark a split between Adam's guilt and the penalty—guilt of one, penalty of all. Do you not see what follows? The penalty then fails to match the guilt: a guilt that is not common is avenged by a common penalty, and punishment falls on people who have no guilt.

If the penalty is everyone's and the guilt only one man's, then all but one are guiltless—how are they justly punished? If the guilt is one man's and not common, why impute it to all? Say that though it is one man's, imputation makes it common to all, and you still do not escape. What is not my guilt ought not to be imputed to me. Imputation does not make it mine so that it can then be charged; rather, because it is mine, it is charged. Otherwise the charge is false and unjust.

And if Adam's guilt is mine only by imputation, then God the Judge—I shudder to think it—made me a sinner by His act of imputing; He did not find me one. Imputation is the judge's act, not mine. Strip away imputation and I am free of that guilt; it is not mine, but was Adam's alone. So the judge—that is, God—made me sinner and guilty (see where this imputation leads, and shudder with me), and becomes the cause of my first sin and first reatus. In law Adam's penalty belongs to me no more than his guilt. If his guilt is not mine in the thing itself, but only by imputation, the same must be said of the penalty.

source_text: His ego absurdis non urgeor, qui culpam volo esse tam communem omnibus, quam poenam: communem inquam reapse, non imputatione sed propagatione, ac nobis imputari, quia intra nos est. Culpa autem illa est vitium originale nobis singulis inhaerens, quam ipsam nolo proprie loquendo poenam esse ob eas causas, quas mox aperiam cap. sequente.
english: These absurdities do not press me. I hold that the guilt is as common to all as the penalty—common in the thing itself, not by imputation but by propagation—and that it is imputed to us because it is within us. That guilt is the original vice inhering in each of us. I refuse to call that vice a penalty in the proper sense, for reasons I will open in the next chapter.

source_text: Laudo etiam haec tua verba, Quemadmodum fons infectus rivos etiam inficit, & sicut radix producit surculos secundum speciem suam, malos scilicet, si mala est, EODEM PRORSUS MODO primus homo corruptus & peccator genuit & protulit filios corruptos & peccatores. Subsumo, atqui fons infectus inficit rivos & radix mala profert malos surculos ea tantummodo lege Naturae, qua sibi quodque simile gignit. Cur igitur non idem statuis de primo homine, si nos eodem prorsus modo corruptus corruptos genuit? Si lex ista naturae sufficit ad peccati originalis propagationem ante peccatum constituta & sancita, quid est quamobrem eam dei justitiae, dei judicis sententiae imputes non sine magno meo scandalo, qui sic magnam Dei justitiae fieri injuriam queror? atque hujus te rei ipsum propagationis nomen admonere potuit: est enim propagatio opus naturae, quae suas in ea leges sequitur, Deo, ut est naturae author & conservator, leges illas suo concursu conservante & constabiliente, pendent enim ex decreto, quod ordine naturae decretum de lapsu permittendo mihi videtur antecessisse. Itaque posteriore decreto rescindi nec potuerunt, nec debuerunt.
english: I also praise these words of yours: just as a polluted spring pollutes its streams, and as a root puts out shoots after its own kind—bad shoots if the root is bad—IN EXACTLY THE SAME WAY the first man, corrupted and a sinner, begot and brought forth corrupted, sinful children.

I take that up. A polluted spring infects its streams, and a bad root yields bad shoots, only by nature's law that each thing begets its like. Why not say the same of the first man, if corrupted he begot us corrupted in exactly that way? If that natural law, already set and sanctioned before the sin, is enough to propagate original sin, why charge it to God's justice and to the sentence of God the Judge—to my great scandal, who complain that God's justice is deeply wronged? The very word "propagation" could have warned you: propagation is nature's work, following nature's laws, while God, as nature's author and conserver, keeps those laws in force by His concurrence. They hang on a decree that, in nature's order, seems to me to have come before the decree permitting the fall. A later decree neither could nor should undo them.

source_text: Placet etiam mihi valde, quod hanc labem & corruptionem in omnes homines transfusam & transmissam fuisse clare nos doceri affirmas Rom. 5. 12. 14. 15. 16. 19. quibus versibus graece & latine pro tuo more citatis, concludis haec manifeste probare primum illud hominis peccatum in omnes homines transfusum, transmissum universos infecisse, & morti addixisse. Nam si illis versibus clare docetur in omnes homines transfusa corruptio, contendo ex iisdem illis versibus nulla arte concludi posse, primum Adami peccatum actuale toti ejus posteritati proxime & immediate imputari. Id quod haec nostra disputatio, Deo favente, faciet liquidum. Interim quid est primum illud primi hominis peccatum in omnes homines transfusum & transmissum, nisi inhaerens omnibus ab ipso ortu labes & corruptio ab ea, quae fuit in Adamo, numero differens? nam, neque ejus actio, quae simul ac commissa est esse desiit, in nos transfundi, neque imputatio, extra nos in dei mente facta, transfusio & transmissio in nos dici, neque inhaerens Adamo corruptio de subjecto in subjectum eadem numero migrare potuit. Memineris igitur te primi Adae peccati nomine haereditariam corruptionem insignivisse.
english: I am also very glad you affirm we are clearly taught that this stain and corruption was poured and passed into all people (Rom. 5:12, 14–16, 19). From those verses, cited in Greek and Latin as is your way, you conclude they plainly prove that man's first sin, transfused into all, infected them all and bound them over to death.

If those verses clearly teach that corruption was transfused into all, I contend the same verses cannot by any art prove that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all his posterity proximately and immediately. God willing, this disputation will make that plain.

Meanwhile, what is that first sin of the first man poured and passed into all, if not the stain and corruption that inheres in each from birth, differing in number from the corruption that was in Adam? His act ceased as soon as it was done, so it could not be poured into us; an imputation made outside us in God's mind is not a transfusion or transmission into us; and Adam's inherent corruption could not migrate, the same in number, from one subject into another. Remember, then: under the name of Adam's first sin you yourself marked hereditary corruption.

source_text: Laudo denique quod hoc vitium, & peccatum appellas, & sic vocatum ab Apostolo agnoscis, & morti homines universos addixisse fateris, teque hortor ut in ea doctrina, quam Scriptura, & secundum scripturam Ecclesiae omnes protestantium unanimi consensu docent, perseveres constanter.
english: Finally I praise that you call this vice a sin, acknowledge the Apostle so names it, and confess it bound the whole race over to death. I urge you to hold fast to that doctrine which Scripture teaches, and which, following Scripture, all the Protestant churches teach with one consent.

source_text: CAPUT IV. Rursus quaedam observata & reprehensa in eodem Cap. II. Notavi quaedam, Reverende & dilectissime in Christo Frater, in secundo Capite Tui tractatus. Patere me etiam quaedam refellere. Dicis enim quaedam de spiraculo vitae, de ligno vitae, deque morte interminata Adamo, quae, nec probo, nec quid momenti ad id conferant, quod tu eo capite probare instituisti, satis assequor, refutata autem meam causam juvare possunt.
english: Chapter IV. Further observations and censures on the same chapter II.

I marked several points, Reverend and most beloved Brother in Christ, in the second chapter of your treatise. Allow me to answer some of them as well. You say things about the breath of life, the tree of life, and the death threatened to Adam. I neither approve those claims, nor see what they do for the thesis you set out to prove in that chapter—but once answered, they can help my case.

source_text: Rem ab ovo ut aiunt exorsus observas, Deum inspirasse homini spiraculum triplicis vitae, animalis, quae est corporis per unionem animae illud vivificantis, spiritualis, quae est animae per unionem Spiritus sancti illam sanctificantis, & beatae, quae est animae & corporis per unionem cum Deo utrumque beatum reddentis. Idque hoc uno argumento probas, quia textus hebraeus habet in plurali Numero חַיִּים vitas. Quod mihi videtur debilissimum: passim enim usurpatur plurale illud pro singulari, pro ea una vita, quam tu animalem vocas: obvia sunt exempla: vide Gen. 3. 14. & 23. 1. & 25. 7. 17. & 27. 45. Ps. 17. 14. & 31. 11. Eccles. 2. 17. & 9. 9. Et passim alibi. Immo pro ea imperfecta, qualis est brutorum ut Gen. 7. 15. 22. quibus locis etiam brutis animantibus tribuitur נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים spiraculum, ut tu loqueris, vitarum, nec tamen, opinor, alia vita quam animalis, & quidem destituta ratione.
english: Starting from the beginning, as they say, you hold that God breathed into man the breath of a threefold life: animal life of the body through the soul's union that keeps it alive; spiritual life of the soul through the Holy Spirit's union that sanctifies it; and blessed life of soul and body through union with God that beats both. Your one proof is that the Hebrew text has the plural חַיִּים, "lives."

That seems to me a very weak prop. The plural is used everywhere for the singular—for that one life you call animal. The examples lie ready: Gen. 3:14; 23:1; 25:7, 17; 27:45; Ps. 17:14; 31:11; Eccles. 2:17; 9:9; and many more. Indeed Gen. 7:15, 22 give even brute animals נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים, the "breath of lives" as you would say—and yet, I think, no life but the animal one, and that without reason.

source_text: Itaque interpretes omnes quos viderim, vitam verterunt non vitas, & vel nihil mysterii in plurali חַיִּים quaesierunt, vel putarunt eo innui eas vitas, quae ad hominis essentiam & naturam sunt absolute necessariae, vegetativam, sensitivam, & rationalem, quae Zanchii & Parei opinio est non contemnenda: quam enim formatio Corporis, tam haec quoque נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים inspiratio ad hominis fabricationem & compositionem, ac constitutionem pertinebat, ad quam etiam sanctitatem & beatitudinem, introductione Adami, postquam creatus fuit, in paradisum, auctam, libenter refero. Habebat enim se sanctitas ad animam, ut sanitas ad corpus.
english: So every interpreter I have seen rendered "life," not "lives." Either they found no mystery in the plural חַיִּים, or they took it to hint at the lives strictly needed for human essence and nature—vegetative, sensitive, and rational—which is Zanchius's and Pareus's view, and not to be scorned.

As the body's formation belonged to making and composing the human being, so did this inspiring of נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים. To that same constitution I gladly also refer sanctity and blessedness, increased when Adam, after he was made, was brought into paradise. Sanctity stood to the soul as health stands to the body.

source_text: Itaque quemadmodum in corpore non erat duplex vita, quarum altera posita esset in sanitate, sic non arbitror sanctitatem animae augere numerum vitarum, quibus praeditus fuit Adamus. Magnum enim discrimen observo inter Adami & nostram in Christo sanctitatem. Illa naturalis fuit simul cum natura humana & creata, &, nisi amissa fuisset, propaganda secundum leges naturae, ac propterea mutabilis: haec vero pendet ex dono supernaturali Spiritus Sancti a Christo capite in nos eius membra delapso, quo regeneramur, vivificamur, & veluti animamur ac regimur. Sanctitas Adami conditio erat eius vitae Adami, quam animalem appellas, sine qua creari non potuit a Deo justissimo sanctissimoque, & qua fiebat ut Adamus esset bene comparatus ad objecta naturalia. Nostra tota pendet a revelatione supernaturali, tota tendit in objectum supernaturale, nosque supra conditionem illam naturalem & animalem & mutabilem Adami longe evehit. Itaque natura divina a Petro appellatur, & imago gloriae Christi a Paulo. Sed haec obiter: nihil enim faciunt ad rem quam agimus.
english: Just as the body did not have a double life with one part seated in health, so I do not think the soul's sanctity adds to the tally of lives Adam had. I see a great gap between Adam's sanctity and ours in Christ. His was natural, created with human nature, and—had it not been lost—would have been passed on by nature's laws, and so was changeable. Ours hangs on the supernatural gift of the Holy Spirit come down from Christ the head into us his members, by which we are regenerated, made alive, and as it were animated and ruled.

Adam's sanctity was a condition of that animal life of his, as you call it—without which the most just and holy God could not have made him, and by which he was well fitted to natural objects. Ours hangs wholly on supernatural revelation, aims wholly at a supernatural object, and lifts us far above Adam's natural, animal, changeable state. So Peter calls it divine nature, and Paul the image of Christ's glory. But this is by the way; it does not touch the point in hand.

source_text: Eodem nixus plurali חַיִּים vis arborem vitae certam spem fecisse Adamo harum vitarum continuandarum. Atqui non potuit certam spem fecisse continuandae sanctitatis, in qua vitam spiritualem ponis. Hanc enim continuationem Deus ab Adamo exigebat, non ipsi promittebat: qui si eam promisisset, fecisset procul dubio Adamum impeccabilem: fuisset enim promissio ridicula, efficiam ut perseveres in sanctitate & justitia, modo ne pecces.
english: On the same plural חַיִּים you would have the tree of life give Adam a sure hope of continuing these lives. It could not give a sure hope of continuing the sanctity in which you place spiritual life. God was requiring that continuance from Adam, not promising it to him. Had He promised it, He would beyond doubt have made Adam unable to sin—for the promise would have been absurd: I will make you persevere in sanctity and justice, provided you do not sin.

source_text: Huic triplici vitae triplicem opponis privationem seu mortem denunciatam a Deo Adamo ut poenam verbis, morte morieris, asserisque hominem, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuum esse.
