At length you conclude that sin is imputed when it is attributed, considered, and held for sin and punished as sin; on the opposite side, that sin is not imputed when it is not considered as sin, but is covered, pardoned, and remitted. Which certainly is not fitted to our question.

source_text: Cum enim affirmo, peccatum actuale Adami nobis non imputari, non hoc volo peccatum illud non considerari ut peccatum, sed tegi, condonari, & remitti nobis. (vides alienam esse hanc tuam non imputandi explicationem a mea mente, & ab hac quaestione,) non quaeritur inter nos, utrum peccatum Adami nobis condonetur: talis non imputatio est a misericordia; sed quaeritur inter nos, utrum de jure, ex justitia nobis imputetur, necne? Tu proculdubio statuis non imputari, hoc est, remitti fidelibus: attamen idem contendis me adversus omnibus hominibus imputari, & quidem ita imputari, ut in omnibus puniatur actu: non quaero hoc loco quomodo ista punitio consistat cum justificatione seu remissione, & non imputatione illius peccati.
english: For when I affirm that Adam's actual sin is not imputed to us, I do not mean by this that that sin is not considered as sin, but that it is covered, pardoned, and remitted to us. (You see that this explanation of yours of 'not imputing' is alien from my mind and from this question.) It is not asked between us whether Adam's sin is forgiven us: such non-imputation is from mercy; but it is asked between us whether of right, from justice, it is imputed to us or not. You doubtless hold that it is not imputed—that is, that it is remitted to the faithful—and yet the same you contend against me is imputed to all men, and indeed so imputed that in all it is punished in act. I do not ask in this place how that punishment consists with justification or remission and the non-imputation of that sin.

source_text: Sed, quicquid sit, Contendo peccatum illud Adami actuale nostrum peccatum non esse. Itaque nobis jure imputari non posse. Fateor imputare esse tribuere, attribuere, adscribere: sed quaedam sunt hoc loco observanda, in primis distinctio illa imputationis in antecedentem & consequentem seu immediatam & mediatam, quam, dum statum quaestionis constituerem, Cap. 2. explicavi, nec hic repeto: ejus ut memineris te rogo. Deinde illud etiam cogitationi nostrae obversari debet, agi inter nos de imputatione non qualibet, sed judiciaria, quam punitio justa sequatur.
english: But, whatever the case, I contend that that actual sin of Adam is not our sin. Therefore it cannot justly be imputed to us. I grant that to impute is to ascribe, to attribute, to write to one's account: but certain things are to be observed in this place—first of all that distinction of imputation into antecedent and consequent, or immediate and mediate, which, when I was setting the state of the question, I explained in Cap. 2, and do not repeat here: I ask you to remember it. Next this also ought to meet our thought: that what is in dispute between us is not any imputation whatever, but a judicial one, which just punishment follows.

source_text: Est autem ejusmodi imputatio peccati, actus judicis sententia sua peccatum alicui tribuentis, hoc est, aliquem certi cujusdam peccati reum esse pronunciantis, ac propterea poena afficiendum. Tribuitur autem alicui peccatum vel tanquam peccatori, vel tanquam peccatoris personam ultro sustinenti, vadi: illi ut suum, huic ut alienum. Nobis si peccatum Adami actuale imputatur, tribuitur, non ut alienum, sed ut nostrum: suam enim quisque nostrum, cum concipitur & nascitur, personam, non Adami, cujus vas non est, gerit.
english: Now such an imputation of sin is the act of a judge ascribing sin to someone by his sentence—that is, pronouncing someone guilty of a certain sin, and therefore to be visited with punishment. But sin is ascribed to someone either as to a sinner, or as to one who voluntarily sustains the sinner's person, as a surety: to the former as his own, to the latter as another's. If Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, it is ascribed not as another's, but as ours: for each of us, when he is conceived and born, bears his own person, not Adam's, whose surety he is not.

source_text: Considera igitur mecum, quaeso, & perpende, quomodo nobis peccatum illud primum actuale, possit imputari vere an falso, juste an injuste? Fuit actio quaedam singularis, quae non potuit reum peragere, nisi aut imperantem, aut exequentem, aut consentientem. Eam autem neque imperavimus, aut suasimus Adamo, neque ipsi, qui non eramus, commisimus, neque ei, vel antequam essemus, vel in utero materno delitescentes actu consensimus. Dic igitur, amabo te, quomodo nobis vere & juste singulis attribuatur & adscribatur? Si respondeas, vitium illud haereditarium, quod ab illa actione productum in nos manavit, esse peccati illius veluti reliquias & semen, & habitualem, ut ita loquar, voluntatis nostrae consensum; Itaque jure nobis imputari, descendes in meam sententiam, qui imputationem mediatam, quae haereditariam corruptionem sequatur, & in ea fundata sit, ultro agnosco, & doceo.
english: Consider with me, then, I ask, and weigh how that first actual sin can be imputed to us truly or falsely, justly or unjustly. It was a certain singular action, which could not make a man guilty except as one commanding, or executing, or consenting. But we neither commanded it, nor advised Adam to it, nor ourselves—who did not yet exist—committed it, nor consented to it in act, either before we were, or while we lay hidden in the mother's womb. Tell me, then, I beg you, how it is truly and justly attributed and ascribed to each of us? If you answer that that hereditary vice, which flowed into us as produced from that action, is as it were the remnants and seed of that sin, and a habitual—so to speak—consent of our will, and that therefore it is justly imputed to us, you will come down to my opinion, who freely acknowledge and teach mediate imputation, which follows hereditary corruption and is founded in it.

source_text: CAPUT VI. Examen Cap. IV. Rursus Cap. IV. tui tractatus manum admoves statui quaestionis constituendo, expoliendo, illustrando; inque ea re totum Cap. IV. consumis. Doleo nos tamdiu detineri a te in vestibulo famelicos & appetentes tuarum rationum, ad quas percipiendas nos tui tractatus Cap. primo invitaveras. Hic tamen decet me tecum paulisper commorari, & colloqui. Quaeritur, inquis, quomodo peccatum illud actuale, quod fuit personae, sufficiat ad condemnationem omnium. Atqui prius illud oportet distinctione praesupponendum: in eo enim ipso vertitur cardo hujus controversiae: nam si hoc vis, peccatum illud actuale per se ipsum unum immediate sufficere ad condemnationem omnium hominum, id praesupponis quod versatur in quaestione, quodque ego pernego. Sin vis sufficere ad eam condemnationem mediante corruptione, quam produxit, propagata in omnes homines, tibi assentior.
english: CAPUT VI. Examination of Cap. IV. Again in Cap. IV of your treatise you set your hand to constituting, polishing, and illustrating the state of the question; and on that matter you spend the whole of Cap. IV. I am sorry that we are detained so long by you in the vestibule, hungry and eager for your reasons, to the perceiving of which Cap. I of your treatise had invited us. Yet here it becomes me to linger with you a little and converse. It is asked, you say, how that actual sin, which was of a person, suffices for the condemnation of all. But first that point must be presupposed by a distinction: for on it turns the very hinge of this controversy. If you mean that that one actual sin by itself immediately suffices for the condemnation of all men, you presuppose what is in question, and what I deny. But if you mean it suffices for that condemnation by means of the corruption which it produced, propagated into all men, I assent to you.

source_text: Sed tuam responsionem audiamus. Respondeo, inquis, omnes homines ex Adamo natos considerari tanquam unum hominem in Adamo & omnes peccasse in illo, ita ut primum peccatum, quod actualiter commisit, illis imputetur, & tribuatur, & satis sit ut habeantur pro peccatoribus, & morti adjudicentur. Licetne mihi quaerere, unde id habeas, ex Scriptura, an aliunde? nam a quo vis considerari omnes homines tanquam unum hominem, nisi a Deo? Unde igitur tibi iste mentis divinae internus actus innotuit? Tacet Scriptura, reclamat ratio.
english: But let us hear your answer. I answer, you say, that all men born from Adam are considered as one man in Adam, and all sinned in him, so that the first sin which he actually committed is imputed and ascribed to them, and it is enough that they be held for sinners and adjudged to death. May I ask whence you have that—from Scripture, or elsewhere? For by whom do you want all men to be considered as one man, if not by God? Whence, then, did that inner act of the divine mind become known to you? Scripture is silent; reason protests.

source_text: Nam quomodo omnes homines considerantur tanquam unus homo in Adamo? an quomodo dixit Porphyrius participatione speciei multos homines esse unum, unitate scilicet specifica? at id juvare non potest imputationem peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus: actiones enim sunt suppositorum, non autem generis, aut speciei: nec positis, quibus inter se distinguuntur, differentiis propriis omnes homines magis sunt Adamus, quam alius quilibet homo: continetur enim sub hominis specie Adamus haud secus quam reliqui individui homines. An vis omnes homines consideratos fuisse tanquam unum numero hominem in Adamo? nihil fingi posset falsius ista consideratione. Quid igitur tibi vis hac propositione? Ea, fateor ingenue, non intelligo quem sensum non ineptum habere possit.
english: For how are all men considered as one man in Adam? As Porphyry said—by participation of the species many men are one, that is, by specific unity? But that cannot help the imputation of Adam's actual sin to all men: for actions belong to individuals (supposits), not to genus or species; and when the proper differences by which they are distinguished among themselves are set down, all men are no more Adam than any other man whatever is: for Adam is contained under the species of man no less than the remaining individual men. Or do you mean that all men were considered as one man numerically in Adam? Nothing falser could be feigned than that consideration. What, then, do you mean by this proposition? I frankly confess I do not understand what sense not foolish it can have.

source_text: GAR. Respons. 1. omnes homines fuisse unum hominem in Adamo, non commentum recens est, sed vetus Catholicorum, ac nominatim Augustini adversus Pelagianos disputantis doctrina, quam saepius in operibus suis repetit. Sufficiat nunc unus ille locus ex Epist. 106. ad Bonifac. Quicunque ex illo uno multi in seipsis futuri erant, in illo unus homo erant. Si ab Augustino quaeras, unde id habeat, respondebit ex Apostolo se habere, ubi testatur omnes in Adamo peccasse. In Adamo peccarunt: itaque unum fuerunt in Adamo. Quod & Martyr, unus ex gravissimis Theologis, quorum auctoritatem obtendit in hoc negotio vir doctus, evidenter significavit ubi scripsit, Adamo peccante idem fuisse, ac si omnes praesentes fuissent, & cum Adamo peccavissent. PLAC. Aliud quaesivi, aliud respondet. Non enim quaesivi, unde haberet, omnes homines fuisse unum hominem in Adamo; sed unde haberet, Deum considerasse omnes homines tanquam unum hominem in Adamo, ita ut illis primum illud peccatum actuale Adami imputaverit immediate? De illa consideratione, de illo interno mentis divinae actu agebatur: de quo tamen altum in hac responsione silentium.
english: GAR. Response 1. That all men were one man in Adam is not a recent fiction, but the old doctrine of the Catholics, and namely of Augustine disputing against the Pelagians, which he often repeats in his works. Let one place from Epistle 106 to Boniface suffice for now: Whoever from that one were to be many in themselves were one man in him. If you ask Augustine whence he has it, he will answer that he has it from the Apostle, where he testifies that all sinned in Adam. They sinned in Adam: therefore they were one in Adam. Which Martyr also, one of the weightiest theologians whose authority the learned man urges in this matter, clearly signified when he wrote that Adam's sinning was the same as if all had been present and had sinned with Adam. PLAC. He answers something other than I asked. For I did not ask whence he had it that all men were one man in Adam, but whence he had it that God had considered all men as one man in Adam, so that He immediately imputed to them that first actual sin of Adam. The debate was about that consideration, about that inner act of the divine mind—on which, however, there is deep silence in this reply.

source_text: Deinde quaesivi, unde haberet, hoc est, ex qua divina Scriptura. Talis enim actus mentis divinae aliunde quam ex Dei revelatione cognosci nequit. Ille vero confugit ad Augustinum, & Martyrem, quibus talis divinus actus non est, opinor, nominatim caelitus revelatus. Tum non negavi omnes homines aliquomodo unum fuisse in Adamo, nempe unitate speciei, & originis, tantum negavi inde sequi fuisse ita a Deo tanquam unum consideratos, ut illis primum Adami peccatum actuale immediate imputaverit. Negavi etiam fuisse consideratos tanquam unum numero, seu individuum hominem. Itaque ille probat quod concedo, quod nego ne attingit quidem. GAR. 2. Cum Apostolica verba, in quo omnes peccaverunt, imputationem Adamici peccati denotent, ut est supra confirmatum: imputatio autem illa sit actus Dei declarantis omnes ob Adami peccatum reos, consequens est, ut, si ea verba significant omnes in Adamo consideratos ut unum hominem, designent eadem ratione, a Deo ita fuisse consideratos. PLAC. Nec Apostolus dixit omnes in Adamo peccavisse; Nec si id dixisset, verba illa denotarent imputationem Adami peccati, saltem immediatam, uti & supra ostendimus, & infra confirmabimus.
english: Next I asked whence he had it—that is, from what divine Scripture. For such an act of the divine mind cannot be known from elsewhere than from God's revelation. But he flees to Augustine and Martyr, to whom such a divine act was not, I think, revealed from heaven by name. Then I did not deny that all men were somehow one in Adam—namely by unity of species and of origin; I only denied that it follows from that that they were so considered by God as one that He immediately imputed to them Adam's first actual sin. I also denied that they were considered as one numerically, or as an individual man. Therefore he proves what I concede; what I deny he does not even touch. GAR. 2. Since the Apostolic words 'in whom all sinned' denote the imputation of Adam's sin, as was confirmed above, and that imputation is an act of God declaring all guilty on account of Adam's sin, it follows that if those words signify that all were considered in Adam as one man, they designate by the same reason that they were so considered by God. PLAC. Neither did the Apostle say that all sinned in Adam; nor, if he had said it, would those words denote the imputation of Adam's sin, at least not immediate, as we both showed above and will confirm below.

source_text: GAR. 3. Unus homo dicuntur omnes in Adamo fuisse, non unitate vel specifica, vel numerica, sed tum unitate originis; quia omnes ex uno sunt sanguine, Actor. XVII. 26. & omnis homo terrenus nihil est origine, nisi Adam, ut loquitur Augustinus Retract. Lib. 1. cap. 13. Tum unitate repraesentationis: ab uno enim Adamo sunt omnes repraesentati, quia unus Adamus omnium personam sustinebat, ut & Theologi consentienter docent, & non diffitetur Clariss. Amyraldus Thesib. de trib. foeder. Thes. 8. Ex illa duplici unitate colligitur peccati Adae imputatio. PLAC. Agnosco unitatem originis: quanquam aliud est omnes homines esse unum hominem, aut considerari tanquam unum hominem, aliud omnium hominum esse unam originem, hoc est, stirpem, seu principium. Hoc ex unitate originis sequitur, non illud. Sed unitatem repraesentationis probari mihi e Scriptura cupio, ut & illud quod affertur probationis loco, unum Adamum peccando omnium hominum personam sustinuisse. Hoc enim ipsum unde habeatur, scire aveo. Ponitur enim a quibusdam, sed probatur a nemine.
english: GAR. 3. All are said to have been one man in Adam not by specific or numeric unity, but by unity of origin—because all are of one blood, Acts 17:26, and every earthly man is by origin nothing but Adam, as Augustine speaks, Retractations Book 1, chapter 13—and by unity of representation: for by one Adam all were represented, because one Adam sustained the person of all, as theologians also teach with one consent, and as the most distinguished Amyraut does not deny in the Theses on the three covenants, Thesis 8. From that double unity the imputation of Adam's sin is gathered. PLAC. I acknowledge unity of origin—although it is one thing for all men to be one man, or to be considered as one man, and another for all men to have one origin, that is, stock or principle. The latter follows from unity of origin, not the former. But I desire unity of representation to be proved to me from Scripture, and likewise that which is brought forward in place of proof, that one Adam by sinning sustained the person of all men. For I long to know whence that very thing is had. It is posited by some, but proved by no one.

source_text: Idne igitur revelavit Deus in Scriptura? Proferatur locus. Potestne ex natura colligi? adferatur ratio. Affirmanti enim aliquid ejusmodi, praeter naturae & Scripturae librum assentiri nec teneor, nec expedit. Nec vero id ex Augustini aut Clariss. Amyraldi verbis colligi potest. Quae enim consequentia, omnis homo nihil est origine nisi Adam. Ergo omnes homines fuerunt a Deo considerati tanquam unus homo in Adam. Vel, Ergo Adamus in peccando sustinebat omnium hominum personam? Quod ait Vir Doctus, naturalem conjunctionem idoneam causam esse posse, cur aliquis pro alterius crimine poenis subjaceat, verum non est in foro divino; nisi aut sit etiam inter eos conjunctio peccati, aut saltem sit in eo, qui punitur, peccatum dignum illa poena, aut sit ipse peccatorum vas. Quod subjungit, propter unitatem repraesentationis, Adamo peccante idem fuisse, ac si omnes peccatum commisissent, probatione eget. Non enim quicquid facit qui alterum repraesentat, huic continuo sive consentiat, sive non consentiat, imputandum est. Pepigit Deus foedus cum genere humano in Noacho, & cum Israelitis in Abrahamo, neutrius tamen, opinor, aut bona opera aut peccata posteris imputata sunt.
english: Did God then reveal it in Scripture? Let the place be produced. Can it be gathered from nature? Let a reason be adduced. For to one affirming something of that kind I am neither bound nor is it expedient to assent beyond the book of nature and of Scripture. Nor indeed can it be gathered from the words of Augustine or of the most distinguished Amyraut. For what consequence is this: every man is by origin nothing but Adam—therefore all men were considered by God as one man in Adam—or, therefore Adam in sinning sustained the person of all men? What the learned man says, that a natural conjunction can be a fit cause why someone should undergo penalties for another's crime, is not true in the divine forum, unless there is also between them a conjunction of sin, or at least in the one who is punished a sin worthy of that penalty, or he himself is a vessel of sins. What he subjoins, that because of unity of representation Adam's sinning was the same as if all had committed the sin, needs proof. For not whatever one who represents another does is at once to be imputed to that other, whether he consents or does not consent. God struck a covenant with the human race in Noah, and with the Israelites in Abraham; yet of neither, I think, were good works or sins imputed to their posterity.

source_text: GAR. 4. Imputatio primi peccati colligitur non ex eo simpliciter, quod omnes sunt ab Adamo oriundi, sed ex eo quod ita docemur ab Apostolo Roman. v. ut audivimus, & quod per peccatum illud excussit Adamus gratiam omnem foederis illius primarii, quod in ipso cum omnibus hominibus initum fuerat, ut saepius dictum. PLAC. Non docemur ab Apostolo Rom. 5. imputationem immediatam primi peccati. Id hactenus neque vir doctus, neque alius quisquam probavit, ut partim ex dictis, partim ex dicendis cernere est. Addit alteram rationem, sed eam non intelligo. Velim enim mihi exponi quale foedus in Adamo cum omnibus hominibus initum intelligat. Nam si ea fuisse conditione censet, ut, si peccaret Adamus, imputaretur ejus primum peccatum actuale omnibus ejus posteris immediate; id foedus adferendum non fuit ad probandam imputationem immediatam. Non enim minus in quaestione versatur quam illa ipsa imputatio: deque eo merito quaeri potest, undenam habeatur? Ex naturae inspectione? An ex divina per Scripturam revelatione? Aliunde enim si habetur, ob id ipsum rejici debet.
english: GAR. 4. The imputation of the first sin is gathered not simply from the fact that all are sprung from Adam, but from this: that we are so taught by the Apostle in Romans 5, as we have heard, and that by that sin Adam shook off all the grace of that primary covenant which had been struck in him with all men, as has often been said. PLAC. We are not taught by the Apostle in Rom. 5 the immediate imputation of the first sin. That neither the learned man nor anyone else has thus far proved, as may be seen partly from what has been said and partly from what is to be said. He adds another reason, but I do not understand it. For I would have him explain to me what covenant struck in Adam with all men he understands. For if he judges it to have been on this condition, that if Adam sinned his first actual sin would be immediately imputed to all his posterity, that covenant ought not to have been brought forward to prove immediate imputation. For it is no less in question than that imputation itself; and concerning it one may rightly ask whence it is had. From inspection of nature? Or from divine revelation through Scripture? For if it is had from elsewhere, for that very reason it ought to be rejected.

source_text: Visne omnes homines considerari ut unam rempublicam, unum corpus, cujus caput sit Adamus, reliqui autem homines singuli membra? Fuit igitur Adamus caput sine corpore, ut nos hodie membra sine capite. GAR. Hoc rationis genus, si L. Crasso venisset in mentem ea dissertatione quam habuit cum Q. Mutio Scaevola apud Tullium lib. 1. de Oratore, non poterat ille plausibili argumento dictum Scaevolae traducere, Socratem vocantis fontem & caput Philosophorum, qui longa serie post exemptum humanis Socratem in Graecia floruerunt: nimirum, quia & Socrates ante natos illos Philosophos fons fuisset sine rivulis, & caput sine membris; & illi post Socratem Philosophi, rivi fuissent absque fonte, & membra sine capite.
english: Do you want all men to be considered as one republic, one body, whose head is Adam, and the remaining men each members? Then Adam was a head without a body, as we today are members without a head. GAR. This kind of reasoning, if it had come into L. Crassus's mind in that dissertation which he held with Q. Mucius Scaevola in Cicero, On the Orator, book 1, he could not by a plausible argument have turned aside Scaevola's saying that calls Socrates the fountain and head of the philosophers who in a long series flourished in Greece after Socrates was removed from human affairs—namely, because Socrates before those philosophers were born would have been a fountain without streams and a head without members; and those philosophers after Socrates would have been streams without a fountain and members without a head.

source_text: PLAC. Egregiam refutationem! Agebatur de Adamo relatè ad id tempus, quo primum peccavit, diu antequam nobis gignendis operam daret. Dixi eum tunc nondum fuisse caput nostrum, quomodo exercitus caput est dux, reipublicae magistratus, regni rex: quia caput fuisset sine membris. Num eo sensu Socratem Scaevola fontem & caput appellavit? Num ejus temporis respectu, cum nondum ullus esset ejus auditor, ullusve alius praeter eum philosophus? Num propterea aliqua Socratis actio omnibus aliis philosophis imputari immediate potuit aut debuit? Nihil quicquam a Socrate in sequentes philosophos imputatione descendit. GAR. Atqui si rem serio agimus, quidni vulgatissimam distinctionem in memoriam revocamus, ut caput proprie dictum discernatur ab improprie dicto, id est, physicum a morali? Nam in physico certe capite, quod natura suis nervis & vinculis cum reliquo corpore colligavit, ita res habet, ut neque caput dicetur, nisi cum adsunt membra; neque membra του παντός vocentur, nisi quae actu cum capite conjuncta sunt. At vero cum Adamum dicunt Theologi esse generis humani caput, impropriam sine dubio significationem usurpant, ut denotent originem esse & principium seminale generis humani, unde scilicet humana natura sumpserit initium. Quomodo scilicet Abrahamus Judaicae gentis caput dicitur.
english: PLAC. An excellent refutation! The discussion concerned Adam with reference to that time when he first sinned, long before he set himself to begetting us. I said that he was not yet then our head, as a general is head of an army, a magistrate of a republic, a king of a kingdom—because he would have been a head without members. Did Scaevola call Socrates fountain and head in that sense? With respect to that time, when there was not yet any hearer of his, nor any other philosopher besides him? Could or ought some action of Socrates therefore to be immediately imputed to all other philosophers? Nothing whatever descended from Socrates to the following philosophers by imputation. GAR. But if we treat the matter seriously, why should we not recall the most common distinction, so that head properly so called may be discerned from that improperly so called—that is, the physical from the moral? For in a physical head, which nature has bound by its nerves and ties with the rest of the body, the matter stands so that neither will it be called a head unless members are present, nor will members of the whole be so called unless they are actually joined with the head. But when theologians say Adam is the head of the human race, they without doubt use an improper signification, to denote that he is the origin and seminal principle of the human race, from which of course human nature took its beginning. Just as Abraham is called the head of the Jewish people.

source_text: PLAC. Putavitne Vir Doctus me ita insanivisse ut caput proprie dictum intellexerim, qui disertis verbis dixi corpus improprie dictum, seu morale, tanquam rempublicam? Manifestum enim est rempublicam non esse corpus physicum: Et tamen, quamvis natura rempublicam cum capite suo rege, vel magistratu non colligaverit nervis & vinculis, nemo dixerit hominem tunc fuisse caput reipublicae, cum ipse viveret privatus, nondum nata republica: neque respublica quae nunc est corpus dicetur illius principis, qui ante centum aut mille annos desiit esse in vivis. Tale caput, tale corpus politicum intellexi. Nam alioqui non nego, neque negavi unquam, quin sit Adamus caput generis humani eo sensu quem Vir doctus hoc loco exponit. Sed quid ad immediatam imputationem peccati Adamici facit ista capitis ratio? An sic caput fuit Adamus duntaxat dum peccavit? An propterea quod Abrahamus gentis Judaicae caput fuit, eo modo ejus aliqua actio omnibus & singulis Judaeis imputatur?
english: PLAC. Did the learned man think I had so lost my mind as to understand a head properly so called, when I said in express words an improperly so called, or moral, body, as a republic? For it is plain that a republic is not a physical body. And yet, although nature has not bound a republic to its kingly or magisterial head by nerves and ties, no one would say that a man was then head of the republic when he himself lived as a private person, the republic not yet born; nor will the republic which now is be called the body of that prince who a hundred or a thousand years ago ceased to be among the living. Such a head, such a political body, I understood. For otherwise I do not deny, nor have I ever denied, that Adam is the head of the human race in that sense which the learned man explains in this place. But what does that account of the head do for the immediate imputation of Adam's sin? Was Adam head in that way only while he sinned? Or because Abraham was head of the Jewish people, is some action of his in that way imputed to all and each of the Jews?

source_text: Et omnia peccata Adami nobis, nostra vicissim omnia Adamo imputari debuerunt; par enim est ratio: conveniunt enim toti corpori & quae capitis, & quae aliorum membrorum sunt. Me etiam perturbant ista verba, considerantur tanquam unus homo in Adamo; videris enim illum unum hominem ab Adamo distinguere. Porro quaecunque illa consideratio fuerit, cum ea extra nos esset, nec quicquam vel in Adamo, vel in nobis poneret, capere animo non possum, quid ad hoc contulerit, ut nos revera commiserimus peccatum illud actuale Adami tanto ante quam essemus. Adde quod si committente alia peccata Adamo perduravit, quid est quamobrem illa quoque nobis pariter non imputentur? Sin dum solum primum illud admitteret, obtinuit, mirabor, aut desiisse nos esse in Adamo confestim post primum illud peccatum admissum, aut, quamvis in eo ut antea essemus, non fuisse tamen amplius consideratos tanquam unum hominem in ipso. Subjicis nos peccasse in Adamo. Vide quam non sim difficilis, tibi id concedo, modo hoc etiam mihi concedas nos eo modo peccasse in Adamo, quo in eo fuimus. In eo autem fuimus, non quia ejus esse nobis imputetur, aut sit causa meritoria cur sumus, sed quia nos propagatione naturali per intermedios nostros parentes genuit: Eodem modo nos in eo peccasse confiteor, quia peccatum ejus nostrum peccatum longa propagationum serie procreavit.
english: And all Adam's sins ought to have been imputed to us, and all ours in turn to Adam; for the reason is equal: for what belongs to the head and what belongs to the other members suit the whole body. Those words also disturb me—'they are considered as one man in Adam'; for you seem to distinguish that one man from Adam. Further, whatever that consideration was, since it was outside us and put nothing either in Adam or in us, I cannot grasp in mind what it contributed to this—that we truly committed that actual sin of Adam so long before we existed. Add that if it endured while Adam was committing other sins, why are those also not equally imputed to us? But if it obtained only while he admitted that first one, I shall marvel either that we ceased to be in Adam immediately after that first sin was admitted, or that, although we were in him as before, we were nevertheless no longer considered as one man in him. You subjoin that we sinned in Adam. See how little difficult I am: I grant you that, provided you also grant me that we sinned in Adam in the same way in which we were in him. Now we were in him not because his being is imputed to us, or is a meritorious cause why we exist, but because by natural propagation through our intermediate parents he begot us. In the same way I confess that we sinned in him, because his sin by a long series of propagations begot our sin.

source_text: Caeterum hanc tuam responsionem interrogationibus firmas. Nam, inquis, qui potest aliter reddi ratio hujus infectionis & reatus? cur quaeso Adam peccando perdidit, & morti subjecit, non tantum personam, sed etiam totam naturam humanam? Cum caeteri homines peccatis suis actualibus laedant personas, & se mortis reos efficiant. Qui potest nobis peccatum actuale juste imputari, quod neque fecimus ipsi, neque jussimus, neque suasimus, neque ullo voluntatis nostrae consensu probavimus, quodque nostro respectu nullo modo voluntarium fuit? Horumne tu rationem reddere potes? Annon igitur satius esset propagationem corruptionis inhaerentis & reatus qui eam sequitur, docente Scriptura, contestante experientia, firmiter credere; modum autem quem non capis Deo permittere, quam praeter & contra Scripturam imputationem excogitare aeque, aut magis difficilem captu, ac Dei justitiam pervertentem, & maculantem?
english: For the rest, you shore up this answer of yours with questions. For, you say, who can otherwise give the reason of this infection and guilt? Why, I ask, did Adam by sinning destroy and subject to death not only a person but also the whole human nature—whereas other men by their actual sins wound persons and make themselves liable to death? How can an actual sin be justly imputed to us which we ourselves neither did, nor ordered, nor advised, nor approved by any consent of our will, and which with respect to us was in no way voluntary? Can you give the reason of these things? Would it not then be better firmly to believe the propagation of inherent corruption and of the guilt which follows it—Scripture teaching, experience bearing witness—and to leave to God the mode which you do not grasp, than beside and against Scripture to invent an imputation equally, or more, hard to grasp, and one that perverts and stains the justice of God?

source_text: Subjungis hoc cogit nos fateri, primum illud Adami peccatum fuisse alio modo consideratum, & justo Dei judicio imputatum, & adscriptum toti naturae humanae. Mallem fateri meam ignorantiam: neque hujus confessionis me puderet: caecum enim esse arbitror qui non sentit se multo plura quam scit ignorare. Quam multa sunt in natura, quorum rationes cur sic fiant reddere nequimus? Satius mea sententia id esset, quam in Dei arcanam mentem irrumpentes, ei considerationem & judicium sine ulla revelatione tribuere, quod forte nec fuit, nec eum decet. Nosti enim illud Esai. 55. cogitationes meae non sunt ut cogitationes vestrae. Quam alti sunt coeli supra terram, tam altae sunt cogitationes meae supra cogitationes vestras: Et illud, quis novit mentem Domini?
english: You subjoin that this compels us to confess that that first sin of Adam was considered in another way, and by God's just judgment imputed and ascribed to the whole human nature. I would rather confess my ignorance; nor would I be ashamed of this confession: for I judge him blind who does not feel that he is ignorant of far more than he knows. How many things there are in nature whose reasons why they happen so we cannot give? Better that, in my judgment, than bursting into God's secret mind and ascribing to Him without any revelation a consideration and judgment which perhaps neither was nor becomes Him. For you know that word of Isaiah 55: my thoughts are not as your thoughts. As the heavens are high above the earth, so high are my thoughts above your thoughts. And that: who has known the mind of the Lord?

source_text: GAR. Hic vero inprimis ego quoque profiteor, malle me credere, hanc non esse affectatam ignorantiam, de qua dicunt illi apud Jobum cap. 21. 14. Recede a nobis, scientiam viarum tuarum nolumus, quam sinistram aliquam de Viro docto opinionem fovere. PLAC. Ecquam quaeso verbis illis sinistram de me opinionem fovendi ansam praebui, aut quid est in mea ista modesta & religiosa ignorantia, qua nolo sapere praeter Scripturam, simile abominandae illorum apud Jobum sceleratorum impietati?
english: GAR. Here indeed I also first profess that I prefer to believe that this is not the affected ignorance of which those speak in Job chapter 21 verse 14—'Depart from us; we do not want the knowledge of your ways'—rather than to foster some sinister opinion of the learned man. PLAC. What handle, I ask, did I give by those words for fostering a sinister opinion of me, or what is there in this modest and religious ignorance of mine, by which I refuse to be wise beyond Scripture, like to the abominable impiety of those criminals in Job?

source_text: GAR. Miror solum, qua ratione ductus, eos arbitretur in arcanam Dei mentem irrumpere, qui corruptionis Originalis, & omnium poenarum in posteros ab ipsa nativitate incumbentium causam quaerunt in imputatione, adeoque participatione primi peccati; cum non ignoret veteres & Recentiores Theologos, hoc & docere, & profiteri se hausisse ex Apostoli doctrina Roman. v. Sicut postea frequentissimis testimoniis probabitur. Hos omnes gravissima accusatione urgere, quasi in arcanam Dei mentem temerario ausu irrumpentes, & limites illos transeuntes, quos Deus homini praestituit Deuter. XXIX. 29. nescio an fideciore satis consentaneum sit. PLAC. Primum agebatur de eo Dei actu interno, quo dicebatur Deus omnes homines considerasse tanquam unum hominem in Adamo. Idne veteres & Recentiores Theologi dixerunt? Idne colligi potest ex Apostoli doctrina Roman. v? Attulitne Vir doctus frequentissima testimonia ut id probaret? Tribuere Deo considerationem, actum quendam mentis & voluntatis internum praeter Scripturam, praeter rationem, quid est irrumpere in arcanam Dei mentem, si hoc non est?
english: GAR. I only marvel by what reason he judges that those who seek the cause of original corruption, and of all the penalties lying upon posterity from birth itself, in the imputation—and so the participation—of the first sin are bursting into God's secret mind, when he is not unaware that older and more recent theologians both teach this and profess that they drew it from the Apostle's doctrine in Romans 5, as will afterward be proved by most frequent testimonies. To press all these with so grave an accusation, as if by rash daring bursting into God's secret mind and crossing those limits which God set for man in Deuteronomy 29:29—I do not know whether it is sufficiently agreeable to faithfulness. PLAC. First the debate was about that inward act of God by which God was said to have considered all men as one man in Adam. Did the older and more recent theologians say that? Can that be gathered from the Apostle's doctrine in Romans 5? Did the learned man bring most frequent testimonies to prove it? To ascribe to God a consideration—a certain inward act of mind and will—beyond Scripture, beyond reason: what is it to burst into God's secret mind, if this is not?

source_text: Idem, fateor, de immediata illa imputatione, in qua causa quaeritur originalis corruptionis, dici potest, si quidem ex sacris literis colligi nequit. Est enim ipsa quoque internus divinae mentis & voluntatis actus. Frustra me praejudiciis gravat; frustra Theologorum in me animos irritat: neque enim eos accuso, sed fraterne moneo, ut caveant sibi ab hoc scopulo. Humanum enim est errare, sed monitum in errore perseverare, turpe admodum, & periculosum est. Miror autem Theologos Reformatos talibus uti adversus fratres suos praejudiciis, quibus olim, & hoc tempore nihil veritati cognoscendae magis obstitit. Non enim quod hic, aut ille docuit, regula est fidei nostrae, sed id tantum, quod unicus noster doctor per suos Apostolos & Prophetas docuit. Illam autem imputationem neque Scriptura, neque plerique veteres Theologi, neque recentiores quidam agni nominis docuerunt: Et quosdam ipse contra se Vir doctus laudat. Exemplo sit Ludovicus Lavaterus insignis Theologus Tigurinus (unum enim attulisse exemplum sufficiet hoc loco) cujus haec verba ex Comm. in 2. Paralip. 25. citat cap. XVIII. pag. 629. Quisque scelerum suorum poenas luat. Hac lege Deus non obstringitur. Juste enim punit in omnibus hominibus peccatum primorum parentum, quod vitio originis sit cuique proprium. Quid potest magis opponi doctrinae Viri docti, passim affirmantis, peccatum primorum parentum nonnisi imputatione fieri nostrum?
english: The same, I confess, can be said of that immediate imputation in which the cause of original corruption is sought, if indeed it cannot be gathered from the sacred letters. For that too is an inward act of the divine mind and will. In vain he loads me with prejudices; in vain he stirs up the minds of theologians against me: for I do not accuse them, but brotherly warn them to beware this reef for themselves. For it is human to err, but to persist in error when warned is very shameful and dangerous. And I marvel that Reformed theologians use against their own brothers such prejudices as once, and in this time, have more than anything hindered the knowing of the truth. For not what this man or that taught is the rule of our faith, but only that which our one Teacher taught through His Apostles and Prophets. But that imputation neither Scripture, nor most of the older theologians, nor certain more recent ones of fair name taught: and some the learned man himself praises against himself. Let Ludovicus Lavater, the distinguished Zurich theologian, be an example (for to have brought one example will suffice in this place), whose these words from the Commentary on 2 Chronicles 25 he cites at Cap. XVIII, page 629: Let each pay the penalties of his own crimes. God is not bound by this law. For He justly punishes in all men the sin of the first parents, which by the vice of origin is each one's own. What can more oppose the doctrine of the learned man, who everywhere affirms that the sin of the first parents becomes ours only by imputation?

source_text: Quid si quaeram ex te rationem, cur primum illud Prorsus enim me fugit. Quanquam tu ultro nec rogatus videris reddere voluisse, addis enim haec verba, quia sc. Adam fuit primus homo, origo & stirps, seu radix omnium hominum. Agnosco, hinc intelligo potuisse una cum natura humana suum propagare vitium in posteros: at nego propterea ejus peccatum actuale nostrum fuisse, aut nobis debuisse imputari: nego inde considerationem illam & judicium, quod tu Deo tribuis, posse confici. Ego non video, quomodo peccatum illud actuale Adami, actio illa singularis magis nostra actio, nostrum peccatum fuerit, quam ejus persona fuit nostra persona. Si id vides, ostende quaeso mihi & explica: magnam tibi habebo gratiam.
english: What if I ask of you the reason why that first— for it wholly escapes me. Although you seem of your own accord, unasked, to have wished to give a reason, for you add these words: because, namely, Adam was the first man, the origin and stock, or root, of all men. I acknowledge it; from this I understand that he could, together with human nature, propagate his vice into posterity: but I deny that therefore his actual sin was ours, or ought to have been imputed to us; I deny that from that the consideration and judgment which you ascribe to God can be made out. I do not see how that actual sin of Adam, that singular action, was more our action, our sin, than his person was our person. If you see that, show it to me, I beg, and explain: I will hold great gratitude to you.

source_text: GAR. Huic ergo primae inobedientiae, non quidem praecise sumptae, sed una cum corruptione quam effecit in Adamo nobis imputatur, sicut supra vir doctus agnoscebat, erit sane etiam per eam imputationem nostra. Quidni ergo & Adami persona nobis imputetur, & dicatur etiam fuisse persona nostra? Aut hoc vir doctus concedat, aut suam argumentandi rationem condemnet & eliminet: & fateatur quod res est, nunquam auditum alienas personas imputari, sed actionum imputationem rem esse omnium ore atque sermone tritam, &c. PLAC. Quo sensu dixerim, & quam is minime causae quam ago obsit, actionem illam primam inobedientiae cum corruptione quam peperit nobis imputari, supra expositum est pag. 162. 163. Quod inde colligit, illam actionem etiam per eam imputationem nostram esse; non agnosco. Nam corruptio nostra est, quia in nos propagata est. Actio autem illa nostra fit non imputatione, sed, ut dicebat Lavaterus, vitio originis: quia nempe vitium originis seu corruptio est inobedientiae illius communicatio, & habitualis in eam consension: itaque non est nostra, quia nobis imputatur; sed contra nobis imputatur, quia nostra est.
english: GAR. To this first disobedience, then—not indeed taken precisely by itself, but together with the corruption which it effected in Adam—is imputed to us, as the learned man above acknowledged; it will indeed also be ours through that imputation. Why then should not Adam's person also be imputed to us, and be said also to have been our person? Let the learned man either grant this, or condemn and eliminate his way of arguing: and confess what the fact is—it was never heard that alien persons are imputed, but that the imputation of actions is a thing worn in everyone's mouth and speech, etc. PLAC. In what sense I said—and how little that hinders the cause I am pleading—that that first action of disobedience with the corruption which it bore is imputed to us, was set out above at pages 162–163. What he gathers from that, that that action is ours also through that imputation, I do not acknowledge. For the corruption is ours because it was propagated into us. But that action becomes ours not by imputation, but, as Lavater said, by the vice of origin: because of course the vice of origin or corruption is the communication of that disobedience, and a habitual consent to it; and so it is not ours because it is imputed to us; but on the contrary it is imputed to us because it is ours.

source_text: Certe Chamierus negavit actionem illam Adami esse nostram actionem, lib. 1. de hom. corrupt. c. 8. § 9. Dico, inquit, nullum peccatum unum numero posse esse commune omnibus hominibus. Nam peccatum, vel qualitas est, vel actio. Qualitas, ut peccatum originale. Actio, ut peccatum quodlibet actuale. At nulla qualitas, una eademque numero potest pluribus subjectis communicari: ut candor qui est in nive, idem numero non potest esse in cygno, aut lana. Actiones autem sunt suppositorum. Quare idem homicidium a Caino patratum non potest esse a Lamecho. Itaque nego peccatum illud Adami esse peccatum Originale. Non enim potest omnibus esse commune, sive numero, quia est actio: sive specie, quia est individuus actus. Et rursus eodem capite § 11. Omne peccatum vel qualitas est, vel actio, ut diximus, eius cujus dicitur peccatum. At hic actus Adami, neque qualitas est nostra: nam ne est quidem: ac proinde non potest esse qualitas: tum actio, qualitasque longe differunt: neque est etiam actus noster: quia idem numero actus non est variorum suppositorum. Ergo is actus Adami non est nostrum peccatum: nedum sit nostrum originale. Haec eius ratio eadem est cum hac mea, si actio Adami est nostra, eius suppositum est nostrum: Sunt enim actiones suppositorum.
english: Certainly Chamier denied that that action of Adam is our action, book 1 On the corruption of man, chapter 8, § 9. I say, he says, that no sin one in number can be common to all men. For sin is either a quality or an action. A quality, as original sin. An action, as any actual sin whatever. But no quality, one and the same in number, can be communicated to several subjects: as the whiteness which is in snow cannot be the same in number in a swan, or in wool. But actions are of individuals (supposits). Therefore the same homicide perpetrated by Cain cannot be by Lamech. Therefore I deny that that sin of Adam is Original sin. For it cannot be common to all, whether by number, because it is an action: or by species, because it is an individual act. And again in the same chapter § 11. Every sin is either a quality or an action, as we have said, of him of whom it is called a sin. But this act of Adam is neither a quality of ours: for it does not even exist: and therefore it cannot be a quality: then action and quality differ widely: nor is it even our act: because the same act in number is not of various subjects. Therefore that act of Adam is not our sin: much less is it our original. This reason of his is the same as this of mine: if Adam's action is ours, his subject is ours: for actions are of subjects.

source_text: Justitia enim non modo non exigit, sed ne patitur quidem, ut judiciaria imputatione peccatum fiat eius peccatum, cujus alioqui peccatum non fuisset. Faceret enim peccatorem judex, alioqui non peccatorem, id quod cum judicis officio pugnat, ut quod maxime. Itaque frustra observat vir doctus alienas personas non imputari, sed actiones. Non enim sic argumentabar; si actio Adami nobis imputatur, etiam nobis imputatur eius persona: Sed contendebam nullam reddi posse causam idoneam, cur illa actio nobis imputetur immediate; ac inter caeteras hanc excludebam, nostram esse actionem illam Adami: ac proinde nobis jure imputari. Intelligebatur igitur esse nostra, non per imputationem immediatam, sed ante illam: quo modo dici non potest, cur magis nostra sit, quam ipsa persona Adami. Non igitur id quod dixi vir doctus oppugnat, sed aliud quid.
english: For justice not only does not require, but does not even suffer, that by judicial imputation a sin should become the sin of him whose sin it would otherwise not have been. For the judge would make a sinner of one otherwise not a sinner—which conflicts with the judge's office as much as anything can. Therefore the learned man observes in vain that alien persons are not imputed, but actions. For I was not arguing thus: if Adam's action is imputed to us, his person also is imputed to us. But I was contending that no fit cause can be given why that action should be imputed to us immediately; and among the rest I was excluding this—that that action of Adam is ours, and therefore is justly imputed to us. It was understood, then, to be ours not through immediate imputation, but before it: in which way it cannot be said why it is more ours than Adam's person itself. Therefore it is not what I said that the learned man attacks, but something else.

source_text: Interim quaero dum alia peccata committeret (commisisse enim haud dubie non negabis) an non fuerit etiam tum primus homo, origo, stirps, seu radix omnium hominum? Fuisse proculdubio concedas: fueruntne igitur ea quoque eodem modo considerata, & justo Dei judicio omnibus hominibus imputata? Si negas, fatearis oportet hujus considerationis judicii & imputationis primi peccati, quam protulisti in medium, rationem hanc non esse, quia Adam primus homo fuit, & origo, & stirps omnium hominum. Si affirmas, Revincet te Apostolus Rom. v. tam unitatem peccati quam hominis unitatem inculcans. Quaererem etiam libenter de Setho, de Noacho, aliisque ejusmodi stirpibus totius, quod extat, generis humani, num eorum quoque peccata eodem modo fuerint & considerata, & imputata posteris? Si fuerunt, multos homines dicere debuit Apostolus Rom. v. non unum, &, nos antequam nascamur miserrimi, qui tot peccata commisimus. Si non fuerunt, discriminis peto rationem: sed vereor ne sim longior hoc loco quam necesse est.
english: Meanwhile I ask: while he was committing other sins (for you will scarcely deny that he committed them), was he not even then the first man, the origin, stock, or root of all men? That he was, you will doubtless grant: were those also, then, considered in the same way, and by God's just judgment imputed to all men? If you deny, you must confess that this reason of the consideration, judgment, and imputation of the first sin which you brought forward is not this—because Adam was the first man, and the origin and stock of all men. If you affirm, the Apostle in Romans 5 will refute you, inculcating the unity of the sin as much as the unity of the man. I would also gladly ask about Seth, about Noah, and other such stocks of the whole human race that remains, whether their sins also were in the same way both considered and imputed to posterity. If they were, the Apostle in Romans 5 ought to have said many men, not one, and we, before we are born, are most wretched, who have committed so many sins. If they were not, I ask the reason of the distinction: but I fear I may be longer in this place than is necessary.

source_text: GAR. Quod vero docent Theologi Adamum peccasse ut caput hominum, & jure posteris imputari primam illam eius inobedientiam, variis quaestionum & erotematum machinis quatit, quibus & alii nonnulla etiam addunt, quae omnia hic in unum fasciculum compingemus. PLAC. Nec Adamo elogium capitis hominum detraho, nec jure posteris imputari primam illam eius inobedientiam nego, si imputari intelligatur mediante corruptione ex ipsa in nos propagata. Tantum nego ita Adamum ut caput hominum peccasse, ut nobis possit, aut debeat prima eius inobedientia imputari immediate. Sunt autem hae quaestiones partim e Thesibus meis, partim ex hoc posteriore Manuscripto omnes, praeter unam, excerptae. Itaque non omnes sunt hujus loci; non erit tamen inutile eas hoc loco a responsionibus viri docti tutas praestare: quoniam in illis de causa agitur, ob quam peccatum illud immediate dicitur imputari; cui investigandae hoc caput destinatum est.
english: GAR. But what the theologians teach—that Adam sinned as the head of men, and that that first disobedience of his is rightly imputed to posterity—he shakes with various engines of questions and erotemata, to which others also add some things, all of which we will here bind into one fascicle. PLAC. Neither do I strip Adam of the title of head of men, nor do I deny that that first disobedience of his is rightly imputed to posterity, if it is understood to be imputed by means of the corruption propagated from it into us. I only deny that Adam so sinned as the head of men that his first disobedience can or ought to be imputed to us immediately. Now these questions are all excerpted partly from my Theses, partly from this later Manuscript, except one. Therefore not all are of this place; yet it will not be useless to keep them safe in this place from the learned man's replies: since in them the debate is about the cause on account of which that sin is said to be immediately imputed—to the investigating of which this chapter is destined.

source_text: GAR. 1. Si peccavit ut caput generis humani, cur non etiam puniri debuit eo nomine? 2. Cur potius Adami peccatum posteris, quam posterorum Adae imputatur? 3. Cum Adamus post illud peccatum, confestim non desierit esse caput, cur non sequentia Adami peccata aeque posteris imputantur atque primum? 4. Cur potius actuale peccatum, quod est actio transiens, imputari dicitur, quam habituale, quod fuit vitium permanens? 5. Si primus actus peccandi fuit actus naturae, cur non etiam primus actus generandi? Nemo tamen dixerit nos in Adamo Cainum aut Sethum genuisse. 6. Si ut Christi justitia nobis imputatur, ita & peccatum Adae nostrum est imputatione, cur non, ut Christus dicitur, justitia nostra, dicitur etiam Adamus peccatum nostrum? 7. Cum dicimur peccasse in Adamo, estne propria, an impropria locutio? Propria dici non potest, nisi dicamus, aliquid simul esse & non esse: proprie enim loquendo, tum cum Adamus peccavit, fuissemus, non fuissemus. Si propria non est, revocanda est ad propriam. Quid autem significat proprie nos fuisse in Adamo, nisi nos ducere ab Adamo originem, vel esse Adami esse causam nostri esse?
english: GAR. 1. If he sinned as the head of the human race, why ought he not also to have been punished under that title? 2. Why is Adam's sin rather imputed to posterity than posterity's to Adam? 3. Since Adam after that sin did not at once cease to be head, why are Adam's following sins not equally imputed to posterity as the first? 4. Why is actual sin, which is a transient action, rather said to be imputed than habitual, which was a permanent vice? 5. If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not also the first act of begetting? Yet no one would say that we in Adam begot Cain or Seth. 6. If as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin is ours by imputation, why is Christ called our righteousness, but Adam is not also called our sin? 7. When we are said to have sinned in Adam, is it proper or improper speech? It cannot be called proper unless we say that something simultaneously is and is not: for properly speaking, when Adam sinned, we would have been, we would not have been. If it is not proper, it must be reduced to the proper. But what does it properly signify that we were in Adam, except that we draw origin from Adam, or that Adam's being is the cause of our being?

source_text: GAR. VII. Nos vero respondemus. I. Generaliter. Si ejusmodi interrogationum punctulis locus esse debeat, non minus speciose sollicitari posse doctrinam de corruptione Originali a Pelagii aut Socini sectatoribus, quam haec de imputatione doctrina hic vexatur. Quaeretur enim 1. Cur Adami corruptio moralis posteros potius infecit, quam corruptio posterorum inquinavit Adamum? 2. Cur Adami peccatum in posteros necessario descendit, caeterorum patrum non ita descendit? 3. Cur Adami peccatum Caino nocuit, Caini peccatum Adamo minime nocuit? 4. Cur primum peccatum nos potius corrupit, quam sequentia? 5. Cur Adamus ab illa corruptione liberatus est ... infantes omnes ... non liberantur? 6. Cur Christus justitia & sanctificatio nostra dicitur, Adamus non dicitur peccatum & corruptio nostra? Haec & alia adversus doctrinam de corruptione ingenita queri possunt, quae si non obstant quominus Viri docti corruptionem illam agnoscere debeant; neque debent quaestiunculae illae impedimento nobis esse, quominus in antiqua & Catholica imputationis fide perseveremus. PLAC. Itane antiqua & catholica est imputationis immediatae fides? Id neque probatum est hactenus, neque probari potest.
english: GAR. VII. But we answer. I. Generally. If there ought to be room for such pinpoint interrogations, the doctrine of Original corruption can be no less speciously harassed by the followers of Pelagius or Socinus than this doctrine of imputation is vexed here. For it would be asked 1. Why Adam's moral corruption rather infected posterity than posterity's corruption stained Adam? 2. Why Adam's sin necessarily descended into posterity, and that of other fathers not so? 3. Why Adam's sin hurt Cain, and Cain's sin hurt Adam not at all? 4. Why the first sin rather corrupted us than Adam's following sins? 5. Why was Adam freed from that corruption ... and all infants ... not freed? 6. Why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, and Adam not called our sin and corruption? These and other things can be asked against the doctrine of inborn corruption, which if they do not hinder the learned man from having to acknowledge that corruption, neither ought those little questions to be an impediment to us from persevering in the ancient and Catholic faith of imputation. PLAC. Is the faith of immediate imputation thus ancient and catholic? That has neither been proved thus far, nor can it be proved.

source_text: Frustra autem istas de corruptione originali quaestiones nostris opponit: non enim sunt pares, nec ullam prorsus probandi vim habent. Respondeo ad primam, Cur Adami corruptio moralis posteros potius infecit, quam corruptio posterorum inquinavit Adamum? quia corruptio moralis non aliter quam per generationem carnalem propagatur: sunt autem posteri Adamaeo geniti, non autem Adamus ab illis. Ad 2. Cur Adami peccatum in posteros necessario descendit, caeterorum patrum non ita descendit? quia peccatum Adami fuit mutatio finis ultimi, atque adeo universalem in Adami naturam corruptionem induxit: immundus autem non potuit non immundum, caro non carnem gignere. Peccata vero aliorum patrum, hujusmodi corruptionis causae esse non poterunt, cum jam esset in eis producta, sed effecta quibus ipsa sese exercuit, & conservavit. Itaque quamvis a proximis parentibus eam proxime traxerimus, tamen Adamo, ut illius primo autori & scaturigini ascribi debet.
english: But he opposes those questions about original corruption to ours in vain: for they are not equal, nor have they any proving force at all. I answer the first: Why did Adam's moral corruption rather infect posterity than posterity's corruption stain Adam? Because moral corruption is propagated in no other way than by carnal generation: and posterity are begotten from Adam, but Adam is not begotten from them. To the second: Why did Adam's sin necessarily descend into posterity, and that of other fathers not so? Because Adam's sin was a change of the last end, and so brought a universal corruption into Adam's nature: but the unclean could not but beget the unclean, flesh not but flesh. Now the sins of other fathers could not be causes of this kind of corruption, since it was already produced in them, but effects by which it exercised and preserved itself. Therefore although we have drawn it most nearly from our nearest parents, yet it ought to be ascribed to Adam as its first author and spring.

source_text: Ad 3. Cur Adami peccatum Caino nocuit, Caini peccatum Adamo minime nocuit? quia Adamus genuit Cainum, non Cainus Adamum. Ad 4. Cur primum peccatum nos potius corrupit, quam sequentia Adami peccata? quia illud naturam Adami corrupit, ista corruptionem jam factam consequuta sunt ut causam effecta. Ad 5. Cur Adamus ab illa corruptione liberatus est, quam sua actione sibi comparavit; infantes omnes, qui nihil mali egerunt, non liberantur? Liberatus est ab illius corruptionis reatu gratia justificationis, & ab inhaerentia poenarum gratia regenerationis, quia credidit & resipuit; credidit autem, quia fuit electus. Idem evenit aliis omnibus electis. Cur autem hic potius quam ille fuerit electus, alii causae quam liberrimae Dei voluntati, de suo quod vult facientis, tribui nequit. Genuit autem non secundum gratiam, sed secundum naturam, conceptus corruptos, sicut arte circumcissus gignit incircumcisos.
english: To the third: Why did Adam's sin hurt Cain, and Cain's sin hurt Adam not at all? Because Adam begot Cain, not Cain Adam. To the fourth: Why did the first sin rather corrupt us than Adam's following sins? Because that corrupted Adam's nature; those followed corruption already made as effects follow a cause. To the fifth: Why was Adam freed from that corruption which by his action he procured for himself, and all infants, who have done no evil, are not freed? He was freed from the guilt of that corruption by the grace of justification, and from the inherence of penalties by the grace of regeneration, because he believed and repented; and he believed because he was elect. The same happens to all other elect. But why this one rather than that was elect can be ascribed to no other cause than the freest will of God, who does what He will with His own. And he begot not according to grace, but according to nature, conceiving corrupt ones, just as one circumcised by art begets the uncircumcised.

source_text: Ad 6. Cur Christus justitia & sanctificatio nostra dicitur, Adamus non dicitur peccatum & corruptio nostra? Quia nulla alia justitia justificamur, nulla alia virtute sanctificamur, quam Christi. Itaque in eo omnis nostra justitia & sanctificatio quaerenda. Non possumus similiter dicere, nullo nos peccato damnari, quam Adami. Nam & multorum aliorum sumus rei, & ad universalem corruptionem, quam ab Adamo traximus, multos habitus, seu particulares ad certa objecta determinationes nimis saepe adjungimus, & illud ipsum Adami peccatum non est nostrum donatione, aut imputatione ut Christi justitia, sed ratione propagati ex eo vitii nobis inhaerentis, quod vim habet nos condemnandi, non quia est Adami, aut profluxit ab Adamo, sed quia natura sua vitium est legi Dei repugnans. Ejus pro Pelagio & Socino quaestiunculis respondi: nunc videamus quomodo respondeat nostris.
english: To the sixth: Why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, and Adam not called our sin and corruption? Because we are justified by no other righteousness, sanctified by no other power, than Christ's. Therefore in Him all our righteousness and sanctification is to be sought. We cannot similarly say that we are damned by no sin but Adam's. For we are guilty of many others too, and to the universal corruption which we drew from Adam we too often add many habits, or particular determinations to certain objects; and that very sin of Adam is not ours by gift, or by imputation as Christ's righteousness is, but by reason of the vice propagated from it and inherent in us, which has power to condemn us not because it is Adam's, or flowed from Adam, but because by its nature it is a vice opposed to God's law. I have answered his little questions for Pelagius and Socinus: now let us see how he answers ours.

source_text: GAR. Nobis certa responsio suppetit, imputationem primi peccati esse actionem Dei liberam & voluntariam, ex certo Dei consilio judicioque, non ex solius naturae ordine dependentem. Neminem autem fuisse Dei consiliarium, qui ea nosse, & de iis respondere teneatur, quae Deus in verbo suo revelare noluit. Sufficere nobis ipsius rei notitiam, omnes scilicet in Adamo peccasse, & ipsius reatum super omnes venisse in condemnationem, atque ita primum illud peccatum in omnes imputatione descendere. Rationes illius judicii penes Deum esse cujus viae sunt impervestigabiles, & eius judicia abyssus multa. Rom. xi. 33. Psalm. xxxvi. 7. PLAC. Si immediata imputatio primi peccati est actio Dei libera & voluntaria, ea nisi in Scriptura revelata fuerit, sciri non potest. Atqui non est in Scriptura revelata, neque ad eam probandam ullam vim habent loca a viro docto hic repetita, ut partim jam patuit, partim ex dicendis manifestum fiet.
english: GAR. We have a sure reply ready: that the imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary action of God, from God's fixed counsel and judgment, not depending on the order of nature alone. And that no one was God's counselor, bound to know those things and to answer concerning them which God refused to reveal in His word. That it is enough for us to know the thing itself—namely that all sinned in Adam, and his guilt came upon all unto condemnation, and so that first sin descends upon all by imputation. That the reasons of that judgment are with God, whose ways are unsearchable, and His judgments a great deep. Romans 11:33. Psalm 36:7. PLAC. If the immediate imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary action of God, it cannot be known unless it has been revealed in Scripture. But it is not revealed in Scripture, nor do the places repeated here by the learned man have any force to prove it, as has partly already appeared, and will partly be made plain from what is to be said.

source_text: Deinde si est actio Dei libera, quo modo est actio Dei judiciaria? Liberam enim, opinor, intelligit, quae potest absque ulla justitiae aut legis violatione omitti. Quomodo ergo judiciaria dicitur, si eam a Judice neque lex, neque justitia exigit? Si nemo tenetur ea nosse, quae Deus in verbo suo revelare noluit, certe nemo tenetur illam imputationem nosse, siquidem, ut contendo, Deus eam non revelavit in verbo suo. Caeterum quaestionibus illis oppugno potissimum rationes, quae reddi solent, cur unum illud peccatum primum nobis omnibus immediate imputetur. Iis igitur renunciandum est, ac ad solam Dei voluntatem confugiendum, cui placuit illud unum, non alia, imputare, aut nostris istis interrogatis respondendum. Denique cum Deus nihil faciat nisi sapientissime, & justissime, & optime, si ejusmodi imputatio aut justitiae, aut sapientiae, aut bonitati repugnare videatur, quominus tribuatur Deo pia refugit conscientia, nec potest id a se impetrare, nisi, vel tollatur illa repugnantia, vel disertis Scripturae testimoniis, quae profecto nulla sunt, ad eam credendam aliquo modo cogatur.
english: Next, if it is a free action of God, how is it a judicial action of God? For by free he means, I think, what can be omitted without any violation of justice or of law. How then is it called judicial, if neither law nor justice requires it of the Judge? If no one is bound to know those things which God refused to reveal in His word, certainly no one is bound to know that imputation—if, as I contend, God did not reveal it in His word. For the rest, by those questions I chiefly attack the reasons which are usually given why that one first sin is immediately imputed to us all. Therefore either those reasons must be renounced, and refuge taken in God's will alone, to whom it pleased to impute that one and not others, or our interrogations must be answered. Finally, since God does nothing except most wisely, and most justly, and most well, if such an imputation seems to clash with justice, or wisdom, or goodness, a pious conscience shrinks from ascribing it to God, and cannot force that upon itself unless either that clash is removed, or it is somehow compelled to believe it by express testimonies of Scripture—of which there are in fact none.

source_text: GAR. Neque tamen quaestionum nodi putandi sunt insolubiles. Itaque nunc secundo loco Erotemata singula consideremus. Quaeritur primo. Si Adam peccavit, ut caput generis, cur non puniri debeat ut caput? Resp. Adamo cum tribuitur capitis nomen, rationem haberi non tantum originis carnalis, sed etiam foederis universalis illius, quod in Adamo Deus cum humano genere iniit. Cum ergo peccasse dicitur ut caput, non tantum denotatur, eum fuisse principium radicale totius generis, verum etiam ea conditione constitutum fuisse generis caput & principium, ut quamprimum ab obedientia praescripta deflecteret, non ipse tantum peccati sui reatu obstringeretur, sed & posteros omnes reos efficeret, ac proinde poena dignos. Hoc est ergo peccasse ut caput, se & posteros ob peccatum illud reatu involvisse. PLAC. Ita nodus non solvitur, sed augetur alio nodo: Nam praeter liberam & voluntariam illam actionem, quae Deo sine Scriptura tribuebatur, ecce aliam, nempe foederis cujusdam universalis pactionem, de qua ne gry quidem in Scriptura; & quod deterius est, conditio fingitur Deo haud satis digna.
english: GAR. And yet the knots of the questions are not to be thought insoluble. Therefore now in the second place let us consider the erotemata one by one. It is asked first: If Adam sinned as the head of the race, why ought he not to be punished as head? Reply: When the name of head is given to Adam, account is taken not only of carnal origin, but also of that universal covenant which God struck in Adam with the human race. When therefore he is said to have sinned as head, it denotes not only that he was the radical principle of the whole race, but also that he was constituted head and principle of the race on this condition: that as soon as he turned aside from the obedience prescribed, not he alone would be bound by the guilt of his sin, but he would also make all posterity guilty, and so worthy of penalty. This, then, is what it is to have sinned as head: to have involved himself and posterity in guilt on account of that sin. PLAC. So the knot is not loosed, but enlarged by another knot: for besides that free and voluntary action which was ascribed to God without Scripture, see another—namely the pact of some universal covenant, of which there is not even a syllable in Scripture; and what is worse, a condition is invented hardly worthy of God.

source_text: Si quod enim foedus cum homine contrahit, id facit hominis causa, & quia bonum est homini. Hoc vero foedus, cuius ea est, quam Vir Doctus declarat, conditio, non poterat non esse Adami posteris damnosum. Multo plus enim ex eo erat metuendum mali, quam sperandum boni: nam ut inde ad nos aliqua utilitas rediret, opus erat ut Adamus toto vitae curriculo perseveraret in obedientia & fide erga Deum: nec tamen propterea, si Viro Docto fides habetur, nobis eius imputata fuisset obedientia, tantum qualis fuisset, tales nos genuisset: at, si vel semel ab obedientia deflecteret, prima eius inobedientia nobis omnibus imputanda erat ad mortis aeternae reatum, nec id tantum, sed ut ob imputatum illud peccatum puniremur infligenda nobis erat corruptio illa hereditaria quae vere peccatum est, & fons peccatorum. Qui factum est, ut Deus, qui ipsa bonitas est, & genus humanum amabat, aequiorem ei non tulerit conditionem, & qui Adamus non rogavit Deum, quandoquidem contrahebat cum Deo ut totius generis humani procurator, ut ab eo conditionem impetraret tolerabiliorem? Nam certe talis conditio ab odio potius quam ab amore profecta videri possit; nec quid ad Dei gloriam, ut omnia quae facit Deus, per se se conferre possit ullo modo intelligitur.
english: For if He contracts any covenant with man, He does it for man's sake, and because it is good for man. But this covenant, whose condition is what the Learned Man declares, could not but be harmful to Adam's posterity. For far more evil was to be feared from it than good hoped for: since for any utility to return from it to us, Adam had to persevere through the whole course of life in obedience and faith toward God; and yet even then, if the Learned Man is believed, his obedience would not have been imputed to us—he would only have begotten us such as he was; but if he once turned aside from obedience, his first disobedience was to be imputed to us all unto the guilt of eternal death, and not that only, but that we might be punished for that imputed sin there was to be inflicted on us that hereditary corruption which is truly sin, and the fountain of sins. How came it that God, who is goodness itself and loved the human race, did not offer it a fairer condition, and that Adam did not ask God—seeing he was contracting with God as procurator of the whole human race—to obtain from Him a more tolerable condition? For surely such a condition might seem to have sprung from hatred rather than love; nor is it in any way understood how it could of itself contribute to God's glory, as all things God does ought.

source_text: Adde quod ea ratione aliter ad Adamum pertinuisset mandatum, aliter comminatio: illud ut ad caput generis humani, haec ut ad privatam personam: & vice versa ad nos pertinuisset comminatio, non item mandatum. Denique cur non ea conditione contractum est istud foedus, ut quemadmodum peccaret, sic etiam puniretur ut caput generis humani? Si recurras ad voluntatem Dei, quid opus erat ad has quaestiones alia responsione, quam generali ista, quia Deus ita voluit? Sed vide ne ei voluntatem attribuas pro tuo ingenio eius virtutibus minime convenientem, ac praeter Scripturam.
english: Add that on that account the command would have belonged to Adam one way, the threat another: the former as to the head of the human race, the latter as to a private person; and conversely the threat would have belonged to us, not likewise the command. Finally, why was that covenant not contracted on this condition, that as he sinned, so also he should be punished as head of the human race? If you fall back on the will of God, what need was there of any other answer to these questions than that general one, because God so willed? But see that you do not ascribe to Him a will suited to your own ingenuity, least fitting to His virtues, and beyond Scripture.

source_text: GAR. Quaeritur secundo, Cur potius Adami peccatum posteris, quam posterorum Adamo imputatur? Resp. 1. Hoc inde esse, quod posteri omnes in Adamo radicaliter & seminaliter fuerunt. Adamus in posteris hoc modo non fuit. 2. Quod peccatum imputari, est poenam propter peccatum irrogari. Atqui poena peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur, nunquam antecedit. Non potuit igitur Adamus poenas dare peccatorum, quae nondum erant, praesertim cum non ipse, sed Christus peccata hominum portare debuerit, & portando expiare.
english: GAR. It is asked second: Why is Adam's sin rather imputed to posterity than posterity's to Adam? Reply 1. This is because all posterity were in Adam radically and seminarily. Adam was not in posterity in this way. 2. That to impute sin is to inflict penalty on account of sin. But penalty always follows sin in the order of nature, never precedes it. Therefore Adam could not pay penalties for sins that did not yet exist, especially since not he, but Christ, ought to bear the sins of men, and by bearing to expiate them.

source_text: PLAC. Hac interrogatione non oppugnavi immediate imputationem immediatam primi peccati, sed rationem qua firmabatur, ideo scilicet primum illud Adami peccatum omnibus eius posteris imputari, quoniam Adamus componebat cum suis posteris unum corpus, cuius ipse caput erat, nos omnes eius posteri membra, quod autem facit caput toti corpori imputatur: objiciebam, si valet haec ratio, causam non esse, cur non itidem quae faciunt membra capiti, aut etiam toti corpori imputentur, quia reciproca est capitis & membrorum relatio. Itaque non attendens ad mentem meam, & loci, unde hanc interrogationem deprompsit, circumstantiam, Vir Doctus non ad rem respondet. Nam ad primam eius responsionem quod spectat, primo non est de ratione capitis ut sint in eo membra radicaliter & seminaliter. Deinde si de propagatione ageretur naturali, optima quidem esset ratio, cur propagatum fuerit peccatum ab Adamo in posteros, potius quam a posteris in Adamum, quia nempe posteri sunt ab Adamo, non Adamus a posteris: sed cum agatur de imputatione immediata, quae sit libera Dei actio, si spectavit posteros Adami tanquam eius membra unum cum eo corpus componentes, cur non potuit Deus aeque posterorum Adamo, atque Adami posteris peccatum imputare, praesertim cum posteri nullo modo causa fuerint peccati Adami, Adamus vero causa fuerit peccati posterorum?
english: PLAC. By this interrogation I did not immediately attack the immediate imputation of the first sin, but the reason by which it was fortified—namely that that first sin of Adam is imputed to all his posterity because Adam composed with his posterity one body of which he was head, we all his posterity members, and what the head does is imputed to the whole body: I objected that if this reason holds, there is no cause why what the members do should not likewise be imputed to the head, or even to the whole body, because the relation of head and members is reciprocal. And so, not attending to my mind, and to the circumstance of the place whence he drew this interrogation, the Learned Man does not answer to the point. For as to his first reply: first, it is not of the nature of a head that members be in it radically and seminarily. Next, if the question were of natural propagation, it would indeed be an excellent reason why sin was propagated from Adam into posterity rather than from posterity into Adam, because posterity are from Adam, not Adam from posterity; but when the matter is immediate imputation, which is a free act of God, if He regarded Adam's posterity as his members composing one body with him, why could God not equally impute posterity's sin to Adam and Adam's to posterity—especially since posterity were in no way the cause of Adam's sin, but Adam was the cause of posterity's sin?

source_text: Ad alteram autem eius responsionem quod attinet, primum vivente Adamo eius filii & nepotes peccaverunt. Deinde ultimi diei judicium quae sequetur poena posterior erit peccatis posterorum Adami, & quidem omnium. Tertio cum imputatio sit actio Dei, & Deus tum habuerit praesentes omnes Adami posteros, habuit etiam praesentia eorum peccata, cur ergo ea imputare non potuit? Denique, si poena peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur, nunquam antecedit, certe etiam peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur existentiam eius cui imputatur, nunquam antecedit. GAR. Quaeritur tertio. Cum Adamus post peccatum illud primum continuo non desierit esse caput generis humani, cur non sequentia eius peccata aeque imputantur ac primum? Resp. 1. Quia unam unius offensam & inobedientiam, non plures memorat Apostolus, ob quam homines peccatores constituti fuerint. 2. Quia Adamus per primum illud peccatum suum, excussus est beneficio foederis illius, quod Deus cum toto genere in Adami persona pactus fuerat. Itaque etiamsi non desierit esse caput relatione originis, desiit tamen esse relatione foederis. Ad imputationem autem de qua loquimur, utrumque necessarium fuit, ut scilicet Adamus, & radix esset, unde genus humanum oriretur, & foederis depositarius, quod sibi & suis, aut conservaret, aut amitteret.
