For it is to be considered, he says, that just as the body's diverse members are parts of one man's person, so all men are parts and as it were certain members of human nature: whence Porphyry says that by participation in the species many men are one man.

source_text: Diversa membra corporis sunt partes integrantes totius hominis. Omnes vero homines non sunt partes integrantes naturae humanae. Non componitur natura ex multis hominibus. Alioqui cum mihi natura humana insit integra, inessent mihi omnes homines. Sed sunt partes Logicae, sive subjectivae, ut vulgo loquuntur in scholis, & natura abstracta & praecisa ab individuis, ac universalitate donata totum est Logicum seu universale: sed hanc rationem totius non habet a parte rei, sed per mentis nostrae operationem. Itaque Metaphysice loquendo contra res habet. Persona est totum, natura pars: persona est id quod agit, natura id quo agit. Addit Thomas, videmus autem quod actus peccati exercitus per aliquod membrum, puta per manum, vel pedem, non habet rationem culpae ex voluntate manus vel pedis, sed ex voluntate totius hominis, a qua sicut a quodam principio derivatur motus peccati ad singula membra. Et similiter a voluntate Adae, qui fuit principium humanae naturae, tota inordinatio naturae habet culpae rationem in omnibus ad quos pervenit, quantum ad hoc quod susceptivi sunt culpae. Adverte quaeso quam non bene procedat ista similitudo.
english: The body's diverse members are integrating parts of the whole man. But all men are not integrating parts of human nature. Nature is not composed of many men. Otherwise, since human nature is in me entire, all men would be in me. They are Logical or subjective parts, as the schools say, and nature abstracted and cut off from individuals and given universality is a Logical or universal whole—but it has that reason of a whole not from the side of the thing, but through our mind's operation. So Metaphysically speaking the matter is the contrary. Person is the whole, nature the part: person is what acts, nature that by which it acts. Thomas adds: we see that an act of sin exercised through some member—say hand or foot—has the nature of fault not from the hand's or foot's will but from the whole man's will, from which as from a principle the motion of sin is derived to the several members. And likewise from Adam's will, who was the principle of human nature, the whole inordination of nature has the nature of fault in all to whom it reaches, insofar as they are capable of fault. Mark, I pray, how badly this likeness proceeds.

source_text: In praecedentibus verbis componebat naturam cum persona, omnes homines cum membris corporis. Unde oriebatur haec similitudo, ut se habet persona ad membra corporis, sic se habet natura ad omnes homines. Satis, ut innui, male: Non enim ut persona est principium quod actionis, membrum quo; sic natura est principium quod, homines principia quibus peccat. Sed contra, ut iam dixi. Iam autem quomodo istam comparationem ad institutum accommodat? Actus, inquit, peccati exercitus per aliquod membrum non habet rationem peccati ex voluntate illius membri, sed totius personae. Expectabam ut concluderet, ergo actus peccati exercitus per aliquem hominem non habet rationem peccati ex voluntate illius hominis, sed ex voluntate naturae humanae. Verum ille mutatis terminis, loco actus exerciti per homines aut hominem, posuit totam inordinationem naturae, & pro voluntate naturae humanae posuit voluntatem Adae qui fuit principium naturae humanae. Atqui primum accurate loquendo falsum est, Adam fuisse principium naturae humanae: Imo contra potius, natura humana fuit principium Adami. Est enim natura quodammodo pars suppositi: pars autem principium aliquomodo eius quod componit. Et, ut Logici loquuntur, natura humana prior est Adamo existendi consequentia. Est igitur Adamus principium seu causa, non absolute naturae humanae, sed naturae humanae quae in eius posteris fuit: quomodo pater quilibet principium est naturae posterorum, non suae. Deinde voluntas Adae tam eius personae voluntas fuit, quam mea meae; nec intelligo cur naturae voluntas dici debeat. Nam si Adamus principium fuit naturae humanae, inde non sequitur eius voluntatem fuisse voluntatem naturae, sequitur tantum Adamum fuisse principium voluntatis naturae humanae, aut certe naturam humanam non habere voluntatem, aut ad summum voluntatem Adami fuisse principium voluntatis naturae.
english: In the preceding words he was composing nature with person, all men with the body's members. Whence arose this likeness: as person stands to the body's members, so nature stands to all men. Badly enough, as I hinted: for it is not that as person is the principle-which of the action and the member the principle-by-which, so nature is the principle-which and men the principles-by-which it sins. Rather the contrary, as I already said. Now how does he fit that comparison to the point? An act of sin exercised through some member, he says, has the nature of sin not from that member's will but from the whole person's. I expected him to conclude: therefore an act of sin exercised through some man has the nature of sin not from that man's will but from human nature's will. But he, changing terms, put in place of an act exercised through men or a man the whole inordination of nature, and in place of human nature's will put Adam's will who was the principle of human nature. Yet first, accurately speaking, it is false that Adam was the principle of human nature: rather, on the contrary, human nature was Adam's principle. For nature is somehow a part of the supposit; and a part is somehow a principle of what it composes. And as the Logicians say, human nature is prior to Adam in the consequence of existing. Therefore Adam is principle or cause not of human nature absolutely, but of the human nature that was in his posterity—as any father is principle of his posterity's nature, not of his own. Next, Adam's will was his person's will as mine is mine; nor do I understand why it should be called nature's will. For if Adam was principle of human nature, it does not follow that his will was nature's will—only that Adam was principle of human nature's will, or that human nature has no will, or at most that Adam's will was the principle of nature's will.

source_text: Piget me diutius immorari in isto scholastico pulvere inanium subtilitatum, quibus tu me Thomae opera implicuisti, quem alioqui fabellis plurium rationum possem in suos autores dispellere, & dissipare: sed satis erit hoc loco duas huius similitudinis claudicationes observasse. Primum enim ideo actus per membrum aliquod corporis exercitus non habet rationem culpae ex voluntate illius membri, sed totius hominis, quia membro illi nulla est propria voluntas. At sua cuique homini propria est voluntas. Itaque membrum separatum nihil peccat, nihil agit. Homines singuli multa & agunt, & peccant separati ab Adamo, eorumque actiones peccata sunt, non quia proficiscuntur a voluntate Adami, sed quia, profectae a propria cuiusque voluntate, pugnant cum lege Dei. Deinde discere velim, cur haec comparatio locum habeat duntaxat respectu primi illius peccati actualis, non autem sequentium? desiitne simul ac peccavit Adamus, eius voluntas esse voluntas naturae, aut Adamus esse principium naturae humanae? Effecerit igitur ista comparatio, ut, non minus quam primum, reliqua Adami peccata nobis imputentur, contradicente Apostolo Rom. 5. Addam & tertiam claudicationem, idcirco actiones membrorum corporis rationem culpae habent ex voluntate totius hominis, quoniam membra corporis sunt voluntatis totius hominis organa, seu instrumenta, & eius imperio moventur; quo fit ut eorum actiones tribuantur voluntati personae ut causae principali, membris tantummodo ut causae instrumentali. Nos autem, opinor, organa non sumus Adami, nec movemur a voluntate Adami, nec ab eo imperantur actiones nostrae, nec, cum quis generat, id facit ut causa instrumentalis, Adami voluntati obsequens. Praeter hos omnes defectus quos memoravi, laborat alio vitio haec Thomae Aquinatis similitudo & ratiocinatio, eoque maximo. Non enim propositae difficultati ullo modo satisfacit. Urgere enim id possum, quod etiam doctissimus Chamierus adversus Pighium & Salmeronem urget. Eius verba ascribam: Cum peccatum dicitur esse voluntarium, intelligendum est de voluntate eius, cuius peccatum esse dicitur. At hoc certe sensu non potest dici in nobis peccatum illud Adami esse voluntarium, multo minus actus nostrae voluntatis. Neque enim est in nostra voluntate, neque a nostra voluntate: quia reipsa nostra voluntas nunquam fuit voluntas Adami. Si ergo nostrae voluntatis respectu voluntarium non est Adami peccatum, sed tantum respectu voluntatis Adami, certe nostrum peccatum non est, sed solius Adami.
english: It irks me to linger longer in that scholastic dust of empty subtleties with which you have entangled me by Thomas's work—whom otherwise I could scatter back to his authors with the little stories of many reasons: but it will be enough here to have noted two limps of this likeness. First: an act exercised through some bodily member has the nature of fault from the whole man's will, not that member's, because that member has no proper will of its own. But each man has his own proper will. So a separated member sins nothing, does nothing. Individual men do and sin many things separated from Adam, and their actions are sins not because they proceed from Adam's will, but because, proceeding from each one's own will, they clash with God's law. Next I would learn why this comparison holds only respecting that first actual sin, not the following ones: did Adam's will cease to be nature's will, or Adam to be human nature's principle, the moment he sinned? Then this comparison would make Adam's later sins no less imputed to us than the first—contradicting the Apostle, Rom. 5. I add a third limp: members' actions have fault from the whole man's will because the body's members are organs or instruments of the whole man's will and are moved by his command; so their actions are ascribed to the person's will as principal cause, to the members only as instrumental. But we, I think, are not Adam's organs, nor are we moved by Adam's will, nor are our actions commanded by him, nor when someone generates does he do it as an instrumental cause obeying Adam's will. Besides all these defects I have mentioned, this likeness and reasoning of Thomas Aquinas labors under another and greatest vice. For it in no way satisfies the difficulty proposed. I can press what the most learned Chamier also presses against Pighius and Salmeron. I will copy his words: When sin is said to be voluntary, it is to be understood of the will of him whose sin it is said to be. But in that sense Adam's sin cannot be said to be voluntary in us, much less an act of our will. For it is neither in our will nor from our will: because in very deed our will never was Adam's will. If therefore Adam's sin is not voluntary with respect to our will, but only with respect to Adam's will, certainly it is not our sin, but Adam's alone.

source_text: Tu quidem ais, voluntatem Adami, cum peccavit, fuisse voluntatem omnium hominum: sed affirmanti, nec rationem afferenti oppono Chamierum, voluntas nostra nunquam fuit voluntas Adami. Cum enim haec propositio sit negans, convertitur simpliciter in hanc, Voluntas Adami nunquam fuit voluntas nostra. Vin' tui huius dicti protraham in lucem absurditatem? 1. Si voluntas Adami fuit voluntas omnium hominum; igitur fuit voluntas universalis. Atqui constat tam singularem fuisse, quam alius cuiusvis. 2. Si voluntas Adami fuit, exempli causa, mea voluntas, igitur etiam eius anima fuit mea anima, & eius corpus fuit meum corpus, & eius os fuit meum os, & eius uxor fuit mea uxor &c. 3. Si voluntas Adami fuit mea voluntas, igitur duas habeo voluntates, unam aliquot millibus annorum antequam essem; alteram creatam nuper, annis abhinc fere quinquaginta, alteram ab altera realiter, immo localiter, divisam & separatam, unam communem, alteram propriam. Porro si duas voluntates habeo, etiam duas animas, duo corpora. Itaque qui me unum hominem esse putabam, evasi in duos, unum communem, alterum proprium; illum pridem fato suo functum, hunc adhuc viventem. Noli confugere ad figuras sermonis. Vis enim nobis omnibus vere & proprie imputari peccatum Adami, ac proinde nos illud vere & proprie commisisse. Non commisimus autem vere & proprie, nisi voluntas Adami qua commissum est vere & proprie nostra fuerit voluntas. 4. Si voluntas Adami fuit voluntas omnium hominum, igitur actus voluntatis Adami fuerunt actus omnium hominum: idem dicendum de actibus mentis. Quod si actus voluntatis eius eliciti fuerunt actus omnium hominum, etiam proculdubio actus eius voluntatis imperati. Cum loquebatur, loquebantur omnes homines; cum ambulabat, ambulabant omnes; cum edebat, edebant omnes; cum gignebat, gignebant omnes. Hoccine tibi probatur? nisi fortasse vis hoc privilegium habuisse voluntatem Adami ut nostra esset voluntas, pro eo duntaxat momento quo peccavit: mallem fuisset alio potius tempore.
english: You indeed say that Adam's will, when he sinned, was the will of all men: but to one who affirms without bringing a reason I oppose Chamier—our will never was Adam's will. And since that proposition is negative, it converts simply into this: Adam's will never was our will. Shall I drag the absurdity of your saying into the light? 1. If Adam's will was the will of all men, then it was a universal will. Yet it is clear it was as singular as anyone else's. 2. If Adam's will was, for example, my will, then also his soul was my soul, and his body my body, and his mouth my mouth, and his wife my wife, &c. 3. If Adam's will was my will, then I have two wills—one some thousands of years before I was; another created lately, nearly fifty years ago—one really, even locally, divided and separated from the other, one common, one proper. Further, if I have two wills, also two souls, two bodies. So I who thought myself one man have turned out two—one common, one proper; that one long since dead, this one still living. Do not flee to figures of speech. For you want Adam's sin truly and properly imputed to us all, and so us to have truly and properly committed it. But we did not truly and properly commit it unless Adam's will by which it was committed was truly and properly our will. 4. If Adam's will was the will of all men, then Adam's acts of will were acts of all men—the same of acts of mind. And if his elicited acts of will were acts of all men, then doubtless also his commanded acts of will. When he spoke, all men spoke; when he walked, all walked; when he ate, all ate; when he begot, all begot. Does this please you?—unless perhaps you want Adam's will to have had this privilege of being ours only for that moment when he sinned: I would rather it had been at some other time.

source_text: GAR. Respondeo. Voluntatem Adae fuisse voluntatem omnium, satis tritum est apud Theologos, neque Augustino ignoratum. Per unius enim Adami voluntatem malam omnes in eo peccaverunt, quando omnes ille unus fuerunt, inquit de Nupt. & Concup. lib. 1. cap. 5. Et tamen hoc dictum non modo tanquam dubium, aut improbabile, aut falsum vir doctus exagitat; verum etiam, tanquam ineptum & fatuum, & anilium fabularum nugamenta superans, traducit, atque subsannat. PLAC. Negavi, praeeunte Chamiero praestanti Theologo, Adami voluntatem fuisse nostram voluntatem, & quae, si dicatur fuisse nostra voluntas, sequantur absurda, absque ullo asperiore verbo, ostendi. Fecine ea in re quicquam praeter officium meum? At voluntatem Adae fuisse voluntatem omnium satis tritum est apud Theologos. Quaeso, apud quos? Eorum certe autoritas non impedivit, quominus Chamierus, & ipse, opinor, Theologus, id negaret. Cur mihi quoque id negare non licuit? Opponitur mihi Augustinus, qui tamen totus meus est.
english: GAR. I answer. That Adam's will was the will of all is worn enough among Theologians, and not unknown to Augustine. For by the one Adam's bad will all sinned in him, when all were that one, he says in De Nuptiis et Concupiscentia book 1 chapter 5. And yet the learned man assails this saying not only as doubtful or improbable or false, but even traduces and scoffs at it as inept and fatuous and surpassing old wives' fables. PLAC. I denied, with the excellent theologian Chamier going before, that Adam's will was our will, and without any harsher word I showed what absurdities follow if it is said to have been our will. Did I do anything in that beyond my duty? But that Adam's will was the will of all is worn enough among Theologians. Among whom, I ask? Their authority certainly did not keep Chamier—himself a theologian, I think—from denying it. Why may I not deny it too? Augustine is opposed to me—who yet is wholly mine.

source_text: Dixitne voluntatem Adami fuisse voluntatem omnium? Non, sed per unius illius voluntatem malam omnes in eo peccasse, quando omnes ille (malim ille) unus fuerunt, de quo propterea singuli peccatum originale traxerunt. Quando autem unus fuerunt? nimirum quando ipsi non fuerunt, sed unus fuit unde suum esse traxerunt. Quomodo in eo tunc peccaverunt? nimirum ipsi tunc non peccaverunt, sed ille peccavit cuius ex peccato suum singuli peccatum originale traxerunt. Id autem peccatum, non per voluntatem omnium, sed per voluntatem unius illius commissum est. Cum ergo dicit fuisse voluntatem unius illius, non affirmat, sed negat potius fuisse voluntatem omnium. At dicit omnes fuisse illum unum, nempe quando ille unus fuit, & ipsi non fuerunt. Simul enim ac ipsi esse coeperunt, non fuerunt amplius unus, sed ab eo uno diversi: id quod arguit vox quando: innuit enim quo tempore loquebatur, eos non esse amplius unum. Si ex quo sumus, non sumus unus ille homo, certe ex quo sumus eius voluntas non est nostra voluntas, nec ad eam similem habemus relationem ei quam habent membra ad voluntatem totius hominis, ut verbis Thomae asseverabaris cum quo disputabam. Mihi igitur favet potius Augustinus quam nocet.
english: Did he say Adam's will was the will of all? No—but that by that one's bad will all sinned in him when all were that one (I prefer "he"), from whom therefore each drew original sin. When were they one? Namely when they themselves were not, but one was from whom they drew their being. How did they then sin in him? Namely they themselves did not then sin, but he sinned from whose sin each drew his own original sin. And that sin was committed not through the will of all, but through that one's will. So when he says it was that one's will, he does not affirm but rather denies it was the will of all. Yet he says all were that one—namely when he was one and they were not. For as soon as they began to be, they were no longer one, but diverse from that one: which the word "when" proves; it hints that at the time he was speaking they were no longer one. If from the time we are we are not that one man, then from the time we are his will is not our will, nor have we to it a relation like that which members have to the whole man's will, as you were asserting in Thomas's words with whom I disputed. So Augustine favors me rather than hurts me.

source_text: Vis scire quomodo per voluntatem unius peccavimus? Ex voluntate, inquit, peccatum est. Quaerit forte etiam & originale peccatum. Respondeo prorsus originale peccatum, quia & hoc ex voluntate primi hominis seminatum est, ut & in illo esset, & in omnes transiret. Putavitne cum viro docto id per imputationem transire, & huius causam unicam esse Dei voluntatem? Contra plane; contendit neque Deo, neque naturae humanae ut est a Deo, sed concupiscentiae seu libidini quae a parente in liberos transit per semen debere ascribi. Non vult immediate ab Adamo per imputationem vitium descendere, sed mediate, & a proximi cuiusque parentis vitio per carnalem generationem trajici in prolem. Cumque inquirat, quomodo quod dimissum est in parente trahatur in prolem, id quidem miris modis fieri dicit, sed tamen fieri: & illustrat exemplo olivae ex qua nascitur oleaster. Si idem cum viro docto sensisset, non confugisset ad naturam, non ad carnalem generationem, non ad vitium proximorum parentum, non ad oleastri exemplum, sed ad voluntatem Dei, cui placuit omnibus Adami posteris peccatum actuale immediate imputare, & ut illud imputatum puniret, & satisfaceret justitiae, ipsis omnibus vitium illud originale infligere. Aliter enim illius rei rationem reddi non posse clamat vir doctus multis locis, ac nominatim cap. 11. §. 8. de quo supra pag. 125.
english: Do you want to know how we sinned through one will? From the will, he says, there is sin. Perhaps he seeks original sin too. I answer: original sin altogether, because this too was sown from the first man's will so that it might be in him and pass into all. Did he think with the learned man that it passes by imputation, and that its sole cause is God's will? Plainly the contrary; he contends it should be ascribed neither to God nor to human nature as from God, but to concupiscence or lust which passes from parent to children through seed. He does not want the vice to descend immediately from Adam by imputation, but mediately, and to be carried into the offspring from each nearest parent's vice by carnal generation. And when he asks how what is remitted in the parent is drawn into the offspring, he says it happens in wondrous ways, yet happens—and illustrates with the olive from which a wild olive is born. Had he sensed with the learned man, he would not have fled to nature, carnal generation, nearest parents' vice, or the wild-olive example, but to God's will, which was pleased immediately to impute Adam's actual sin to all his posterity and, to punish that imputed sin and satisfy justice, to inflict that original vice on them all. For otherwise, the learned man cries in many places—and namely cap. 11 §8, above at p. 125—no account of the matter can be given.

source_text: GAR. Videamus tamen, an ista colligendi ratio, ut jocularis argutiola laudem habere potest, ita soliditatis habeat. Etenim respondeo, eam Adami voluntatem, de qua loquimur, & singularem fuisse, & universalem. Singularem actus proprietate; universalem repraesentationis jure. Singularem, quia ab uno ex individuis humanis profecta est: universalem, quia individuum illud repraesentavit universum genus, ut eo per voluntatem suam primum peccante, idem fuerit, ac si omnes per propriam suam voluntatem peccassent. 2. Voluntatem Adae cum dicimus fuisse voluntatem omnium, non loquimur de voluntate prout significat facultatem illam volendi, quae Adamo ex naturae principiis inerat, & sine qua ne homo quidem fuisset: sed voluntatis nomine intelligimus volitionem, sive actum illum volendi quem exercuit circa fructum arboris vetitae, & quo se reum fecit inobedientiae illius primae. Neque dicimus actum illum volendi fuisse omnium proprie, formaliter, aut personaliter, sed interpretative & per imputationem. Itaque quae inde nectuntur conclusiunculae, Adami animam, corpus, uxorem fuisse nostra; nos habere duas voluntates, animas, corpora, & esse duos homines, eo loco possit habere aliquis, quo haberi voluit vir doctus illud Theologorum effatum.
english: GAR. Yet let us see whether that way of gathering, as it can have praise as a joking quibble, so has solidity. For I answer that that will of Adam of which we speak was both singular and universal: singular by the property of the act; universal by right of representation. Singular, because it proceeded from one of the human individuals; universal, because that individual represented the whole race, so that when he first sinned by his will it was the same as if all had sinned by their own proper will. 2. When we say Adam's will was the will of all, we do not speak of will as signifying that faculty of willing which was in Adam from nature's principles and without which he would not even have been a man: but by the name of will we understand volition, or that act of willing which he exercised about the fruit of the forbidden tree and by which he made himself guilty of that first disobedience. Nor do we say that act of willing was everyone's properly, formally, or personally, but interpretatively and by imputation. So the little conclusions thence woven—that Adam's soul, body, wife were ours; that we have two wills, souls, bodies, and are two men—someone may put in the place where the learned man wanted the Theologians' saying held.

source_text: PLAC. Ergo, si fides habetur viro docto, cum voluntas Adami dicitur voluntas omnium, nihil aliud significatur, nisi volitionem illam qua primum peccavit, hoc est, primam eius inobedientiam esse omnium per imputationem: id quod toto hoc libro refellimus. Sed quo jure est omnium? Est, inquit, universalis repraesentationis jure. Estne igitur, ut loquuntur, universalis in repraesentando? Non, opinor, hoc voluit. Quid ergo voluit? nam quo fuit voluntas omnium, eo fuit voluntas universalis; universale enim & commune idem videntur significare. Fuit autem, si illi creditur, omnium imputatione. Probabilius est eum intellexisse jus repraesentationis, quo scilicet Adamus repraesentavit omnes homines. At si repraesentavit omnes homines, potuit non minus quam sua voluntas, dici homo universalis: quo tamen elogio nondum, ut opinor, a quoquam est insignitus. Deinde merito quaeri potest, quo fundamento istiusmodi repraesentatio, & repraesentationis jus nitatur. Proferetur fortasse foedus illud initum cum toto genere humano in Adamo, quod ad imputationem immediatam tuendam viri quidam docti praeter Scripturam & naturam excogitarunt: Sed de eo & jam dictum est, & nihil necesse est nunc disputare. Haec enim obiter hoc loco observare volui: redeo ad id de quo agebatur in Manuscripto, & quod mihi videtur vir doctus hac sua responsione detorsisse in alienum sensum. Patet enim ex verbis Thomae, quibus suam mentem is vir doctus, quicum mihi res erat, exposuit, per voluntatem, non ipsam volitionem, sed volitionis principium intelligi, sicut per membra, non actiones membrorum, sed harum principia significantur. Considerantur enim a Thoma omnes homines tanquam partes seu membra naturae humanae, & voluntas Adami ut voluntas totius naturae, vel, ut loquitur, principii naturae humanae: quae comparatio flagitat, ut quemadmodum membra non significant actiones membrorum, sed illarum principia, sic voluntas non significet actionem voluntatis, sed eius principium.
english: PLAC. Therefore, if the learned man is credited, when Adam's will is called the will of all, nothing else is meant than that the volition by which he first sinned—that is, his first disobedience—is everyone's by imputation: which this whole book refutes. But by what right is it everyone's? It is, he says, universal by right of representation. Is it then, as they say, universal in representing? I do not think he meant that. What then did he mean?—for insofar as it was the will of all, it was a universal will; universal and common seem to signify the same. Yet if he is believed, it was everyone's by imputation. More probably he meant the right of representation by which Adam represented all men. But if he represented all men, he could no less than his will be called a universal man—an elogium with which, I think, no one has yet marked him. Next it may fairly be asked on what foundation such representation and right of representation rest. Perhaps that covenant entered with the whole human race in Adam will be brought forward, which certain learned men invented beyond Scripture and nature to guard immediate imputation: but of that enough has already been said, and there is no need to dispute now. These things I wished to note in passing here: I return to what was treated in the Manuscript, and what the learned man seems to me by this reply to have twisted into an alien sense. For it is clear from Thomas's words, by which that learned man with whom I had to do expounded his mind, that by will not the volition itself but the principle of volition is understood, just as by members not the members' actions but their principles are signified. For Thomas considers all men as parts or members of human nature, and Adam's will as the will of the whole nature, or, as he speaks, of the principle of human nature: which comparison demands that as members do not signify the members' actions but their principles, so will not signify the act of will but its principle.

source_text: GAR. Quid si accedat aliquis de Socini schola, & arma mutuatus a viro docto similibus conclusionum tormentis agat adversus id quod habet Gallica S. Coenae liturgia, virtutem mortis Christi ad justitiam nobis imputari, non minus quam si eam nos ipsi pertulissemus? Si actus ille voluntatis Christi, quo se in mortem obtulit, tam tuus est, quam si tu actu proprio voluntatis tuae teipsum obtulisses, quiani etiam tua fuerit anima, corpus, mater Christi? Quidni duas voluntates habere dicaris, unam antequam esses, alteram postquam fuisti? &c. PLAC. Dixitne liturgia illa, voluntatem Christi fuisse voluntatem omnium nostrum? Aut actum illum voluntatis Christi, quo se in mortem obtulit, fuisse actum omnium nostrum? Minime: dixit tantum, virtutem mortis Christi ad justitiam nobis imputari. Aliud autem est virtus mortis Christi, aliud voluntas Christi. Nihil igitur video in verbis liturgiae unde tales consequentiae deduci possint. Cur autem virtus mortis Christi nobis imputatur? Annon quia mortem luere tenebamur, ille, ut vas noster, eam loco nostro luit? Itaque nostra est Dei & Christi donatione, nostraque per fidem acceptione. Num similiter Adamus vas noster fuit, ut loco nostro peccaret? Aut eius peccatum factum est dono Dei, & Adami, & nostra acceptione, nostrum?
english: GAR. What if someone from Socinus's school should come, and borrowing arms from the learned man should with like engines of conclusions fight against what the French Lord's Supper liturgy has—that the virtue of Christ's death is imputed to us unto righteousness, no less than if we ourselves had borne it? If that act of Christ's will by which he offered himself unto death is as much yours as if by your own act of will you had offered yourself, why then was not Christ's soul, body, mother also yours? Why not be said to have two wills—one before you were, another after you had been? &c. PLAC. Did that liturgy say Christ's will was the will of us all? Or that that act of Christ's will by which he offered himself unto death was an act of us all? Not at all: it said only that the virtue of Christ's death is imputed to us unto righteousness. But the virtue of Christ's death is one thing, Christ's will another. So I see nothing in the liturgy's words from which such consequences can be drawn. Why then is the virtue of Christ's death imputed to us? Is it not because we were bound to pay death, and he, as our surety, paid it in our place? So it is ours by God's and Christ's gift, and ours by acceptance through faith. Was Adam likewise our surety so as to sin in our place? Or did his sin become ours by gift of God and of Adam and by our acceptance?

source_text: Reliqua quae addit hoc loco vir doctus egere non videntur refutatione, praesertim si memineris, candide lector, eorum quae dicta sunt a nobis supra pag. 163. Cum assertionem, voluntatem Adami fuisse voluntatem omnium, oppugnavi, non putabam illius hunc esse sensum, volitionem, quam Adamus circa arborem vetitam exercuit, omnibus imputari. Sequentia Thomae verba quae tu adscripsisti etsi verum continent praetermittenda non sunt. Et sicut peccatum actuale, quod est peccatum personae, trahitur ad singula membra per aliquem actum personalem, ita peccatum originale trahitur ad singulos homines per actum naturae qui est generatio. Rursus peccatum actuale distinguit ab originali, & utrumque vult in Adamo fuisse: illud personae, hoc naturae. Necesse est igitur ut per originale corruptionem intelligat ex peccato actuali ortam. Quare non voluit peccatum actuale, quod personae est, nobis imputari: immo nec vitium naturae quatenus in Adamo haesit, ut mox videbimus: alioqui imputanda etiam nobis esset generatio, qua secundum nostrum parentem Sethum Adamus genuit, quandoquidem illa teste Thoma actus fuit naturae. Subjicit, Et ita sicut per generationem humana natura trahitur, ita etiam per generationem traducitur defectus humanae naturae qui est consecutus ex peccato primi parentis. Nihil verius. Mea haec est sententia. Unde concludo, quemadmodum natura humana trahitur per generationem absque imputatione naturae Adami, sic trahi per generationem defectus naturae humanae absque imputatione peccati actualis Adami. Trahitur nempe vitium naturae per actum naturae, non per actum Dei imputantis nobis peccatum Adami, & hos defectus infligentis.
english: The rest the learned man adds here does not seem to need refutation, especially if you remember, candid reader, what we said above at p. 163. When I opposed the assertion that Adam's will was the will of all, I did not think its sense was that the volition Adam exercised about the forbidden tree is imputed to all. Thomas's following words which you wrote out, though they contain truth, must not be passed by. And just as actual sin, which is a person's sin, is drawn to the several members by some personal act, so original sin is drawn to individual men by the act of nature which is generation. Again he distinguishes actual from original, and wants both to have been in Adam: that of the person, this of nature. So by original he must mean the corruption arisen from actual sin. Therefore he did not want the person's actual sin imputed to us—nor even nature's vice as it stuck in Adam, as we shall soon see: otherwise the generation by which Adam begot Seth our second parent would also be imputed to us, since that, by Thomas's witness, was an act of nature. He adds: And so just as human nature is drawn by generation, so also by generation is traduced the defect of human nature which followed from the first parent's sin. Nothing truer. That is my sentence. Whence I conclude: as human nature is drawn by generation without imputation of Adam's nature, so the defect of human nature is drawn by generation without imputation of Adam's actual sin. Namely nature's vice is drawn by nature's act, not by an act of God imputing Adam's sin to us and inflicting these defects.

source_text: Adjunxisti alia eiusdem Thomae verba in quibus occurrit verbum imputandi, quod tu majusculis literis pinxisti. Subit mirari qui in caeteris controversiis Thomae Aquinatis, aliorumque scholasticorum Pontificiorum authoritatem nullo loco habent, in hac quaestione ea apud eos niti qui eam ipsi quoque contemnunt: nempe dogma istud de imputatione peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus nec antiquum est, & non aliunde primum fluxit quam ex lacunis quorundam scholasticorum, quos ne nominare quidem Lombardus Thomae magister, adeo obscuri erant, voluit. Thomas autem quamvis & imputandi verbo usus sit & tuae causae in speciem favere videatur, tamen revera abest a tua sententia haud parum, & mirum est te id non vidisse in his ipsis verbis quae citas, Adam, inquit, peccans vitavit naturam humanam, sed postmodum in aliis Natura vitiata (non igitur imputatio peccati actualis Adae) inficit personam, dum scilicet genito imputatur ad culpam NATURAE VITIUM propter voluntatem primi parentis, ut dictum est. Nonne vides verbi imputatur nominativum esse naturae vitium? dabis autem proculdubio mihi vitium naturae non esse peccatum actuale Adami, quod Thomas constanter docet fuisse peccatum personae. Nempe omnis in eo erat Thomas ut ostenderet quomodo ista nobis inhaerens naturae infectio seu vitium culpae rationem habere possit, cum sit involuntaria. Affirmat igitur ut actus per membrum exercitus habet rationem culpae & imputatur membro propter voluntatem non ipsius membri sed totius personae, sic vitium tractum ab Adamo & genito inhaerens culpae rationem habere & imputari genito ad culpam, non propter voluntatem geniti cuius respectu involuntarium est, sed propter voluntatem primi parentis. Itaque addidit ut dictum est, nempe verbis praecedentibus quae nos a te citata expendimus. Ausim affirmare imputationem peccati actualis Adami toti eius posteritati & inflictionem privationis justitiae originalis omnibus hominibus in poenam illius peccati imputati ignotas fuisse Thomae Aquinati, & possem id si opus esset necessariis argumentis demonstrare.
english: You added other words of the same Thomas in which the verb "to impute" occurs, which you painted in capital letters. One wonders that those who in other controversies give Thomas Aquinas and other Pontifical scholastics no place lean on them in this question though they themselves also contemn them: for that dogma of imputing Adam's actual sin to all men is not ancient, and first flowed from nowhere but the puddles of certain scholastics whom even Lombard, Thomas's master, would not name, so obscure were they. But though Thomas used the word "impute" and seems in appearance to favor your cause, in truth he is not a little distant from your sentence, and it is strange you did not see it in these very words you cite: Adam, he says, sinning vitiated human nature, but afterward in others a vitiated Nature (not therefore imputation of Adam's actual sin) infects the person, namely when to the one begotten is imputed unto fault NATURE'S VICE on account of the first parent's will, as was said. Do you not see that the nominative of "is imputed" is nature's vice? And you will doubtless grant me that nature's vice is not Adam's actual sin, which Thomas constantly teaches was a person's sin. For Thomas's whole aim was to show how that infection or vice of nature inhering in us can have the nature of fault though involuntary. So he affirms that as an act exercised through a member has the nature of fault and is imputed to the member because of the will not of the member itself but of the whole person, so the vice drawn from Adam and inhering in the begotten has the nature of fault and is imputed to the begotten unto fault, not because of the begotten's will in respect of which it is involuntary, but because of the first parent's will. So he added "as was said"—namely in the preceding words we weighed from your citation. I would dare affirm that imputing Adam's actual sin to all his posterity and inflicting privation of original justice on all men as penalty of that imputed sin were unknown to Thomas Aquinas, and I could prove it by necessary arguments if need were.

source_text: Tertiam similitudinem petis a corpore civili. Ea bimembris est. Primum enim nobis ob oculos constituis Regem inferentem bellum vicinae genti, qui non solum ipse qui inferre voluit, & in consilio decrevit, & armis persecutus est, habetur pro hoste, sed etiam omnes subditi, quorum plerique nec voluerunt, nec consenserunt huic bello, & quanquam non agunt, & domi manent, si tamen in manus hostium veniant, excipiuntur incauti, concutiuntur, & jure belli interficiuntur. Attende, quaeso, quam non quadret haec similitudo. Principio si admittatur, fatendum erit, quemadmodum ab hoste capiuntur, & necantur qui nec bellum probant, nec in id consentiunt, nec ullo modo consilii Regis sunt participes, sic etiamsi nihil in nobis esset vitii, atque a peccato voluntas nostra abhorreret, tamen nobis imputari peccatum actuale Adami: quod qui tecum sentiunt multi non audent fateri. Deinde, consequens esset non solum primum peccatum Adami, sed reliqua etiam eius peccata actualia nobis esse imputanda: quippe cum generis humani caput fuerit quamdiu vixit. Tertio, si peccatum Capitis imputatur corpori, cur non etiam peccatum corporis imputetur capiti? nam si Adam & reliqui homines unum simul corpus sive totum constituunt, quam toti corpori membra singula conveniunt, tam etiam singulorum membrorum attributa conveniunt toti.
english: You seek a third likeness from the civil body. It is two-membered. First you set before our eyes a King making war on a neighboring people, who is held an enemy not only himself—he who willed to make it, decreed it in counsel, and pursued it with arms—but also all subjects, most of whom neither willed nor consented to this war, and though they do not act and stay at home, if they come into the enemies' hands they are caught unawares, shaken, and by right of war killed. Mark, I pray, how this likeness does not fit. First, if it is admitted, it must be confessed that as those who neither approve the war nor consent to it nor share the King's counsel are taken and slain by the enemy, so even if there were no vice in us and our will abhorred sin, Adam's actual sin would still be imputed to us—which many who feel with you dare not confess. Next, it would follow that not only Adam's first sin but also his other actual sins must be imputed to us, since he was head of the human race as long as he lived. Third, if the Head's sin is imputed to the body, why not also the body's sin to the head? For if Adam and the rest of men constitute one body or whole together, as the several members suit the whole body, so also the attributes of the several members suit the whole.

source_text: Corpus enim non est unum membrum, sed multa: nec si pes caput non est, consequens est pedem non esse ex corpore. Imputatur autem toti corpori non modo quod caput facit, sed etiam quod pes. Itaque cum populum suum Deus consideraret ut unum corpus in deserto, toti populo ob unius Achan, qui populi illius caput non erat, iratus est. Si ergo omnes homines coalescunt cum Adamo in unum corpus, non unius Adami unum peccatum, sed omnia Adami, omnia aliorum hominum peccata toti corpori imputanda sunt. Quod tamen nec Apostolus, nec tu secundum Apostolum probas. Quarto, quid obstat quominus haec similitudo accommodetur etiam aliis stirpibus & parentibus respectu posterorum? Exempli causa, cur Noachus etiam non sit secundi mundi caput, Abrahamus Israelitarum, & ita de reliquis; unde magna exurget moles peccatorum imputandorum? Caput enim dicitur Adamus, & regi comparatur, non quia primus homo fuit, sed quia ab eo ducimus originem. Negatione relationis ad priorem ad nos minime refertur, sed relatione, quam generando sibi acquisivit, ad posteros. Quinto, si quis in manus hostium incidat quem certo noverint a bello fuisse & voluntate, & opere alienum, nec in id consensisse, hunc si interficiunt innocentem, mihi immanes & crudeles esse videntur. Alioqui qua Regis est mens bellum inferentis, eadem praesumitur esse mens omnium subditorum. Transfugis autem, iisque qui se dedunt, parci solet.
english: For the body is not one member but many: and if the foot is not the head, it does not follow that the foot is not of the body. And what the head does is imputed to the whole body, and also what the foot does. So when God considered his people as one body in the desert, he was angry with the whole people for one Achan, who was not that people's head. If therefore all men coalesce with Adam into one body, not one sin of one Adam but all Adam's and all other men's sins must be imputed to the whole body. Yet neither the Apostle nor you according to the Apostle approve that. Fourth, what stands in the way of fitting this likeness also to other stocks and parents respecting their posterity? For example, why should Noah not also be head of the second world, Abraham of the Israelites, and so of the rest—whence a great mass of sins to be imputed would arise? For Adam is called head and compared to a king not because he was the first man, but because we draw origin from him. He is not referred to us by negation of relation to a prior, but by the relation he acquired to posterity by generating. Fifth, if someone falls into enemies' hands whom they know for certain was alien to the war in will and deed and did not consent to it, if they kill that innocent man they seem to me monstrous and cruel. Otherwise the mind of the King making war is presumed to be the mind of all subjects. But deserters and those who surrender are usually spared.

source_text: Sexto, Rex bellum infert vicinae genti non per se solum, sed per subditos. Ipse imperat, subditi exequuntur. Ipse est causa principalis, subditi instrumentalis: ac illi ipsi, qui bello se non immiscent, subditi tenentur parere Regi, eumque pro viribus tueri & juvare. Adamus vero peccavit solus, ipse sibi, non nobis peccatum illud suum imperavit; ipse solus quod sibi imperavit, mandavit executioni, & opere perfecit. Posterorum nemo actioni illi interfuit, aut mentem manumve admovit suam. Non igitur ipse causa principalis fuit illius peccati, posteri causae instrumentales. Non ad committendum illud peccatum nos ei ut membra, ut organa, ut subditi, vel famuli accommodavimus, sed ipse solus, ut tunc extabat in rerum natura, ita peccatum illud per se ipsum commisit, nec posterorum quisquam illi adfuit. Bellum est commune Regis & subditorum opus, fitque a corpore regni: peccatum actuale Adami, ut tu ipse loqueris, unius personae fuit.
english: Sixth. A King does not wage war on his neighbors by his own hand alone: he orders, and subjects carry out; he is the principal cause, they the instrumental—and even those who never take the field remain bound, as subjects, to obey him and to shield and aid him with their strength. Adam is not like that King. He sinned by himself. He laid that command of sin on himself, not on us; he alone executed what he had commanded himself and finished it in deed. No one among his posterity joined that action, nor lent mind or hand. So the scheme of principal and instrumental causes fails here: we did not lend ourselves to him as members, organs, subjects, or servants for committing that crime. He alone, as he then stood among the things that were, committed it through himself, and none of posterity stood with him at it. War is the shared work of King and subjects and is done by the kingdom's body; Adam's actual sin—as you yourself speak—was of one person only.

source_text: Septimo, peccati imputatio, & poenae inflictio, actiones sunt judiciariae. Fieri debent a judice secundum leges. Lex autem est, Anima quae peccaverit ipsa morietur. Non feret iniquitatem filii pater, nec patris filius. Contra in bello leges silent, &, ut in statu perturbato, omnia vi fiunt: nec finis est ut fiat justitia, sed victoria, cuius causa gens cui bellum infertur in id unum intenta est, ut inferenti incommodet. Quoniam autem Regis potentia in subditorum multitudine & opibus sita est, eam ut atterant, & imminuant, & evertant, subditos Regi pro viribus, & bonis, & vita spoliare conantur: in quo scopus est & regi aegre facere, illique incommodare, & se tueri, ac opibus augere. Deus vero cum peccatum hominibus imputat & vindictam exercet, Judicis partibus fungitur.
english: Seventh. To impute sin and to inflict a penalty are acts of a court. A judge must do them according to laws. And the law runs: The soul that has sinned shall itself die. A father shall not bear a son's iniquity, nor a son a father's. War is another regime: laws fall silent, and, as in a broken order, all things are done by force; nor is the end that justice be done, but victory—for whose sake the people under attack work only to harm the one who makes war. Because a King's strength sits in his subjects' numbers and wealth, they try to grind that strength down, diminish it, and overthrow it by stripping subjects of force and goods and life: both to vex the King and hurt him, and to save themselves and grow richer. God, when he charges men with sin and takes vengeance, does not play that war-game: he takes a Judge's part.

source_text: Deus vero cum peccatum hominibus imputat & vindictam exercet, Judicis partibus fungitur, nihilque habet ob oculos praeter justitiam, qua suum cuique tribuit. Itaque nulli alienum peccatum attribuit, nulli poenam irrogat ob peccatum, quod nec in se habuit, nec admisit: summa est justitiae eius puritas, summus nitor, & splendor. Octavo, Rex cum bellum denunciat vel infert, actu Rex est, & qua Rex caput subditorum, & ad subditos relationem actu habet, & vicissim subditi ad eum. Itaque, cum actu & plures sint, & se mutuis relationibus respiciant, actu unum corpus constituunt, ex Rege & subditis constans. Adamus vero cum peccavit actu pater non erat, actu relationem ad nos nullam habebat, non erat actu caput nostrum, & vicissim nos ad eum nullam relationem actu habebamus. Tum demum nata est haec relatio, cum pater esse, & liberos habere coepit. Est autem, postquam creatus fuerat, centum & triginta annis demum Seth natus, ex quo nos omnes sumus. Itaque qui nulli tum eramus, cum eo coire in societatem, aut componere corpus non potuimus. Subditi enim sunt actu, sunt actu subditi, actu Rex eorum est caput, actu eius imperata tenentur exequi, actu cum eo corpus componunt, actu eum vel consilio vel opibus, vel manu, vel saltem votis juvant. Deinde, an quia eramus in Adamo potentia, sequitur quod ille fecit nos fecisse, nobisque eius actiones imputari debere?
english: But God, when he imputes sin to men and exercises vengeance, plays a Judge's part, and has nothing before his eyes but justice, which gives each his due. So he attributes no alien sin to anyone, nor lays a penalty on anyone for a sin he neither had in himself nor committed: the purity of his justice is highest, its brightness and splendor highest. Eighth: when a King declares or makes war, he is actually King, and as King head of subjects, and actually has relation to subjects, and they to him. So when they actually are many and regard one another by mutual relations, they actually constitute one body consisting of King and subjects. But Adam, when he sinned, was not actually father, actually had no relation to us, was not actually our head, and we actually had no relation to him. That relation was born only when he began to be a father and have children. And after he was created, only at a hundred and thirty years was Seth born, from whom we all are. So we who then were nothing could not join society with him or compose a body. Subjects actually are subjects; actually their King is head; actually they are bound to execute his commands; actually they compose a body with him; actually they help him by counsel or wealth or hand or at least by vows. Next: because we were in Adam potentially, does it follow that what he did we did, and that his actions ought to be imputed to us?

source_text: Tu eras in eo potentia, an igitur fuisti vel actu, vel potentia maritus Evae primae parentis nostrae? An actu vel potentia genuisti Sethum secundum parentem generis humani? An in eo actu vel potentia resipuisti a peccato? Nempe illam unam actionem tu in eo fecisti, concupivisti scilicet fructum arboris vetitae, gustasti eius suavitatem, blanditiis & suasionibus uxoris tuae Evae te persuaderi sivisti, cupiditate sciendi bonum & malum flagrasti, divinitatem quandam affectasti, manum arbori prohibitae admovisti, fructum eius dentibus comminuisti. Equidem non capio cur istam unam actionem in Adamo ediderimus, a caeteris autem eius actionibus abstinuerimus. Alterum similitudinis membrum, seu, si ita mavis, similitudinem integram his verbis expressisti. Eodem modo si in urbe populus sit rebellis, & seditionem moveat in principis ministros, vel satellites, & eam ob causam princeps populum illum rebellionis damnet, & armis persequatur, seditio illa non tantum eorum esse censetur, qui se commoverunt primi, & injuriam fecerunt satellitibus, sed etiam imputatur coetui & toti communitati, seu societati civium. Omnes habentur rei rebelles, bona proscribuntur, nec parcitur vitae; quia sunt ex corpore, & societate illius urbis rebellis. Sic se res habet in genere humano. Primus homo tanquam caput omnium hominum, rebellans Deo & peccans in Deum, justo Dei judicio punitus est; non tantum ipse in persona sua, sed tota natura humana & omnes homines, qui sunt tanquam unum corpus, & coeunt in unam societatem; Et haec rebellio capitis, quae totam naturam pervasit, tribuitur & imputatur omnibus hominibus.
english: You were in him potentially—were you then actually or potentially husband of Eve our first parent? Did you actually or potentially beget Seth, second parent of the human race? Did you in him actually or potentially repent of sin? Namely you did that one action in him: you coveted the fruit of the forbidden tree, tasted its sweetness, let yourself be persuaded by Eve your wife's blandishments and suasions, burned with desire to know good and evil, affected a kind of divinity, put your hand to the forbidden tree, crushed its fruit with your teeth. I for my part do not grasp why we should have performed that one action in Adam and yet abstained from his other actions. You expressed the other member of the likeness—or, if you prefer, a whole likeness—in these words. In the same way if in a city the people are rebellious and raise sedition against the prince's ministers or satellites, and for that cause the prince condemns that people of rebellion and pursues them with arms, that sedition is judged not only theirs who first stirred and injured the satellites, but is also imputed to the assembly and whole community or society of citizens. All are held guilty rebels, goods are proscribed, nor is life spared; because they are of the body and society of that rebellious city. So it stands with the human race. The first man as head of all men, rebelling against God and sinning against God, was punished by God's just judgment; not only himself in his person, but all human nature and all men, who are as one body and gather into one society; And this rebellion of the head, which pervaded all nature, is attributed and imputed to all men.

source_text: Quae ad praecedentem similitudinem dicta sunt hanc ipsam quoque evertunt. Addam tamen pauca. Modo Adamum comparabas Regi bellum inferenti: Nunc eundem comparas populo rebellanti adversus Regis ministros. At quid habet Adamus commune cum seditiosa & tumultuante plebe alicuius urbis, in societatem rebellionis ipsos suos magistratus trahente, nisi eam coerceant pro virili, & se Regi purgent? Hinc facilius concludas multitudinis hominum peccata ipsi Adamo, quam unius Adami primum peccatum actuale toti hominum multitudini imputari debere. Deinde, putasne justum & aequum Regem id crimen illud rebellionis imputare, quos pro comperto habet in rebellionem non consensisse in illa urbe? Discernit proculdubio pro sua aequitate inter rebelles & non rebelles, seditiosos & in officio constantes. Praeterea, annon inde sequeretur multo propius & certius, multitudinis impiae peccata imputari paucis inter improbos delitescentibus piis, quam unius hominis peccatum unum, nullo alio homine praesente, immo existente, commissum omnibus hominibus imputari? Attamen ab illa imputatione Dei justitia abhorret. Absit tibi, dicebat Abraham Gen. 18. 25. Ut facias tale quidpiam, morti tradendo justum cum injusto, ut ita sit justo sicut injusto: Absit tibi; An judex totius terrae non exerceret jus? Vides quantopere pater credentium pugnare cum divina justitia credebat, si paucissimi justi magnae civitatis rebellis & peccatricis punitione cum civium multitudine involverentur, & nos eius filii audebimus Deo eiusmodi justitiam tribuere, quae unius hominis culpam imputet omnibus, non modo ad mortem aeternam, sed etiam ad eam poenam quae sit ipsa proprie malum culpae, & causa omnium peccatorum? Absit, absit a nobis talis, de Deo nostro, de mundi judice, cuius aequitas & justitia nobis notissima est, cogitatio!
english: What was said against the preceding likeness overturns this one too. Yet I will add a few things. Just now you compared Adam to a King making war: now you compare the same man to a people rebelling against the King's ministers. But what has Adam in common with the seditious and tumultuous commons of some city, drawing even their own magistrates into the society of rebellion unless they curb it with all their might and clear themselves to the King? From this you would more easily conclude that the multitude's sins ought to be imputed to Adam himself than that one Adam's first actual sin ought to be imputed to the whole multitude of men. Next, do you think a just and equitable King would impute that crime of rebellion to those he knows for certain did not consent to the rebellion in that city? He doubtless discerns by his equity between rebels and non-rebels, the seditious and those constant in duty. Further, would it not follow much more nearly and surely that the sins of an impious multitude are imputed to a few pious men lurking among the wicked, than that one sin of one man, committed with no other man present—indeed existing—is imputed to all men? Yet God's justice abhors that imputation. Far be it from you, said Abraham Gen. 18:25, to do such a thing, delivering the just to death with the unjust, so that it be with the just as with the unjust: Far be it from you; shall the Judge of all the earth not do right? You see how strongly the father of believers thought it would clash with divine justice if the fewest just of a great rebellious and sinning city were involved in punishment with the multitude of citizens—and shall we his sons dare attribute to God a justice that imputes one man's fault to all, not only unto eternal death, but even unto that penalty which is itself properly the evil of fault and the cause of all sins? Far, far from us such a thought of our God, the world's Judge, whose equity and justice are most known to us!

source_text: GAR. Mittamus nunc quidem Rhetoricationes, & quod de poena dicitur, quae sit ipsa specie malum culpae, quia de hoc & aliquid dictum est superius, & recurret postea ea de re fusius disputandi occasio. Argumenti duntaxat vim attendamus, quod ita pertexi potest. Justos cum injustis eadem condemnatione & morte involvi, alienum est a Dei justitia, teste Abrahamo. Atqui in alieni peccati imputatione, justi cum injustis, eadem condemnatione & morte involverentur. Ergo alieni peccati imputatio est a Dei justitia aliena. PLAC. Qua occasione, & quam apposite testimonium Abrahami fuerit a me allatum Lector prudens, si placet, considerabit. Interim Argumentum quod hic vir doctus contexuit libenter pro meo habebo, modo in minore alieni peccati imputatio, non quaelibet intelligatur, sed ea duntaxat, de qua inter nos lis est, nempe antecedens omne peccatum nobis inhaerens aut a nobis commissum.
english: GAR. Let us now drop the rhetorics, and what is said of a penalty that is itself in kind the evil of fault—something was said of this above, and occasion will return later to dispute it more fully. Let us attend only to the force of the argument, which can be woven thus. That the just be involved with the unjust in the same condemnation and death is alien to God's justice, Abraham witnessing. But in the imputation of another's sin, the just would be involved with the unjust in the same condemnation and death. Therefore the imputation of another's sin is alien to God's justice. PLAC. On what occasion, and how aptly, Abraham's testimony was brought by me the prudent Reader will consider if he please. Meanwhile the Argument the learned man has woven here I gladly take as my own, provided that in the minor "imputation of another's sin" is not understood of any whatever, but only of that about which the dispute between us is—namely that which precedes every sin inhering in us or committed by us.

source_text: GAR. Hic primum responderi posset, qua ab Abrahamo causa disceptatur, eam a Quaestione imputatae Adami inobedientiae longe abesse. Abrahamus enim de iis loquitur, qui non omnes eadem conditione agebant, sed alii justi erant, alii injustitiae mancipati: & quorum ea erat ratio, ut non modo justi propter impios, quibus commixti erant, in earundem poenarum consortium trahi possent, sed etiam impii propter justos eiusdem beneficii & conservationis esse participes; Unde Abrahamus utrumque a Deo precibus contendit, tum ut ne justi propter impiorum scelera pereant, tum ut impiis propter justos ignoscatur. Atqui longe aliter res habet in nostro negotio. Nam primo inter eos quibus Adae peccatum imputatur, hoc quidem respectu, nulla est justitiae injustitiaeve distinctio; neque enim solus Adamus injustus est, posteri vero justi & innocentes, sed omnes naturae seminis corruptione polluti, sicut explicatum est cap. 2. Deinde nec quinquaginta, nec viginti, nec decem, ac ne unus quidem est in hoc ordine carnaliter generatorum, propter cuius justitiam Deus caeteris parcere aut velit, aut debeat. Itaque ex Abrahami verbis duci non potest legitima adversus imputationem peccati Adae consequentia. PLAC. Horum duorum discriminum prius quidem appositum est, si de imputatione mediata agitur, quae supponit & consequitur inhaerentem corruptionem seu injustitiam.
english: GAR. Here it could first be answered that the cause Abraham debates is far from the Question of Adam's imputed disobedience. For Abraham speaks of those who were not all in the same condition, but some were just, others enslaved to injustice: and whose ratio was such that not only could the just be drawn into partnership of the same penalties for the impious with whom they were mixed, but also the impious could share the same benefit and preservation for the just; Whence Abraham pressed God with prayers for both—that the just not perish for the impious' crimes, and that the impious be pardoned for the just. Yet our business stands far otherwise. For first among those to whom Adam's sin is imputed, in this respect there is no distinction of justice or injustice; for not Adam alone is unjust and posterity just and innocent, but all are polluted by corruption of the seed's nature, as was explained in cap. 2. Next there are neither fifty nor twenty nor ten nor even one in this order of those carnally generated for whose justice God would or ought to spare the rest. So from Abraham's words no legitimate consequence against imputation of Adam's sin can be drawn. PLAC. Of these two discriminations the former is indeed apt if mediate imputation is in view, which presupposes and follows inhering corruption or injustice.

source_text: Ideo enim eadem condemnatione & morte cum injusto Adamo involvimur, quoniam & ipsi in nobis ipsis injusti sumus: sed si de imputatione immediata, quam solam impugno, agitur, falsum est; antecedit enim imputatio corruptionem haereditariam ut culpae poenam. Itaque nostra injustitia huiusmodi imputationem & condemnationem sequitur ut effectum, non antecedit ut causa. Non ideo eadem cum injusto Adamo condemnatione involvimur, quia sumus injusti, sed contra ideo sumus injusti, quia eadem cum injusto Adamo condemnatione involvimur: ita enim sumus imputatione peccati actualis ab Adamo commissi peccatores, id est, rei, & ut puniatur imputatum nobis illud peccatum sumus inhaerenter injusti. Sepósita igitur hac imputatione seu condemnatione nocens est Adamus, nos innocentes. Quare illa imputatio seu condemnatio, judice Abrahamo, pugnat cum Dei justitia. Posterius discrimen quid ad rem faciat, de qua agitur, non video.
english: For that is why we are involved in the same condemnation and death with unjust Adam—because we ourselves are unjust in ourselves: but if immediate imputation, which alone I impugn, is in view, that is false; for the imputation precedes hereditary corruption as the penalty of the fault. So our injustice follows this kind of imputation and condemnation as effect, and does not precede as cause. We are not involved in the same condemnation with unjust Adam because we are unjust, but on the contrary we are unjust because we are involved in the same condemnation with unjust Adam: for so by imputation of the actual sin Adam committed we are made sinners—that is, guilty—and that that imputed sin may be punished we are made inherently unjust. Set aside this imputation or condemnation and Adam is the guilty one, we innocents. Therefore that imputation or condemnation, Abraham judging, clashes with God's justice. What the latter discrimination does for the matter at hand, I do not see.

source_text: GAR. Verum ad istam solutionem, progrediendum est ulterius in deprecationis huius Abrahamicae consideratione. Dicimus ergo non esse simpliciter & absolute concedendum, abhorrere omnino a justitia Dei ut justi sive personaliter innocentes eadem aliquando poena involvantur cum injustis & criminosis, quantumvis inde suae deprecationis argumentum desumat Abrahamus. 1. quia Deus ipse expressis & disertis verbis testatur se contrarium aliquando facere. Ita enim Prophetam suum alloquitur, Ezech. XXI. 8. 9. Dic terrae Israelis, Sic ait Jehovah; ecce ego exeram gladium meum e vagina sua, ut exscindam ex te justum & improbum: ut exscindam ex te justum & improbum: idcirco prodibit gladius meus e vagina sua contra omnem carnem a Meridie ad Aquilonem.
english: GAR. But against that solution one must go further in considering this Abrahamic deprecation. We say, then, that it is not to be conceded simply and absolutely that it wholly abhors God's justice that the just, or personally innocent, should sometimes be involved in the same penalty with the unjust and criminal, however much Abraham takes from that the argument of his plea. 1. because God himself testifies in express and clear words that he sometimes does the contrary. For so he addresses his prophet, Ezek. 21:8–9: Say to the land of Israel, Thus says Jehovah; behold, I will draw my sword from its sheath, that I may cut off from you the just and the wicked: that I may cut off from you the just and the wicked: therefore my sword shall go forth from its sheath against all flesh from the South to the North.

source_text: 2. Quia eius divinae dispensationis exempla quaedam Abrahamus ignorare non poterat, quae Deus omnium oculis obiecerat, primo in diluvio generali, deinde in Sodomorum subversione, tertio in Abimelechi familia, quae omnia supra suo loco produximus. PLAC. Hoc vero non est nodum solvere, sed secare. Quid si Ezech. 21 per justum intelligitur is, qui sibi, aut aliis, justus videtur, ut quibusdam placet interpretibus? Quid si justus intelligitur per comparationem cum aliis nequioribus? juxta illud Mich. 7: 4. optimus eorum est similis spinae; rectissimus prae pineto est.
english: 2. Because Abraham could not have been ignorant of certain examples of that divine dispensation which God had set before the eyes of all—first in the general flood, then in the overthrow of Sodom, third in Abimelech's household—all of which we produced above in their place. PLAC. But this is not to untie the knot, but to cut it. What if in Ezek. 21 by 'the just' is meant one who seems just to himself or to others, as it pleases some interpreters? What if 'just' is understood by comparison with others more wicked?—according to that word of Mic. 7:4: the best of them is like a thorn; the most upright is worse than a thorn-hedge.

source_text: Quid, quod nullus est omnino justus, & qui non peccet: omnes peccaverunt & destituti sunt gloria Dei: ipsi infantes recens nati inhaerente vitio polluti sunt, ac propterea illis poenis digni quibus a Dei justitia afficiuntur. Taceo communes poenas aliter sese in piis habere, aliter in impiis. Illorum enim respectu sunt castigationes, & poenae paternae, & vitae peccato & miseriae obnoxiae in perfecte sanctam ac beatam commutatio; itaque nulla iis fit injuria, uti nec impiorum liberis, qui ita ob peccatum originale, quo parentibus similes sunt, moriuntur, ut tamen a multis peccatis, quae si prorogata illis vita fuisset, commisissent, & a multis calamitatibus in quas incidissent, praeserventur; id quod in aliquo beneficio reponi potest. Minime igitur pugnat hoc Dei apud Ezech. oraculum cum Abrahami testimonio. Exempla divinae dispensationis quae vir doctus subjungit, eius causae obsunt. Non enim eadem cum impiis condemnatione Noachum in diluvio generali, nec Lothum in Sodomorum subversione Dei justitia involuit. Novit enim Dominus pios e tentatione eripere, injustos autem in diem judicii poenas dantes servare: quanquam Sodomorum subversio secuta est non antecessit, ut memoria lapsus supponere videtur Vir doctus, istud Abrahami cum Deo colloquium. Idem de edito in Abimelechi familia exemplo dici debet: narratur enim eius historia demum Gen. cap. 20. & ita narratur, ut appareat idem cum Abrahamo sensisse Abimelechum de Dei justitia.
english: What of this—that there is no one at all who is just and who does not sin: all have sinned and are destitute of the glory of God: even infants newly born are polluted by inherent vice, and therefore worthy of those penalties with which they are afflicted by God's justice. I pass over that common penalties stand otherwise in the pious, otherwise in the impious. For in respect of the former they are chastisements and paternal penalties, and a commuting of a life liable to sin and misery into one perfectly holy and blessed; so no injury is done them—nor to the children of the impious, who so die for original sin, by which they are like their parents, that they are yet preserved from many sins they would have committed if life had been prolonged to them, and from many calamities into which they would have fallen; which can be counted for some benefit. Least of all, then, does this oracle of God in Ezekiel clash with Abraham's testimony. The examples of divine dispensation which the learned man subjoins stand against his cause. For God's justice did not involve Noah in the same condemnation with the impious in the general flood, nor Lot in the overthrow of Sodom. For the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation, but to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished: although the overthrow of Sodom followed and did not precede—as the learned man's slip of memory seems to suppose—that colloquy of Abraham with God. The same must be said of the example published in Abimelech's household: for its history is narrated only at Gen. 20, and is so narrated that Abimelech appears to have felt the same as Abraham concerning God's justice.

source_text: GAR. Quomodo igitur, inquies, illud semel & iterum Capite 18. Abrahamus ingerit, abesse debere a Deo ut perimat justum cum injusto? Resp. 1. De hac Abrahae deprecatione ita indicare nonnullos, ut non modo negent, usquequaque certam esse, quam probat sententiam, sed affirment etiam multiplicem habere confutationem. Ita enim Pererius, qui ubi eam confutationem proponit, concludit tandem in hac verba. Abraham similis oratori pessimam causam defendenti, in omnes se partes versanti, ut, undecunque potest, rapiat qualecunque defensionis praesidium, miscet verba, variatque sententias, involvit rationes etiam non admodum probabiles, nec proposito suo valde congruentes, omnem demum movet lapidem, ut impetret quod a Deo postulat, non tam sententiarum pondere, aut robore argumentorum cum Deo agens, quam ardore charitatis & flagrantissimo pietatis erga miseros illos homines affectu. PLAC. Probatne, an improbat Vir doctus illa Pererii verba? Si improbat, cur laudat? Si probat, miror eum probare potuisse tam audacia, tantoque Patriarcha, patri credentium, tam injuriosa Jesuitae verba. Equidem qui me filium esse Abrahae Dei beneficio maximo credo, & laetor, vix ferre possum tam inverecunde de meo patre loquentem. Quantus enim erat Patriarcha, Dei confederatus, Dei amicus, Dei colloquio tam saepe dignatus, insignis Propheta? Quis credat eum voluisse apud Deum pessimam causam defendere, & rationibus tanquam necessariis uti minus probabilibus? Quid, quod Deus illam rationem non reprehendit, sed admisit, & nos decet credentes Patris credentium imitari fidem?
english: GAR. How then, you will say, does Abraham once and again in chapter 18 press that it ought to be far from God to destroy the just with the unjust? Reply 1. Some so treat this deprecation of Abraham that they not only deny the opinion he proves is altogether certain, but even affirm it has a manifold confutation. So Pererius, who when he sets out that confutation concludes at last in these words: Abraham, like an orator defending a worst cause, turning himself every way so that from wherever he can he may snatch any shield of defense, mixes words and varies sentences, wraps in reasons not very probable nor much fitting his purpose, and finally moves every stone to obtain what he asks of God, dealing with God not so much by the weight of sentences or the strength of arguments as by the heat of charity and the most burning affection of piety toward those wretched men. PLAC. Does the learned man approve, or disapprove, those words of Pererius? If he disapproves, why does he praise them? If he approves, I marvel that he could approve words so bold, and so injurious to so great a Patriarch, the father of believers, from a Jesuit. For my part, who by God's greatest gift believe myself a son of Abraham and rejoice in it, I can scarcely bear one speaking so shamelessly of my father. For how great was the Patriarch, confederate of God, friend of God, so often honored with God's colloquy, a distinguished Prophet? Who would believe he meant to defend a worst cause before God, and to use less probable reasons as if they were necessary? What of this—that God did not rebuke that reason but admitted it, and it becomes us believers to imitate the faith of the Father of believers?

source_text: GAR. 2. Abrahamo certa quidem fuit & immota haec regula quam nullus fidelis non agnoscit, fieri nunquam omnino posse, ut Deus injuste quidquam designet: sed in speciali videre non poterat, quomodo haec innocentium clades cum justitia Dei convenire posset. Quaerit ergo non obluctandi animo, sed ut hunc scrupulum sibi eximat, an Deus justum perditurus sit cum impio. Sic. PLAC. Suntne igitur illa verba dubitantis, aut simpliciter quaerentis, Abfit tibi ut facias tale quidpiam, morti tradendo justum cum injusto, ut ita sit justo sicut injusto: Abfit tibi. An judex totius terrae non exerceret jus? Quae sunt assertiones vehementes ac fortes, tanquam certae & indubitatae, si hae non sunt? Certe igitur sciebat, nec Deum posse quicquam inique designare, nec justum esse apud Deum judicem, ut pariter justus ac injustus damnetur, itaque hoc unum flagitabat, non modo ut Deus justos propter impios non damnaret, id quod ei videbatur nimis a Dei justitia alienum, sed ut propter paucos justos parceret vel impiis, vel saltem ipsi loco seu urbi, id quod Dei bonitatem summam non dedecere videbatur. Agebatur enim non de qualicunque castigatione, sed de poena judiciaria, & quodammodo aeterna: cuiusmodi poena certum est nunquam justos propter impios puniri.
english: GAR. 2. To Abraham this rule was indeed certain and unmoved, which no believer fails to acknowledge—that it can never at all come to pass that God should appoint anything unjust: but in the special case he could not see how this slaughter of innocents could agree with God's justice. He asks, therefore, not with a mind to resist, but that he may clear this scruple for himself, whether God is about to destroy the just with the wicked. So. PLAC. Are those then the words of one doubting, or simply asking: Far be it from you to do any such thing, delivering the just to death with the unjust, so that it should be with the just as with the unjust: Far be it from you. Shall the Judge of all the earth not do right? What are vehement and strong assertions, as certain and undoubted, if these are not? He knew for certain, then, both that God cannot appoint anything iniquitous, and that it is not just before God as judge that the just and the unjust be damned alike; and so he begged this one thing—not only that God should not damn the just for the sake of the unjust, which seemed to him too alien from God's justice, but that for the sake of a few just he should spare even the unjust, or at least the place or city itself, which seemed not unworthy of God's highest goodness. For the matter was not about any chastisement whatever, but about judicial punishment, and in a manner eternal: of which kind of punishment it is certain the just are never punished for the sake of the unjust.

source_text: GAR. 3. Cum Deus in exequendis judiciis suis, aliquando ex justitiae rigore agat, aliquando justitiam aequitate temperet, dico Abrahamum, pro charitate sua in Sodomitas, percupiisse, ut Deus judicium illud aliqua misericordiae testificatione temperaret: Itaque seposito nunc quidem Dei rigorosiori modo, unice haesisse in ordinaria & communiori justitiae divinae dispensatione, cum praesertim alte animo ipsius insideret foedus illud cum ipso nuper initum Gen. 17. nimirum foedus gratiae, in quo Deus promisit se non imputaturum aliena peccata, Ierem. XXXI. 29. 30. Et cujus foederis nonnullam aliquando suavitatem etiam iis exhibet, qui ad illud non pertinent. PLAC. Duae sunt partes orationis Abrahami: altera asserit non convenire justitiae Dei, ut justus pereat cum impio: altera petit a Deo, ut propter paucos justos parcat urbi; id quod, fateor, non exspectaretur esse, sed testificationem potius misericordiae: itaque haec pars ad rem quam agimus non facit. Ab altera illa ductum est argumentum nostrum, quae est non aequitati modo, sed rigori etiam justitiae, omni ex parte congruens. Quare quo spectet ista responsio, & quid argumento meo afferat novi, nullus video. Illud tantum reponam, Si in foedere gratiae Deus promisit se non imputaturum aliena peccata, igitur cum nobis non imputare peccatum actuale primum Adami: Quomodo ergo nos ob illud peccatum punit, inflictâ scilicet poena judiciaria, nempe corruptione originali? Caeterum non eo inficias, quin Deus nonnunquam eadem condemnatione temporali pios cum impiis involvat; quippe, nullus est ita pius & justus, ut non peccet interdum, & pii non, uti par est, eorum, quibus admixti sunt, peccata detestantur fugiunt, redarguunt. Interim tamen huiusmodi calamitates cedunt piis in castigationes paternas, quibus cavetur ne aeternum pereant cum impiis. Nos autem in hac causa de imputatione judiciaria agimus & damnatione ad poenas proprie dictas & justitiae satisfactorias, quales illae sunt quas lex comminatur & justitia, ut sibi satisfiat, exigit, quas ob aliena peccata portare innocentes minime nocentium vades, contendimus cum Abrahae testimonio, cum Dei justitia & aequitate pugnare.
english: GAR. 3. Since God, in executing his judgments, sometimes acts from the rigor of justice, sometimes tempers justice with equity, I say Abraham, for his charity toward the Sodomites, earnestly desired that God would temper that judgment with some testimony of mercy: and so, setting aside for now God's more rigorous mode, he clung only to the ordinary and more common dispensation of divine justice—especially since that covenant lately struck with him in Gen. 17 sat deep in his mind, namely the covenant of grace, in which God promised he would not impute others' sins, Jer. 31:29–30. And of which covenant he sometimes shows some sweetness even to those who do not belong to it. PLAC. There are two parts of Abraham's speech: one asserts that it does not agree with God's justice that the just perish with the wicked; the other asks of God that for the sake of a few just he spare the city—which, I confess, would not be looked for as due, but rather as a testimony of mercy: so this part does not serve the matter we are treating. From that other part our argument is drawn, which agrees not only with equity but also with the rigor of justice in every respect. So what this reply aims at, and what new thing it brings to my argument, I see none. I will only reply this: If in the covenant of grace God promised he would not impute others' sins, then he does not impute to us Adam's first actual sin: How then does he punish us for that sin, namely by inflicting a judicial penalty—original corruption?
