I say it is original vice or hereditary corruption inhering in individual humans, but not Adam's actual sin immediately imputed to individual humans. Your opinion the reasons you brought do not prove: for to them, as you see, I have replied.

source_text: Ego meam sic probo. Si quod peccatum Apostolus docet Rom. v. fuisse ab Adamo cum omnibus hominibus communicatum, illud profecto est, quod per Adamum docet in mundum introiisse, & per id mortem, ita ut mors in omnes homines pertransierit. Atqui peccatum illud, quod docet per Adamum in mundum introiisse, & per id mortem, est corruptio haereditaria, non autem peccatum actuale Adami praecise sumptum. Ergo si aliquod peccatum Apostolus docet, uti revera docet, ab Adamo cum omnibus hominibus communicatum, illud profecto est corruptio haereditaria, non autem peccatum actuale Adami. Maiorem non negabis: est enim manifesta. Certe peccatum per quod ait mortem introiisse in mundum, hoc est, ut ipse exponit, & tu post eum, in omnes homines, est illud cui proxime generis humani mortem & condemnationem ascribit. Minorem probo. Primam rationem mihi ministrat ipsum nomen peccati ἡ ἁμαρτία: sic enim (ut doctissimus Beza ad hunc versum notavit) vocare solet Apostolus morbum illum haereditarium: adeo quidem ut vix apud Paulum addito articulo aliud declaret. Morbus autem haereditarius non est peccatum actuale Adami, sed corruptio, & vitium ab illo ortum.
english: I prove mine thus. If any sin the Apostle teaches in Rom. 5. was communicated by Adam with all humans, that certainly is what he teaches entered into the world through Adam, and through it death, so that death passed through unto all humans. But that sin which he teaches entered into the world through Adam, and through it death, is hereditary corruption, not however Adam's actual sin taken precisely. Therefore if the Apostle teaches any sin, as he truly does, communicated by Adam with all humans, that certainly is hereditary corruption, not however Adam's actual sin. You will not deny the Major: for it is manifest. Certainly the sin through which he says death entered into the world, that is, as he himself exposes, and you after him, into all humans, is that to which he nearest ascribes the death and condemnation of the human race. I prove the Minor. The first reason the very name of sin he hamartia supplies me: for so (as the most learned Beza noted on this verse) the Apostle is accustomed to call that hereditary disease: so much so that scarcely in Paul with the article added does it declare anything else. But a hereditary disease is not Adam's actual sin, but corruption, and vice arisen from it.

source_text: GAR. Etsi saepius peccatum originale, inhaerens in visceribus hominum, nomine ἡ ἁμαρτία designat Apostolus, non est tamen necessarium, ut ubicumque vocabulum illud usurpat, intelligatur id peccatum: quod facile agnoscet, qui Paulum legerit de peccato loquentem, Rom. VI. 2. 6. 23: 2. Cor. 15. 56: 2. Thess. 2. 3. Heb. XII. 4.
english: GAR. Although the Apostle more often designates original sin, inhering in the entrails of humans, by the name he hamartia, it is nevertheless not necessary that wherever he uses that word, that sin be understood: which anyone will easily recognize who has read Paul speaking of sin, Rom. VI. 2. 6. 23: 2. Cor. 15. 56: 2. Thess. 2. 3. Heb. XII. 4.

source_text: PLAC. Haec prima mea ratio non est mea, sed maximi viri, Bezae, quem Vir doctus per latus meum ferit. Vide sis eius Annot. ad Rom. 5. 12. Per peccatum eo loco id intelligo, quod Calvinus, Beza, Martyr, aliique eiusmodi primae notae Theologi, intellexerunt, à quibus caeteri, qui me innovatae doctrinae accusant, discedunt: quod ne pateret, mentionem Bezae, eiusque verba, unde nervus & robur argumenti pendebat, (adeo quidem ut vix apud Paulum addito articulo aliud declaret,) alto silentio Vir doctus praeteriit.
english: PLAC. This my first reason is not mine, but of a most great man, Beza, whom the learned man strikes through my side. See if you will his Annot. on Rom. 5. 12. By sin in that place I understand what Calvin, Beza, Martyr, and other theologians of first note of that kind understood, from whom the rest, who accuse me of innovated doctrine, depart: which lest it lie open, mention of Beza, and his words, from which the nerve and strength of the argument hung, (so much so that scarcely in Paul with the article added does it declare anything else,) the learned man passed by in deep silence.

source_text: Non enim ex eo argumentor, quod ἁμαρτία eo nomine peccatum inhaerens Apostolus designet, sed quod tam saepe, ut vix unquam aliud addito articulo declaret, hic autem additur articulus. Quis vero nescit, usitatissimam significationem anteponendam esse rarissimae, nisi forte gravis impediat ratio, quae hic nulla apparet, aut à viro docto affertur. Imo quae exempla affert, ea rationem nostram confirmant potius quam evertunt: in eis enim locis peccati nomine inhaerens vitium vel solum, vel cum fructibus suis intelligitur.
english: For I do not argue from this, that by that name hamartia the Apostle designates inhering sin, but that so often, that scarcely ever with the article added does it declare anything else, and here the article is added. But who does not know that the most usual signification is to be preferred to the rarest, unless perhaps a grave reason blocks it, which here appears none, or is brought forward by the learned man. Nay, the examples he brings confirm our reason rather than overturn it: for in those places by the name of sin inhering vice either alone, or with its fruits, is understood.

source_text: GAR. 2. Cum imputatio primi peccati, & corruptio haereditaria, sint ἀχώριστα, etiam hic peccati nomine, ex vi consequentiae, intelligi posse corruptionem illam, non inficiamur. PLAC. Si essent ἀχώριστα, quandiu manet corruptio, tandiu maneret imputatio: id quod cum omnium Theologorum sententia, quotquot non sunt Pelagiani, pugnat. Tollitur enim imputatio remissione peccati originalis, quae fit, non ut ne sit, sed ut ne imputetur amplius. Quod si peccati quod per unum hominem introiit in mundum nomine corruptio haereditaria intelligitur, quo argumento probabunt illi, qui nobis in hac causa adversantur, peccatum actuale intelligi quod nostrum non sit factum nisi per imputationem? Nam intelligendum esse peccatum inhaerens & nomen ἁμαρτία cum articulo, & maximorum theologorum autoritas, & confessio Adversariorum satis confirmant.
english: GAR. 2. Since the imputation of the first sin, and hereditary corruption, are inseparable, even here we do not deny that by the name of sin, by force of consequence, that corruption can be understood. PLAC. If they were inseparable, as long as corruption remains, so long would imputation remain: which fights with the opinion of all theologians, as many as are not Pelagians. For imputation is taken away by the remission of original sin, which is done, not so that it may not be, but so that it may no longer be imputed. But if by the name of the sin which entered into the world through one man hereditary corruption is understood, by what argument will those who oppose us in this cause prove that actual sin is understood which was not made ours except by imputation? For that inhering sin must be understood, and the name hamartia with the article, both the authority of the greatest theologians, and the adversaries' confession, sufficiently confirm.

source_text: Secundam rationem mihi suppeditant verba sequentia, εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε in mundum introiit. Per mundum autem omnes homines intelligi cum tu & fere omnes interpretes fateamini, nihil opus est probare. Sic igitur ratiocinor, Peccatum, quod per Adamum in omnes homines introiit, non est peccatum actuale Adami, sed corruptio haereditaria. Atqui Apostolus loquitur de peccato quod per Adamum in omnes homines introiit. Ergo loquitur non de peccato actuali Adami, sed de corruptione haereditaria.
english: A second reason the following words supply me, eis ton kosmon eiselthe, entered into the world. But that by the world all humans are understood, since you and almost all interpreters confess it, there is no need to prove. I reason therefore thus: The sin which entered through Adam into all humans is not Adam's actual sin, but hereditary corruption. But the Apostle speaks of the sin which entered through Adam into all humans. Therefore he speaks not of Adam's actual sin, but of hereditary corruption.

source_text: Minor est liquida. Maior quomodo negari possit non video. Constat enim & convenit inter nos per Adamum corruptionem haereditariam quae vere peccatum est in omnes homines ingressam esse: quo posito, quid est quamobrem de ea non accipiamus Apostoli verba?
english: The Minor is clear. How the Major could be denied I do not see. For it is agreed and convenes between us that through Adam hereditary corruption which is truly sin entered into all humans: which being posited, what is there why we should not take the Apostle's words of it?

source_text: GAR. Actuale peccatum Adae in homines omnes non minus transit quam corruptio. Nimirum corruptio inhaesione, peccatum Adae reatu & imputatione.
english: GAR. Adam's actual sin passes into all humans no less than corruption. Namely corruption by inhesion, Adam's sin by reatus and imputation.

source_text: PLAC. Itane non minus in homines omnes transit, seu ut loquitur Apostolus, introiit, quam corruptio? Estne igitur peccatum actuale Adami intra nos, non minus quam corruptio? aut potestne intra nos esse, & tamen nobis non inesse, non inhaerere? Imputatio illa extra nos est, in Deo, diuque antequam essemus, facta: actuale quoque Adami peccatum desiit esse aliquot annorum millibus antequam esse inciperemus. Qui igitur dici potest in nos introiisse, & quidem illa imputatione?
english: PLAC. Does it then pass into all humans no less, or as the Apostle speaks, enter, than corruption? Is Adam's actual sin therefore inside us, no less than corruption? Or can it be inside us, and yet not be in us, not inhere? That imputation is outside us, in God, and was made long before we were: Adam's actual sin also ceased to be some thousands of years before we began to be. How then can it be said to have entered into us, and indeed by that imputation?

source_text: Deinde convenit inter nos peccatum habituale per unum hominem in omnes homines intrasse, idque ipsa experientia confirmat; sed non convenit peccatum actuale per unum hominem in omnes homines intrasse; hoc enim pernegamus, neque potest probari. Nostra igitur interpretatio negari non potest, cum sit in confesso. Suam igitur qui nobis adversantur, probent interpretationem necesse est, antequam admitti aut possit aut debeat. Denique cum duo illi introeundi modi, quorum alter fingitur, alter est certus & confessus, prorsus sint diversi, alterque alterius respectu, vel nullus vel figuratus sit, qui potest tam diversa unum introeundi verbum semel usurpatum significare?
english: Next it is agreed between us that habitual sin entered through one man into all humans, and experience itself confirms it; but it is not agreed that actual sin entered through one man into all humans; for this we flatly deny, and it cannot be proved. Our interpretation therefore cannot be denied, since it is in confession. Those who oppose us must therefore prove their interpretation, before it can or ought to be admitted. Finally since those two modes of entering, of which one is feigned, the other is certain and confessed, are wholly diverse, and one with respect to the other is either nothing or figurative, how can things so diverse be signified by one verb of entering used once?

source_text: GAR. Cum causam justificationis, non sanctificationis hic tractet Apostolus, nihil mirum est, si ex primaria sua intentione hic potius peccatum actuale Adami, quam corruptionem illam inhaerentem spectare voluerit, cum peccatum ab Adamo patratum, reatus ex illo consequens, respondeat justitiae Christi, & justificationi per eam nostrae: corruptio vero interna, non illi Christi justitiae proprie, sed potius inhaerenti per Spiritum Sanctum in nobis sanctitati respondeat. Qua corruptio quanquam hic etiam propter illam quam diximus connexionem comprehendi potest, non tamen Apostolicum scopum directe respicit, sicut in sequentibus de illa aperte agetur a Paulo.
english: GAR. Since the Apostle here treats the cause of justification, not of sanctification, it is no wonder if from his primary intention he wished here rather to look at Adam's actual sin than at that inhering corruption, since the sin committed by Adam, and the reatus following from it, answers to the righteousness of Christ, and to our justification through it: but internal corruption answers not properly to that righteousness of Christ, but rather to the holiness inhering in us through the Holy Spirit. Which corruption, although here also because of that connection we have named it can be comprehended, yet does not directly regard the Apostolic aim, as in what follows Paul will treat of it openly.

source_text: PLAC. Quid? Nonne corruptio est vere peccatum? Nonne ex illa consequitur reatus? Nonne omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragit? Nonne ab ea nos imprimis justificari oportet? Mirum est qui nos innovatae doctrinae accusant, tam aperte a recepta ab omnibus Protestantibus doctrina discedere.
english: PLAC. What? Is corruption not truly sin? Does reatus not follow from it? Does it not make all and each human, not even little ones excepted still hiding in their mothers' womb, guilty of eternal death before God? Must we not first of all be justified from it? It is strange that those who accuse us of innovated doctrine depart so openly from the doctrine received by all Protestants.

source_text: Deinde planum est peccatum actuale Adami, cum actio fuerit singularis, &, ut tu ipse loqueris, personalis, quae simul ac fuit praeteriit, non potuisse in omnes homines ingredi. Neque potes respondere actionem illam singularem & numero unicam tanto antequam nasceremur admissam in omnes homines imputatione introiisse: quis enim unquam fando audivit hanc phrasim, in aliquem introire, significare, alicui imputari? Noli, quaeso, ut tuam sententiam tuearis vim facere Dei verbo. Actio illa Adami nunquam intra nos fuit, sed neque eius imputatio, quae si ulla esset, Dei actio esset intra Deum manens, non intra nos. Si dixeris actionem illam Adami qua peccatum eius actuale fuit, introiisse in nos dici, non quidem ratione sui, sed ratione poenae quam est nobis commerita, videlicet corruptionis haereditariae, primum rursus abuteris verbo introeundi: nam aliud est poenam peccati aliud peccatum in aliquem intrare. Imputata sunt peccata nostra Christo vadi nostro, nemo tamen dixerit per nos peccata in Christum introiisse, quamvis eorum poenam in se susceperit.
english: Next it is plain that Adam's actual sin, since it was a singular action, and, as you yourself speak, personal, which as soon as it was passed away, could not have entered into all humans. Nor can you reply that that singular action and one in number, committed so long before we were born, entered into all humans by imputation: for who ever heard by report that this phrase, to enter into someone, signifies to be imputed to someone? Do not, I ask, to defend your opinion do violence to the word of God. That action of Adam was never inside us, but neither was its imputation, which if any existed would be God's action remaining inside God, not inside us. If you shall say that that action of Adam by which his actual sin was, is said to have entered into us, not indeed by reason of itself, but by reason of the penalty which it earned for us, namely of hereditary corruption, first again you abuse the verb of entering: for it is one thing for the penalty of sin, another for sin, to enter into someone. Our sins were imputed to Christ our surety, yet no one will say that through us sins entered into Christ, although he took their penalty upon himself.

source_text: GAR. Resp. 1. Eadem subtilitate ostendi posse, per illud peccatum, non esse intelligendum (quod tamen volunt qui his rationibus utuntur) corruptionem haereditariam, unicuique nostrum ab origine inhaerentem. Nam ea corruptio non potest dici intrare in nos: cum sit innata & ingenita, & penetissime infita a principio in natura nostra: illud autem intrare aliquo dicitur, quod foris eo delatum est, aut venit aliunde, & antea ibi non erat. Certe nemo nostrum prius fuit, quam fuit corruptus.
english: GAR. Resp. 1. By the same subtlety it can be shown that by that sin is not to be understood (which yet those who use these reasons want) the hereditary corruption inhering in each of us from origin. For that corruption cannot be said to enter into us: since it is innate and inborn, and most deeply fixed from the beginning in our nature: but that is said to enter somewhere, which has been brought there from outside, or comes from elsewhere, and before was not there. Certainly none of us was earlier than he was corrupt.

source_text: PLAC. Eadem quidem esset subtilitas, si posset argumentum meum aeque corruptioni ac peccato actuali accommodari: nunc vero cum haec viri docti subtilitas in argumento a meo valde diverso sita sit, intelligere non possum, cur eadem subtilitas dicatur, aut quid argumentis meis noceat? Quanquam vim nullam habet. Quis enim non videt per illum peccati introitum non esse intelligendum introitum situm in motu locali qui proprius est corporum & substantiarum?
english: PLAC. It would indeed be the same subtlety, if my argument could be accommodated equally to corruption and to actual sin: but now since this subtlety of the learned man is situated in an argument very diverse from mine, I cannot understand why it is called the same subtlety, or what it harms in my arguments? Although it has no force. For who does not see that by that entry of sin is not to be understood an entry situated in local motion which is proper to bodies and substances?

source_text: Quis etiam, nisi sit Pelagianus, non intelligit peccatum intrasse in homines propagatione naturali simul ac gignimur, ac proinde in genitos non fuisse foris delatum? nempe dicitur in nos intrasse, quia revera intra nos est, nec tamen est a creatione, aut ab ipsa humana natura, sed aliunde, a tentatione serpentis & peccato primi hominis actuali. Itaque revera per unum hominem vitium illud in naturam humanam ubi antea non erat, nec esse debebat, intravit, & una cum natura in nos omnes, id quod de peccato actuali dici non potest. Quod igitur innatum est, id si non est a natura, quominus per parentes in liberos introiisse dicatur, nihil potest prohibere. Sic potest dici per parentem in liberos lepra aut podagra intraisse, quamvis lepra insit liberis ab ortu. Non quidem prius tempore, at prius tamen natura fuimus quam corrupti fuimus. Non potest enim corruptio naturae non esse posterior ipsa natura. Caeterum si prius non fuimus quam corrupti fuimus, & corruptio sequitur, Non entis nulla sunt accidentia.
english: Who also, unless he is a Pelagian, does not understand that sin entered into humans by natural propagation as soon as we are begotten, and therefore was not brought from outside into those already born? namely it is said to have entered into us, because it truly is inside us, and yet is not from creation, or from human nature itself, but from elsewhere, from the serpent's temptation and the first man's actual sin. And so truly through one man that vice entered into human nature where before it was not, nor ought to be, and together with nature into us all, which cannot be said of actual sin. What therefore is innate, if it is not from nature, nothing can prohibit that it be said to have entered through parents into children. So it can be said that through a parent leprosy or gout entered into children, although leprosy is in the children from birth. Not indeed earlier in time, but earlier yet by nature we were than we were corrupt. For corruption of nature cannot but be later than nature itself. But if we were not earlier than we were corrupt, and corruption follows, Of a non-being there are no accidents.

source_text: GAR. 2. Non est absurdius si dicatur peccatum, aut actio singularis Adae introiisse, quam si dicatur Christi justitia introisse. At ita loquitur Clar. Amyr. in paraphrasi huius versus, per unum hominem qui Iesus Christus est, vera justitia introducta est in mundum, quod de justitia imputata, non minus quam de inhaerente dicitur. Quibus non displicet si dicatur justitia imputata introduci vel intrare, quidni placeat, si dicatur etiam, peccatum imputatum introire?
english: GAR. 2. It is not more absurd if it is said that sin, or Adam's singular action, entered, than if it is said that Christ's righteousness entered. But so speaks the distinguished Amyraut in a paraphrase of this verse: through one man who is Jesus Christ, true righteousness was introduced into the world, which is said of imputed righteousness no less than of inhering. To those whom it does not displease if imputed righteousness is said to be introduced or to enter, why should it not please, if imputed sin also is said to enter?

source_text: PLAC. Dixitne Clar. Amyr. justitiam quae Christo inhaesit, per eum unum in homines intrasse? Non certe: Attamen id ab eo dici oportuit, ut posset eius locutione expositio viri docti defendi. Nempe justitiae nomine, quae per unum hominem in mundum introducta est, aut vehementer fallor, aut cum Calvino remissionem peccatorum intellexit, eamque introductam voluit non in omnes homines, aut in omnes credentes sola imputatione, sed impetratam a Christo & donatam a Patre & praedicatione Evangelii oblatam omnibus & fide acceptam a credentibus, in quibus constans permanet: id quod de actuali Adae peccato dici similiter non potest.
english: PLAC. Did the distinguished Amyraut say that the righteousness which inhered in Christ entered through him alone into humans? Certainly not: And yet that ought to have been said by him, so that by his locution the learned man's exposition could be defended. Namely by the name of righteousness which through one man was introduced into the world, either I am badly mistaken, or with Calvin he understood the remission of sins, and wished it introduced not into all humans, or into all believers by imputation alone, but obtained by Christ and given by the Father and offered to all by the preaching of the Gospel and accepted by faith by believers, in whom it remains constant: which cannot similarly be said of Adam's actual sin.

source_text: GAR. 3. Quod sine introduci dicitur saepius, quod tum demum esse incipit, ut apud Graecos εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν intrare in iudicium, est incipere litem. Et Christus dicitur intrasse, & introductus fuisse in mundum, cum in mundo incepit esse secundum humanitatem suam. Act. 1. 21. Heb. 1. 6. Ergo cum peccatum incepit esse primum in genere humano, quod fuit per primorum parentum inobedientiam, merito dicitur in mundum intrasse.
english: GAR. 3. What is often said to be introduced is that which then at last begins to be, as among the Greeks eis to dikasterion eiselthein, to enter into judgment, is to begin a suit. And Christ is said to have entered, and to have been introduced into the world, when in the world he began to be according to his humanity. Acts 1. 21. Heb. 1. 6. Therefore when sin first began to be in the human race, which was through the first parents' disobedience, it is rightly said to have entered into the world.

source_text: PLAC. More eorum qui submerguntur, obvium quodque arripit vir doctus: sed frustra. Significet enim phrasis εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν apud Graecos incipere litem, num sequitur, idem verbum cum quovis alio nomine constructum pro incipere usurpari? Num ex. g. εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸν οἶκον, vel εἰς τὴν πόλιν, erit incipere domum vel urbem, aut ita incipere esse in domo vel urbe, ut antea non fueris?
english: PLAC. After the manner of those who are drowning, the learned man seizes whatever meets him: but in vain. For grant that the phrase eis to dikasterion eiselthein among the Greeks signifies to begin a suit, does it follow that the same verb constructed with any other noun is used for 'to begin'? Will, for example, eiselthein eis ton oikon, or eis ten polin, be to begin a house or a city, or so to begin to be in a house or city, that you were not there before?

source_text: Perperam laudatur locus Act. 1. 21. nam ingredi & egredi Hebraismus est, neque nativitatem neque mortem significans, sed conversationem, & vel publicorum vel privatorum officiorum functiones. vide Bez. Ann. in illum locum.
english: The place Acts 1. 21. is wrongly praised: for to go in and to go out is a Hebraism, signifying neither birth nor death, but conversation, and the functions of either public or private offices. See Beza's Annot. on that place.

source_text: Alter quoque Heb. 1. 6. virum doctum refellit: intelligendus enim non est de nativitate Christi, sed de secundo eius gloriosissimo adventu, ut patet ex verbis Apostoli, & toto Ps. 97. unde sunt desumpta. Caeterum hanc viri docti responsionem refutavit Bellarminus multis rationibus lib. 4. de amiss. Grat. cap. 3. & post eum Chamierus, sed brevius, lib. 1. de hom. corrupt. cap. 5. §. 9.
english: The other place also, Heb. 1. 6., refutes the learned man: for it is not to be understood of Christ's nativity, but of his second most glorious advent, as is plain from the Apostle's words, and from the whole of Ps. 97. from which they are taken. Moreover Bellarmine refuted this reply of the learned man with many reasons in book 4. de amiss. Grat. chapter 3. and after him Chamier, but more briefly, in book 1. de hom. corrupt. chapter 5. section 9.

source_text: Quidni ergo dixerim peccata nostra in Christum εἰσελθεῖν, cum Scriptura dicat, ea venisse in Christum? Dominus fecit venire, vel incurrere in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Esai. LIII. 6. Et similiter, peccatum Adae in nos ἐλθεῖν, in nos venisse, quia eius reatum sustinemus, id est, quia illud imputatum nobis est? Itaque quanquam introire simpliciter positum, non sit idem quod imputare, tamen peccatum introire, vel venire in aliquem, si res aut locus, ubi phrasis habetur, ita exigit, potest idem esse quod peccatum illud ipsi imputari.
english: Why then may I not say that our sins eiselthein into Christ, when Scripture says they came into Christ? The Lord made the iniquities of us all to come, or to fall upon him. Isaiah 53. 6. And likewise, that Adam's sin elthein upon us, came upon us, because we sustain its reatus, that is, because it has been imputed to us? And so although to enter simply put is not the same as to impute, yet for sin to enter, or to come upon someone, if the matter or place where the phrase is held so requires, can be the same as for that sin to be imputed to him.

source_text: PLAC. Non potuit diligentius Pighii expositio defendi, quam sit a viro docto hoc quidem in loco: nullum enim lapidem non movet ut extorqueat e manibus orthodoxorum argumentum, quod soliti sunt adversus Pelagium & Pighium ex verbis Apostoli ducere, per unum hominem peccatum introiit in mundum. Sed frustra laborat. Expugnari veritas non potest. Quid est, quare sibi dari Vir doctus postulet, compositum εἰσελθεῖν, nihil significatione differre a simplici ἐλθεῖν? Aut quis ferat dicentem peccata nostra introiisse in Christum, aut per nos peccatum intrasse in Christum? Nonne talem locutionem pia refugit conscientia?
english: PLAC. Pighius's exposition could not have been defended more carefully than it is by the learned man in this place: for he moves no stone that he may wrest from the orthodox the argument which they are accustomed to draw against Pelagius and Pighius from the Apostle's words, through one man sin entered into the world. But he labors in vain. Truth cannot be stormed. What is it, why the learned man demands to be granted to himself, that the compound eiselthein differs in signification not at all from the simple elthein? Or who will bear one saying that our sins entered into Christ, or that through us sin entered into Christ? Does not a pious conscience flee such a locution?

source_text: Locus Esai. LIII. 6. ad rem non est, tum quia non est idem verbum: הִפְגִּיעַ enim non est fecit ingredi seu introire, sed fecit occurrere, vel incurrere; tum quia iniquitas eo loco non ipsum peccatum, sed poenam peccati significat. Occurrit enim Christo, incurrit, irruit in eum, &, si ita vis, intravit in eum non peccatum, sed sola peccati poena. Hic autem peccatum a peccati poena distinguitur: sequitur enim, & per peccatum mors. Itaque probari non potest idem esse posse, peccatum in aliquem ingredi, & peccatum alicui imputari. Quod si peccatum, quatenus a poena distinguitur, ingressum est in Christum, quid est cur Christus non potuerit dici peccator? Si hoc est absurdum, illud quoque absurdum esse confitendum est.
english: The place Isaiah 53. 6. is not to the point, both because it is not the same verb: for hiphgia is not 'he made to enter' or 'to go in,' but 'he made to meet,' or 'to fall upon'; and because iniquity in that place signifies not the sin itself, but the penalty of sin. For it met Christ, falls upon him, rushes upon him, and, if you will, entered into him—not sin, but only the penalty of sin. But here sin is distinguished from the penalty of sin: for there follows, and through sin death. And so it cannot be proved that it can be the same, for sin to enter into someone, and for sin to be imputed to someone. But if sin, insofar as it is distinguished from penalty, entered into Christ, what is there why Christ could not have been called a sinner? If this is absurd, that also must be confessed to be absurd.

source_text: Sed, ut omnis expugnetur pertinacia, loco introiit pone imputatum est, vide quam belle procedet Apostoli oratio, per unum hominem peccatum imputatum est mundo, & per peccatum mors. Num imputata est mors? num imputata est per peccatum? num peccatum est imputatum per Adamum? Nonne ridiculum, quantum in ipsis est, qui sic contra me disputant, faciunt Apostolum?
english: But, that every obstinacy may be stormed, in place of introiit put imputatum est, see how finely the Apostle's speech will proceed: through one man sin was imputed to the world, and through sin death. Was death imputed? Was it imputed through sin? Was sin imputed through Adam? Do they not make the Apostle ridiculous, as far as in them lies, who so dispute against me?

source_text: GAR. 5. Itaque quamquam singularis actio, ratione substantiae suae non potest dici introire in alium, tamen ratione reatus introire recte dicitur, quatenus propter actionem illam alius reus habetur, adeoque poenis subiacet.
english: GAR. 5. And so although a singular action, by reason of its substance, cannot be said to enter into another, yet by reason of reatus it is rightly said to enter, insofar as because of that action another is held guilty, and so lies under penalties.

source_text: PLAC. Atqui 1. aliud est actio, aliud reatus. Illa est actio, haec relatio, illa transit, hoc manet. Num igitur si reatus recte dicitur introire, recte etiam dicitur introire actio? Num quicquid dicitur de reatu, dici etiam potest de actione? Num actio est relatio? num manet postquam actio transiit? num sequitur actionem? 2. Aliud est propter actionem reum haberi, aliud reatum actionis introire in aliquem: illud externam tantum denominationem significat, hoc aliquid importat amplius. Imo ipse reatus, cum sit relatio, introire dici non potest, nisi aut ratione fundamenti, hoc est, peccati sive sit actio, sive habitus, aut termini, hoc est, poenae, tantum abest ut ratione reatus actio dici possit in alium introire.
english: PLAC. But 1. action is one thing, reatus another. That is an action, this a relation, that passes, this remains. Is it then, if reatus is rightly said to enter, rightly also said that the action enters? Can whatever is said of reatus also be said of the action? Is action a relation? Does it remain after the action has passed? Does it follow the action? 2. It is one thing to be held guilty because of an action, another for the reatus of the action to enter into someone: that signifies only an external denomination, this imports something more. Nay the reatus itself, since it is a relation, cannot be said to enter, except either by reason of the foundation, that is, of sin whether it be action or habit, or of the term, that is, of penalty, so far is it from it that by reason of reatus the action can be said to enter into another.

source_text: GAR. 6. Denique imputatio peccati, est illa quidem actio Dei, a Deo tanquam judice profecta, sed in homines tendens, tanquam in terminum, & eo respectu in hominem intrans aut veniens, propter effectus quos in ipso producit, id est, propter poenas quibus eum afficit. Sic maledictio est actio Dei Gen. XII. 3. Malach. 2. 2. Et tamen intrare dicitur in homines aliquos Psal. CIX. 18. Maledictio ingredietur, velut aqua, intra eum, & velut oleum in ossa eius. Quod autem imputatio peccati sit actio Dei intra Deum manens Theologi vix concedant, qui cum Dei actiones distinguere soleant in immanentes & transeuntes; immanentes eas vocant, quae in ipso Deo terminantur, ut intellectionem, & volitionem, qua seipsum intelligit & diligit: transeuntes, quae terminantur in creaturas, quales sunt actiones divinae providentiae. Sed haec aliis disceptanda relinquo.
english: GAR. 6. Finally the imputation of sin is indeed that action of God, proceeding from God as judge, but tending into humans, as into a term, and in that respect entering or coming into a human, because of the effects which it produces in him, that is, because of the penalties with which it afflicts him. So curse is an action of God Gen. XII. 3. Malachi 2. 2. And yet it is said to enter into some humans Psalm 109. 18. The curse shall enter, like water, within him, and like oil into his bones. But that the imputation of sin is an action of God remaining inside God theologians hardly grant, who are accustomed to distinguish God's actions into immanent and transeunt; they call immanent those which terminate in God himself, as intellection, and volition, by which he understands and loves himself: transeunt, those which terminate in creatures, such as the actions of divine providence. But these I leave to be disputed by others.

source_text: PLAC. Quis unquam negavit Dei actiones alias esse immanentes, alias transeuntes; illas in Deo, has in creaturis esse? Et quis nescit in hoc posteriore genere ponendam esse maledictionem quae est actio Dei? Quanquam per maledictionem Ps. CIX. 18. non significatur actio, sed effectum potius Dei irati, nempe miseria, infortunium, malum poenae. Vult Propheta huiusmodi hominem omnibus malis corporalibus & spiritualibus omni ex parte induti & penetrari. Itaque praecessit, optavit ut maledictio eveniret ei, & sequitur, Hoc esto praemium adversantium mihi &c. Quid autem hoc ad rem, qua de agimus, facit? Quaeritur quo sensu dixerit Apostolus per unum hominem peccatum introiisse in mundum, id est, in homines? Dicis per peccatum intelligendam esse actionem Adami. Quaero, quomodo actio Adami, quae diu antequam ulli alii homines essent, fuerat praeterita ac esse desierat, dici potuit in omnes homines introiisse? Dicis introiisse imputatione. Repono, imputationem illam non esse actionem unius illius hominis, sed solius Dei. Non igitur per unum hominem, sed per Deum peccatum introiisse in omnes homines: quo nihil dici potest absurdius.
english: PLAC. Who ever denied that God's actions are some immanent, some transeunt; those in God, these in creatures? And who does not know that into this latter kind must be placed the curse which is an action of God? Although by the curse in Psalm 109. 18. is not signified the action, but rather the effect of an angry God, namely misery, misfortune, the evil of penalty. The Prophet wants a man of this kind to be clothed and penetrated on every side with all bodily and spiritual evils. And so it preceded, he wished that the curse would befall him, and there follows, Let this be the reward of those opposing me, etc. But what does this do for the matter we are treating? It is asked in what sense the Apostle said that through one man sin entered into the world, that is, into humans? You say that by sin Adam's action must be understood. I ask, how could Adam's action, which long before any other humans were, had been past and had ceased to be, be said to have entered into all humans? You say it entered by imputation. I reply, that imputation is not the action of that one man, but of God alone. Not therefore through one man, but through God, did sin enter into all humans: than which nothing more absurd can be said.

source_text: Repono etiam, non fieri imputatione illa ut peccatum actuale, seu actio illa praeterita Adami, unquam intra nos fuerit, aut esse possit. Repono denique imputationem, aut esse actionem mentis seu iudicii divini reputantis nos esse reos actionis illius Adamicae, aut illius divini iudicii declarationem lata sententia sermone externo, aut poenae inflictionem.
english: I reply also, that by that imputation it does not come about that the actual sin, or that past action of Adam, ever was inside us, or can be. I reply finally that imputation is either an action of the mind or of the divine judgment reckoning us to be guilty of that Adamic action, or a declaration of that divine judgment by a sentence passed in external speech, or the infliction of penalty.

source_text: Si primum eligis, actio est Dei immanens: non enim alibi est aut esse potest quam in Deo, in Dei mente. Vocant quidem nonnulli Theologi actiones divinae mentis & voluntatis, actiones ad extra, quia habent pro obiecto creaturas: at non eas ideo faciunt minus immanentes, ut facit hoc loco vir doctus, <PRIVATE_ADDRESS> inconsiderate.
english: If you choose the first, it is an immanent action of God: for it is not elsewhere, nor can it be, than in God, in God's mind. Some theologians indeed call the actions of the divine mind and will actions toward the outside, because they have creatures for their object: but they do not therefore make them less immanent, as the learned man does in this place, rather inconsiderately.

source_text: Si secundum, ubi & quando facta est illa declaratio, & num extra nos, an intra nos?
english: If the second, where and when was that declaration made, and is it outside us, or inside us? The learned man does not say.

source_text: Si tertium, repugnat Apostolus qui peccatum hoc loco distinguit a poena peccati quam mortem vocat. Inflictione poenae, hoc est, mortis, intrat quidem mors seu poena, sed non intrat peccatum. Alius est in verbis Apostoli introitus peccati, alius introitus mortis, ille causa est huius.
english: If the third, the Apostle conflicts, who in this place distinguishes sin from the penalty of sin which he calls death. By the infliction of penalty, that is, of death, death or penalty indeed enters, but sin does not enter. One thing in the Apostle's words is the entry of sin, another the entry of death; that is the cause of this.

source_text: Deinde, si peccatum actuale Adami non intravit in mundum, nisi ratione corruptionis haereditariae, fatendum est hoc attributum intrasse in mundum, seu homines, convenire per se & proprie & proxime corruptioni haereditariae, remote tantum, & illius corruptionis ratione, peccato actuali Adami. Si igitur corruptio illa est vere & proprie peccatum, etiam post baptismum, ut nostri adversus Pontificios tuentur, nonne manifestum est, peccatum quod in mundum intravit, eius potius descriptionem esse quam peccati actualis Adami?
english: Next, if Adam's actual sin did not enter into the world except by reason of hereditary corruption, it must be confessed that this attribute of having entered into the world, or into humans, agrees of itself and properly and nearest with hereditary corruption, only remotely, and by reason of that corruption, with Adam's actual sin. If therefore that corruption is truly and properly sin, even after baptism, as ours hold against the Papists, is it not manifest that the sin which entered into the world is rather its description than that of Adam's actual sin?

source_text: Huc accedit quod Apostolus ait per hoc peccatum mortem introiisse in mundum. Introitus in mundum commune est peccati & mortis attributum. Utrumque in mundum introiit, sed peccatum per se, mors per peccatum. Mors autem introiit reapse, non imputatione, & mors quae introiit in mundum non est mors unius Adami, sed totuplex quot sunt homines. Cum ergo constet esse peccatum, nempe corruptionem haereditariam, quod eodem prorsus modo introierit in mundum, quid est, cur id hoc loco non intelligamus potius, quam id quod neque introitu in mundum, neque numero morti correspondeat?
english: To this is added that the Apostle says that through this sin death entered into the world. Entry into the world is a common attribute of sin and of death. Both entered into the world, but sin of itself, death through sin. But death entered in very deed, not by imputation, and the death which entered into the world is not the death of one Adam, but as manyfold as there are humans. Since therefore it is agreed there is a sin, namely hereditary corruption, which entered into the world in exactly the same way, what is there why we should not understand that in this place rather than that which corresponds to death neither by entry into the world, nor by number?

source_text: Denique si per peccatum quod in mundum introiit, peccatum actuale Adami intelligitur, necesse est, ut Apostolus, vel prorsus omiserit corruptionem inhaerentem, vel eam mortis nomine comprehenderit. Hoc utrumque est falsum; Ergo & illud.
english: Finally if by the sin which entered into the world Adam's actual sin is understood, it is necessary that the Apostle either wholly omitted inhering corruption, or comprehended it under the name of death. Both of these are false; Therefore that also.

source_text: Nam, si dixeris eum corruptionem haereditariam praetermisisse, sequentur duo: Unum, eam ex hac tota collatione, quam inter primum & secundum Adamum Apostolus instituit, colligi non posse. Non enim alia mala ex Adamo in genus humanum manasse sequentibus versibus docet, quam quae hoc v. 12. nominavit. Id autem Pighii causam valde iuvabit.
english: For if you shall say that he passed over hereditary corruption, two things will follow: One, that it cannot be gathered from this whole collation which the Apostle instituted between the first and the second Adam. For in the following verses he does not teach that other evils flowed from Adam into the human race than those which he named in this v. 12. But that will greatly help Pighius's cause.

source_text: & quamvis alia extent in sacris literis loca, ex quibus effici possit, nos nasci corruptos peccato, tamen fere alius nullus est, qui eam corruptionem doceat ab ipso Adamo profectam in omnes homines invasisse.
english: And although there are other places in the sacred letters from which it can be made out that we are born corrupt with sin, yet there is almost no other which teaches that that corruption, proceeding from Adam himself, invaded into all humans. That scarcity matters here.

source_text: Alterum, aut eam corruptionem nullam esse, aut Apostolum aberrasse a suo scopo. Si prius, vicerunt Pelagiani, estque adhuc in integro liberum arbitrium. Posterius patet.
english: The other, either that that corruption is nothing, or that the Apostle wandered from his aim. If the former, the Pelagians have won, and free choice is still intact. The latter is plain.

source_text: Scopus enim Apostoli est docere quae mala a primo Adamo, quae contra bona a secundo Adamo in genus humanum fluxerint, ut intelligamus mirum non esse, cum unus homo ad nos perdendos tam potens fuerit, unum hominem, Iesum Christum, nos posse servare. Itaque bona ab hoc in nos profecta malis ab illo profectis accurate comparat. Quis igitur credat eum voluisse id malum silentio praeterire, quod constat & ex Adamo in nos derivari, & causam omnium nostrorum peccatorum esse?
english: For the Apostle's aim is to teach what evils from the first Adam, what goods by contrast from the second Adam, flowed into the human race, so that we may understand it is not wonderful, when one man was so powerful to destroy us, that one man, Jesus Christ, can save us. And so he accurately compares the goods proceeded from this one into us with the evils proceeded from that one. Who therefore would believe that he wished to pass over in silence that evil which it is agreed both is derived from Adam into us, and is the cause of all our sins?

source_text: Si vero dixeris, Apostolum mortis nomine corruptionem illam haereditariam, quae peccatum est, comprehendisse, primum discedes ab omnium (quos viderim) interpretum consensu. Deinde causam Pelagianorum adversus Augustinum iuvabis, mortis nomen de morte animae accipientium.
english: But if you shall say that the Apostle comprehended that hereditary corruption, which is sin, under the name of death, first you will depart from the consent of all interpreters (whom I have seen). Next you will help the cause of the Pelagians against Augustine, who take the name of death of the death of the soul.

source_text: Tum Apostolum induces contra suum morem nomine mortis absolute posito, & sine ulla additione, eiusmodi corruptionem significantem, unumque & idem nomen semel positum, semel intelligendum, simul proprie & figurate accipientem. Praeterea, quis credat mortem cum a peccato distinguitur, ut fit hoc loco, peccatum significare?
english: Then you will bring in the Apostle against his custom, with the name of death set absolutely, and without any addition, signifying corruption of that kind, and one and the same name set once, to be understood once, taking it at once properly and figuratively. Besides, who would believe that death, when it is distinguished from sin, as is done in this place, signifies sin?

source_text: Adde quod Apostolus probat hoc loco omnes homines esse peccatores, peccatum in mundo, id est in hominibus, hoc argumento, quod omnes moriuntur. Putasne probare eum peccatum esse in hominibus, quia sit in hominibus peccatum, nimirum corruptio haereditaria? Num a latente corruptione morali, quae ipsa erat probanda, ducit argumentum, cum suppeteret a patente & nota omnium morte?
english: Add that the Apostle proves in this place that all humans are sinners, that sin is in the world, that is in humans, by this argument, that all die. Do you think he proves that sin is in humans, because there is sin in humans, namely hereditary corruption? Does he draw the argument from a latent moral corruption, which itself was to be proved, when it was at hand from the open and known death of all?

source_text: Certe condemnatio & mors sunt apud Apostolum hoc capite correlata. Condemnamur ad mortem, non ad peccatum. Mors non est condemnationis causa, sed effectum. Contra peccatum (est autem corruptio haereditaria, ut iam saepius dixi, peccatum) condemnationis causa, non effectum.
english: Certainly condemnation and death are correlatives with the Apostle in this chapter. We are condemned to death, not to sin. Death is not the cause of condemnation, but the effect. On the contrary sin (but hereditary corruption is sin, as I have already often said) is the cause of condemnation, not the effect.

source_text: Denique, ut ne sim aequo prolixior, cum ait Apostolus vers. 21. regnasse peccatum in mortem, sitne verisimile alio modo accipi mortem, quam in antecedenti disputatione Apostoli, cuius versus ille conclusio est? At profecto eo versu id significare non potest, quod sit vere peccatum. Praecessit enim illud vers. 20. lex praeterea introiit, ut peccatum abundaret. ubi autem peccatum abundavit, ibi gratia superabundavit. Illud enim peccati regnum, haec peccati redundantia id omne in homine complectitur, quod vere peccatum sit, & liquet ex Rom. VI. & VII. id peccatum, quod per legem redundavit & regnavit, esse concupiscentiam, sive corruptionem haereditariam.
english: Finally, that I may not be too prolix, when the Apostle says in verse 21. that sin reigned unto death, is it likely that death is taken in another way than in the Apostle's preceding dispute, of which that verse is the conclusion? But surely in that verse it cannot signify that which is truly sin. For that preceded in verse 20. the law moreover entered, that sin might abound. But where sin abounded, there grace superabounded. For that reign of sin, this overflow of sin, embraces all that in a human which is truly sin, and it is clear from Rom. VI. and VII. that that sin which overflowed and reigned through the law is concupiscence, or hereditary corruption.

source_text: Putabis fortasse te horum argumentorum aciem declinare posse, dicendo, per peccatum τὴν ἁμαρτίαν intelligi utrumque & peccatum actuale Adami, & natum ex eo vitium originale; sed id tibi non licet per statum quaestionis, quae inter nos versatur. Est enim instituta de peccato actuali Adami praeciso a vitio haereditario. Vis enim primum peccatum actuale Adamo & nobis fuisse imputatum, & quia imputatum, inflictam Adamo & nobis hanc poenam, nimirum vitium seu corruptionem originalem. Itaque secundum tuam sententiam corruptio ista cum peccato actuali Adami non cohaeret, nisi divinae imputationis interventu. Quare imputatio naturae ordine corruptionem antecedit. Est igitur peccati actualis Adami praecisi a corruptione haereditaria imputatio tibi probanda, non autem cum ea coniuncti ac confusi.
english: You will perhaps think you can turn aside the edge of these arguments by saying that by sin, ten hamartian, both are understood, both Adam's actual sin, and the original vice born from it; but that is not allowed you by the status of the question which is treated between us. For it is instituted concerning Adam's actual sin cut off from hereditary vice. For you will have the first actual sin to have been imputed to Adam and to us, and because imputed, this penalty to have been inflicted on Adam and on us, namely original vice or corruption. And so according to your opinion that corruption does not cohere with Adam's actual sin except by the intervention of divine imputation. Wherefore imputation in the order of nature precedes corruption. Therefore the imputation of Adam's actual sin cut off from hereditary corruption must be proved by you, not however of it joined and confused with that.

source_text: Id quod mihi alia suggerit argumenta, sed, vitandae hoc loco nimiae prolixitatis causa, conferenda in alium locum. Adde quod iam probavi peccatum actuale non introiisse in mundum, hoc est, in homines: unde sequitur hoc attributum in mundum introiit sibi iungere peccatum, non qua significat peccatum actuale, sed qua significat vitium ex eo mea sententia immediate, tua vero mediante Dei imputatione ortum. Sic opinor meum argumentum firmavi satis.
english: Which suggests other arguments to me, but, for the sake of avoiding too much prolixity in this place, to be conferred to another place. Add that I have already proved that actual sin did not enter into the world, that is, into humans: whence it follows that this attribute entered into the world joins sin to itself, not insofar as it signifies actual sin, but insofar as it signifies the vice arisen from it in my opinion immediately, but in yours by the mediation of God's imputation. So I think I have confirmed my argument enough.

source_text: Vides prima verba Apostoli, quae sequentium sunt basis; at eorum saltem nullius vestigium deprehendo in tuo tractatu. Quid si ego inde aliquid eliciam sententiae tuae adversum. Dabisne mihi per mortem hoc loco intelligendam esse eam mortem, quam lex Adamo fuerat comminata, poenam scilicet, & stipendium peccati? non video quo iure id negare possis, praesertim cum sentias eam legem ad totum genus humanum spectare, & Adamum, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuum esse. Dabis saltem mortem hoc loco significare poenam peccati, quod in mundum introiit.
english: You see the Apostle's first words, which are the basis of those that follow; but of them at least I detect no vestige in your treatise. What if I from there elicit something adverse to your opinion. Will you grant me that by death in this place is to be understood that death which the law had threatened to Adam, namely the penalty, and the wages of sin? I do not see by what right you can deny that, especially since you hold that that law regards the whole human race, and that Adam, as God had threatened, died. You will at least grant that death in this place signifies the penalty of the sin which entered into the world.

source_text: Tu autem vis illud peccatum esse peccatum actuale Adami, & illius poenam esse non tantum mortem corporis & aeternam, sed imprimis mortem spiritualem animae, positam in privatione iustitiae originalis, & corruptione haereditaria: Ex quo sequitur istam corruptionem nomine mortis hoc loco contineri. Atqui iam probavi non contineri. Quod si Apostolus mortis nomine quicquid poenae per Adamum in posteros derivatum est significavit, nec tamen eo nomine corruptionem haereditariam seu vitium complexus est, ut iam probavi, vides quid sequatur, nempe vitium illud haereditarium non esse in numero poenarum quas Adamus mundo intulit, ac proinde peccatum eius actuale non esse mundo imputatum ad illam poenam, videlicet vitium haereditarium.
english: But you will have that sin to be Adam's actual sin, and its penalty to be not only the death of the body and eternal death, but chiefly the spiritual death of the soul, placed in the privation of original righteousness, and in hereditary corruption: from which it follows that that corruption is contained under the name of death in this place. And yet I have already proved that it is not contained. But if the Apostle by the name of death signified whatever of penalty was derived through Adam into his posterity, and yet did not under that name embrace hereditary corruption or vice, as I have already proved, you see what follows, namely that that hereditary vice is not in the number of the penalties which Adam brought upon the world, and therefore that his actual sin was not imputed to the world unto that penalty, namely hereditary vice.

source_text: Veniamus ad sequentes voces ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. Hic magnum scilicet causae tuae putas te reperisse praesidium. In verbis ἐφ' ᾧ consistis paululum, mox iis desertis ad verbum ἥμαρτον te confers. Nempe tu versionem, qua utuntur Ecclesiae nostrae, noluisti prorsus reiicere, quamvis satis aperte prae te feras, eam tibi non probari. Itaque, inquis, stabiliatur & maneat versio nostra gallica, quae est Iohannis Calvini, eo quod, vel quando omnes peccaverunt. Adversus eam tamen nonnulla obicis hoc cap. & cap. ix. quae cum ad illud caput pervenero, Deo bene iuvante, ad examen revocabo.
english: Let us come to the following words, eph' hoi pantes hemarton. Here, forsooth, you think you have found a great defense of your cause. You linger a little on the words eph' hoi, presently, leaving them, you betake yourself to the word hemarton. Namely you were unwilling wholly to reject the version which our Churches use, although you openly enough show that it does not please you. And so, you say, let our French version stand and remain, which is John Calvin's, because, or when, all have sinned. Yet against it you cast some things in this chapter and in chapter ix., which, when I shall have come to that chapter, God helping, I will call back to examination.

source_text: Et quamvis mea fere nihil intersit quomodo ἐφ' ᾧ reddatur, eo quod, sive in quo, tamen ostendam vertendum esse eo quod, ac tuebor versionem, quam Ecclesiae nostrae probant. Interim tu vis explicari haec verba eo quod vel in quo omnes peccaverunt ex prima parte versiculi. At tibi iam primam illam partem extorsi. Si ergo peccasse omnes dicuntur eo peccato quod in mundum introiit,
english: And although it almost nothing concerns me how eph' hoi is rendered, because, or in which, yet I will show that it is to be turned because, and I will defend the version which our Churches approve. Meanwhile you will have these words explained because or in which all have sinned, from the first part of the verse. But I have already wrested that first part from you. If therefore all are said to have sinned by that sin which entered into the world,

source_text: Id autem peccatum non probasti esse peccatum actuale Adami, ego vero probavi esse vitium inhaerens, quid superest, nisi ut illud peccaverunt interpretemur cum Calvino de vitio nobis singulis innato & insito? Ita peccare, inquit, est corruptos esse & vitiatos. Gallice: Or ce peche, duquel il parle icy, ne signifie autre chose sinon que nous sommes tous corrompus: illa enim naturalis pravitas quam e matris utero afferimus, tametsi non ita cito fructus suos edit, peccatum tamen est coram Domino, & eius ultionem meretur. Et paulo post, peccavimus igitur omnes, quia naturali corruptione omnes imbuti sumus: ideoque iniqui ac perversi.
english: And that sin you have not proved to be Adam's actual sin, but I have proved it to be an inhering vice: what remains, except that we interpret that they sinned with Calvin of the vice innate and implanted in each of us? So to sin, he says, is to be corrupt and vitiated. In French: Now this sin, of which he speaks here, signifies nothing else but that we are all corrupted: for that natural depravity which we bring from our mother's womb, although it does not so soon put forth its fruits, is yet sin before the Lord, and deserves his vengeance. And a little after, we have therefore all sinned, because we are all imbued with natural corruption: and therefore iniquitous and perverse.

source_text: Id tamen negas tibi satisfacere: non enim, inquis, dicit Apostolus quoniam peccatum est in omnibus (immo hoc dicit versu sequente) sed, quoniam omnes peccaverunt, ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, & utitur verbo activo, ut significet peccatum actuale, cuius omnes sint participes. In peccato autem originali non peccavimus actu, nisi quatenus in Adamo peccavimus: nam cum peccavit pro omnibus suis posteris peccavit, & omnes homines qui ex illo nati sunt in illo peccaverunt, quia in illo omnes fuerunt. Vis probandi, si qua est, in tuis istis verbis, in hoc consistit, quod verbum ἥμαρτον peccaverunt, activum cum sit, significat peccatum actuale. Reliqua petitiones sunt τοῦ ἐν ἀρχῇ. Atqui verbum illud activum, si significat peccatum actuale, profecto peccatum actuale significat ab eo ipso commissum qui peccavit. Profer, si potes, contrarium exemplum. Vide igitur ne haec tua observatio Pelagio faveat.
english: Yet you deny that this satisfies you: for, you say, the Apostle does not say since sin is in all (nay, he says this in the following verse) but, since all have sinned, eph' hoi pantes hemarton, and he uses an active verb, that he may signify actual sin, of which all are partakers. But in original sin we have not sinned by act, except insofar as we sinned in Adam: for when he sinned he sinned for all his posterity, and all men who were born of him sinned in him, because in him all were. The force of proving, if there is any, in those words of yours, consists in this, that the word hemarton, they sinned, being active, signifies actual sin. The rest are petitions of what was in the beginning. And yet that active verb, if it signifies actual sin, surely signifies actual sin committed by him himself who sinned. Bring forward, if you can, a contrary example. See therefore lest this observation of yours favor Pelagius.

source_text: Deinde te non fugit peccatum actuale ab originali omnes Theologos distinguere. Si ergo hoc verbum peccaverunt actuale peccatum significat, igitur non significat originale, quod tu ipse ab actuali hoc loco discernis. Non ergo loquitur Apostolus de peccato originali hoc loco. Sic nobis, quantum in te est, extorques arma quibus ex hoc loco Pelagium, Pighium & Socinum conficiamus. Sed iuvat te alia via aggredi, quamvis enim nunc quidem meae sint partes respondere, tuae argumentari, tamen mihi temperare non possum quin argumenta, quibus mea causa abundat, ubique disseminem. Dic mihi igitur, quaeso, quomodo omnes homines intelligas peccasse peccato actuali Adami? Inculcas passim peccatum illud actuale nostrum esse non posse, nisi per imputationem. Si nostrum non est nisi imputatione, utique eo non peccavimus nisi imputatione. Quid erit igitur illud omnes peccaverunt? omnibus peccatum actuale imputatum est? Atqui aliud est aliquem peccare, aliud alicui peccatum imputari.
english: Next it does not escape you that all theologians distinguish actual sin from original. If therefore this word they sinned signifies actual sin, then it does not signify original, which you yourself in this place distinguish from the actual. Therefore the Apostle does not speak of original sin in this place. So, as much as in you lies, you wrest from us the weapons with which from this place we overthrow Pelagius, Pighius, and Socinus. But it pleases you to attack by another way: for although now indeed my part is to answer, yours to argue, yet I cannot restrain myself from scattering everywhere the arguments with which my cause abounds. Tell me therefore, I pray, how you understand all men to have sinned by Adam's actual sin? You inculcate everywhere that that actual sin cannot be ours except by imputation. If it is not ours except by imputation, then surely we have not sinned by it except by imputation. What then will that be, all have sinned? Actual sin has been imputed to all? And yet it is one thing for someone to sin, another for sin to be imputed to someone.

source_text: GAR. Respondeo 1. Aliud est si dicas simpliciter aliquem peccare, aliud si dicas aliquem in alio peccavisse. Nam illud sane ex vi vocis non significat imputationem peccati, sed hoc posterius designat imputationem. Quomodo enim qui multis post saeculis exstiterunt, dici possunt iam antea in alio peccasse, nisi quia ille eorum actum exercuit, & qui posterorum ita reputatur, ac si ipsi illum commisissent?
english: GAR. I answer 1. It is one thing if you say simply that someone sins, another if you say that someone has sinned in another. For the former, surely by force of the word, does not signify imputation of sin, but this latter designates imputation. For how can those who existed many ages afterward be said to have already before sinned in another, except because he exercised their act, and he of the posterity is so reputed, as if they themselves had committed it?

source_text: Sic satisfacere aliquem, & alicui satisfactionem imputari, sunt sane longe diversa, & tamen cum docent Theologi nos in Christo satisfecisse, non aliud sibi volunt, quam Christi satisfactionem nobis imputari, sive Christum eam satisfactionem exhibuisse, quae propter unionem, quam cum eo habemus tanquam capite nostro spirituali & mystico, nobis imputetur, ita ut apud Deum habeamur, quasi ipsi per nos satisfecissemus.
english: So for someone to satisfy, and for satisfaction to be imputed to someone, are surely far diverse. And yet when the theologians teach that we have satisfied in Christ, they mean nothing else than that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us. Or that Christ exhibited that satisfaction which, because of the union which we have with him as our spiritual and mystical head, is imputed to us, so that before God we are held as if we ourselves had satisfied through ourselves.

source_text: PLAC. Primum, non dicit Scriptura nos in Adamo peccasse. Deinde, non video cur illa locutio vim significet imputationem, qua peccatum alienum, nempe Adami, fiat aut existat nostrum. Dicimur enim mori in Adamo, nec tamen mors Adami nobis imputatur.
english: PLAC. First, Scripture does not say that we sinned in Adam. Next, I do not see why that manner of speaking should signify imputation by which another's sin, namely Adam's, becomes or exists as ours. For we are said to die in Adam, and yet Adam's death is not imputed to us.

source_text: Dici possumus in Adamo creati fuisse, creati fuisse iusti & beati, eiecti fuisse e paradiso &c., nec tamen eius creatio, aut iustitia originalis, aut eiectio e paradiso nobis imputatur. Potuimus ergo dici in eo peccasse, quomodo dici possumus in eo fuisse, quia ille quam naturam tam peccatum suum nobiscum communicavit propagatione naturali.
english: We can be said to have been created in Adam, to have been created just and blessed, to have been cast out of paradise, and so on, and yet neither his creation, nor original righteousness, nor casting out of paradise is imputed to us. Therefore we could be said to have sinned in him, in the way we can be said to have been in him, because he communicated to us both his nature and his sin by natural propagation.

source_text: Ad satisfactionem Christi quod attinet, cum dicimur in Christo satisfecisse, nihil aliud intelligi mihi videtur, nisi Christum loco nostro pro nobis satisfecisse: num igitur similiter Adamus loco nostro pro nobis peccavit? Tenebamur pro se quisque satisfacere. Id erat nobis impossibile. Christus, qui non tenebatur, vadem nostrum sese constituit, & pro nobis satisfecit. Potestne idem de nobis & Adamo dici? Tenebamurne peccare? num sese Adamus vadem nostrum constituit, ut pro nobis peccaret?
english: As for Christ's satisfaction, when we are said to have satisfied in Christ, nothing else seems to me to be understood, except that Christ in our place satisfied for us: did Adam therefore likewise in our place sin for us? Each of us was bound to satisfy for himself. That was impossible for us. Christ, who was not bound, constituted himself our surety, and satisfied for us. Can the same be said of us and of Adam? Were we bound to sin? Did Adam constitute himself our surety, that he might sin for us?

source_text: Peto etiam, quando in Christo satisfecimus? opinor quando passus est. Num igitur tunc nobis imputata est Christi satisfactio? Tunc igitur fuimus iustificati, nondum existentes, nondum credentes. Non ergo per fidem sumus iustificati, quandoquidem iustificatio nostra tanto nostram & existentiam & fidem antecessit. Adde quod unionem cum Christo tanquam capite nostro spirituali & mystico non habemus nisi per fidem, sequitur ergo fidem nostram imputatio satisfactionis Christi seu iustificatio nostra. Quid est cur non dicamus similiter nos unionem non habere cum Adamo tanquam capite peccatorum, nisi per vitium haereditarium, quo suum nobiscum peccatum communicavit. Itaque posteriorem esse eo vitio peccati Adamici imputationem.
english: I ask also, when did we satisfy in Christ? I think when he suffered. Was Christ's satisfaction therefore then imputed to us? Then therefore we were justified, not yet existing, not yet believing. We are therefore not justified by faith, seeing that our justification so far preceded both our existence and our faith. Add that we do not have union with Christ as our spiritual and mystical head except by faith; it follows therefore that the imputation of Christ's satisfaction, or our justification, follows our faith. What reason is there why we should not similarly say that we do not have union with Adam as head of sinners except by the hereditary vice by which he communicated his sin with us? And so the imputation of Adam's sin is later than that vice.

source_text: GAR. 2. Neque ignotum est in Scriptura peccandi verbum aliquando significare reatum ex peccato consequentem, secundum illam loquendi rationem qua ponitur antecedens pro consequente.
english: GAR. 2. Nor is it unknown in Scripture that the word of sinning sometimes signifies the guilt consequent from sin, according to that manner of speaking by which the antecedent is put for the consequent.

source_text: Ut cum Iudas secum Beniaminem in Aegyptum abducturus, patrem Iacobum ita alloquitur, Genes. XLIII. Ego spondeo pro eo, de manu mea reposcito eum: Si non reduxero eum ad te, & statuero eum coram te, omnino peccavero tibi omnibus diebus, id est, ero tibi reus, & a te habebor pro scelerato: Sic Bethsabea ad Davidem 1. Regum I. 21. cum occubuerit Dominus Iesus Rex cum patribus suis, ego & filius meus Schelomoh erimus peccatores; id est, agetur nobiscum tanquam cum sontibus & reis, ut exponunt interpretes.
english: As when Judah, about to take Benjamin with him into Egypt, addresses his father Jacob thus, Genesis XLIII. I pledge for him; of my hand require him: If I do not bring him back to you, and set him before you, I shall altogether have sinned against you all my days, that is, I shall be guilty to you, and shall be held by you for a criminal: So Bathsheba to David, 1 Kings I. 21. when the lord king sleeps with his fathers, I and my son Solomon shall be sinners; that is, it shall be dealt with us as with the guilty and the accused, as the interpreters explain.

source_text: Quid igitur in eo novi erit, si eandem metalepsin Hebraeis familiarem hic usurpari doceamus, ut dicamur in Adamo peccare, id est, pro reis haberi, non minus quam si, Adamo peccante, nos ipsi peccavissemus?
english: What then will be new in this, if we teach that the same metalepsis familiar to the Hebrews is used here, so that we are said to sin in Adam, that is, to be held as guilty, no less than if, Adam sinning, we ourselves had sinned?. Mark that well.

source_text: PLAC. Cum haec responsio Pighiana sit, ac nostris olim obiecta, eam, me tacente, refellat Martyr, Comm. in Rom. 5. 9. & locor. Comm. Class. 2. cap. 1. §. 8. Postremo, inquit, habemus a Paulo, per inobedientiam unius hominis, multos constitutos esse peccatores; quod indicat, in illis qui nascuntur ex Adamo esse vitium, propter quod peccatores dici possint. Sed hoc Pighius putat se posse eludere, quod peccatores interdum dicantur propter reatum quamvis actio peccandi praeterierit, neque amplius extet.
english: PLAC. Since this reply is Pighian, and was formerly objected to our men, let Martyr refute it while I am silent, Commentary on Romans 5. 9. and Common Places, Class 2. chapter 1. section 8. Finally, he says, we have from Paul, that by the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners; which indicates that in those who are born of Adam there is a vice because of which they can be called sinners. But Pighius thinks he can elude this, because sinners are sometimes so called because of guilt although the act of sinning has passed and no longer exists.

source_text: Quamvis hoc ita sit, nunquam tamen ostendere potest e Scripturis, quemquam peccatorem appellari, quin aut in seipso vitium habeat, aut certe antea admiserit: nisi dicere velit, Deum homines reos facere, absque ipsorum aliquo peccato. Fateor igitur, qui puniuntur aut calamitate opprimuntur, peccatores dici, sed non apud Deum, nisi peccatum ipsi aut commiserint, aut in se habuerint: Et vero manifestum est Apostolum in eo esse hoc loco, ut doceat vere peccatum esse in omnes homines propagatum, non autem aliquid quod non sit peccatum, sed peccati tantum consequens.
english: Although this is so, yet he can never show from the Scriptures that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has vice in himself, or has certainly committed it before: unless he would say that God makes men guilty without some sin of their own. I confess therefore that those who are punished or oppressed by calamity are called sinners, but not before God, unless they themselves have either committed sin, or have it in themselves: And truly it is manifest that the Apostle is at this in this place, that he may teach that sin has truly been propagated into all humans, not however something which is not sin, but only a consequent of sin.

source_text: Si peccati nomen non accipitur proprie hoc loco, sed figurate, ea figura, qua ponitur antecedens pro consequente, quomodo ex hoc loco argumentantur adversus Pelagium & Pighium Orthodoxi? Et, si accipitur proprie, quomodo simul accipitur figurate?
english: If the name of sin is not taken properly in this place, but figuratively, by that figure by which the antecedent is put for the consequent, how do the Orthodox argue from this place against Pelagius and Pighius? And, if it is taken properly, how is it at the same time taken figuratively?

source_text: Imputant nonnunquam homines vel ignari, vel iniusti, aliis hominibus peccata, qui non peccarunt; & qui peccarunt, his nonnunquam Deus peccata non imputat: Et, si cui Deus peccatum imputat, imputat quia peccavit, non facit imputando ut peccaverit. Ordine naturae prius peccatur, quam peccatum imputatur.
english: Men, whether ignorant or unjust, sometimes impute to other men sins who have not sinned; and to those who have sinned God sometimes does not impute sins: And, if to anyone God imputes sin, he imputes because he has sinned; he does not by imputing make him to have sinned. In the order of nature it is first sinned, before sin is imputed.

source_text: GAR. Resp. 3. Deus nemini peccatum imputat, quin ille peccaverit vel in se, vel in alio, id est, quin vel in se peccatum commiserit, vel alius, quocum arcte coniunctus est; sicut Sauli peccatum filiis eius imputavit, non quia ipsi commisissent, sed quia pater eorum commiserat. Et item Deus testatur in lege, se visitare peccata patrum in filiis.
english: GAR. Answer 3. God imputes sin to no one unless he has sinned either in himself, or in another, that is, unless either he has committed sin in himself, or another with whom he is closely joined; as he imputed Saul's sin to his sons, not because they themselves had committed it, but because their father had committed it. And likewise God testifies in the law that he visits the sins of the fathers upon the children.

source_text: Deus imputando peccatum alicui, non facit ut peccaverit, sed supponit eum peccavisse, sive in se, sive in alio. Est enim imputatio peccati actus Dei iudicialis, quo declarat aliquem esse reum & dignum poena ob peccatum, ut ab initio dictum.
english: God, by imputing sin to someone, does not make him to have sinned, but supposes him to have sinned, whether in himself or in another. For the imputation of sin is a judicial act of God, by which he declares someone to be guilty and worthy of penalty on account of sin, as was said from the beginning.

source_text: Peccatur prius ab aliquo, quam peccatum imputetur; sed non est necessarium, ut ab eo ipso cui peccatum imputatur, prius actu peccatum fuerit; sed necessarium est, ut aliquam habeat coniunctionem cum eo qui peccavit, & cuius peccatum ei imputatur, sicut antea docuit Clar. Amyraldus.
english: It is sinned first by someone, before sin is imputed; but it is not necessary that by that very one to whom sin is imputed, sin should first have been by act; but it is necessary that he have some conjunction with him who sinned, and whose sin is imputed to him, as the learned Amyraut taught before.

source_text: PLAC. Idem sonare mihi videntur tres istae Viri docti responsiones; simul igitur omnes refellam. Principio distinguenda est coniunctio cum peccatore: alia enim est coniunctio cum peccatore quatenus est peccator, alia cum peccatore quatenus est homo a quo ducimus originem. Vacare peccato non potest qui cum peccatore coniunctus est quatenus est peccator: particeps enim est eiusdem peccati, vel consensione, vel propagatione, vel imitatione &c.
english: PLAC. Those three replies of the learned man seem to me to sound the same; I will therefore refute them all together. First the conjunction with the sinner must be distinguished: for one is conjunction with the sinner insofar as he is a sinner, another with the sinner insofar as he is the man from whom we draw our origin. He cannot be free from sin who is joined with the sinner insofar as he is a sinner: for he is a partaker of the same sin, whether by consent, or by propagation, or by imitation, and so on.

source_text: At coniunctio cum alio, quatenus homo est a quo ducimus originem, sola non sufficit, ut peccatum ab alio commissum imputetur: alioqui omnia Adami, omniaque parentum nostrorum peccata, nobis possent iure imputari, quod, opinor, nemo dixerit: nulla tamen alia coniunctio nos inter & Adamum, ante communicatam ab eo corruptionem haereditariam, esse potuit. Nec iuvat Virum doctum exemplum Saulis: Nam eius filii, cum in se peccatores erant ac digni ob propria peccata illis poenis quas perpessi sunt, tum peccati illius paterni participes, ut patet ex verbis ipsius Dei 2. Sam. 21. 1. Propter Saulem, & domum eius sanguinariam, eo quod interfecit Gibeonitas. Non igitur solus Saul erat sanguinarius, sed eius domus seu familia.
english: But conjunction with another, insofar as he is the man from whom we draw origin, alone does not suffice for a sin committed by another to be imputed: otherwise all Adam's sins, and all our parents' sins, could rightly be imputed to us, which, I think, no one would say: yet no other conjunction between us and Adam could have existed before the hereditary corruption communicated by him. Nor does the example of Saul help the learned man: For his sons, when they were sinners in themselves and worthy on account of their own sins of those penalties which they suffered, were then also partakers of that paternal sin, as is clear from the words of God himself, 2 Samuel 21. 1. For Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Therefore not Saul alone was bloody, but his house or family.

source_text: Deinde non videtur Vir doctus sibi satis constare. Dixerat enim paragrapho praecedente aliquem in alio peccare ex vi vocis designare imputationem, idemque esse in alio peccare ac peccatum alienum imputari. Nunc vult esse diversa; & prius esse peccare in alio, quam peccatum alienum imputari; hocque tanquam posterius, illud supponere, tanquam prius & causam.
english: Next the learned man does not seem to himself to stand consistent enough. For he had said in the preceding paragraph that for someone to sin in another designates imputation by force of the word, and that to sin in another and for another's sin to be imputed are the same. Now he will have them to be diverse; and that to sin in another is prior to another's sin being imputed; and that this as the later, that as the prior and cause.

source_text: Deinde passim inculcat peccatum Adami nostrum non esse nisi imputatione: unde sequitur, nos in Adamo non peccasse nisi imputatione. At tamen nunc vult peccatum Adami nobis imputari, quia nos in Adamo peccavimus. Quomodo autem in Adamo peccavimus, si peccatum Adami nostrum non fuit? Ut igitur prius in Adamo peccavimus, quam eius peccatum nobis fuit imputatum, sic prius nostrum fuit Adami peccatum, quam nobis imputaretur. Quomodo ergo passim inculcat nostrum non esse, nisi per imputationem?
english: Next he inculcates everywhere that Adam's sin is not ours except by imputation: whence it follows that we did not sin in Adam except by imputation. And yet now he will have Adam's sin imputed to us, because we sinned in Adam. But how did we sin in Adam, if Adam's sin was not ours? Therefore as we first sinned in Adam before his sin was imputed to us, so Adam's sin was first ours before it was imputed to us. How then does he inculcate everywhere that it is not ours except by imputation?

source_text: Denique Deus, inquit, imputando peccatum alicui non facit ut peccaverit. Non facit igitur Deus imputando posteros Adami esse peccatores. Nam peccator non est qui non peccavit. Quomodo ergo dicit Vir doctus peccatum actuale Adami propter imputationem, nos inobedientia Adami constitui peccatores imputatione? Uno verbo, si peccatores sumus antequam Deus nobis imputet peccatum Adami, peccatum Adami non introiit in mundum imputatione, sed imputatio introitum illum sequitur: id quod mihi erat probandum.
