english: Finally God, he says, by imputing sin to someone does not make him to have sinned. Therefore God by imputing does not make Adam's posterity to be sinners. For he is not a sinner who has not sinned. How then does the learned man say that by Adam's actual sin, because of imputation, we are constituted sinners by Adam's disobedience by imputation? In one word, if we are sinners before God imputes Adam's sin to us, Adam's sin did not enter into the world by imputation, but imputation follows that entry: which was what I had to prove.

source_text: Deinde tu vis omnes peccasse in Adamo. Dabis autem fuisse in Adamo quomodo in Adamo peccaverunt: prius enim est esse quam agere vel peccare. Fuimusne ergo in Adamo imputatione qua esse eius? negabis procul dubio: cur ergo vis nos in eo peccasse imputatione qua peccare ipsius?
english: Next you will have all to have sinned in Adam. But you will grant that they were in Adam in the way they sinned in Adam: for it is prior to be than to act or to sin. Were we therefore in Adam by an imputation of his being? You will deny it far from doubt: why then will you have us to have sinned in him by an imputation of his sinning?

source_text: Dices fortasse istud peccare non significare peccatum imputari. Hinc inferam, igitur peccasse omnes peccato actuali, non quia ipsis imputetur, sed alio modo, quem mihi a te explicari cupio, qui toties negas peccatum actuale Adami nostrum esse alio modo quam per imputationem.
english: You will perhaps say that that to sin does not signify sin to be imputed. From this I will infer, therefore all sinned by actual sin, not because it is imputed to them, but in another way, which I desire to be explained to me by you, who so often deny that Adam's actual sin is ours in any other way than by imputation.

source_text: Sed praeterea quaero. Quando peccavimus in Adamo eius peccato actuali? an cum illud peccavit, an alio tempore? haud dubie cum illud commisit in paradiso: nullum aliud tempus assignare potes. Audi quid inde sequatur. Qui peccarunt ita ut iustam condemnationem mortis aeternae sibi commeriti sint, illi vere & proprie peccarunt. Qui autem vere & proprie peccarunt, illi tunc cum peccaverunt vere & proprie fuerunt. Qui ergo hodie incipit esse & nascitur infans, ille vere & proprie loquendo fuit iam tum, cum Adamus esset in paradiso, ante aliquot annorum millia: quippe qui tum vere & proprie peccavit. Itaque quod de se dixit Christus Ioh. 8. 58. Antequam Abraham nasceretur ego sum, nemo fuerit nostrum, qui idem dicere de semetipso non possit.
english: But besides I ask. When did we sin in Adam by his actual sin? when he sinned it, or at another time? without doubt when he committed it in paradise: you can assign no other time. Hear what follows from that. Those who have so sinned that they have merited for themselves the just condemnation of eternal death, those have truly and properly sinned. But those who have truly and properly sinned, those then when they sinned were truly and properly. Therefore he who today begins to be and is born an infant, he truly and properly speaking already then was, when Adam was in paradise, some thousands of years before: inasmuch as he then truly and properly sinned. And so what Christ said of himself, John 8. 58. Before Abraham was born I am, there will be none of us who cannot say the same of himself.

source_text: GAR. Resp. 1. Ex verbis Domini & Dei nostri, commata Hebrae, ut alios ludibrio exponas, an sit iocus, an sit serio, aliorum iudicium esto. Malim ego sane perire mihi centum iocos, quam ut vel sacrae Scripturae verbulo abuti velim.
english: GAR. Answer 1. From the words of our Lord and God, Hebrew commas—whether you expose others to mockery in jest or in earnest—let others' judgment be. I would rather lose a hundred jokes for myself than be willing to abuse even a little word of sacred Scripture.

source_text: PLAC. Ego ne hic iocos aut commata nexui? Imo serio, maxime, inquam, serio argumentatus sum, imputationisque immediatae absurditatem revelavi. Quid enim est ioci in hoc argumento? Ex qua opinione sequitur, unumquemque nostrum posse idem de semetipso dicere quod de se Christus dixit, Antequam Abraham fieret ego sum, illa est falsa & absurda. Id autem sequitur, ex opinione qua dicimur vere & proprie peccasse, atque adeo fuisse tunc cum Adamus esset adhuc in paradiso terrestri. Ergo illa opinio est falsa & absurda. Cum sic argumentor, videorne tibi, Lector, iocari, & ad iocum abuti Scriptura? Non arbitror. Nihil tamen aliud verba quibus sum usus continent quam hoc argumentum.
english: PLAC. Have I here woven jokes or commas? Nay, in earnest, most of all, I say, I have argued in earnest, and have uncovered the absurdity of immediate imputation. For what jest is there in this argument? From which opinion it follows that each one of us can say of himself what Christ said of himself, Before Abraham was, I am—that is false and absurd. But that follows from the opinion by which we are said to have truly and properly sinned, and so to have been then when Adam was still in the earthly paradise. Therefore that opinion is false and absurd. When I so argue, do I seem to you, Reader, to jest, and to abuse Scripture for a joke? I do not think so. Yet the words I have used contain nothing else than this argument.

source_text: GAR. Et quaedam ratio esse potest, ut quis ad infantem vel hominem quemcumque applicet ea verba, quibus teste Calvino Christus eximit se a vulgo hominum, sibiique solius divinam virtutem vindicat, cuius sensus ab initio usque mundi in omnia saecula diffusus fuerit. Putasne passurum Sanctum Augustinum, ut hic locus vel ioco, vel serio ad creaturam accommodaretur, qui cum ea verba diligenter meditatus esset, exclamat, Agnoscite Creatorem, discernite creaturam?
english: GAR. And there can be some reason why someone should apply to an infant or to any man whatever those words by which, Calvin testifying, Christ exempts himself from the common crowd of men, and claims for himself alone the divine power, whose sense from the beginning of the world has been diffused through all ages. Do you think holy Augustine would have suffered this place to be accommodated to a creature, whether in jest or in earnest—he who, when he had diligently meditated those words, exclaims, Acknowledge the Creator, discern the creature?

source_text: PLAC. Pro me, contra se, disputare Vir doctus videtur. Idem enim cum Calvino & Augustino sentio, idque Disp. xi. lib. 1. pro Divina Domini nostri Iesu Christi natura, satis, opinor, testatum feci; Nuncque etiam testor, qui ideo vestram opinionem reiicio hoc loco, quia ex ea sequitur maximum absurdum, nempe verba illa Christi cuilibet alii homini convenire posse. Si videtur vobis absurdum hoc consequens, ut est certe, & quidem tam absurdum quam quod maxime, cur non videtur vobis pariter absurdum antecedens unde ducitur?
english: PLAC. The learned man seems to dispute for me, against himself. For I think the same with Calvin and Augustine, and that, I think, I have sufficiently testified in Disputation xi. book 1. for the Divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ; and now also I testify, who for that reason reject your opinion in this place, because from it follows the greatest absurdity, namely that those words of Christ can suit any other man. If this consequent seems absurd to you, as it certainly is, and indeed as absurd as can be, why does the antecedent from which it is drawn not seem equally absurd to you?

source_text: GAR. 2. Sed ratiocinii vanam subtilitatem considera in exemplo simili. Ita imputatur nobis Christi satisfactio, ut in Christo satisfecisse dicamur. Accedat e Socinianorum grege quispiam; adversus eam doctrinam arma mutua biturus, Viro docto & in veritatem subtili argumentatione consurget. Quando vero demum satisfacimus in Christo, satisfactione eius actuali? An cum Christus ipse satisfecit in cruce? An alio tempore? Certe cum satisfecit in cruce. Sed audi. Qui satisfecerunt, ita ut iram Dei placarent, illi vere & proprie satisfecerunt. Qui vere & proprie satisfecerunt, tunc cum satisfecerunt, vere & proprie fuerunt. Ergone Christianus qui nunc vivit vere fuit, cum Christus penderet in cruce? Quid videtur? Annon valide contortum telum? Dissolvat nodum qui nectere docuit. Nec enim Socinianum refellet, ut non & eadem ratione subtilitatem suam traducat.
english: GAR. 2. But consider the vain subtilty of the reasoning in a like example. So Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us, that we are said to have satisfied in Christ. Let someone from the flock of the Socinians approach; about to take mutual arms against that doctrine, he will rise against the learned man and against the truth with subtle argumentation. When then at last do we satisfy in Christ, by his actual satisfaction? When Christ himself satisfied on the cross? Or at another time? Surely when he satisfied on the cross. But hear. Those who have satisfied so as to placate the wrath of God, those have truly and properly satisfied. Those who have truly and properly satisfied, then when they satisfied, truly and properly were. Therefore has the Christian who now lives truly been, when Christ hung on the cross? What seems? Is it not a strongly twisted dart? Let him who taught to knot it loose the knot. For he will not refute the Socinian so as not also by the same reason to traduce his own subtilty.

source_text: PLAC. Hoc exemplum non est simile, nec meam ratiocinationem ullo modo evertit. Imputatur quidem nobis credentibus Christi satisfactio, sed ea imputatio fidem nostram sequitur, non antecedit, nedum ut antecedat nostram existentiam. Iustificamur enim fide, non ante fidem. Cum igitur dicimur satisfecisse in Christo, ut locutio non extat in Scriptura, sic commode accipi debet, nec proprie intelligi potest. Sensus alius esse non debet quam iste, Christus satisfecit pro nobis.
english: PLAC. This example is not like, nor does it in any way overturn my reasoning. Christ's satisfaction is indeed imputed to us believing, but that imputation follows our faith, does not precede it, still less so as to precede our existence. For we are justified by faith, not before faith. When therefore we are said to have satisfied in Christ, as the phrase does not stand in Scripture, so it ought to be taken conveniently, and cannot be understood properly. The sense ought to be no other than this, Christ satisfied for us.

source_text: Nos non satisfecimus, sed alius, nempe Christus, pro nobis satisfecit. Idemne dici potest de peccato, Nos non peccavimus, sed alius peccavit pro nobis, aut loco nostro?
english: We have not satisfied, but another, namely Christ, has satisfied for us. Can the same be said of sin: We have not sinned, but another has sinned for us, or in our place?

source_text: Deinde quaestio, Quando vero demum satisfacimus in Christo satisfactione eius actuali? parum abest quin sit ridicula: innuit enim duplicem satisfactionem, actualem & habitualem; cum tamen non, ut est peccatum aliud actuale ab Adamo commissum, aliud habituale in nos propagatum ac nobis inhaerens, sic ulla sit satisfactio praeter eam quae a Christo loco nostro praestita est.
english: Next the question, When then at last do we satisfy in Christ by his actual satisfaction? is not far from ridiculous: for it hints a double satisfaction, actual and habitual; whereas yet not, as there is one actual sin committed by Adam, another habitual propagated into us and inhering in us, so is there any satisfaction besides that which was performed by Christ in our place.

source_text: Praeterea propositio quando satisfacimus in Christo, cum propria non sit, eget expositione, & revocanda est ad propriam: alioqui committitur fallacia plurium interrogationum: continet enim has duas quaestiones: 1. Quando Christus satisfecit? 2. Quando nobis Christi satisfactio imputatur? Ad illam respondeo, quando passus est in cruce; Ad hanc, quando credimus in eum.
english: Besides, the proposition when we satisfy in Christ, since it is not proper, needs exposition, and is to be recalled to the proper: otherwise the fallacy of many questions is committed: for it contains these two questions: 1. When did Christ satisfy? 2. When is Christ's satisfaction imputed to us? To that I answer, when he suffered on the cross; to this, when we believe in him.

source_text: Quod si similiter resolvas quaestionem, Quando peccavimus in Adamo? in has duas, Quando peccavit Adamus? &, Quando imputatur nobis eius peccatum? Facilis erit responsio ad primam, quando manducavit fructum vetitum in paradiso; ad secundam, ut taceam supponi imputationem, cum tamen, ut dici possimus peccasse in Adamo, non sit necessaria imputatio, sufficiat propagatio peccati, respondeo, quando geniti sumus ab Adamo vitiati & corrupti.
english: But if you similarly resolve the question, When did we sin in Adam? into these two, When did Adam sin? and, When is his sin imputed to us? the answer to the first will be easy, when he ate the forbidden fruit in paradise; to the second, not to say that imputation is supposed, whereas yet, that we may be said to have sinned in Adam, imputation is not necessary, propagation of sin suffices, I answer, when we were begotten of Adam vitiated and corrupted.

source_text: Quid in eo est absurdi? Nec tamen sic potuit respondere Vir doctus, quippe qui velit peccatum Adami nobis, iam ab eo tempore quo lapsum est Adam, fuisse imputatum.
english: What absurdity is there in that? And yet the learned man could not so answer, inasmuch as he will have Adam's sin to have been imputed to us already from that time when Adam fell.

source_text: Caeterum quam multa sint inter Christi satisfactionem & Adami peccatum discrimina iam aliquoties observavimus, & ad Rom. 5. 19. observaturi sumus.
english: For the rest, how many discriminations there are between Christ's satisfaction and Adam's sin we have already observed several times, and will observe at Romans 5. 19.

source_text: GAR. 3. Sed & Pelagianus telum arripiet, & in nos contorquebit. Nam ubi dicit Apostolus nos in Adamo peccasse, quid intelligit Vir doctus peccati voce? Corruptionem haereditariam, vitium illud originale nostrum, & nobis ingenitum. Itaque in Adamo peccasse, erit in Adamo corruptos & vitiatos esse.
english: GAR. 3. But the Pelagian also will seize a dart, and will twist it against us. For where the Apostle says that we have sinned in Adam, what does the learned man understand by the word sin? Hereditary corruption, that original vice of ours, and inborn in us. And so to have sinned in Adam will be to have been corrupt and vitiated in Adam.

source_text: Insurget iam Pelagianus, & hac argumentatione fretus quaeret, Quando corrupti sumus in Adamo peccato eius? An cum ipse peccavit, & peccando se corrupit, an alio tempore? Certe cum ipse peccavit, & peccando se corrupit. Multi, imo omnes peccato pro nobis, sed & vitio illius lapsi moniti sunt. Audi iam. Qui ita corrupti fuerunt, ut mortis aeternae rei facti sint, illi vere & proprie corrupti fuerunt. Qui vere & proprie corrupti fuerunt, illi tunc cum corrupti sunt, vere & proprie fuerunt. Ergone infans qui nunc nascitur, vere fuit, cum Adamus peccaret, & peccando seipsum corrumperet? Ita qui laqueos aliis confecerant, in eos se induunt, & quam foveam aliis paraverant in eam ipsimet incidunt.
english: The Pelagian will now rise, and relying on this argumentation will ask, When were we corrupted in Adam by his sin? When he himself sinned, and by sinning corrupted himself, or at another time? Surely when he himself sinned, and by sinning corrupted himself. Many, nay all, have been warned by the sin for us, but also by the vice of that fall. Hear now. Those who were so corrupted that they were made guilty of eternal death, those were truly and properly corrupted. Those who were truly and properly corrupted, those then when they were corrupted truly and properly were. Therefore has the infant who is now born truly been, when Adam was sinning, and by sinning corrupting himself? So those who had made snares for others put themselves into them, and into the pit which they had prepared for others they themselves fall.

source_text: PLAC. Hi laquei nulli sunt, neque facile expedio. Primum enim Apostolus non dixit nos in Adamo peccasse, & ut dixisset, propositio nos esse corruptos & vitiatos in Adamo quem sensum habere possit, considerandum est. Sensus est nos derivata ab Adamo corruptione corruptos esse, vel, quod eodem redit, corruptionem Adami fuisse fontem unde nostra scaturiit corruptio, vel, corruptum fuisse Adamum, & corruptionem Adami in nos propagatam fuisse.
english: PLAC. These snares are none, nor do I easily get free. For first the Apostle has not said that we have sinned in Adam, and even if he had said it, what sense the proposition that we are corrupt and vitiated in Adam can have must be considered. The sense is that we are corrupted by corruption derived from Adam, or, which comes to the same, that Adam's corruption was the fountain from which our corruption sprang, or, that Adam was corrupted, and Adam's corruption was propagated into us.

source_text: Si ergo quaero, Quando Adamus corruptus fuit? respondebo, cum primum peccavit. Quando corrupti fuimus vi communionis quam cum Adamo habemus? Resp. quando geniti sumus. Quid est in ea re difficultatis?
english: If therefore I ask, When was Adam corrupted? I will answer, when he first sinned. When were we corrupted by force of the communion which we have with Adam? Answer, when we were begotten. What difficulty is there in that matter?

source_text: Taceo Virum doctum uti fallacia a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter. Aliud enim est esse corruptum secundum quid, seu cum hac limitatione in Adamo, aliud esse corruptum simpliciter seu absque eiusmodi limitatione. Hoc ex illo non sequitur, si temporis illius ratio habeatur, cum primum Adamus corruptus fuit: significatur enim corruptio radicis seu fontis, non ramorum aut rivorum, quoniam nondum erant: prius autem est esse quam esse corruptum.
english: I pass over that the learned man uses the fallacy from what is said in a certain respect to what is said simply. For it is one thing to be corrupt in a certain respect, or with this limitation in Adam, another to be corrupt simply or without such a limitation. This does not follow from that, if the reason of that time is had, when Adam was first corrupted: for the corruption of the root or fountain is signified, not of the branches or streams, because they were not yet. But it is prior to be than to be corrupt.

source_text: Id quod mihi respondere non potest, quoniam, ut iam observavi, imputationem oppugno quae diu fuisse creditur, antequam esse inciperemus, & qua factum sit ut vere & proprie peccatores & rei fieremus.
english: Which he cannot answer me, because, as I have already observed, I oppose the imputation which is believed to have long been, before we began to be. And by that imputation it was brought about that we truly and properly became sinners and guilty.

source_text: GAR. 4. At sic argumentantur, eos memores esse oportebat eorum quae prius dixerunt. Si peccatum Adami accipiatur non pro actione ipsa praecise sumpta, sed simul cum corruptione quam peperit, recte dici Adami peccatum posteris imputari. Nam ita peccatum erit, & ipsa Adami actio & corruptio consequens.
english: GAR. 4. But so they argue: they ought to have been mindful of those things which they said before. If Adam's sin is taken not for the act itself precisely taken, but together with the corruption which it begot, Adam's sin is rightly said to be imputed to the posterity. For so it will be sin, both Adam's act itself and the following corruption.

source_text: Itaque ut recte dicimur peccare in Adamo propter corruptionem in nobis ab Adamo descendentem: Ita & vere peccare dicemur in eo, propter actionem quam Adamus praecessit.
english: And so as we are rightly said to sin in Adam because of the corruption descending into us from Adam: so also we shall be said truly to sin in him, because of the act which Adam performed before.

source_text: PLAC. Quomodo id antea fuerit dictum, & quantum faveat imputationi antecedenti, satis patere arbitramur ex dictis supra pag. 151. 152. 153. Quorsum igitur pertineat, & quam vim habeat haec Viri docti responsio, non intelligo.
english: PLAC. How that was said before, and how much it favors antecedent imputation, we judge to appear sufficiently from what was said above at pages 151, 152, 153. Whither therefore this reply of the learned man pertains, and what force it has, I do not understand.

source_text: Certe corruptio nostra est, quia in nos propagata, intra nos est; actio vero quae corruptionem peperit non est nostra nisi quatenus corruptio eius quaedam participatio, & in eam consensio est.
english: Certainly the corruption is ours, because propagated into us, it is within us; but the act which begot the corruption is not ours except insofar as the corruption is a certain participation of it, and there is consent unto it.

source_text: GAR. 5. Negatur illud, cui totam suam rationem superstruit Vir doctus, Qui peccarunt, ita ut iustam condemnationem meriti sint, eos vere & proprie peccasse. Quid si vere & proprie peccare est in propria sua persona peccare, & suo non alieno peccato delinquere? Proprium enim alieno opponitur.
english: GAR. 5. That is denied on which the learned man builds his whole reason, that those who have so sinned that they have merited just condemnation have truly and properly sinned. What if to sin truly and properly is to sin in one's own person, and to offend by one's own, not by another's, sin? For one's own is opposed to another's.

source_text: At etiam qui alieno peccato peccant, id est, quibus alienum peccatum imputatur, & iustam condemnationem merentur. Nam filii Saulis peccaverunt alieno, nempe patris, peccato, & tamen iustam mortis condemnationem ex Dei mandato perpessi sunt, adeoque meruerunt, quia iusta sunt Dei iudicia. Et peccata, quibus patres actu peccarunt, non sunt proprie peccata filiorum, quia non sunt ab iis personaliter patrata; & tamen iuxta Decalogi comminationem, propter ea filii in varias poenas & iustam condemnationem incurrunt. Ita ergo possumus in Adamo peccasse, ut iustam mortis sententiam meriti simus, & tamen non ideo huc deveniendum est ut dicamus nos proprie sive personaliter peccasse, cum Adamus peccavit; sed tantum ita censeri apud Deum, ac si cum ipse peccavit omnes peccassemus.
english: And yet even those who sin by another's sin, that is, to whom another's sin is imputed, also merit just condemnation. For Saul's sons sinned by another's, namely the father's, sin, and yet they suffered the just condemnation of death by God's command, and so merited it, because God's judgments are just. And the sins by which the fathers actually sinned are not properly the sons' sins, because they were not personally committed by them; and yet according to the Decalogue's threat, because of them the sons incur various penalties and just condemnation. So therefore we can have sinned in Adam so as to have merited the just sentence of death, and yet we need not for that reason come to this, that we say we properly or personally sinned when Adam sinned; but only that we are so reckoned before God, as if when he himself sinned all of us had sinned.

source_text: PLAC. Putabam vere opponi falso, & proprie improprie sive infigurate, atque ita accipiebam; sed docet me nunc Vir doctus utrumque hoc loco idem valere quod personaliter, vel in propria persona.
english: PLAC. I used to think "truly" was opposed to "falsely," and "properly" to "improperly" or "figuratively," and I took them that way; but the learned man now teaches me that in this place both mean the same as "personally," or "in one's own person."

source_text: Quaero igitur, qui ita peccaverunt ut iustam & propriam condemnationem sint commeriti, verumne vere, an falso peccaverint? Falso, opinor, nemo dixerit. Qui enim dicitur ita peccasse ut iustam condemnationem sit promeritus, si potest probare id falso dici, fieri non potest ut ob eiusmodi peccatum damnetur ab iudice iusto.
english: I ask, then: those who have so sinned that they have earned a just and proper condemnation—have they sinned truly, or falsely? Falsely, I suppose, no one will say. For if someone is said to have so sinned that he has merited just condemnation, and yet one can prove that this is said falsely, it cannot be that he is damned by a just judge for a sin of that kind.

source_text: Rursus quaero an proprie dici possit peccasse, necne, hoc est, non figurate, aut metaphorice? Nemo etiam dixerit, peccasse tantum metaphorice aut figurate: cum enim poena & peccatum sibi mutuo respondeant, poena vere & proprie dicta supponit peccatum vere & proprie dictum, alienum quidem cum poena infligitur alicui ut vadi peccatoris, suum vero, cum infligitur ut peccatori poenam proprie dictam commerito.
english: Again I ask whether he can be said to have sinned properly or not—that is, not figuratively or metaphorically. No one will say he sinned only metaphorically or figuratively: for since penalty and sin answer each other, a penalty truly and properly so called presupposes a sin truly and properly so called—another's, when the penalty is inflicted on someone as surety for the sinner; one's own, when it is inflicted on him as on a sinner who has earned a properly so-called penalty.

source_text: Nec negari potest quin nascamur ex Adamo vere & proprie peccatores, ab eoque peccatum vere & proprie sic dictum trahamus. Adde quod negat Augustinus, negant theologi alii magni nominis ob alienum peccatum quenquam damnari. Vide si placet verba Martyris a nobis laudata sup. pag. 196. ex loc. Com. Class. 2. cap. 1. §. 11. Necnon verba Calvini & Chamieci laudata sup. p. 95. 96. 97. 98.
english: Nor can it be denied that we are born from Adam truly and properly sinners, and from him draw a sin truly and properly so called. Add that Augustine denies, and other theologians of great name deny, that anyone is damned for another's sin. See, if you will, the words of Martyr we cited above, p. 196, from Loci Communes, Class. 2, ch. 1, §11; and also Calvin's and Chamier's words cited above, pp. 95–98.

source_text: Addam haec pauca Martyris, ex eodem loco Com. §. 7. "Huic commento (intelligit commentum Pighii) nos nec possumus nec debemus acquiescere: nam ira Dei non nisi iuste provocatur. Neque enim ea eiusmodi est, ut temere aut fortuito inflammari possit. Quare oportet in natura nostra aliquid esse pravi, ad quod ulciscendum, ira divina excitetur." Alioqui, quomodo mereremur veram & proprie dictam condemnationem, si nullum esset nostrum eiusmodi condemnationis meritum? Est nostrum, inquies, imputatione. Facit ergo, inquam, imputatio ut mereamur poenam aeternam, quam alioqui non meremur.
english: I will add these few words of Martyr from the same place, Loci §7: "We neither can nor ought to rest in this comment"—he means Pighius's comment—"for God's wrath is provoked only justly. Nor is it of such a kind that it can be kindled rashly or by chance. So there must be something evil in our nature, for the avenging of which the divine wrath is stirred." Otherwise, how would we merit a true and properly so-called condemnation, if we had no merit of that kind of condemnation of our own? "It is ours," you will say, "by imputation." So imputation, I reply, makes us merit an eternal penalty that otherwise we do not merit.

source_text: Id ne Dei aequitatem deceat, rogo te, Lector, diligenter considera. Cum enim scopus nobis propositus debeat esse Dei gloria, vide, quaeso, num id sit Deo gloriosum, & an eius aequitatem & iusticiam faciat clariorem. Vide etiam an deceat eius veritatem? peccavimus in Adamo, iustam mortis sententiam meriti sumus, idque sine dubio nec falso nec figurate: tamen non proprie sive personaliter peccavimus cum Adamus peccavit; sed tantum censemur apud Deum, ac si cum ipse peccavit, omnes peccassemus. Hoccine iudicium est secundum veritatem? gloriosum Deo?
english: Whether that befits God's equity, I ask you, reader, to consider carefully. For since the end set before us ought to be God's glory, see, I pray, whether that is glorious to God, and whether it makes his equity and justice clearer. See also whether it befits his truth. We sinned in Adam; we merited the just sentence of death—and that without doubt neither falsely nor figuratively: yet we did not properly or personally sin when Adam sinned; we are only reckoned before God as if, when he himself sinned, we all had sinned. Is this judgment according to the truth? Glorious to God?

source_text: At, inquiet aliquis, censemur apud Deum ac si iusti essemus. Nempe reuera iusti sumus, non iustitia legali sed evangelica, non iustitia operum sed fidei, non iustitia a nobis profecta aut acquisita, sed data a Deo & per fidem accepta. Dispar est ratio peccati: non promittitur, non datur a Deo, non accipitur a nondum existente.
english: But someone will say: we are reckoned before God as if we were just. Yes—we truly are just, not by a legal righteousness but by an evangelical one; not by a righteousness of works but of faith; not by a righteousness that proceeds from us or is acquired by us, but given by God and received through faith. The case of sin is different: it is not promised, not given by God, not received by one who does not yet exist.

source_text: Verba Augustini causae meae non obsunt: fateor enim ab Adami vitio neminem esse immunem. Ad exemplum filiorum Saulis iam respondimus, eos paterni peccati fuisse participes. Peccata patrum visitantur in filiis, ut dixi, cum reperiuntur in filiis. Dicuntur patrum quia patres priores illa commiserunt, filiis ut committerent autores fuerunt, vel exemplo & autoritate, vel educatione & institutione, vel etiam lege.
english: Augustine's words do not hurt my case: for I grant that no one is immune from Adam's vice. As for the example of Saul's sons, we have already answered that they were partakers of the father's sin. The fathers' sins are visited on the sons, as I said, when they are found in the sons. They are called the fathers' because the fathers first committed them, and were authors to the sons that they should commit them—by example and authority, or by education and training, or even by law.

source_text: Objicies, quod etiam hoc loco subiungis Apostolum dixisse Levi fuisse decimatum in Abrahamo quia adhuc in lumbis patris erat, cum ei occurreret Melchisedec. Sed Apostolus satis innuit phrasim illam non modo non esse propriam, sed duram, cum eam emollivit hac praefatione ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν. Deinde ad locum illum respondi in thesibus, & tu meam responsionem tibi sumis refellendam in extremo cap. 9. tui tractatus; quam bene, cum tuis vestigiis insistens ad eum locum pervenero, Deo iuvante, ostendam, eademque opera ratiocinationem Apostoli retegam longe solidissimam, sed ab imputatione, quae inter nos controvertitur, alienam omnino.
english: You will object that here too you add the Apostle's saying that Levi was tithed in Abraham because he was still in his father's loins when Melchizedek met him. But the Apostle plainly hints that that phrase is not only not proper, but harsh, when he softens it with the preface "so to speak." Next, I answered that place in the theses, and you take my answer to refute it at the end of chapter 9 of your treatise; how well, when following your steps I reach that place, God helping, I will show—and by the same work I will uncover the Apostle's reasoning as most solid, yet altogether foreign to the imputation disputed between us.

source_text: Objicis etiam similem phrasim in re simili eiusdem Apostoli: in Adam omnes moriuntur. Sed ea tuam sententiam evertit. Non vult enim omnes mori in Adamo illa ipsa singulari morte, qua mortuus est Adamus, quae scilicet omnibus imputetur, sed sua quisque propria morte. Sic vivificamur, seu resurgimus in Christo; non per imputationem resurrectionis Christi, sed reali, & quam quisque in se suscipit, resurrectione.
english: You also object a like phrase in a like matter from the same Apostle: in Adam all die. But that overturns your view. For he does not mean that all die in Adam by that very singular death by which Adam died, as if it were imputed to all, but each by his own proper death. So we are made alive, or rise, in Christ—not by imputation of Christ's resurrection, but by a real resurrection which each receives in himself.

source_text: Et cum versu praecedente Apostolus sic loquitur: quandoquidem per hominem est mors, etiam per hominem est resurrectio mortuorum, non intelligit unius Adami mortem reliquis hominibus imputatam nec unius Christi resurrectionem imputatam, sed mortem & resurrectionem specie unam, numero multam, qua omnes, quisque sua, moriuntur & resurgunt. Id ita manifestum est ut probatione non egeat.
english: And when in the preceding verse the Apostle speaks thus—since by a man comes death, by a man also comes the resurrection of the dead—he does not mean one Adam's death imputed to the rest of men, nor one Christ's resurrection imputed, but death and resurrection one in kind, many in number, by which all die and rise, each his own. That is so plain it needs no proof.

source_text: Concludamus igitur, cum idem Apostolus ait, per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introisse, intelligendum esse non singulare illud actuale peccatum quod unus ille homo commisit, sed peccatum ab illo natum, & in omnes homines sparsum ac propagatum: Et, cum ait, omnes peccasse in Adamo (quanquam id non dicit) intelligendum esse omnes peccasse, non uno illo singulari peccato actuali Adami illis imputato, sed suo quemque, sibi infito ac proprio peccato, quod ab illo Adami ducit originem. Morimur ergo in Adamo; id est, vi communionis naturalis quae nobis cum Adamo intercedit, non autem in ipsa Adami persona; & vivificamur in Christo, non in ipsa persona Iesu Christi, sed vi communionis nostrae supernaturalis cum ea: sed hac de re rursus cum ad Theses ventum fuerit.
english: Let us conclude, then: when the same Apostle says that through one man sin entered the world, it is to be understood not as that singular actual sin which that one man committed, but as the sin born from him and spread and propagated into all men. And when it is said that all sinned in Adam (though he does not say that), it is to be understood that all sinned—not by that one singular actual sin of Adam imputed to them, but each by his own inborn and proper sin, which takes its origin from that of Adam. We die, then, in Adam—that is, by the force of the natural communion that joins us to Adam, not in Adam's own person; and we are made alive in Christ, not in the very person of Jesus Christ, but by the force of our supernatural communion with him: but of this again when we come to the Theses.

source_text: GAR. Resp. I. Qui negant nos in ipsa Adami persona fuisse morti addictos, illi manifeste deserunt Confessionem Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quae id docet & dicit expresse Art. 10.
english: GAR. Resp. I. Those who deny that we were devoted to death in Adam's own person plainly desert the Confession of our churches, which teaches and expressly says that in Art. 10.

source_text: PLAC. Egone illam Confessionem desero, quam totam amplector, arcteque teneo, imprimis articulum illum decimum? At nego nos in ipsa Adami persona fuisse morti addictos. Primum illa verba, fuisse morti addictos, mea non sunt: neque praeterito usus sum, sed praesenti, neque de addictione locutus sum, sed de ipsa morte. Verba enim Apostoli sic aiunt: in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur; de praesenti eiusmodi addictione intelligi non possunt, ut ex futuro, vivificabuntur, perspicuum est.
english: PLAC. Do I desert that Confession, which I wholly embrace and tightly hold, especially that tenth article? Yet I deny that we were devoted to death in Adam's own person. First, those words "were devoted to death" are not mine: I did not use the past tense but the present, and I did not speak of devotion (addiction) but of death itself. For the Apostle's words run thus: in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive; they cannot be taken of a present devotion of that kind, as is clear from the future "will be made alive."

source_text: Loquor igitur de morte qua quisque moritur, de resurrectione qua quisque formaliter resurgit. Nec aliud volo, cum nego nos mori in ipsa Adami persona, quam nos mori ipsa morte Adami nobis imputata; cum nego nos resurgere in ipsa Christi persona, quam resurgere resurrectione Christi nobis imputata, ut patet ex verbis ipsis antecedentibus.
english: I speak, then, of the death by which each dies, and of the resurrection by which each formally rises. And when I deny that we die in Adam's own person, I mean nothing else than that we die by Adam's own death imputed to us; when I deny that we rise in Christ's own person, nothing else than that we rise by Christ's resurrection imputed to us—as is plain from the very words that went before.

source_text: Contrariumne docet Art. ille Confessionis decimus? Cur igitur cum illo committo? At dicit nos in ipsius (Adami) persona spoliatos bonis illis omnibus, in omnem hanc miseriam & maledictionem incidisse. Ergo morimur in ipsa Adami persona, hoc est morte Adami nobis imputata. Nihil tale sequitur ex illis Confessionis verbis. Imo ne imputatio quidem ulla ex ijs colligi potest, vel donorum illorum, vel spoliationis illius, ut plenius declarabitur cap. XII.
english: Does that tenth article of the Confession teach the contrary? Why then am I set against it? But it says we were spoiled of all those goods in his (Adam's) person, and fell into all this misery and curse. Therefore we die in Adam's own person—that is, by Adam's death imputed to us. No such thing follows from those words of the Confession. Indeed not even any imputation can be drawn from them, either of those gifts or of that spoiling—as will be shown more fully in chapter XII.

source_text: GAR. 2. Unionem cum Adamo naturalem non tantum agnoscimus, sed etiam imputationis illius, de qua agitur, fundamentum esse dicimus.
english: GAR. 2. We not only acknowledge a natural union with Adam, but also say that it is the foundation of that imputation which is under discussion.

source_text: PLAC. Si imputatio intelligitur antecedens seu immediata, non est illius fundamentum unio illa. Sed pergat.
english: PLAC. If the imputation is understood as antecedent or immediate, that union is not its foundation. But let him go on.

source_text: GAR. Nec minus certum est unumquemque nostrum mori morte sua propria, & habere corruptionem internam sibi propriam, & personaliter distinctam a corruptione quam peccatum actuale fecit in Adamo. Habere autem utrumque ex vi conjunctionis illius quae nobis cum Adamo tanquam capite generis intercedit. Illa tamen non impediunt, quominus ad imputationem ea verba Apostoli pertinere dicantur, cum testatur, nos in Adamo mori.
english: GAR. It is no less certain that each of us dies by his own proper death, and has an internal corruption proper to himself and personally distinct from the corruption which actual sin made in Adam. Yet we have both by the force of that conjunction which joins us to Adam as head of the race. Still those facts do not keep the Apostle's words from being said to pertain to imputation when he testifies that we die in Adam.

source_text: PLAC. Itane, ad imputationem mortis Adami? Quis unquam audiverat, mortem Adami nobis imputari? Manet igitur responsio mea, vel si ita vis, argumentatio: si propositio in Adamo morimur vera est, quamvis mors Adami nobis non imputetur, etiam propositio in Adamo peccavimus vera esse potest, quamvis peccatum Adami nobis non imputetur.
english: PLAC. Really—to the imputation of Adam's death? Who ever heard that Adam's death is imputed to us? So my answer—or if you will, my argument—stands: if the proposition "we die in Adam" is true even though Adam's death is not imputed to us, the proposition "we sinned in Adam" can also be true even though Adam's sin is not imputed to us.

source_text: GAR. Unde contrario modo concludo, atque collegit Vir doctus: Si dictum Apostoli, in Adamo morimur, ad imputationem spectat: Ergo & quod ait, in Adamo peccasse. Atqui illud ad imputationem spectat; ut certa ratione ostendi potest. Nam neque in Noacho, neque in quocumque alio maiorum nostrorum mori dicimur, sed tantum in Adamo. Et tamen sicuti dicimur ab Adamo prognati, ita dici possumus prognati a patribus & omnibus maioribus nostris.
english: GAR. From which I conclude the opposite way from the learned man: if the Apostle's saying "we die in Adam" looks to imputation, then so does what he says about having sinned in Adam. And that saying does look to imputation, as can be shown by a sure reason. For we are not said to die in Noah, nor in any other of our ancestors, but only in Adam. And yet just as we are said to be descended from Adam, so we can be said to be descended from our fathers and all our ancestors.

source_text: Cuius discriminis aliquam prorsus causam esse oportet. Non est autem illa simpliciter quaerenda in conjunctione naturali, aut propagatione qua descendimus ab Adamo. Nam non minus a maioribus alijs nostris propagati sumus, neque minus sumus cum iis coniuncti, quam cum Adamo; imo propinquior est cum iis, quam cum Adamo, communio ratione temporis. Neque etiam in eo, quod Adam principium est nostrae originis, sive ille a quo genus humanum incepit. Nam ea quidem legitima causa esse potest, quare in Adamo mori dicamur: sed non est legitima causa quare idem de alijs maioribus dici non possit. &c.
english: There must be some cause at all of this discrimination. But it is not to be sought simply in the natural conjunction or propagation by which we descend from Adam. For we are no less propagated from our other ancestors, nor less joined to them than to Adam; indeed our communion with them is nearer in time than with Adam. Nor again simply in this, that Adam is the principle of our origin, or the one from whom the human race began. For that can indeed be a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam; but it is not a legitimate cause why the same cannot be said of other ancestors. Etc.

source_text: PLAC. Quomodo certa ratione ostendi potest, dictum Apostoli in Adamo morimur, ad imputationem spectare, si sine imputatione causa legitima est, quare in Adamo mori dicamur? Agebatur enim de eo quod ab Apostolo dicitur, non de eo quod non dicitur. At quare idem de alijs maioribus non dicitur? Si saepius diceretur ac inculcaretur in Scriptura nos in Adamo mori, merito quaeri posset, quare saepe rem illam repetens Scriptura, perpetuo unius Adami, nunquam aliorum maiorum meminisset: nunc, cum semel dictum sit, mirum videri non debet, si alij maiores silentio praeteriti sunt, nec locus est silentii illius rationem quaerendi.
english: PLAC. How can it be shown by a sure reason that the Apostle's saying "we die in Adam" looks to imputation, if without imputation there is already a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam? For the point was what the Apostle says, not what he does not say. But why is the same not said of other ancestors? If Scripture said and drove home more often that we die in Adam, one might fairly ask why, repeating that matter often, it always remembered one Adam and never other ancestors; now, since it is said only once, it ought not seem strange if other ancestors are passed over in silence, and there is no place to hunt a reason for that silence.

source_text: Si tamen eius ratio reddenda est, ab imputatione arcessiri non debet: succresceret enim statim alia quaestio, cur non aeque in alijs maioribus, ac in Adamo, quod imputaretur posteris fuisset? Tandemque ad Dei voluntatem esset confugiendum, quae sine imputatione posset hoc loco pro ratione afferri. Sed non est opus: succurrunt enim aliae rationes, & quidem duae. Prima, a voce omnes. Sicut, inquit Apostolus, omnes in Adamo morimur. Iam autem manifestum est omnes in solo Adamo mori. Altera inde peti potest, quod notatur primus fons, prima origo mortis. Reliqui maiores veluti canales fuerunt, per quos peccatum & mors ab illo fonte in nos dimanarunt: solus Adamus primus fuit author mortis.
english: Yet if a reason for it must be given, it ought not be fetched from imputation: for at once another question would grow up—why was there not equally in other ancestors, as in Adam, something to be imputed to posterity? And at last one would flee to God's will, which without imputation could be offered here as the reason. But there is no need: other reasons come to hand, and two of them. First, from the word "all." As the Apostle says, we all die in Adam. And it is already plain that all die in Adam alone. Second, it can be drawn from this, that the first source, the first origin of death, is marked. The other ancestors were like channels through which sin and death flowed down from that source into us: Adam alone was the first author of death.

source_text: Sic, communis omnium peccatum Ieroboami vocatur, non autem Iudaeorum Israelis idolatria tam alicuius alterius regis, propterea quod primus illius autor Ieroboamus fuerat.
english: So the common sin of all is called Jeroboam's sin—not Israel's idolatry as of some other king—because Jeroboam had been its first author.

source_text: Interim nonne vides omnes homines eodem modo accipi ab Apostolo, cum in eos mortem transire, & cum eos peccasse dicit? Mors, inquit, in omnes transiit, quoniam omnes peccaverunt. Utrobique vox omnes eosdem homines, eodem modo, significat.
english: Meanwhile, do you not see that all men are taken in the same way by the Apostle, both when death passes into them and when he says they sinned? Death, he says, passed into all, because all sinned. In both places the word "all" signifies the same men, in the same way.

source_text: Alioqui vitiosus esset Apostoli syllogismus, & ex quatuor terminis componeretur, quem sic forms: Quicumque peccaverunt, in eos mors transiit; Omnes peccaverunt; Igitur in omnes mors transiit. Nam in conclusione vox omnes notat personas omnium hominum inter se & a persona Adami distinctas & separatas. Ergo necesse est ut in minore eadem vox omnium itidem hominum personas distinctas & separatas cum inter se tum ab Adamo significet.
english: Otherwise the Apostle's syllogism would be faulty and composed of four terms, which you may form thus: Whoever sinned, into them death passed; all sinned; therefore into all death passed. For in the conclusion the word "all" marks the persons of all men, distinct among themselves and from Adam's person. So in the minor the same word must likewise signify the distinct and separate persons of all men, both among themselves and from Adam.

source_text: Iam autem manifestum est, omnium hominum personas distinctas & separatas a persona Adami non commisisse peccatum illud actuale unum idemque numero quod Adamus commisit, & tam impossibile esse ut omnium personarum generis humani sit unicum numero peccatum actuale, quam ut sit unica numero mors omnium.
english: But it is already plain that the distinct and separate persons of all men, apart from Adam's person, did not commit that one actual sin, one and the same in number, which Adam committed. And it is as impossible that there should be one numerical actual sin of all the persons of the human race as that there should be one numerical death of all.

source_text: GAR. Resp. Huius rationis vim satis ad assignandam peccati Adami imputationem videre difficile est & dicere. Nam aut longe fallor, aut nemo eorum qui pro hac imputatione pugnant, unquam somniavit personam suam, vel alterius cuiuscumque hominis, esse confusam cum persona Adami, aut ita indistinctam, ut in unum ὑπόστασιν cum ea coaluerit. Hoc ne quidem animo concipi potest. &c.
english: GAR. Resp. It is hard enough to see and say how the force of this reason assigns the imputation of Adam's sin. For either I am far wrong, or none of those who fight for this imputation ever dreamed that his own person, or any other man's, is confused with Adam's person, or so indistinct as to have coalesced into one hypostasis with him. That cannot even be conceived in the mind. Etc.

source_text: PLAC. Quandoquidem videre huius rationis vim Vir doctus non potuit, eam explicabo. Meminerit igitur, Lector, si placet, me non impugnare imputationem mediatam seu consequentem, quae cuiusque existentia & corruptione posterior est.
english: PLAC. Since the learned man could not see the force of this reason, I will explain it. Let the reader remember, if he will, that I am not attacking mediate or consequent imputation, which is later than each one's existence and corruption.

source_text: sed immediatam & antecedentem, quam Vir doctus communem appellat & ita describit Cap. 1. §. xiii. Imputatio, inquit, peccati Adami communis est, qua peccatum Adami non ipsum modo reum fecit, sed etiam totum genus, quod in ipso seminaliter & radicaliter continebatur, eodem reatu implicuit, iam ab eo tempore, quo lapsus est Adam.
english: But the immediate and antecedent imputation, which the learned man calls "common" and so describes in Cap. 1 §13: "The common imputation of Adam's sin," he says, "is that by which Adam's sin made not only him guilty, but also implicated the whole race, which was contained in him seminaliter and radicaliter, in the same guilt, already from the time when Adam fell."

source_text: Et paulo post inquit: Existente autem humana natura in individuo illo principiali, in illo etiam dici possunt homines communiter extitisse. Extiteruntne scilicet a persona Adami distantes & separati? Non arbitror quenquam hoc dicturum. Et Cap. 2. §. xvii. Communis, inquit, illa sive immediata, quemadmodum posterior fuit prima actuali Adami transgressione, ita prior fuit personali cuiuscumque hominis ex Adamo prognati existentia atque adeo etiam corruptione illa quae in singulos naturali generatione descendit, quatenus ab initio resuerunt omnes communiter in Adamo.
english: And a little later he says: "But with human nature existing in that principal individual, men can also be said to have existed commonly in him." Existed, that is, distant and separate from Adam's person? I do not think anyone will say that. And Cap. 2 §17: "That common or immediate [imputation]," he says, "just as it was later than Adam's first actual transgression, so it was prior to the personal existence of each man born of Adam, and so also to that corruption which descends into individuals by natural generation, insofar as from the beginning all flowed commonly in Adam."

source_text: Facta est igitur ista imputatio cum nondum essemus personae separatae & distantes ab Adamo: vel, ut loquitur is quicum mihi res erat, cum consideraremus a Deo tanquam unus homo in Adamo. Nunc, opinor, quam vim habeat argumentum, ipse per te, Lector, satis intelligis.
english: That imputation was therefore made when we were not yet persons separate and distant from Adam—or, as the one I was dealing with puts it, when we were considered by God as one man in Adam. Now, I think, you yourself, reader, sufficiently see what force the argument has.

source_text: Rectius igitur mea sententia fecisses, si Calvini interpretationi acquiescens non contempsisses id quod legere potuisti in Clavi Scripturae ad nomen peccatum, his verbis: significat quoque crebro verbum חטא peccavit in prima conjugatione non actionem, sed qualitatem inhaerentem, seu sortem ac conditionem hominis, seu esse peccatorem, esse reum, sicut solent verba hebraea saepissime tantum existentiam rei, non actionem aut passionem aliumve motum indicare.
english: You would therefore, in my judgment, have done better if, resting in Calvin's interpretation, you had not despised what you could read in the Clavis Scripturae under the name peccatum. He writes that the verb "sinned" in the Qal conjugation often signifies not an action, but an inherent quality, or a man's lot and condition, or to be a sinner, to be guilty—just as Hebrew verbs very often indicate only the existence of a thing, not an action or passion or other motion.

source_text: Et paulo post: sic Rom. v. in Adamo omnes peccaverunt: id est, scelerati ac Dei hostes fuerunt. Quae quasi habitualis significatio verbi & nominis peccati diligenter observanda est.
english: And a little later: so Rom. 5, in Adam all sinned—that is, they were wicked and enemies of God. Which quasi-habitual sense of the verb and noun "sin" is to be carefully observed.

source_text: Et rursus, Romanorum quinto: sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pervasit, in quo omnes peccaverunt: non actionem sed potius habituale, aut sortem innatum & essentiale malum significat, quod nempe per Adamum omnes facti sint corrupti &c.
english: And again, Romans 5: as through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, in whom all sinned. It signifies not an action but rather a habitual, or innate and essential, evil lot: namely that through Adam all have been made corrupt, etc.

source_text: Eodem sensu Logici notare solent verba in definitionibus posita aptitudinem, non actum designare, ut cum definitur albedo, Color qui visum disgregat, id est, qui aptus natus est visum disgregare.
english: In the same sense logicians usually note that words set in definitions mark an aptitude, not an act—as when whiteness is defined as a color that scatters sight, that is, that is born apt to scatter sight.

source_text: Sic cum Dominus dicit omnem arborem malam malos ferre fructus, male colligeret qui infidelium irregenitos infantulos malas arbores esse negaret, quod non ferant malos fructus; haud secus certe ac qui legisset, omnem volucrem volare, male inde concluderet, aviculam recens exclusam, quod nondum volet, volucrem non esse.
english: So when the Lord says every bad tree bears bad fruit, he would gather poorly who denied that the unregenerate infants of unbelievers are bad trees because they do not yet bear bad fruit. No otherwise than if, reading that every bird flies, he concluded that a chick just hatched, because it does not yet fly, is not a bird.

source_text: Itaque Anabaptistis quibusdam idem quod tu obiicientibus, peccare esse verbum activum & actionem significare, Georgius Sohnius nihil respondit, nisi verba apud Hebraeos non tantum significare actualiter, sed etiam habitualiter; hoc est, non tantum actionem, sed etiam defectum & pravitatem inhaerentem.
english: And so to certain Anabaptists objecting—as you do—that "to sin" is an active verb and signifies an action, Georgius Sohnius answered nothing except that among the Hebrews words signify not only actually but also habitually. That is, not only an action, but also an inherent defect and wickedness.

source_text: Caeterum non satis intelligo tua ista verba, In peccato originali non peccavimus actu, nisi quatenus in Adamo peccavimus. Quid enim? Visne nos actu peccavisse in Adamo tum cum peccavit?
english: For the rest I do not well enough understand those words of yours: "In original sin we did not sin by act, except insofar as we sinned in Adam." What then? Do you mean that we sinned by act in Adam at the time when he sinned?

source_text: Id Zanchius, quem tu pro tua sententia laudas Cap. tui tractatus vii. negat, addita hac ratione, quia nondum eramus actu. Nam qui fieri potuit, ut, quum nondum essemus actu, peccaremus actu?
english: That Zanchius—whom you praise for your view in chapter 7 of your treatise—denies, adding this reason: because we were not yet in act. For how could it be that, when we were not yet in act, we should sin by act?

source_text: Unde sic argumentor: Moriuntur homines actu. Ergo peccaverunt actu. Absurdum enim est ut qui potentia tantum peccavit, non autem actu, puniatur actu, & quidem poena gravissima. Atqui non peccaverunt actu in Adamo cum peccavit actualiter. Aliud igitur sit oportet peccatum ob quod actu moriantur homines, nempe vitium illud originale, quo quod omnibus & singulis inest vere & proprie, actu, inhaerenter; tam certe actu quam fuit in ipso Adamo.
english: From which I argue thus: Men die by act. Therefore they have sinned by act. For it is absurd that one who has sinned only in potency, not in act, should be punished in act—and with a most heavy penalty. And yet they did not sin by act in Adam when he sinned actually. There must therefore be another sin because of which men die by act: namely that original vice which is in all and each truly and properly, by act, inherently—as certainly by act as it was in Adam himself.

source_text: Minus etiam capio quae subnectis, cum Adamus peccavit, pro omnibus suis posteris peccavit. Si intelligis eum magno omnium posterorum malo peccasse, nihil verius. Hinc enim natum est vitium illud quod genus humanum invasit & morti addixit. Sed si intelligis eum loco nostro peccavisse, nihil dici potuit a te minus considerate.
english: Still less do I grasp what you add: when Adam sinned, he sinned for all his posterity. If you mean he sinned to the great harm of all his posterity, nothing is truer. For from that was born the vice that invaded the human race and devoted it to death. But if you mean he sinned in our place, nothing less carefully considered could have been said by you.

source_text: Nam neque id Scriptura dicit uspiam, & valde absurdum est. Satisfecit quidem loco nostro Christus iustitiae divinae: quippe nos enim tenebamur satisfacere. Moriendum erat omnibus nobis, ipse mortem loco nostro gustavit. Puniendi eramus omnes, ipse omnium loco passus est.
english: For Scripture nowhere says that, and it is exceedingly absurd. Christ did indeed satisfy divine justice in our place—for we were bound to satisfy. All of us had to die; he tasted death in our place. All of us were to be punished; he suffered in the place of all.

source_text: Num igitur peccare tenebamur, ut nostro loco Adamus peccaret? Mihi quidem hactenus inauditum fuit peccare aliquem loco alterius tanquam eius vadem posse.
english: Were we then bound to sin, so that Adam might sin in our place? For my part it has so far been unheard-of that anyone can sin in another's place as his surety.

source_text: Sed fortasse nostrae partes erant legem, tunc Adamo latam, tunc observare, atque adeo audire, memoriae mandare, intelligere, exequi. Adamus autem ut nos hac molestia levaret se suffecit in locum nostrum qui nostrum officium impleret, nostras partes ageret. Apage tales cogitationes.
english: But perhaps our part was then to keep the law then given to Adam—to hear it, commit it to memory, understand it, carry it out. And Adam, to relieve us of that trouble, put himself in our place to fulfill our duty and play our part. Away with such thoughts.

source_text: Profecto, si loco omnium posterorum Adamus legem illam implevisset, eius posteri ad eandem legem implendam ipsi in propriis suis personis non fuissent amplius obligati, quemadmodum quia loco nostro Christus iustitiae divinae satisfecit, non tenemur amplius ei satisfacere.
english: Truly, if Adam had fulfilled that law in the place of all his posterity, his posterity would no longer have been bound to fulfill the same law in their own persons—just as, because Christ satisfied divine justice in our place, we are no longer bound to satisfy it.

source_text: Certe quemadmodum tunc temporis nulla erat in mundo persona humana praeter Adamum & Evam, sic nulla praeter eos duos persona humana aut poterat, aut debebat legi illi pro illo tempore parere. Neque vero Adamus ea mente peccavit ut loco nostro peccaret, neque, si mens ea ipsi fuisset, in cuiusquam potestate est loco alterius non consentientis peccare. Neque id naturae lex exigebat ut posterorum loco peccaret, neque Dei bonitatem & iustitiam decebat id efficere & constituere.
english: Certainly, just as at that time there was no human person in the world besides Adam and Eve, so no human person besides those two either could or ought to obey that law for that time. Nor did Adam sin with the mind of sinning in our place; and even if that had been his mind, it is in no one's power to sin in the place of another who does not consent. Nor did nature's law require that he sin in posterity's place, nor did it befit God's goodness and justice to effect and appoint that.

source_text: Praeterea si loco nostro peccavit & peccatum illud merebatur poenam quae est peccatum, videlicet corruptionem: dic mihi, quaeso, cur non sit etiam loco nostro illa affectus poena? nam quo temporis articulo peccavit, eodem corruptus & vitiosus & iniustus factus est.
english: Besides: if he sinned in our place, and that sin merited the penalty which is sin—namely corruption—tell me, I ask, why was he not also afflicted with that penalty in our place? For at the very moment he sinned, in the same he was made corrupt and vicious and unjust.

source_text: Annon quo nomine peccavit eodem puniri debuit, praesertim eodem momento? nisi velis, quemadmodum sacrificulus pontificius inter celebrandum missam modo Christi personam induit, modo deponit, atque ita diversas agit personas eodem paene momento, sic Adamum similiter modo personam nostram repraesentasse, modo suam unius sustinuisse, atque eodem momento & peccasse loco nostro, & punitum suo, non nostro.
english: Ought he not to have been punished under the same title under which he sinned, especially at the same moment? Unless you mean that, as a pontifical priest celebrating mass puts on Christ's person and then puts it off, and so plays different persons in almost the same moment, so Adam likewise sometimes represented our person, sometimes sustained his own alone—and in the same moment both sinned in our place and was punished in his own, not ours.

source_text: Nam si loco nostro ea poena castigatus fuit quae est peccatum originale, non convenit nos eadem poena affici: quam enim loco nostro peccavit, tam loco nostro punitus est.
english: For if he was chastised in our place with that penalty which is original sin, it does not fit that we should be afflicted with the same penalty: for as he sinned in our place, so he was punished in our place.

source_text: Sicut enim quamvis ipsi in propriis nostris personis peccaverimus, tamen quia Christus loco nostro punitus est, non debemus amplius puniri: ita si pro illo peccato actuali punitus est Adamus loco nostro inflictione peccati originalis, non potest amplius pro eodem illo peccato nobis peccatum originale infligi.
english: For just as, though we ourselves have sinned in our own persons, yet because Christ was punished in our place we ought not to be punished further: so if for that actual sin Adam was punished in our place by the infliction of original sin, original sin can no longer be inflicted on us for that same sin.

source_text: Vides quo te ducat tua ista assertio pro nobis peccasse Adamum: nimirum ad negandum peccatum nostrum originale.
english: You see where that assertion of yours—that Adam sinned for us—leads you: namely to denying our original sin.

source_text: Quod ipsum etiam effici potest hoc argumento, ut videas magis magisque quam perniciosa sit illa sententia, a qua te dimovere cupio & conor.
english: Which very thing can also be brought about by this argument, so that you may see more and more how pernicious that opinion is from which I desire and strive to move you.

source_text: Quod Adami peccatum nobis per imputationem convenit, vel, si ita mavis, nobis proxime & immediate imputatur, id ex quo sumus reipsa neque a nobis commissum est, neque nobis inhaeret. Res manifesta est de peccato actuali Adami: id enim vis nobis imputari, non autem inesse, aut a nobis natis committi.
english: That Adam's sin belongs to us by imputation—or, if you prefer, is proximately and immediately imputed to us—is, as far as we are concerned in the thing itself, neither committed by us nor inherent in us. The matter is plain about Adam's actual sin: for you want that imputed to us, not to be in us, or to be committed by us once born.

source_text: Nam quod per imputationem convenit, non convenit per realem inhaerentiam sive inexistientiam. Duo istiusmodi inter se pugnant. Cur enim aut faciam aut patiar quod alius loco meo vel fecit vel passus est?
english: For what belongs by imputation does not belong by real inherence or inexistence. Those two fight each other. For why should I either do or suffer what another has done or suffered in my place?

source_text: Atqui si peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatur, profecto etiam imputatur eius peccatum habituale sive corruptio inhaerens. Nam quae ratio afferri potest pro imputatione peccati actualis Adami, quae eadem non militet pro imputatione peccati eiusdem habitualis, & quidem validius? Illud enim fuit actio praeteriens, hoc vitium permanens: illud iam pridem praeterierat cum anno aetatis 130. Adamus Sethum genuit, a quo nos ducimus originem; hoc vero tum aderat praesens & inhaerens penitus facultatibus Adami cum generationi operam daret.
english: And if Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, then certainly his habitual sin—or inherent corruption—is imputed too. For what reason can be offered for imputing Adam's actual sin that does not equally—and more strongly—serve for imputing his habitual sin? That was a passing act; this is a permanent vice. That had already long passed when, at age 130, Adam begot Seth, from whom we take our origin; but this was then present and thoroughly inherent in Adam's powers when he gave himself to generation.

source_text: Illud vulgo dicitur esse personae, hoc naturae. Itaque aut aeque aut magis etiam conveniebat Adamo ut capiti nostro & origini, & nostram personam sustinenti, quam peccatum illud actuale, quod actio fuit singularis.
english: That is commonly said to belong to the person; this, to the nature. So it suited Adam as our head and origin, and as sustaining our person, equally or even more than that actual sin, which was a singular act.

source_text: Si ergo peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatur, imputatur etiam nobis eius vitium sive peccatum habituale & insitum. Si imputatur, non est in nobis. Quod enim nobiscum Adamus communicavit imputatione, id non communicavit nobiscum reali existentia. Quod peccatum peccavimus in persona Adami, id non peccavimus realiter in nostris personis postea quam geniti sumus.
english: If therefore Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, his vice—or habitual and implanted sin—is imputed to us too. If it is imputed, it is not in us. For what Adam shared with us by imputation he did not share with us by real existence. The sin we sinned in Adam's person we did not really sin in our own persons after we were born.

source_text: Alioqui magis peccatores ex Adamo nasceremur quam fuit Adam. Nam ei non est imputatum nisi ipsius peccatum actuale & habituale; nobis idem utrumque, quemadmodum Adamo, imputaretur, & praeterea imputaretur idem specie peccatum habituale nobis actu insitum ac inhaerens: nam, velis nolis, corruptio innata peccatum est, nisi condonetur, imputandum ad mortem.
english: Otherwise we would be born from Adam more sinners than Adam was. For to him was imputed only his own actual and habitual sin; to us both would be imputed as to Adam, and besides there would be imputed a habitual sin of the same kind actually implanted and inherent in us—for, like it or not, innate corruption is sin, and unless forgiven is to be imputed unto death.

source_text: Non modo autem imputatio quam tueris tollit vitium originale, quod tamen nobis, proh dolor, omnibus & singulis medullitus infixum est, & Scriptura clamat & experientia contestatur, sed ea quoque Dei φιλανθρωπίαν labefactat.
english: Nor does the imputation you defend only take away original vice—which nevertheless is, alas, fixed marrow-deep in all and each of us, and Scripture cries out and experience bears witness—but it also undermines God’s φιλανθρωπία.

source_text: Quippe qui voluerit Adamum sustinere personam nostram cum peccavit, non voluerit autem nostram personam eundem sustinere cum punitus est.
english: Seeing that he willed Adam to sustain our person when Adam sinned, but did not will that same man to sustain our person when Adam was punished.

source_text: Consideraverit eum cum peccavit ut caput nostrum, noluerit eum eodem modo considerare cum puniretur: voluerit eum peccare loco nostro, noluerit puniri loco nostro.
english: He considered him our head when he sinned, and refused to consider him in the same way when he was being punished.
He willed him to sin in our place, and refused that he be punished in our place.

source_text: Nostras personas ei imposuerit ut peccaret loco nostro, ac eodem momento abstulerit ne puniretur itidem loco nostro: perinde ac si nostra ipsorum qui nihil ipsi peccaveramus, morte delectatus fuisset, nihilque aliud illa personarum nostrarum impositione Adamo captasset quam occasionem nos omnes efficiendi peccatores.
english: He imposed our persons on him so that he might sin in our place, and at the same moment took them away lest he likewise be punished in our place.

It is as if he had delighted in the death of us ourselves, who had ourselves sinned nothing, and by that imposition of our persons on Adam had sought nothing else than an occasion of making us all sinners.

source_text: Quod Petrum Martyrem (qui Calvini & Buceri vestigia secutus totus meus est) ac caeteros dicis agnovisse, omnes homines in Adamo peccasse, mihi non obest, qui clamo omnes homines peccare in Adamo quomodo in Adamo moriuntur, hoc est, vi communionis quam habent cum Adamo, non autem imputatione singularis eius vel peccati, vel mortis.
english: That you say Peter Martyr (who followed the steps of Calvin and Bucer and is wholly mine) and the others acknowledged that all men sinned in Adam does not hurt me.
I cry that all men sin in Adam as they die in Adam—that is, by the force of the communion they have with Adam, not by imputation of his singular sin or of his death.

source_text: Peccavisse omnes homines in Adamo, quomodo in eo fuerunt. Fuerunt autem in eo non imputatione τοῦ εἶναι ipsius, sed quia eius esse est causa τοῦ εἶναι omnium. Peccavisse igitur in eo omnes, non peccati ipsius imputatione, sed quia peccatum eius est causa peccati omnium; causa, inquam, eo modo quo ipsius esse est causa nostri, non imputationis divinae interventu, sed per generationem & propagationem naturalem.
english: All men sinned in Adam as they were in him.
But they were in him not by imputation of his being (τοῦ εἶναι), but because his being is the cause of the being of all.

Therefore all sinned in him not by imputation of his sin, but because his sin is the cause of the sin of all—a cause, I say, in the same way his being is the cause of ours: not by intervening divine imputation, but through natural generation and propagation.
